profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-17T20:43:44.113+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Sòng Běnjì shàng Dìyī
Sòng Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì, personal name Yù,
courtesy name Déyú,
childhood name Jìnú,
was a native of Suīyú Lǐ, Péngchéng Xiàn.
His surname was Liú,
and he was the twenty-first generation descendant of Liú Jiāo, King Yuán of Chǔ of the Hàn dynasty.
Péngchéng was the capital of Chǔ,
hence his descendants made their home there.
When the Jìn dynasty moved east,
the Liú family relocated to Jīngkǒu Lǐ, Dāntú, Jìnlíng.
His imperial grandfather, Jìng,
was the Grand Protector of Dōng'ān during the Jìn dynasty.
His imperial father, Qiáo,
courtesy name Xiǎnzōng,
was the Prefectural Secretary.
The Emperor was born on the night of Rén Yín in the third month of the Kuǐ Hài year (the first year of Xīngníng of Emperor Āi of Jìn).
Divine light illuminated the room, making it completely bright,
and that night, sweet dew fell on the grave trees.
As he grew,
he was heroic, outstanding, and had a magnanimous spirit.
He was seven *chǐ* and six *cùn* tall,
with an extraordinary physique and majestic bearing.
He did not concern himself with minor details of decorum,
and was known for his filial piety towards his stepmother.
Once, when he traveled to Zhúlín Sì in Jīngkǒu,
he slept alone in front of the lecture hall.
Above him appeared a five-colored dragon pattern.
The monks saw it,
and were startled, reporting it to the Emperor.
The Emperor alone was pleased and said:
"Honored sirs, do not speak falsely."
His imperial father's tomb was on Hòushān in Dāntú.
This place was what the Qín historians referred to as having the "aura of an Emperor" between Qǔ'ā and Dāntú.
At that time, there was a man named Kǒng Gōng,
who was skilled in geomancy.
The Emperor once passed by the tomb with him,
and jokingly asked:
"What about this tomb?"
Kǒng Gōng replied:
"This is an extraordinary site."
From this, the Emperor became even more self-assured.
Wherever he went, he sometimes saw two small dragons attached to his wings.
When he was gathering firewood and fishing in the mountains and marshes,
his companions sometimes also witnessed them.
When he rose to prominence,
the dragon forms became larger.
The Emperor had always been poor,
and at that time, few people recognized his potential,
only Wáng Mì of Lángyá deeply respected him.
The Emperor once owed Diāo Kuí thirty thousand in community tax,
and after a long time, had no way to repay it.
He was seized by Kuí.
Mì secretly paid the debt with his own money,
and thus he was released.
Later, while cutting reeds in Xīnzhōu,
he saw a large snake several *zhàng* long.
He shot it,
wounding it.
The next day, he returned to the island,
and faintly heard the sound of a pestle and mortar.
He went to observe it,
and saw several boys, all in green clothes,
pounding medicine in the thicket.
He asked them why,
and they replied:
"Our king was shot by Liú Jìnú,
and we are compounding medicine to apply to him."
The Emperor said:
"Why does your king, being a spirit, not kill him?"
They replied:
"Liú Jìnú is a king; he will not die,
he cannot be killed."
The Emperor shouted at them,
and they all dispersed.
He then collected the medicine and returned.
Once, when he was staying at an inn in Xiàpéi,
he met a Buddhist monk who said to the Emperor:
"The lands south of the Jiāng are about to fall into chaos.
The one who will bring them peace
will it be you?"
The Emperor had previously suffered from a hand wound,
which had not healed for years.
The monk had a yellow medicine,
which he left with the Emperor.
Soon after, he suddenly disappeared.
The Emperor applied the yellow powder to his wound,
and it healed with a single application.
He treasured the remainder, and the medicine he had obtained from the boys,
and whenever he suffered a sword wound,
applying it always proved effective.
Initially, he served as the *Sīmǎ* to Sūn Wúzhōng, the Commander-in-Chief.
In the eleventh month of the third year of Lóng'ān of Jìn (399 CE),
the demon rebel Sūn Ēn caused disturbances in Kuàijī.
The court dispatched General of the Guards Xiè Yǎn and Former General Liú Láozhī to suppress him in the east.
Láozhī invited the Emperor to participate in military affairs,
and ordered him and several dozen men to scout the rebels.
They encountered several thousand rebels.
The Emperor immediately engaged them in battle.
Most of his men died,
but the Emperor wielded his long saber,
killing and wounding many.
Láozhī's son, Jìngxūan, suspected the Emperor was trapped by the rebels,
and therefore rode lightly to find him.
Soon after, all the cavalry arrived,
and they pacified Shānyīn.
Ēn fled into the sea.
In the fifth month of the fourth year (400 CE),
Ēn re-entered Kuàijī,
and killed Xiè Yǎn.
In the eleventh month,
Láozhī again marched east,
sending the Emperor to garrison Gòuzhāng.
Gòuzhāng was a small city with few people.
The Emperor repeatedly broke through enemy lines in battle,
and the rebels retreated to Jiāpukǒu.
At that time, all the generals in the eastern campaign
allowed their soldiers to plunder,
and the common people suffered greatly from it.
Only the Emperor committed no such offenses.
In the spring of the fifth year (401 CE),
Ēn frequently attacked Gòuzhāng.
The Emperor repeatedly defeated him,
and Ēn again fled into the sea.
In the third month,
Ēn moved north to Hǎiyán.
The Emperor built a city at the old Hǎiyán.
The rebels attacked the city daily.
With few soldiers inside the city,
the Emperor selected a death squad to attack and drive them off.
Although he achieved continuous victories,
the Emperor deeply worried about the numerical disparity.
So, one night, he lowered his banners to feign weakness,
observed their complacency,
then launched a vigorous attack,
and thoroughly routed them.
Ēn, knowing the city could not be taken,
advanced towards Hùdú.
The Emperor abandoned the city and pursued him.
Bāo Lòu, the Magistrate of Hǎiyán, sent his son Sìzhī with one thousand Wú soldiers as a vanguard.
The Emperor, knowing the Wú people were not accustomed to fighting,
ordered them to stay behind,
but they did not comply.
That night, the Emperor set up many surprise troops,
and also positioned banners and drums.
The next day during battle,
the ambushes were sprung,
and the rebels retreated.
Sìzhī pursued the fleeing enemy and was trapped and lost.
The Emperor retreated and fought simultaneously.
Nearly all his subordinates were killed or wounded.
He finally stopped at a certain place,
and ordered his attendants to strip clothes from the dead to appear at ease.
The rebels suspected there were still ambushes,
and thus withdrew.
In the sixth month,
Ēn sailed across the sea to Dāntú.
The Emperor marched continuously and arrived with him,
then attacked fiercely and thoroughly defeated him.
When Ēn reached Jiànyè,
he knew the court was prepared,
so he fled to Yùzhōu.
In the eighth month,
the Jìn Emperor appointed the Emperor as Grand Protector of Xiàpéi.
The Emperor again pursued Ēn to Yùzhōu and Hǎiyán,
repeatedly defeating him.
Ēn thereafter suffered from famine,
and fled to Línhǎi.
In the first year of Yuánxīng (402 CE),
Huán Xuán, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, raised an army and moved east.
Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn, the General of Agile Cavalry, sent Láozhī to resist him.
The Emperor again participated in his military affairs.
When Xuán arrived,
the Emperor requested to attack him,
but Láozhī refused,
and instead sent his son Jìngxūan to Xuán to seek peace.
The Emperor and Hé Wújí of Dōnghǎi both strongly remonstrated,
but were not heeded.
Xuán conquered Jiànyè,
and appointed Láozhī as the Grand Administrator of Kuàijī.
Láozhī was afraid,
and invited the Emperor to raise troops in Guǎnglíng.
The Emperor said:
"The people's hearts are gone.
How can Guǎnglíng be obtained either?"
Láozhī eventually hanged himself in Xīnzhōu.
Hé Wújí said to the Emperor:
"Where shall I go?"
The Emperor said:
"You can return with me to Jīngkǒu.
If Xuán observes the loyalty of a minister,
I will serve him with you;
otherwise,
I will plan with you."
This was the banquet!
After the rituals were completed,
the imperial carriage was prepared,
and the emperor proceeded to the Jiànkāng Palace.
He ascended the Tàijí Qián Diàn,
granted a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
Nobility ranks were bestowed two levels higher upon the people.
For the poor, widowed, orphaned, and solitary who could not sustain themselves,
each person was granted five hú of grain.
Outstanding rents and old debts were not to be collected.
Those who had offended local public opinion or clean discourse,
or committed embezzlement, illicit acts, or theft,
were all pardoned.
Those sentenced to long-term imprisonment
were all specially pardoned and released.
Those who had lost official positions, been deprived of noble ranks, been barred from office, or had their service benefits revoked
were all to be reinstated according to previous regulations.
The Jìn emperor was enfeoffed as the King of Línglíng,
receiving a full commandery as his domain,
flying the emperor's banners,
riding the five-colored imperial副車 (fùchē) secondary carriage,
maintaining the Jìn calendar,
performing suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
with rituals, music, and institutions
all following Jìn precedents.
Petitions to him were not to be called memorials,
and his replies to memorials were not to be called edicts.
His palace was located in the former Mòlíng.
His imperial father was posthumously honored as Xiàomù Huángdì,
and his imperial mother as Mù Huánghòu.
The Empress Dowager Wáng was honored as Huáng Tàihòu.
An edict stated:
"The subtle emotions of Yǔ,
the deep sighs for later generations,
the love for people and the cherishing of trees,
these should not be cut down.
Even in different eras,
the principle should not be abandoned or abolished.
The ceremony of demotion
shall fully follow previous precedents.
Shǐxīng Gōng may be demoted to a Xiàn Gōng,
Lúlǐng Gōng to a Cháisāng Xiàn Gōng,
Shǐ'ān Gōng to a Lìpǔ Xiàn Hóu,
Chángshā Gōng to a Lǐlíng Xiàn Hóu,
Kānglè Gōng is immediately demoted to a Xiàn Hóu.
The sacrifices to Wáng Dǎo, Xiè Ān, Wēn Jiào, Táo Kǎn, and Xiè Xuán shall be maintained.
Those who exerted themselves during Yìxī
shall all retain their original ranks."
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Sīkōng Dàolián was appointed Tàiwèi
and enfeoffed as the King of Chángshā.
Nánjùn Gōng Yìqìng was established as the King of Línchuān.
Another edict discussed posthumous honors and rewards, as well as exemptions and reinstatements, for those who died in battle.
On the day Yǐhài,
the imperial prince Guìyáng Gōng Yìzhēn was enfeoffed as the King of Lúlǐng,
Péngchéng Gōng Yìlóng as the King of Yídū,
and Yìkāng as the King of Péngchéng.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
envoys were dispatched to tour the four directions,
to commend the virtuous and promote the good,
to inquire about the people's sufferings,
and to report all cases of judicial misconduct, administrative and penal errors, practices that harmed public morality or disturbed customs, or those not pleasing to the people's ears.
All such matters were to be reported.
On the day Wùyín,
an edict increased the stipends of all officials.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
the Jìn Tàishǐ calendar was changed to the Yǒngchū calendar,
the God of Earth's sacrifice was held in the month of Zǐ,
and the winter sacrifice in the month of Chén.
In the autumn, seventh month, on the day Dīnghài,
remaining bandits who had been confiscated into government custody were pardoned and released.
All families who had been banished
were permitted to return to their hometowns.
Furthermore, due to the burdensome market taxes,
a favorable reduction was ordered.
For those who died on campaigns to Guān and Luò,
not returning their bodies,
their families were granted generous provisions.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
the King of Chénliú, Cáon Qiánsì, passed away.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
the offices of five校三將 (wǔxiào sānjiàng) five colonels and three generals were reinstated,
the number of Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn was increased by twenty,
with others remaining outside the established quota.
On the day Wùxū,
Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Yáng Shèng was promoted to the title of Chējì Dàjiāngjūn.
On the day Jiáchén,
Zhènxī Jiāngjūn Lǐ Xīn was promoted to the title of Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn,
Píngxī Jiāngjūn Qǐfú Chìpán was promoted to the title of Ānxī Dàjiāngjūn,
Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn, King Gāogōulì Gāo Lián was promoted to the title of Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn,
and Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn, King Báijì Fúyú Yìng was promoted to the title of Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn.
The offices of Dōnggōng Rǒngcóng Púshè and Lǚbēn Zhōnglángjiàng were established.
On the day Wùshēn,
the spirit tablets were moved to the Tàimiào,
with the emperor personally officiating.
On the day Rénzǐ,
an edict reformed the temporary regulations,
making them generally lenient and simple.
In the eighth month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
an edict ordered that all old commanderies and counties named "North" be abolished,
and those provisionally established in the south
were permitted to use "South" in their names.
On the day Wùchén,
an edict stated:
"Péngchéng is my ancestral home,
where roots are nurtured and flourishing,
it should be treated like Fēng and Pèi.
Therefore, Péi Commandery and Xiàpī shall both have their land tax and tribute silk reduced for thirty years."
On the day Xīnwèi,
the consort Zāng Shì was posthumously honored as Jìng Huánghòu,
and her mausoleum was named Yǒngníng.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Crown Prince Yìfú was established as the Imperial Crown Prince.
On the day Yǐhài,
those currently convicted were pardoned.
In the intercalary month, on the day Rénwǔ,
guardians were appointed for the tombs of the Jìn emperors.
Distinguished former worthies and sages
were to be carefully honored with sweeping and sacrifices.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
the Kingdom of Línyì sent envoys to present tribute.
In the ninth month, on the day Rénzǐ,
ten Diànzhōng Jiāngjūn were established for the Eastern Palace,
with twenty others outside the quota.
On the day Rénshēn,
the office of Dūguān Shàngshū was established.
This year
was the fifth year of Tàicháng for Emperor Míngyuán of Wèi.
Xīliáng perished.
In the second year, spring, first month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
a sacrifice was made at the southern suburb,
and a general amnesty was granted.
On the day Bǐngyín,
the use of gold and silver plating was prohibited.
Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, King Lúlǐng Yìzhēn, was appointed Sītú.
Shàngshū Púshè Xú Xiànzhī was appointed Shàngshū Lìng and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
the use of copper nails in funeral arrangements was prohibited.
The commandery administration of Kuàijī was abolished.
In the second month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
candidates for Xiù and Xiào from the provinces and commanderies were tested in the Yánxián Táng.
The Kingdom of Wō sent envoys to present tribute.
In the third month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
for the first time, the number of generals allowed in the Jīngzhōu administration was limited to no more than two thousand,
and officials to no more than ten thousand.
For each province, the number of generals was limited to no more than five hundred,
and officials to no more than five thousand.
Soldiers were not included in these limits.
In the summer, fourth month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
illicit sacrifices were prohibited for the first time,
and all private shrines were abolished.
However, shrines established for former worthies based on their merit and virtue
were exempt from this rule.
On the day Wùshēn,
legal cases were heard in the Huálín Yuán.
[二四]
In the fifth month, on the day Jǐyǒu,
the offices of Túnqí, Bùbīng, and Yìjūn Sān Xiàowèi were established for the Eastern Palace.
In the autumn, seventh month, on the day Jǐsì,
there was an earthquake.
In the ninth month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
[二五]the King of Línglíng passed away.
This is recorded in the Sòng Annals.
The emperor, accompanied by all officials, mourned in the imperial court for three days,
following the precedent of Emperor Míng of Wèi mourning for Sānyáng Gōng.
An acting Tàiwèi was dispatched, holding a marshal's staff, to oversee the funeral arrangements,
and the burial was conducted according to Jìn rites.
In the winter, tenth month, on the day Jǐhài,
the Hú chieftain of Liángzhōu, Dàjùqú Méngxùn, was appointed Zhèn Jūn Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the eleventh month, on the day Xīnhài,
Emperor Gōng of Jìn was buried at Chōngpínglíng.
The emperor, accompanied by all officials, viewed and escorted the funeral procession.
In the third year, spring, first month, on the day Jiáchén,
an edict ordered that all penalties, regardless of severity, be pardoned.
[二六]On the day Guǐchǒu,
Shàngshū Lìng and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Xú Xiànzhī was appointed Sīkōng and Lù Shàngshū Shì,
retaining his position as Cìshǐ.
Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Hóng was promoted to Wèi Jiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Tàizǐ Zhānshì Fù Liàng was appointed Shàngshū Púshè.
In the second month, on the day Bǐngxū,
a comet appeared in the constellations Xū and Wēi.
In the third month,
the emperor was unwell.
Tàiwèi, King Chángshā Dàolián, Sīkōng Xú Xiànzhī, Shàngshū Púshè Fù Liàng, Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Xiè Huì, and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Tán Dàojì all attended to his medical care.
The assembled officials requested prayers to the gods,
but the emperor refused,
only allowing Shìzhōng Xiè Fāngmíng to announce his illness to the ancestral temple.
On the day Dīngwèi,
King Lúlǐng Yìzhēn was appointed Shìzhōng, Chējì Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Jǐwèi,
the emperor's illness recovered,
and a general amnesty was granted.
In the summer, fourth month, on the day Yǐhài,
Qiúchí Gōng Yáng Shèng was enfeoffed as the King of Wǔdū Commandery.
On the *rénchén* day of the eleventh month,
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn Hé Mài was imprisoned and died.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Shěn Qìngzhī, newly appointed as Tàiwèi, was killed.
On the *rényín* day,
Empress Lù was enthroned,
and music was played from the four pavilions.
A partial amnesty was granted to Yáng and Nánxú prefectures.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
a royal prince was born;
he was the son of Shàofǔ Liú Méngzhī.
A grand amnesty was declared;
all cases of embezzlement, theft, and lewdness
were pardoned and cleared.
Those who adopted their father's title were granted one rank of nobility.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, the King of Jiàn'ān, XiūRén, was appointed Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
the King of Nánpíng Jìngyóu, the King of Lúlíng Jìngxiān, and the Marquis of Ānnán Jìngshēn were all granted death.
[四一]
At this time, the Emperor's cruelty and perversity grew daily,
and executions followed one another.
Officials, both inside and outside the court,
could not guarantee their safety.
Earlier,
a rumor spread that an Emperor would emerge from Xiāngzhōng.
The Emperor intended to make a southern tour to Jīng and Xiāng to suppress this rumor,
planning to eliminate his four uncles in the morning,
and then depart.
That night, Xiāngdōng Wáng Yù, along with his attendants Ruǎn Diànfū, Wáng Dàolóng, and Lǐ Dào'ér, secretly colluded with eleven of the Emperor's attendants, including Shòu Jìzhī and Jiāng Chǎnzhī,
plotting to depose the Emperor.
Earlier,
the Emperor enjoyed visiting the Zhúlín Táng in the Huálín Yuán,
making women chase each other naked.
One woman refused to obey,
and he had her beheaded.
A short time later,
he dreamed at night that he was wandering in the back hall,
and a woman cursed him, saying:
"The Emperor is perverse and unrighteous;
next year he will not live to see the harvest."
Enraged, the Emperor
searched the palace for someone resembling the woman in his dream and executed her.
That evening, he again dreamed of the executed woman, who cursed him, saying:
"You wrongfully killed me;
I have already appealed to Shàngdì."
By this time,
shamans said,
"There is a ghost in this hall."
The Emperor, along with Shānyīn Gōngzhǔ and hundreds of palace maids, followed the shamans to capture the ghost,
dismissing his guards.
The Emperor personally shot at it.
When the ritual was over,
as he was about to play sensuous music,
Shòu Jìzhī, with a knife in his bosom, rushed in directly,
with Jiāng Chǎnzhī as his deputy.
The concubines scattered and fled,
and the deposed Emperor also ran.
They caught up with him,
and he cried out loudly:
"Jì!
Jì!"
He did this three times.
Unable to lift his hands,
he collapsed in the Huáguāng Diàn,
aged seventeen.
The Tàihuáng Tàihòu ordered Xiāngdōng Wáng Yù to inherit the imperial lineage.
Thereupon, the Emperor was buried west of the suburban altar in Mòlíng County, Dānyáng.
The Emperor had protruding eyes and a beak-like nose,
a long neck and a sharp chin.
He was impetuous and irritable in his youth,
and was often reprimanded by Xiàowǔ in the Eastern Palace.
When Xiàowǔ toured the west,
the Emperor requested to attend to his daily life.
His handwriting was not neat,
and the Emperor admonished him, saying:
"Your handwriting has not improved;
this is one thing.
I hear that lately your studies have all slackened,
and your irritability has grown daily.
How can you be so obstinate!"
When he first ascended the throne,
receiving the imperial seals and ribbons,
he showed no signs of grief.
Cài Xīngzōng withdrew and sighed, saying:
"In ancient times, Lǔ Zhāo showed no sorrow,
and Shūsūn requested death.
The calamity for the state
must be approaching."
Initially, the Emperor was still wary of the senior ministers and Dài Fǎxīng and others.
After Dài Fǎxīng was killed,
none of the senior ministers were not terrified.
Thereupon, he also executed the various dukes,
from Yuán and Kǎi downwards,
all were beaten, dragged, and pulled.
Both inside and outside the court, there was fear and trembling,
and the palace was in turmoil.
The Empress Dowager was gravely ill and
sent for the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
"There are many ghosts among the sick;
it is frightening.
How can I go!"
The Empress Dowager was furious,
and told her attendants:
"Bring a knife and cut open my belly!
How could I have given birth to such a child!"
A few days after the Empress Dowager passed away,
the Emperor dreamed that the Empress Dowager said to him:
"You are inhumane and unfilial,
and originally had no imperial qualities.
Your son is so foolish and perverse,
he is also not destined for the throne.
Xiàowǔ was treacherous and cruel, destroying the Way,
creating resentment among men and gods.
Although he had many sons,
none had the mandate of Heaven;
the great mandate will return
to the sons of Wéndì."
Therefore, the Emperor gathered all his uncles in the capital,
fearing they would cause trouble outside.
Shānyīn Gōngzhǔ was excessively promiscuous
and said to the Emperor:
"Although there is a difference between male and female for Your Majesty and me,
we both inherited our bodies from the late Emperor.
Your Majesty has hundreds of concubines,
while I only have one consort.
This is unfair;
how can it be so extreme!"
The Emperor then provided her with thirty male favorites,
and advanced her title to Huìjī Jùn Zhǎnggōngzhǔ,
with rank equal to a commandery prince,
a bathing and eating fief of two thousand households,
a set of drum and wind instruments,
and an additional twenty sword-bearing guards.
Whenever the Emperor went out,
the Princess and court officials often accompanied his carriage.
The Emperor was fond of reading in his youth,
was quite knowledgeable about ancient affairs,
and had some literary talent.
He personally composed the eulogy for Emperor Xiàowǔ and various other pieces,
which often possessed literary flourish.
Because Wèi Wǔ had Fāqiū Zhōnglángjiàng and Mōjīn Xiàowèi,
he established these two offices,
with Jiàn'ān Wáng XiūRén and Shānyáng Wáng XiūYòu leading them.
Other deeds
are detailed in the various biographies.
A commentary states: Emperor Wén showed exceptional brilliance in his youth,
inherently possessing the virtues of a ruler.
When he assumed the throne and ruled,
for many years,
the administration was fully established,
regulations were clear and precise,
punishments had their categories,
and ranks were not arbitrarily granted.
Thus, he was able to maintain internal order and external peace,
with the four seas tranquil.
However, when dispatching generals and armies,
his actions deviated from the proper division of authority.
His talent was inferior to Guāngwǔ,
yet he remotely directed military strategies,
even regarding the dates and times of attacks,
all had to follow his specific instructions.
Although the army was defeated and lost,
it was not that the generals were inferior to Hán and Bái;
rather, the prolongation of the enemy threat and the shrinking of territory
were due to this.
As for words leaked from the bedchamber,
and disaster arising from malicious servants,
though the calamity came unexpectedly,
it also had its reasons.
Indeed, taking human lives to sustain oneself
is solely the conduct of Jié and Zhòu.
Observing the era of Dàmíng,
was it also to exhaust human lives?
Even with the talent and excellence of Zhōu Gōng,
it would have ended in chaos.
From this perspective,
to die was perhaps fortunate.
As for the matter of the deposed Emperor,
his actions are recorded in this chapter.
If a monarch of average talent
had committed even one such act,
it would have been enough to cause his downfall,
let alone combining all these evils!
How could he have avoided ruin!

Song Dynasty Annals, Volume 3
Tàizōng Míng Huángdì, personal name Yù,
courtesy name Xiūjǐng,
childhood name Róngqī,
was the eleventh son of Wéndì.
Born in the tenth month of the sixteenth year of Yuánjiā.
In the twenty-fifth year,
he was enfeoffed as the King of Huáiyáng,
and in the twenty-ninth year, he was re-enfeoffed as the King of Xiāngdōng.
When Xiàowǔ ascended the throne,
he was successively promoted to ZhènJūn Jiāngjūn and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Ceding,
the imperial court had no worries looking east;
Mǐn and Yuè had the joy of revival.
This, too, is Your Grace’s achievement.
The Xiongnú, with their wild ambition,
plundered the borders.
The vile Jié treacherously
expanded,
their power shaking Péng and Sì.
Your Grace received the command to punish the wicked,
set off at dawn,
and as soon as the war chariots engaged,
the dark mists were swept away.
You consoled the dead and succored the wounded,
widely proclaiming imperial grace,
so that
our Huái and Féi
once again received the flourishing transformation.
This, too, is Your Grace’s achievement.
Thereafter,
the Xiǎnyǔn became fiercely rampant.
Wild boars and long snakes
again cast their gaze on the capital.
As
the old order persisted,
the army had grown old,
and the fortified city with its high walls
was on the verge of falling.
Your Grace, mindful of royal affairs,
was so engrossed that you forgot to eat.
You personally donned armor and helmet,
viewing danger as
ease,
divided and demarcated territories,
and established Qīng and Yǎn.
This, too, is Your Grace’s achievement.
Guìyáng, with its numerous followers,
presumptuously coveted the Jiǔdǐng.
Crowns were ripped apart, mian caps destroyed,
roots were pulled out and sources blocked.
Raging fires burned in the royal city,
flying arrows gathered on the lord’s palace.
The multitude of feudal lords were anxious and fearful,
the commander-in-chief was without a master.
Your Grace, grasping your sword and concentrating your mind,
produced extraordinary strategies that surpassed the world.
Wielding the banner and
commanding,
even cowards became brave.
Within a single night,
Xuānyáng was pacified.
This, too, is Your Grace’s achievement.
The imperial house faced many difficulties,
strife arose among relatives.
Jiànpíng, having lost
its way,
raised troops to insult the interior.
Your Grace directed the Six Armies,
righteousness visible in your demeanor.
Before the campaign exceeded ten days,
Zhūfāng was tranquil.
This, too, is Your Grace’s achievement.
Cāngwú indulged
in tyranny,
all of Xià was in turmoil.
Cruel punishments were carried out,
who then was innocent?
The common people grieved together,
not knowing if they would see the morrow.
Gāozǔ’s legacy had fallen,
Wén and Míng’s path, who would
continue?
Your Grace, drawing far from the righteousness of Yīn and Hàn,
and recently following the ordinances of Wèi and Jìn,
humbly with your small self,
entered to uphold the ancestral temple.
The Seven Temples were purified and tranquil,
the nine regions returned to proper governance.
This,
too, is Your Grace’s achievement.
Yuán and Liú, harboring disloyalty,
created this path of rebellion.
Their vile schemes secretly coalesced,
the crisis covertly erupted.
They occupied Shítóu,
intending to invade Yìng and Lù.
Your Grace’s
divine strategy operated internally,
and frost-like blades were raised externally.
Evil and calamity were dispelled,
the nation’s path became pleasant and peaceful.
This, too, is Your Grace’s achievement.
Shěn Yōubāo’s transgressions
grew more evident with the years.
With greedy eyes
and豺-like voices,
he resisted with his army, secure in his ruthlessness.
He then looked westward,
far akin to a foreign land.
But even with the initial organization,
the nine campaigns were not yet carried out.
His prolonged wickedness remained unrepentant,
and thus he indulged in his brutal rebellion.
Your Grace, wielding the battle-axe, exited the pass,
imposing your might upon the Jiāng territories.
Your upright character shone as brightly as the sun,
your brilliant strategies competed in excellence with autumn clouds.
Moved by your supreme righteousness,
people were inspired a hundredfold.
Years
of unpunished crimes
were brought to manifest execution in a single day.
Jǔpǔ’s currents flowed peacefully,
Zhāngtái’s path was set right.
This, too, is Your Grace’s achievement.
Your Grace possesses the merit of bringing salvation to the world,
further enhanced by your sagacity.
Your way shelters living beings,
your will rectifies the universe.
You have exerted your strength and heart,
toiled for the royal house.
Dangers and
difficulties,
you have experienced them all.
As for the diligence in establishing the ancestral sacrifices,
and the grace of the Creator’s beginning,
like clouds dispersing and mists scattering,
its light covers the six obscurities,
assisting Me, the One Man,
to eternally
purify the Four Seas.
Therefore, fragrant *jù* grass rises in the suburban gardens,
and auspicious stars cast their radiance in the clear Milky Way.
Distant lands overcome barriers and yearn for righteousness,
barbarian regions come to court with multiple interpretations.
How vast and profound it is,
it cannot be fully named.
I have heard that rewarding merit and manifesting virtue
was a grand tradition of former kings.
Erecting marquises and counts,
and establishing states, is a common practice,
whereby Wénmìng achieved
success,
and the dark jade tablet was conspicuously bestowed.
Jī Dàn proclaimed his wisdom,
and Qǔfù was established as a fief.
Some changed jade to extend their influence,
others bestowed land to spread their transformation.
Their rites surpassed ordinary ranks,
their favor surpassed all
feudal lords.
Down to Huán and Wén,
their chariots and attire were of different grades.
Your Grace’s achievements surpass those of previous heroes,
yet the commendation is lacking compared to old statutes.
The ways of ancient and modern times,
how are they so disparate
indeed!
Reflecting with admiration,
there is indeed a deficiency.
Now, I hereby promote Your Grace to Xiàngguó,
with Qí Jùn of Qīngzhōu, Liáng Jùn of Xúzhōu, Lánlíng, Lǔ
Jùn, Lángyé, Dōnghǎi, Jìnlíng, Yìxìng of Nánxúzhōu, and Wú Jùn, Kuàijī of Yángzhōu,
a total of ten commanderies,
and enfeoff Your Grace as Qí Gōng.
I bestow upon you this dark earth,
and wrap it with white *máo* grass,
to establish your state and family,
and thereby found your grand altar to the gods of land and grain.
This is truly the former fief of the Shàngfù,
whose descendants eternally served as alliance leaders,
governing the feudal territories,
following the old rules.
In the past, Zhōu and Shào established
their states,
serving concurrently as Imperial Tutors and Protectors.
Máo and Bì held their jade tablets,
entering to serve as high ministers.
The favors both internal and external
followed the same pattern as in ancient times.

Now I command the Envoy with Imperial Credentials, concurrently Grand Commandant, Palace Attendant, Director of the Central Secretariat, Minister of Works, General of the Guards, Founding Marquis of Yúdū County, Yànhuí,
to present Your Grace with the Xiàngguó’s seal and ribbon, and the Qí Gōng’s seal and sash.
The Envoy with Imperial Credentials, concurrently Vice Minister of
Works and Defender of the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Sēngqián, is to present Qí Gōng with the *máo* grass and earth,
[1-1] the first to fifth left Gold Tiger Tallies,
and the first to tenth left Bamboo Messenger Tallies.
The Xiàngguó’s
position encompasses all high ministers,
its rank surpasses the Three Excellencies.
The duties shift with ceremony,
the title changes with circumstances.
Therefore, by virtue of being Xiàngguó, you will oversee all governmental affairs,
and the title of Director of the Imperial Secretariat is removed.
Return the provisional

credentials, the Palace Attendant’s sable and cicada ornament, the seals and ribbons of Commander-in-Chief of Internal and External Affairs, Grand Tutor, and Grand Commandant, and the seal and tablet of Jìnglíng Gōng.
The titles of General of Agile Cavalry, Governor of Yángzhōu, and Nánxúzhōu
In winter, the intercalary twelfth month, on the day *wùyín*,
the Crown Prince was capped.
Princes, dukes, and officials below them were granted silk, each with different amounts.
Those who were successors to their fathers were granted one rank of nobility.
Distant and nearby regions were ordered to reduce their customary tributes.
In the fourth year, spring, the first month, on the day *gēngwǔ*,
a general amnesty was declared.
On the day *rényín*,
[一七]an edict was issued:
"For those who bear children,
their parents' *diàoyì* (corvée labor and taxes) are waived for one year,
and they are also granted ten *hú* of rice.
For newly married couples,
the husband's corvée labor is waived for one year."
On the day *bǐngchén*,
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Yàn was executed.
[一八]
In the second month, Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Xú Xiàosì was made Shàngshū Lìng.
In autumn, the eighth month, on the day *jiǎwǔ*,
[一九]Wáng Shì, the mother of Jǐng Huáng, was posthumously honored as Gōng Tàihòu.
The Wèi army attacked Miǎnběi.
In winter, the tenth month,
they again pressed Sī and Yōng two prefectures.
On the day *jiǎxū*,
Taìzǐ Zhōng Shùzǐ Xiāo Yǎn and Yòujūn Sīmǎ Zhāng Jì were dispatched to resist them.
In the eleventh month, on the day *bǐngchén*,
[二０]the Dī Yang Língzhēn was appointed Běiqín Cìshǐ,
and enfeoffed as Chóuchí Gōng and Wǔdū Wáng.
In the twelfth month, on the day *dīngchǒu*,
Dùzhī Shàngshū Cuī Huìjǐng was dispatched to lead troops to relieve Yōngzhōu.
In Yǒngtaì元年, spring, the first month, on the day *guǐwèi*, which was the first day of the month,
a general amnesty was declared.
Zhōngjūn Dà Jiàngjūn Xú Xiàosì was granted the privilege of establishing an administration and having a retinue, retaining his original title.
The various commanderies of Miǎnběi,
attacked by Wèi,
fell one after another.
Xīnyě Tàishǒu Liú Sījì responded appropriately to the situation,
[二一]but when food ran out,
they boiled soil for porridge.
No relief troops arrived,
the city was captured,
and he died.
On the day *yǐsì*,
Tàiwèi Chén Xiǎndá was dispatched with a *jié* (credentials) to relieve Yōngzhōu.
On the day *dīngwèi*,

Hédōng Wáng Xuàn, Línhé Wángzǐ Yuè, Xīyáng Wángzǐ Wén, Héngyáng Wángzǐ Jùn, Nánkāng Wángzǐ Lín, Yǒngyáng Wángzǐ Mín, Xiāngdōng Wángzǐ Jiàn, Nánjùn Wángzǐ Xià, Bālíng Wáng Zhāoxiù, and Guìyáng Wáng Zhāocàn were executed.
In the second month, on the day *guǐchǒu*,
Zuǒwèi Jiàngjūn Xiāo Huìxiū was dispatched with temporary credentials to reinforce Shòuyáng.
On the day *xīnwèi*,
Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Péi Shúyè defeated the Wèi army north of the Huái River.
In the third month, on the day *bǐngwǔ*,
the rent and taxes for the counties of Yōngzhōu that had encountered the Wèi army were waived.
On the day *wùshēn*,
an edict was issued to increase the sacrificial offerings to Zhòngní (Confucius).
The Emperor's illness did not improve,
and diviners who observed the *qì* said that the era name should be changed.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day *jiǎyín*,
a general amnesty was declared,
the era name was changed,
and civil and military officials were promoted two ranks.
On the day *jǐwèi*,
Wǔlíng Zhāo Wángzǐ Zǐ Tǎn was established as Héngyáng Wáng.
On the day *dīngchǒu*,
Dàsīmǎ Kuàijī Tàishǒu Wáng Jìngzé raised an army and rebelled.
In the fifth month, on the day *rénwǔ*,
Fǔguó Jiàngjūn Liú Shānyáng was dispatched to lead an army to suppress the rebellion in the east.
On the day *yǐyǒu*,
Wáng Jìngzé was beheaded,
and his head was sent to Jiànyè.
A partial amnesty was granted to the seven commanderies of Wú and Jìnlíng in Zhèdōng.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day *jǐyǒu*,
the Emperor passed away in the Zhèngfú Diàn,
at the age of forty-seven.
His last will stated:
"Xú Xiàosì should again be granted the 'Eight Orders';
his positions as Zhōngshū Jiān and his current official titles shall remain as before.
Shěn Wénjì shall be Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè;
his positions as Chángshì and Hùjūn shall remain as before.
Jiāng Gē shall be Yòu Púyè.
Jiāng Sì shall be Shìzhōng.
Liú Xuān shall be Wèiwèi Qīng.
Major military and political affairs are entrusted to Tàiwèi Chén.
All internal and external affairs, great or small, are entrusted to Xú Xiàosì, Yáoguāng, Tǎnzhī, and Jiāng Gē;
major matters should be discussed with Shěn Wénjì, Jiāng Sì, and Liú Xuān.
Tasks of trust
can be entrusted to Liú Quān, Xiāo Huìxiū, and Cuī Huìjǐng."
His ministers posthumously honored him as Míng Huángdì,
with the temple name Gāozōng,
and he was buried in Xīng'ān Líng.
The Emperor was discerning and possessed administrative talent,
enforcing laws without bias.
He kept his favored relatives and intimates under strict control,
and his officials were upright and pure.
He employed commoners
and did not allow them to use the four-panel umbrella.
He greatly emphasized frugality,
abolishing the Xīnlín Yuàn built by Wǔ Dì,
and returning the land to the common people.
He abolished the Dōngtián built by Wénhuì Tàizǐ,
and sold off the land.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
all gold and silver were removed from carriages and boats,
returned to the main treasury,
and replaced with ivory and horn.
He once used soap-bean pods,
and after finishing,
he gave the remnants to his attendants,
saying:
"These can still be used tomorrow."
When the imperial kitchen presented wrapped and steamed food,
the Emperor marked it with a cross,
saying:
"It can be broken into four pieces,
the rest saved for dinner."
However, the palaces, clothes, and equipage in Wǔ Dì's imperial women's quarters
were left completely unchanged.
Such was his frugality.
He was suspicious by nature
and frequently carried out executions.
He believed in Taoist arts
and used divination.
Whenever he traveled,
he would first divine the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
He was secretive about his movements;
if he planned to go south, he would falsely say he was going west;
if he planned to go east, he would falsely say he was going north.
None of these were true,
and he never went to the southern suburbs for sacrifices.
When he first fell ill,
he did not cease his administrative duties,
and his ministers did not know.
When his illness became severe,
he ordered the offices of the central government to seek white fish for medicine from the official registers,
and only then did the outside world become aware.
He wore crimson robes,
and all his attire was red,
believing it to be for warding off evil.
Shamans said
that "the water from Hòuhú passing through the palace
caused the Emperor's illness."
The Emperor then personally went to the imperial kitchen to inspect the waterways.
His attendants informed him
that "the imperial kitchen cannot operate without this water."
He resolutely decided to block it,
intending to divert the Huái River southward.
He passed away before this could happen,
and the plan was abandoned.
The deposed Emperor, Dōnghūn Hóu, whose personal name was Bǎojuǎn,
courtesy name Zhìzàng,
was Míng Dì's second son.
His original name was Míngxián,
but Míng Dì changed it after he became regent.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he was established as Crown Prince.
In the first year of Yǒngtaì, seventh month, on the day *jǐyǒu*,
Míng Dì passed away,
and the Crown Prince ascended the throne.
In the eighth month, on the day *gēngshēn*,
Zhènběi Jiàngjūn Jìn'ān Wáng Bǎoyì was promoted to Zhēngběi Dà Jiàngjūn and granted the privilege of establishing an administration and having a retinue.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day *jǐwèi*,
an edict was issued to revise and simplify the legal codes.
On the day *guǐhài*,
an edict was issued for Xiāo Tǎnzhī and Jiāng Gē to take turns on duty in the Diànshěng,
supervising the palace guards.
On the day *xīnwèi*,
an edict was issued for Liú Xuān and Jiāng Gē to take turns on duty in the Yánmíng Diànshěng.
In the eleventh month, on the day *wùzǐ*,
Empress Chǔ was established.
On the day *gēngyín*,
Shàngshū Lìng Xú Xiàosì proposed:
"When princes, marquises, and noblemen marry,
the practice of using real silver cups for the *liánjǐn* (nuptial cup ceremony)
is a recent custom;
furthermore, the extravagance of sacrificial candles and embroidered decorations
also deviates from ancient regulations.
Therefore, I propose to abolish gold and silver *liánsuǒ* (linked cups),
and all other new utensils
should be made of pottery.
The lavishness of sacrificial candles and elaborate decorations
should also be discontinued."
The proposal was approved.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán, spring, the first month, on the day *wùyín*, which was the first day of the month,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed.
On the day *xīnmǎo*,
sacrifices were offered at the southern suburbs.
On the day *dīngyǒu*,
Suí Wáng Bǎoróng was re-enfeoffed as Nánkāng Wáng;
Ānlù Wáng Bǎozhì as Xiāngdōng Wáng;
Jìnglǐng Wáng Zhāozhòu as Bālíng Wáng.
In the second month,
Tàiwèi Chén Xiǎndá suffered a defeat at Mǎjuàn.
Shìzǔ Xiàoyuán Huángdì, personal name Yì,
courtesy name Shìchéng,
childhood name Qīfú,
was the seventh son of Wǔdì.
Initially,
Wǔdì dreamt of a one-eyed monk holding an incense burner,
claiming to be reincarnated into the royal family.
Later, when the emperor's mother was serving among the palace women,
as she first drew aside the curtain,
a wind billowed her skirt,
and Wǔdì felt moved to favor her.
The palace woman dreamt of the moon falling into her bosom,
and subsequently became pregnant.
In the eighth month, on the day of Dīngsì, in the seventh year of Tiānjiān, the Emperor was born.
The entire room was filled with an extraordinary fragrance,
and there was the anomaly of a purple caul.
Wǔdì found this remarkable,
and consequently bestowed the surname Ruǎn upon the palace woman,
advancing her to Xiūróng.
In the thirteenth year,
he was enfeoffed as Xiāngdōng Wáng.
In the first year of Tàiqīng,
he was successively promoted to Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn, Dūdū, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the third month of the third year,
Hóu Jǐng captured Jiànyè.
In the fourth month,
the heir apparent Fāngděng arrived from Jiànyè,
learning that Táichéng had not been held.
The Emperor ordered the city of Jiānglíng to be palisaded,
with a circumference of seventy lǐ.
Zhèn Xī Chángshǐ Wáng Chōng and others presented a memorial requesting that he be made Tàiwèi and Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì,
to preside over the alliance under imperial authority.
The Emperor did not permit it,
saying:
"I am not lowly in the empire,
why should I wait for the title of Dūdū?
As the respected son of the Emperor,
why should I rely on a position in the highest court?
Those who propose this should be executed."
He threw down his brush and wept.
Chōng and others pleaded again,
but he did not comply.
They further requested that he be made Sīkōng,
to preside over the various lords,
but he also did not listen.
Instead, he opened the Zhèn Xī Fǔ,
recruiting scholars from all over the empire.
In this month,
the Emperor levied troops from Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Hédōng Wáng Yù,
but Yù refused the order.
Soon after, Shàng Jiǎ Hóu Sháo arrived from Jiànyè,
declaring a secret edict of the fifteenth day of the third month,
bestowing upon the Emperor the position of Jiǎ Huángyuè, Dà Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì, Sītú, and authority to act on behalf of the throne.
Thereupon, an Xíngtái was established in Nánjùn, and officials were appointed there.
In the seventh month,
he sent the heir apparent Fāngděng to campaign against Hédōng Wáng Yù;
the army was defeated,
and he died.
He then sent Zhèn Bīng Jiāngjūn Bào Quán to campaign against Yù.
In the ninth month, on the day of Yǐmǎo,
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Yuèyáng Wáng Chá raised an army and attacked Jiānglíng.
His generals Dù Zè and his brothers surrendered,
and Chá fled.
Bào Quán attacked Xiāngzhōu,
but had not yet captured it;
he then sent Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn Wáng Sēngbiàn to replace him as commander.
When Jiǎnwén Dì ascended the throne,
he changed the era name to Dàbǎo Yuánnián.
The Emperor, believing Jiǎnwén to be under the control of treacherous ministers,
ultimately did not comply with his decrees.
In the first month,
he sent his youngest son Fāngguǐ as a hostage to Wèi;
Wèi did not accept the hostage but formed a brotherhood with him.
In the fourth month,
Xiāngzhōu was captured,
Yù was executed,
and Xiāngzhōu was pacified.
Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Yuèyáng Wáng Chá declared himself Liáng Wáng,
and became a vassal of Wèi;
Wèi sent troops to assist him in attacking Xiāngyáng.
Previously,
Shàolíng Wáng Lún's letter had already spoken of dire events,
but it was kept secret,
awaiting the victory in Xiāngzhōu.
In this month, on the day of Rén Yín,
he first ordered Chén Yíng to announce the news of Wǔdì's death,
and the Emperor wept in the main hall.
In the sixth month,
Jiāngxià Wáng Dàkuǎn, Shānyáng Wáng Dàchéng, and Yídū Wáng Dàfēng came to surrender from Xìn'ān.
In the ninth month, on the day of Xīnyǒu,
the former Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ Nánpíng Wáng Kè was appointed Zhōng Wèi Jiāngjūn, Shàngshū Lìng, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Dàkuǎn was re-enfeoffed as Línchuān Jùnwáng,
Dàchéng as Guìyáng Jùnwáng,
and Dàfēng as Rǔnán Jùnwáng.
In the eleventh month, on the day of Jiǎzǐ,
Nánpíng Wáng Kè and others presented a memorial requesting that he be advanced to Xiàngguó,
to oversee all government affairs.
The Emperor did not comply.
In the third month of the second year,
Hóu Jǐng marched all his troops westward.
In the fourth month,
Jǐng sent his generals Sòng Zǐxiān and Rèn Yuē to attack Yǐngzhōu,
capturing Cìshǐ Fāng Zhū.
On the day of Gēngxū,
Lǐngjūn Wáng Sēngbiàn stationed his army at Bālíng.
In the fifth month, on the day of Guǐwèi,
the Emperor sent generals Hú Sēngyòu and Lù Fǎhé to reinforce Bālíng.
In the sixth month,
Sēngyòu and others defeated Jǐng's general Rèn Yuē's army,
captured Yuē,
and Jǐng lifted the siege and fled by night.
Wáng Sēngbiàn was appointed Zhēng Dōng Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Shàngshū Lìng,
leading his troops to pursue Jǐng,
and was victorious wherever he went.
He advanced to besiege Yǐngzhōu,
capturing the rebel general Sòng Zǐxiān and others.
In the ninth month,
the kingdom of Pánpán presented a tamed elephant.
In the tenth month, on the first day of Xīnchǒu,
purple clouds like a canopy appeared over Jiānglíng city.
In this month,
Jiǎnwén Dì died,
and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī Wáng Sēngbiàn and others presented a memorial urging his enthronement.
The Emperor observed the mourning rites,
mourned greatly for three days,
and the hundred officials wore white mourning clothes,
responding to the memorial by not permitting it.
Sīkōng Nánpíng Wáng Kè, leading the imperial clan,
Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Hú Sēngyòu, leading the officials,
Jiāngzhōu Biéjià Zhāng Yì, leading the civil servants and commoners,
all presented memorials urging his enthronement.
The Emperor firmly declined.
In the eleventh month, on the day of Yǐhài,
Sēngbiàn again presented a memorial urging his enthronement,
but he again did not comply.
At this time, the great bandit still existed,
and the Emperor did not wish to ascend the throne immediately.
However, memorials urging him from all directions
came one after another,
so he issued an order to discontinue such memorials.
In the second month of the first year of Chéngshèng,
Wáng Sēngbiàn's armies departed from Xúnyáng.
The Emperor dispatched circulars throughout the land,
offering a reward for the capture of Jǐng and his rebels:
enfeoffment as Wàn Hù Kāiguó Gōng,
and fifty thousand bolts of silk and cloth.
In the third month,
Sēngbiàn and others pacified Jǐng,
and his head was sent to Jiānglíng.
On the day of Wùzǐ,
the pacification of the rebel was announced to the Míngtáng and Tàishè.
On the day of Jǐchǒu,
Sēngbiàn and others again presented a memorial urging his enthronement, saying: The
armies gathered fully at Jiànkāng on the Wùzǐ day of this month.
The rebel Jǐng, like a bird hiding or a beast cornered,
was repeatedly attacked and repeatedly frustrated.
His treachery exhausted and his deceptions spent,
he fortified himself with deep moats.
Your servants
divided and commanded the martial troops,
converging from a hundred routes.
Elite cavalry and short-range soldiers,
rhino-hide armor and iron shields,
formed into a thousand companies,
holding a million halberds,
stopping Zhòu at seven paces,
and encircling Xiàng
threefold.
With a thunderous crash, they utterly collapsed,
and all the villains were annihilated.
The young and old of the capital
all shouted "Long live!"
The wine and food of Cháng'ān
now commanded higher prices here.
The nine counties cleared,
the six
directions brightened;
how much more so the common people,
who would not leap for joy?
We humbly reflect that Your Majesty chewed sorrow and endured grief,
suffered indignation and bore cruelty.
From the purple court and crimson palace,
barbarian dust rose everywhere.
Dilapidated walls and good fields,
Jì horses gathered like clouds.
Weeping
blood, you faced the army,
tasting gall and swearing oaths to the multitude.
Yet Wú and Chǔ, as one family,
rebelled simultaneously with the Seven States,
and Guǎn and Cài spread rumors,
further causing chaos among the Three Supervisors.
The righteous of Xīliáng
The Emperor sent down two seals:
one said, “Founding Marquis of Jìnglín County,
with an income fief of a thousand households.”
This was for rewarding whoever captured Dàn.
The other said, “Founding Baron of Jiànxīng County,
with an income fief of three hundred households.”
This was for rewarding whoever was first to ascend the walls.
If the outer city was captured, one beacon was to be lit;
if the inner city was captured, two beacons;
if Dàn was captured, three beacons.
On the second day of the seventh month,
Qìngzhī advanced his army
and captured the outer city.
Riding on the victory, he also captured the small city.
When Dàn heard the army had entered,
he ran to the rear garden, fell into the water,
was pulled out and killed.
His head was sent to Jiànyè,
and he was then buried in Guǎnglíng.
His surname was demoted to Liú.
The Emperor commanded that all, great and small, in the city be executed.
Qìngzhī remonstrated against this,
and saved those below five feet in height.
Thereupon, all of Dàn’s partisans were executed.
The women and children in the city were distributed as military rewards,
while the men were killed to form a Jingguān (pyramid of heads).
The dead numbered several thousand,
and every windy dawn and rainy night, there were sounds of wailing and weeping.
Dàn’s mother, Yīn, and wife, Xú, both committed suicide.
Yīn was posthumously granted the title of Zhǎngníng Yuán Shúfēi.
Initially,
when Dàn was Governor of Nánxú Prefecture
in Jīngkǒu,
a great wind at night blew off roof tiles,
and the city gates’ deer antlers were overturned.
Dàn was greatly troubled by this.
When he was later transferred to garrison Guǎnglíng,
as he was about to enter the city,
a violent wind suddenly arose,
stirring up dust,
making the day dark.
He also once sat idly in the middle of the night
when a red light illuminated the room.
All who saw it were startled and horrified.
Dàn’s attendants on duty
dreamed in their sleep that someone told them:
“Your official's hair must be made into a spear-tassel.”
Upon waking, their topknots were already gone.
This happened to dozens of people.
Dàn was very frightened and perplexed.
In the second year of Dàmíng,
people were conscripted to build Guǎnglíng City.
As Dàn was inspecting,
a man stood before his carriage,
shouting loudly and cursing:
“The great army will arrive soon!
Why do you trouble the common people so much?”
Dàn had him seized
and asked about his background.
He replied:
“My surname is Yí, my given name Sūn.
My home is in Hǎilíng.
Heavenly Lord, along with Daoist and Buddhist deities, had a prior discussion,
wanting to burn and eliminate the people here.
The Daoist and Buddhist deities pleaded bitterly,
and by force gained time until now.
A great disaster is coming;
why don’t you establish the 'Six Cautions Gate'?”
Dàn asked,
“What is the ‘Six Cautions Gate’?”
He replied:
“It is an ancient saying:
‘Calamity will not pass the Six Cautions Gate.’”
Dàn, finding his words wild and perverse,
killed him.
Another, a musician from the Five Sounds, suddenly went mad, saw ghosts,
and cried out in terror:
“The enemy army is besieging the city!
White cloth sails are unfurled on the city walls!”
Dàn had him arrested and held for over twenty days before killing him.
On the day the city fell,
clouds and fog made it dark and dim.
A white rainbow descended upon the North Gate,
stretching into the city.
Eight years later,
the former deposed Emperor ascended the throne.
Yìyáng Wáng Chǎng, as Governor of Xú Prefecture,
passed through Guǎnglíng
and showed full grief at Dàn's tomb.
He submitted a memorial requesting Dàn’s reburial.
An edict ordered Dàn and his wife and children to be buried with the rites of commoners.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ of Míngdì,
they were reburied again,
sacrificed with a small offering.
Wáng Yúzhī,
a native of Lángxié,
was talented and resourceful.
All five of his sons were in Jiànyè.
Yúzhī once defended the city walls.
Qìngzhī bound his five sons,
showed them to him and beckoned him,
promising him wealth and high rank.
Yúzhī said:
“I have received great kindness from my lord.
I cannot have two hearts.
In my thirtieth year,
I have not yet found a place to die.
How can I be enticed by my private kin?”
His five sons cried out from outside,
calling their father.
When the city was pacified,
Qìngzhī killed all of them.
Jiànpíng Xuānjiǎn Wáng Hóng, courtesy name Xiūdù,
was the seventh son of Wéndì.
He lost his mother early.
In the twenty-first year of Yuánjiā,
at the age of eleven,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jiànpíng.
Hóng was modest and simple in his youth,
and deeply fond of literature.
Wéndì loved him with unusual favor,
and built a residence for him on Jīlóng Shān,
utilizing all the beauty of the mountains and waters.
The officials of the Jiànpíng principality were one rank higher than those of other principalities.
He successively held the positions of Zhōnghùjūn and Zhōngshūlìng.
When the “Original Fiend” usurped the throne,
and Xiàowǔ entered to suppress him,
Shào confined Hóng within the palace,
making it impossible for him to escape.
Xiàowǔ had previously given Hóng a tablet.
Hóng sent his trusted aide Zhōu Fǎdào with the tablet to Xiàowǔ.
After the matter was settled,
he was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè,
and ordered to welcome the Empress Dowager.
Upon his return, he was additionally appointed Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn and Zhōngshūjiān.
He was humble, frugal, and cautious,
treating the virtuous with respect and welcoming scholars.
He was astute in political affairs,
and the Emperor greatly trusted and relied on him.
He was transferred to Shàngshūlìng.
Hóng suffered from many illnesses in his youth,
and requested to be relieved of the Shàngshūlìng post.
He was granted his original title with the privilege of establishing a government office and being accorded the Three Ducal Ministers’ rites,
He was posthumously granted the title of Sītú.
The Emperor grieved deeply,
personally visiting his spirit on the first and fifteenth day of each month,
and composed his tomb inscription and eulogy himself.
In the fifth year,
the fiefs of other princes, his younger brothers, were increased by a thousand households each.
Deceased princes were not included in this rule,
except for Hóng, whose fief was posthumously increased.
His son, Jǐngsù, succeeded him.
Jǐngsù had his father’s demeanor in his youth,
and held the position of Governor of Nánxú Prefecture,
with the added title of Dūdū.
When Guìyáng Wáng Xiūfàn rebelled,
although Jǐngsù gathered troops to nominally assist the imperial court,
he secretly harbored duplicity.
After the rebellion was quelled,
he was promoted to the title of Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn.
Jǐngsù was fond of literature and books,
and gathered talented and righteous scholars
to acquire a good reputation,
thus drawing attention from both the court and the common people.
However, the later deposed Emperor was crazed and violent, losing the Way,
and everyone, both inside and outside the court, believed Jǐngsù was suitable for the imperial throne.
But the relatives of the deposed Emperor’s birth mother, the Chén clan, resented and envied him,
and Yáng Yùncháng and Ruǎn Tiánfū, both former subordinates of Míngdì,
were greedy to prolong their power through the young emperor.
They feared that if Jǐngsù ascended,
they would not be tolerated by a mature emperor,
and thus deeply feared and disliked him.
When Wǔdì marched north,
Lúnzhī sent the Administrator of Shùnyáng, Fù Hóngzhī, and the Administrator of Fúfēng, Shěn Tiánzǐ, out from Yáoliǔ,
and greatly defeated Yáo Hóng at Lántián.
When Wǔdì received the Mandate,
for his meritorious service in assisting the founding,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāochéng County.
When Shàodì ascended the throne,
he was summoned and appointed Hùjūn.
In the third year of Yuánjiā (426 CE),
he was appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Although Lúnzhī was a quýchǒng (privileged relative of the imperial family),
he lived frugally,
and was by nature rustic and unsophisticated,
often failing to understand human affairs.
Having long held a regional office,
he was wealthy both publicly and privately.
Upon entering court as Hùjūn,
his resources no longer matched his position,
which he took as a demotion.
Guānglù Dàfū Fàn Tài, who enjoyed practical jokes,
joked with him, saying:
“When the position of Sītú Gōng is vacant,
they will certainly use you, old fellow.
I'm not saying you're fit for the role by your qualifications,
but it's simply a matter of external relatives reaching high ranks in due course.”
Lúnzhī was greatly pleased,
and regularly brought wine and food to Tài.
In the fifth year (428 CE),
he died,
and was posthumously named Yuánhóu.
His son, Bófú, succeeded him.
Bófú, courtesy name Rùnyuǎn,
loved archery and horsemanship from a young age,
and served as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
leading the Yìtú (volunteer militia),
and resided north of the palace city.
Whenever a fire broke out or there were robbers,
he would don his armor personally,
and assist the commanderies and counties in pursuit and suppression.
Wǔdì greatly praised him.
When Wéndì ascended the throne,
he was successively promoted to Cìshǐ of Xú and Yǎn provinces.
His governance was harsh and violent;
officials and common people feared him as if living with tigers and wolves,
but robbers fled far away,
none daring to enter the territory.
In the eighteenth year of Yuánjiā (441 CE),
he was summoned to be Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
Previously,
the external supervisors were not subordinate to the Lǐngjūn,
and for those who should be jointly managed,
there would be a separate imperial decree;
only from this point did they come under the Lǐngjūn's overall command.
Later, he became Dānyáng Yǐn.
In the commandery, he was extremely severe;
the sub-offices could no longer bear his orders,
some deserted and were executed,
others jumped into the water and died.
A clerk who made a mistake while taking dictation
was immediately given fifty lashes.
His son, Qiàn, married Wéndì's fourth daughter, Hǎiyán Gōngzhǔ,
and was deeply loved and esteemed.
Qiàn once, in a playful remark,
struck the princess with his hand.
The matter reached the emperor's ears.
Wéndì was enraged,
and divorced them.
Bófú was ashamed and fearful,
fell ill and died,
posthumously named Sù.
The lineage continued to his grandson, Xù.
When Qí received the abdication,
the state was abolished.
Xiāo Sīhuà,
a native of Nánlánlíng,
was the nephew of Empress Xiàoyì of Sòng.
His father, Yuánzhī, courtesy name Jūnliú,
had successively served as Cìshǐ of Xú and Yǎn provinces.
He died in the first year of Yǒngchū (420 CE),
and was posthumously appointed Qián Jiāngjūn.
When Sīhuà was about ten years old,
he had not yet learned to read,
enjoyed riding on roof ridges,
beating slender-waisted drums,
and bullying his neighbors,
who all suffered from his maliciousness.
From then on, he changed his ways,
and within a few years, he gained a good reputation.
He was quite skilled in clerical script,
played the qín well,
and was capable in archery and horsemanship.
Later, he inherited the title of Marquis of Fēngyáng County.
During the Yuánjiā period,
he served as Cìshǐ of Qīng province.
The fugitive Sīmǎ Lángzhī and his brothers gathered a faction to plot rebellion.
Sīhuà sent the Administrator of Běihǎi, Xiāo Wāngzhī, to suppress and execute them.
In the eighth year (431 CE),
a large Wèi army arrived,
and he abandoned his post and fled to Píngchāng.
The Wèi army did not, in fact, arrive,
and consequently, he was summoned and imprisoned in the Shàngfāng.
Earlier, while in Qīng province,
a bronze dipper he often used was inverted under medicine.
Suddenly, he found two dead sparrows under the dipper.
Sīhuà sighed, saying:
“A dipper overturned and two sparrows dead,
is this not ominous?”
Soon after, he was imprisoned.
When the Administrator of Liáng province, Zhēn Fǎhù, caused discord during his tenure,
the Dī chieftain Yáng Nándāng took advantage of this to invade Hànzhōng.
Sīhuà was then released from prison and appointed Cìshǐ of Liáng and Nánqín provinces,
pacified Hànzhōng,
recovered all the encroached territory,
and stationed garrisons at the Jiāméng River.
Sīhuà relocated his administrative seat to Nánzhèng.
Fǎhù was
a native of Wújí, Zhōngshān.
After crossing the river,
he resided as a temporary resident in Nánjùn.
His younger brother, Fǎchóng, became Cìshǐ of Yì province from Shàofǔ.
Fǎhù was arrested by the regional office for the crime of abandoning his post,
and was granted death in prison.
Wéndì, because Fǎchóng held an important regional command,
ordered that Fǎhù be reported as having died of illness.
Wéndì instructed Sīhuà to submit a detailed account of the pacification of Hànzhōng,
and submitted it to the imperial historians.
In the fourteenth year (437 CE),
he was promoted to Píngxī Zhǎngshǐ under Prince Línchuān Yìqìng, and Nánmán Xiàowèi.
Wéndì bestowed upon him a bow and a qín,
with a personal imperial edict stating:
“I previously obtained this qín,
which is said to be an ancient item.
I now lend it to you,
along with a mulberry wood bow,
whose material and craftsmanship are truly excellent.
Good materials and beautiful instruments
should be in places where they can be fully utilized.
Sir, you truly have no one to yield to in this regard.”
He once accompanied Wéndì in ascending the northern ridge of Zhōngshān.
Halfway up, there was a flat rock and clear spring.
The emperor ordered him to play the qín on the rock,
and then bestowed upon him wine in a silver cup,
saying:
“Your appreciation has the spirit of pine and rock.”
He successively served as Níngmán Xiàowèi,
Cìshǐ of Yōng province,
and Supervisor of Military Affairs for four provinces,
before being summoned to be Lìbù Shàngshū.
Sīhuà, thinking that leaving the province meant he would no longer have effective power,
requested nine personal retainers from the palace army.
Wéndì joked with him, saying:
“Sir, you will ultimately not be a farmer in the village.
Why worry about having no one to command?”
Before he was appointed,
he was promoted to Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
At this time,
Wèi attacked Xuánhù.
Wéndì intended to launch a large northern invasion.
While the court officials generally agreed,
Sīhuà strongly advised against it, but was not heeded.
When the Wèi army retreated,
he immediately replaced Xiàowǔ as Cìshǐ of Xú and Yǎn provinces,
and Supervisor of Military Affairs for four provinces.
Later, he failed to capture the besieged Quèqiao City,
and retreated to Lìxià.
He was impeached and dismissed from office by Prince Jiāngxià Yìgōng.
When the primary culprit (the usurper) assassinated the emperor and took the throne,
he was appointed Cìshǐ of Xú and Yǎn provinces.
He immediately raised an army of righteousness to support Xiàowǔ.
When Xiàowǔ ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè.
He firmly declined,
and was instead appointed Zhōngshū Lìng, Dānyáng Yǐn, and Sànqí Chángshì.
At that time, there were many robberies in the capital.
Seventeen occurred within two decades.
He took the blame and offered to resign,
but was not permitted.
Later, he was appointed Cìshǐ of Yǐng province,
and additionally given the title Dūdū.
He died,
and was posthumously appointed Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and posthumously named Mùhóu.
Sīhuà was a highly regarded quýchǒng,
and was entrusted with important responsibilities early on,
serving in twelve provinces,
and holding military command with the imperial insignia nine times.
Although he did not display strikingly pure integrity wherever he served,
he also did not incur any stain of corruption.
He loved talent and appreciated scholars,
and many people gravitated towards him.
During the Tiānjiān era of Liáng,
he served as an aide to Sītú Xiè Fěi.
He was directly assigned to the Wéndé Waiting Chamber to await imperial commands,
where he was ordered to copy books from the Yǐ division.
He was also ordered to compile stories of ancient women.
He had calligraphers Wáng Chēn of Lángyá and Fàn Huáiyuē of Wú Jùn copy them for the rear palace.
Zhāng Shuài obtained leave to return east,
and commentators called this his "world" [of influence].
Zhāng Shuài was fearful,
so he presented the "Fu on the Imperial Attendant" (Dàizhào Fù),
which was greatly praised and admired.
The emperor replied with a personal edict:
"Xiāngrú was skilled but not quick-witted,
Méi Gāo was quick-witted but not skilled.
You can be said to combine the strengths of both gentlemen at the Jīnmǎ Gate."
He also attended a banquet and composed a poem.
Emperor Wǔ separately bestowed a poem upon Zhāng Shuài, saying:
"The southeast has talented sons,
thus they are able to serve in government.
Although I am ashamed compared to antiquity,
the acquisition of such a man makes the present prosperous."
Zhāng Shuài submitted six poems in return.
Later, he was granted an audience in the Yùhéng Hall.
The emperor said:
"You are the hope of the southeast,
which I have heard of since olden times.
You ask who is the Prime Minister –
he does not come from heaven,
nor does he emerge from the earth.
You are a celebrated talent from a renowned family.
If you also focus on rites and laws,
then you will be that person.
The Bìshūchéng (Secretariat Director) is a pure office in the realm.
No prominent family from the southeast has yet held it.
Now I appoint you to it,
to establish your reputation."
Soon after, he was made Bìshūchéng,
in charge of collecting imperial edicts, decrees, and policies.
In the fourth year,
during the Xì festival at Huáguāng Hall,
on that day, the state of Hénán presented a red dragon colt
that could bow and prostrate
and was skilled at dancing.
An edict ordered Zhāng Shuài, Dào Gài, and Zhōu Xīngsì to compose *fu* (rhapsodies).
Emperor Wǔ considered Zhāng Shuài and Zhōu Xīngsì to be the most skilled.
That year,
he left office due to his father's mourning.
His father had dozens of female entertainers.
Among those skilled in singing, some had good looks.
A local gentleman, the Yícáoláng Gù Guāngzhī, sought to marry one.
The singer was unwilling,
and subsequently became a nun.
Once, during a vegetarian gathering at Zhāng Shuài's residence,
Gù Guāngzhī sent a letter alleging an illicit affair with Zhāng Shuài.
The Southern Bureau reported the matter.
Emperor Wǔ, valuing Zhāng Shuài's talent,
shelved the report,
but it still caused public discussion at the time.
After the mourning period ended,
he did not serve in office for a long time.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Zhōngquán Jiàn’ān Wáng Zhōngjìshì Cānjūn (Secretary to the Prince of Jiàn’ān in the Central Army).
Shortly after, he was assigned to the Shòuguāng Bureau,
to revise and copy books from the Bǐng and Dīng divisions.
He was successively promoted to Jìn’ān Wáng Xuānhuì Zīyì Cānjūn (Advisor to the Prince of Jìn’ān).
Zhāng Shuài was in the prince's residence for ten years,
and was treated with great favor and courtesy.
Later, he became Yángzhōu Biéjià (Auxiliary Administrator of Yáng Province).
Although Zhāng Shuài held various official positions,
he never paid close attention to administrative details.
When he became Biéjià and presented reports,
Emperor Wǔ read the documents and questioned him,
but he had no answers,
only replying:
"The matter is in the documents."
The Emperor was displeased.
Later, he served as Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Attendant).
He was sent out as Xīn’ān Tàishǒu (Governor of Xīn’ān Commandery),
but died during the mourning period for his biological mother.
Zhāng Shuài indulged in wine and neglected his duties,
especially forgetting household affairs.
In Xīn’ān, he sent his servants to transport three thousand *shi* of rice back to his residence.
Upon arrival, more than half was gone.
Zhāng Shuài asked the reason,
and they replied:
"Consumed by sparrows and rats."
Zhāng Shuài laughed and said:
"What mighty sparrows and rats!"
He never investigated further.
From a young age, he engaged in writing.
He supplemented the poems and *fu* recorded in *Qīlüè* and *Yìwén Zhì*
whose texts were now lost.
His extant works include *Wén Héng* in fifteen volumes
and a collection of essays in forty volumes, which circulated in the world.
His son was Zhāng Chánggōng.
Zhāng Shuài's younger brother was Zhāng Dùn.
Zhāng Dùn, courtesy name Shìxuān,
was known for his prudence and solemnity.
When he was Wúxī Lìng (Magistrate of Wúxī),
he encountered robbers.
He asked what the robbers needed.
The robbers slashed his cheek with a knife.
Zhāng Dùn said:
"Oh,
oh,
that's not good."
He said nothing else.
Thus, all his possessions were lost,
but he did not take it to heart.
He served as Jìshì (Secretary) to the Xiāngdōng Wáng (Prince of Xiāngdōng),
and later became Jiān Fùyáng Lìng (Overseer of Fùyáng County).
He lived in detached solitude,
without any worldly concerns.
On the day of his death,
his family had no leftover wealth,
only a collection of writings, over a thousand scrolls of books,
and a few jars of wine and rice.
Zhāng Jì, courtesy name Gōngqiáo,
was Zhāng Guī's younger brother.
As a child, he possessed filial piety.
His biological mother, Liú, was not favored [by his father]
and fell ill.
At that time, Zhāng Jì was eleven years old.
He attended to her without loosening his clothes,
and whenever her illness worsened, he would stay awake for several nights.
When she died,
he wasted away excessively,
only able to stand with a cane.
When he saw children his age,
he would choke up and shed tears.
The people of his province called him "Purely Filial."
His eldest brother, Zhāng Wěi, was skilled at playing the *zheng*.
As his mother Liú had previously practiced this art,
when Zhāng Jì heard Zhāng Wěi play a clear melody,
he was overcome with sadness and immediately stopped [listening to it].
He never listened to it again for the rest of his life.
He was unconstrained and easygoing by nature,
bright and intelligent with strategic talent.
He started his career as Zuòzuò Zuǒláng (Assistant in the Secretariat of History),
but did not accept the appointment.
His father, Zhāng Yǒng, and his stepmother, Qiū, died one after another.
He lived in a hut by their graveside for six years.
During the Yǒngmíng era of Qí,
he served as Zhǔbù (Clerk) to the Yùzhāng Wáng Yì (Prince of Yùzhāng).
He and Liú Huì of Péngchéng were both treated with courtesy.
They were never called by their names,
but always addressed as "Liú Four" and "Zhāng Five."
Due to poverty, he sought to be Yǎn Lìng (Magistrate of Yǎn County),
but rarely attended to official duties,
often making trips to small mountains.
〔一０〕When the mountain bandit Táng Yùzhī caused trouble,
Zhāng Jì rallied the local people to protect the entire county.
His biological mother Liú had been temporarily buried at Huángshān in Lángyá.
During the Jiànwǔ era, he revised the funeral rites for her reburial,
and many funeral contributions accumulated.
Although he did not refuse them at the time,
he returned them all after the matter was concluded.
From childhood to adulthood,
for several decades,
he always kept a spirit tablet for Lady Liú.
He would announce his departure and greet it upon his return,
as if she were still alive.
He successively served as Jǐshìzhōng (Attendant Censor) and Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Attendant),
and Tàishǒu (Governor) of Xīnxīng and Yǒngníng Commanderies.
As the commandery's name violated a private taboo,
Yǒngníng was changed to Chángníng.
At the end of the Yǒngyuán era,
he became Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant),
guarding the imperial palace city.
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's army arrived,
Jiāng Yān, who was concurrently Wèiwèi (Palace Guard Commander), fled.
Zhāng Jì then concurrently served as Wèiwèi Qīng (Minister of the Palace Guard),
assisting Wáng Yíng in commanding all military affairs within the city.
At that time, the Dōnghūn Emperor was debauched and cruel.
Wáng Zhēnguó, the Císhǐ (Inspector) of Běixú Province, conspired with Zhāng Jì.
They then had Zhāng Qí, a Zhíhé, assassinate the emperor in the Hándé Hall.
Zhāng Jì then summoned Ròupúshè Wáng Liàng and others to sit in front of the hall, under the western bell.
They discussed sending Guózǐ Bóshì Fàn Yún and Zhōngshū Shèrén Péi Chángmù to Shítóuchéng to meet Emperor Wǔ.
Zhāng Jì was appointed Shìzhōng, Zuǒwèijiāngjūn (General of the Left Guards),
and later promoted to Dàsīmǎ Zuǒsīmǎ (Left Commandant of the Grand Marshal).
knowing why it is called such.
This book is circulated,
so there should be appreciative readers.
The biographies usually give only a general outline,
and there are many subtle points.
Since ancient times,
no one has had such a grand structure
and refined thought.
I fear that the world cannot fully grasp it,
many valuing the old and belittling the new,
which is why I speak wildly out of emotion.
As for music,
my listening skill is not as good as my own playing,
but what I excel at is not refined music, which is regrettable.
However, when it reaches a point of absolute perfection,
how is it any different?
Its
inner charm and appeal
cannot be fully expressed in words.
The meaning beyond the strings,
the sound of the ethereal echoes,
one knows not whence they come.
I have also tried to teach it to others,
but among both scholars and commoners,
not one has been even slightly similar.
This will never be transmitted.
Though my writing has some small intention,
the brushwork is not smooth,
and the rest of it remains unaccomplished,
for which I am always ashamed of this reputation.
Yè's self-preface is genuine and factual,
hence it is preserved.
Ái was neat and clean from a young age;
his clothes never had a speck of dust for a whole year.
He died at the age of twenty.
When Yè was young,
his elder brother Yàn often said:
"This child is keen on profit
and will ultimately ruin the family."
It turned out exactly as he said.
Initially,
Hé Shàngzhī was in charge of personnel selection,
and he claimed there was no talent overlooked in the world.
When Kǒng Xīxiān was arrested,
the Emperor questioned Shàngzhī, saying:
"If Kǒng Xīxiān at thirty was still a Sànqí Shìláng,
why wouldn't he become a bandit?"
After Xīxiān's death,
he again said to Shàngzhī:
"Kǒng Xīxiān had excellent talent,
and his noble lineage was also considerable,
yet he was obscure in official circles.
Was this not a failure of the era's selectors?"
Shàngzhī replied:
"Your subject once mistakenly held the humble post in the selection office,
and indeed had no means to cleanse the corrupt and promote the pure.
However, a gentleman with wisdom and ability
is like a phoenix with beautiful plumage.
He awaits his time to spread his wings
and need not worry about failing to soar above the clouds and mist.
If Xīxiān indeed possessed brilliant talent
but abandoned himself in the mud,
then there is ultimately nothing to discuss."
The Emperor said:
"In the past, those with good talent who did not meet a true appreciative friend,
how could they not leave regrets for later generations?"
Xún Bózǐ,
a native of Yǐngyīn, Yǐngchuān,
was the grandson of Jìn General of Agile Cavalry Xiàn.
His father, Yī,
was a Mìshū Láng.
Bózǐ was fond of learning in his youth,
extensively reading classics and commentaries,
but he was straightforward and enjoyed idle talk,
roaming around villages and neighborhoods,
which caused him to lose the path to a pure career.
He was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi, Fèng Cháoqǐng, and Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
The Zhùzuò Láng Xú Guǎng esteemed his talent and learning,
and recommended Bózǐ and Wáng Sháozhī to be his assistant scribes,
jointly compiling the Jìn History and writing biographies of Huán Xuán and others.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Cíbù Láng.
In the first year of Yìxī,
〔一０〕he submitted a memorial stating:
"The late Grand Tutor, Marquis of Jùpíng, Yáng Hù, his merits assisted in establishing the state
and his achievements in pacifying Wú were great,
yet his succession is cut short,
and there is no one to offer sacrifices.
The Hàn dynasty, considering Xiāo Hé's foundational merit,
ensured that his lineage was continued even if a generation was absent.
Your subject humbly suggests that the enfeoffment of Jùpíng
should be treated the same as the state of Cuózé.
The late Grand Commandant, Duke of Guǎnglíng, Chén Zhǔn, was a partisan of Sūn Xiù,
〔一一〕bringing disaster to Huáinán,
secretly enjoying a great state,
turning crime into profit.
At that time, the Western Court's governance and punishments were out of order,
and the restoration of the dynasty continued it without abolition.
Now that the royal way is renewed,
how can we not make a clear distinction between good and bad?
I propose that the state of Guǎnglíng
should be abolished.
The late Grand Protector, Wèi Guàn, was originally enfeoffed as the Duke of Zīyáng County.
After suffering an undeserved calamity,
his rank was advanced,
he was posthumously granted Lánlíng,
and then subsequently Jiāngxià.
Many high officials in the Central Court
did not die justly.
