Guàn's merits and virtues were not special,
and there is no reason for him alone to receive a singular reward.
It is fitting to restore his original enfeoffment
to rectify the state's regulations."
The emperor ordered it to be submitted to the Ménxià Shěng.
Former Sànqí Chángshì, Duke of Jiāngxià, Wèi Yú, and Yǐngchuān's Chén Máoxiān each presented their ancestors' achievements,
not accepting the demotion.
The emperor ordered both to be submitted to the Ménxià Shěng,
and neither was implemented.
Bózǐ was recommended by his wife's younger brother, Xiè Huì,
and became Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
then appointed Nèishǐ of Línchuān.
General of Chariots and Cavalry Wáng Hóng praised Bózǐ as
"profound and not ostentatious,
possessing the style of the Marquis of Píngyáng."
Bózǐ often prided himself on the beauty of his inherited prestige,
and said to Hóng:
"Among the privileged gentry of the world,
there are only Your Excellency and your humble servant;
those like Xuān Míng are not worth counting."
He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
and again submitted a memorial saying:
"Regarding the order of precedence for officials,
the King of Chénliú is above the King of Línglíng.
Your humble subject secretly harbors doubts about this.
In the past, King Wǔ, upon conquering Yīn,
enfeoffed the descendant of Shénnóng in Jiāo,
the descendant of Huángdì in Zhù,
the descendant of Emperor Yáo in Jì,
the descendant of Emperor Shùn in Chén,
the descendant of the Xià ruler in Yí,
and the descendant of Yīn in Sòng.
Qǐ and Chén were both listed as states,
while Jì, Zhù, and Jiāo are unheard of.
This indicates that the veneration of one's lineage
is prioritized over distant ancestors, which is a clear manifestation.
Therefore, when the Spring and Autumn Annals arranged the feudal lords,
Sòng was placed above Yí and Chén.
Examining recent times,
the matter also has proof.
In the first year of Tàishǐ of Jìn,
an imperial edict granted Liú Kāng, Duke of Shānyáng, and one of his kinsmen the title Guānnèi Hóu,
and Jī Shǔ, Duke of Wèi, and Kǒng Shào, Marquis of Sòng, and one of their kinsmen, Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
Then, in the third year of Tàishǐ,
the Tàicháng reported on the deliberation of the Bóshì Liú Jiā and others,
stating that Duke Shǔ of Wèi was counted among the three honored guests of Great Jìn,
and should be demoted to a Marquis.
Your subject believes that the King of Línglíng's position should be above that of Chénliú."
This was followed.
He served as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and diligently performed his duties,
earning the reputation of being selfless.
He upheld righteousness in court,
and everyone feared him.
In all his impeachments,
he never failed to severely reprimand and criticize,
sometimes even extending to the ancestors,
to demonstrate his directness.
He also mixed in some mockery,
which is why people criticized him for this.
He was appointed Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ,
and died as the Tàishǒu of Dōngyáng.
His collected works were circulated in the world.
His son Chìsōng
became Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
and as a partisan of Xú Zhànzhī,
was killed by the chief rebel.
Bózǐ's clan brother Chǎng, courtesy name Màozǔ,
was distant from Bózǐ by mourning attire.
In the early Yuánjiā era,
he rose to Zhōngshū Láng through his literary talent and integrity.
Chǎng's son was Wànqiū.
When Emperor Shàodì ascended the throne,
Yán Zhī was successively promoted to Grand Protector of Shǐ'ān.
General of the Central Army Xiè Huì said to Yán Zhī:
"In the past, Xún Xù, jealous of Ruǎn Xián,
banished him to Shǐpíng Prefecture.
Now you are also in Shǐ'ān.
One might say it's 'the two Shǐs'."
Yellow Gate Attendant Yīn Jǐngrén also said to him:
"This is what is meant by 'people resent outstanding talent,
the world faults refinement and elegance'."
When Yán Zhī went to his prefecture,
his route passed through Mìtán.
He composed a memorial to Qū Yuán for Zhāng Shào, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, to express his feelings.
In the third year of Yuánjiā (426 CE),
when Xiàn Zhī and others were executed,
he was recalled to serve as Gentleman of the Central Secretariat,
then transferred to Prince's Household Grand Master,
and concurrently Supervisor of Infantry.
He received very generous rewards and treatment.
As Yán Zhī was treated favorably for his talent and scholarship,
most people at the time highly esteemed him.
Only Yuán Shú, who was more than ten years younger than Yán Zhī,
did not hold him in high regard.
Yán Zhī, annoyed, openly challenged him in front of a crowd, saying:
"In ancient times, Chén Yuánfāng and Kǒng Yuánjùn were peers in literature.
Yuánjùn bowed to Yuánfāng beneath the couch.
How is it that you do not bow to me now?"
Shú had no reply.
Yán Zhī was unconventional and unrestrained,
and unable to ingratiate himself with the current age.
Seeing Liú Zhàn and Yīn Jǐngrén monopolizing crucial positions,
he felt indignant.
He often said,
"How can the affairs of the world be settled solely by the wisdom of one person?"
His words were fervent and agitated,
constantly offending powerful figures.
Moreover, when young, he had served as clerk to Liǔ Hòujiāngjūn, Zhàn's father.
Now, he said to Zhàn:
"My official position has not risen,
it must be due to having been your family's clerk."
Zhàn resented this deeply
and spoke about it to Prince Péngchéng Yìkāng,
who had Yán Zhī sent out as Grand Protector of Yǒngjiā.
Yán Zhī was very resentful,
and so composed the "Five Gentlemen's Songs" (Wǔjūn Yǒng),
to describe the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove,
among whom Shān Tāo and Wáng Róng were disparaged for their wealth and prominence.
His song for Jī Kāng said:
"A phoenix's wings are sometimes clipped,
who can tame a dragon's nature?"
His song for Ruǎn Jí said:
"Past things cannot be discussed,
when one reaches the end of the road, how can one not mourn?"
His song for Ruǎn Xián said:
"Repeated recommendations did not gain him office,
a single appointment sent him out to govern."
His song for Liú Líng said:
"Concealing his talent, he drank day and night,
who knew it wasn't a wild banquet?"
These four lines were likely his self-preface.
Zhàn and Yìkāng, deeming his words disrespectful,
were furious
and wanted to demote him to a distant prefecture.
Emperor Wén and Yìkāng issued an edict saying:
"He should be ordered to reflect on his transgressions in his village.
If he still does not mend his ways,
he should be driven to the eastern lands.
As for those who are truly unforgivable,
they can be dealt with according to the circumstances."
Consequently, Yán Zhī secluded himself and did not involve himself in human affairs for seven years.
The Central Secretariat Director Wáng Qiú, as a noble gentleman who disdained involvement in trivial matters,
had a deep affection for Yán Zhī
and often relieved his destitution.
When Empress Gōngsī of Jìn was buried,
all officials were required to attend,
based on appointments made in the first year of Yìxī.
Yán Zhī was serving concurrently as Imperial Household Grandee.
When the district clerk delivered the summons,
Yán Zhī, being drunk,
threw the summons to the ground and said:
"Yán Yánzhī has not been able to serve the living,
how can he serve the dead?"
Emperor Wén once summoned Yán Zhī,
but his messengers repeatedly failed to find him,
as he spent his days naked and singing dirges in taverns,
utterly refusing to respond.
He would only appear on another day after sobering up.
The Emperor once asked him about the talents of his sons.
Yán Zhī said:
"Jùn got my calligraphy,
Cè got my prose,
Huàn got my righteousness,
and Yuè got my wine."
Hé Shàngzhī scoffed:
"Who got your madness?"
He replied:
"My madness is beyond reach."
When Shàngzhī was on duty as Imperial Household Grandee,
Yán Zhī visited him while drunk.
Shàngzhī, seeing him from afar, pretended to be asleep.
Yán Zhī pulled back the curtain, stared intently, and said:
"Rotten wood cannot be carved."
Shàngzhī said to his attendants:
"This man is terrifying when drunk."
When idle and without official duties,
he composed the "Family Admonitions" (Tíng Gào) to instruct his children and younger relatives.
After Liú Zhàn was executed,
Yán Zhī was reinstated as Military Advisor to Prince Shǐxīng Jùn's Rear Army and Censor-in-Chief.
He was relaxed in his post
and did not impeach anyone.
He was promoted to Libationer of the National University and Left Senior Clerk to the Minister of Works.
Hé Shàngzhī had always been close to Yán Zhī,
and wrote to Wáng Qiú saying:
"With Yán Zhī's later appointments,
the prefectural office will no longer have its former brilliance."
He was impeached for buying land from someone and refusing to pay the full price.
Assistant Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs, Xún Chìsōng, memorialized thus:
"Seeking land and asking for houses
is scorned by former sages.
Yán Zhī only sees profit,
boldly encroaching on others,
relying on imperial favor,
and resisting payment of the remaining cost.
Almost a year has passed,
and it is still not settled.
Greedy for profit, he obtains it unscrupulously,
without any scruples.
Yán Zhī was previously banished for his transgressions,
yet was again drawn forth and promoted.
However, he has never mended his ways
and his complaints and slanders are endless.
His associates are unruly,
he is lost in drink,
maliciously raising mockery and slander,
and disparaging court officials.
He presumptuously appropriates undue honor,
inflaming his nature of contempt and disdain.
Privately relying on imperial favor,
he has developed a stubborn and overbearing disposition.
Outwardly he feigns few desires,
but inwardly he harbors ambition and strives for promotion.
He pursues office and prays for advancement,
knowing no bounds.
Attending banquets and sharing wine,
he openly curses those in higher seats.
Like mountains and seas, the imperial court accommodates and tolerates,
always preserving and nurturing.
It cherishes his talent, like the carving of insects,
and cannot bear to cast him far away.
Yet his arrogance and unrestrained behavior grow worse with each passing day.
Your servant hears that a reputation exceeding one's true nature
is what Mèng Kē (Mencius) found shameful,
much less when the reputation is not from external sources,
but the inquiry arises from his own actions.
Although his intelligence and wisdom are meager,
he highly compares himself to others,
his arrogance ostentatiously displayed,
without any shame or fear.
How can such a person
assist in enlightening the five teachings and
add splendor to the imperial court?
I request that Yán Zhī be dismissed from his current office
for his dishonest land dispute,
his reckless presumption before the Emperor,
and his bullying of the weak."
The edict approved.
Later he served as Imperial Secretary,
then Grand Master of Ceremonies,
and then Grand Historian.
At this time, the Buddhist monk Shì Huìlín was esteemed by Emperor Wén for his talent and learning,
and many court policies were discussed with him,
leading to his veneration by both gentry and commoners.
The Emperor always received him,
often letting him sit alone on an elevated couch.
Yán Zhī deeply resented this.
One day, while drunk, he reported to the Emperor:
"In ancient times, even with Tóng Zǐ riding in the same carriage,
Yuán Sī maintained proper decorum.
This is the seat of the Three Ducal Ministers,
how can one who is a eunuch occupy it?"
The Emperor's expression changed.
Yán Zhī's nature was both narrow-minded and impetuous,
and he also had a drinking problem.
He spoke his mind freely and directly,
without any pretense or concealment.
Therefore, many critics did not agree with him,
calling him 'Yán Biāo' (Mad Yan).
His personal life was frugal,
he did not pursue wealth,
wearing plain clothes and eating simple food,
drinking alone in the countryside.
When he was enjoying himself,
he behaved as if no one else was around.
At the age of thirty,
he retired from service.
Jiāng Zhìshēn
was a disciple of Yí.
His father, Sēng'ān,
was a Middle Commandant of the Heir Apparent in Sòng.
Yí had a great reputation;
his son Zhàn also had a pure reputation.
Father and son were both noble and prominent.
Zhìshēn's father had little renown in his youth,
and Zhàn treated him with extreme condescension.
Zhìshēn often resented this,
and would not enter Zhàn's gate except for festivals and new year.
Later, he served as Adjutant in the Rear Army for Súi Wáng Dàn,
stationed in Xiāngyáng.
Dàn treated him very generously.
At that time, Consultative Adjutant Xiè Zhuāng and Chief Clerk Shěn Huáiwén were good friends with Zhìshēn.
Huáiwén often praised him, saying:
"One who has everything he should have and lacks everything he should not lack,
is that not Jiāng Zhìshēn?"
At the end of Yuánjiā,
he was appointed Lang of the Imperial Treasury in the Department of State Affairs.
At that time, high-ranking officials generally did not serve as臺láng.
Zhìshēn, being from an isolated family with few connections,
was uniquely chosen for this,
and was very displeased.
He firmly declined the appointment.
Later, he became Chief Clerk and Adjutant in the Secretariat for Jìnglín Wáng Dàn,
concurrently holding the post of Grand Administrator of Nán Púyáng,
then was promoted to Attendant Censor.
When Dàn was about to rebel,
Zhìshēn perceived his intentions
and requested leave to return home first.
When Dàn's rebellion broke out,
he was immediately appointed Court Gentleman of the Central Secretariat.
Zhìshēn loved literature and refined arts;
his prose was clear and eloquent.
Xiàowǔ deeply appreciated and favored him,
and his grace and courtesy were unsurpassed in court.
The emperor frequently held private banquets,
often inviting groups of five or three officials to gather.
Zhìshēn was always foremost among them.
Before his companions could advance,
he would always be uniquely ushered in,
and he often felt ashamed of being singled out,
never showing a joyful expression.
Whenever he accompanied the emperor on outings,
he would walk with other officials.
When he saw an imperial messenger rushing towards them,
knowing he was about to be summoned,
[一０]he would flinch with shame and embarrassment,
which was evident on his face.
Commentators often praised him for this.
He was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry and Lang of the Bureau of Appointments in the Department of State Affairs.
Whenever the emperor was deeply intoxicated at banquets,
he would disparage his officials
and make them mock and expose each other's faults,
finding it amusing.
Zhìshēn was by nature modest and withdrawn,
and gradually failed to understand the emperor's intentions.
The emperor once ordered him to joke with Wáng Sēnglǎng's son Jǐngwén.
Zhìshēn, with a serious expression, said:
"I fear such a joke would be inappropriate."
The emperor angrily said:
"Jiāng Sēng'ān is a fool,
and fools naturally cherish each other."
Zhìshēn prostrated on the mat, shedding tears,
and from then on, his favor greatly declined.
He was sent out to serve as Chief Clerk of the Northern Army for Xīn'ān Wáng Zǐluán and Grand Administrator of Nán Dōnghǎi,
acting as the affairs of Xiāngzhōu.
Originally,
when the emperor's favored concubine, Noble Consort Xuān, née Yīn, died,
he ordered officials to discuss her posthumous title.
Zhìshēn proposed
"Huái."
The emperor felt this did not fully express her virtues
and greatly resented him for it.
Later, when the imperial carriage visited Nánshān,
reaching the tomb of Lady Yīn on horseback,
all officials rode along.
The emperor pointed his horsewhip at the stone pillar of the tomb and said to Zhìshēn,
"This pillar has no room for the character 'Huái'."
Zhìshēn became even more terrified
and died of worry.
His son, Yún,
was an Attendant Horseman to the Heir Apparent,
and died young.
[一一]Later, the empress of the deposed emperor
was Yún's daughter.
When the deposed emperor ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted Yún the title of Grand Master of the Golden and Purple Light, as the empress's father,
and Yún's wife, Wáng Píngwàng, the title of Xiāng Jūn.
Zhìshēn's nephew Gài was orphaned early,
and Zhìshēn raised him as his own son.
Gài successively served as Lang of the Yellow Gate and Bureau of Appointments,
Attendant,
and Chief Clerk of the Northern Army for Wǔlíng Wáng Zàn.
Jiāng Bǐngzhī, courtesy name Xuánshū,
[一二]was a native of Kǎochéng in Jìyáng.
His grandfather, Yōu,
was Grand Chamberlain during the Jìn dynasty.
His father, Zuǎn,
was a Palace Attendant.
Bǐngzhī was orphaned young,
and his seven younger siblings were all infants.
He devoted all his effort to raising them and arranging their marriages.
During the reign of Sòng Shàodì,
he served as Magistrate of Yǒngshì and Wūchéng,
and was renowned in the eastern region for his good governance.
He was summoned to serve as Magistrate of Jiànkāng.
His administration was strict and observant,
and his subordinates were awestruck.
Later, he became Magistrate of Shānyīn.
With 30,000 households,
government affairs were complex and troublesome,
and lawsuits accumulated,
with hundreds of people always at his courtyard.
Bǐngzhī managed complexity with simplicity,
always maintaining order.
During the Sòng dynasty,
only Gù Jìzhī also achieved results through simplifying affairs;
though others might have rectified legal and administrative matters,
they could not simplify them.
For his competence in the county,
he was appointed Grand Administrator of Xīn'ān.
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā (435 CE),
he was transferred to Línhǎi,
and was praised for his simplicity and frugality,
dying in office.
He distributed all his official salary to his relatives and old friends,
and his wife and children often suffered from hunger and cold.
Someone advised him to manage farmland.
Bǐngzhī replied with a serious expression:
"How can one who receives official salary
compete for profit with farmers?"
While in the commandery, he made one writing desk,
which he left to the treasury upon leaving office.
Bǐngzhī's kinsman Suìzhī, courtesy name Xuányuǎn,
[一三]was quite learned in literature and meaning.
He compiled commentaries on texts that circulated in the world
and held the position of Adjutant to the Minister of Works.
Bǐngzhī's son Huī
was Lang of the Department of State Affairs, Bureau of Revenue,
and Magistrate of Wú.
When Yuán Xiōng murdered Xú Zhànzhī,
Huī was executed as an accomplice.
His son was Mì.
Mì, courtesy name Línghé,
was imprisoned in the Imperial Manufactory
when his father Huī met disaster.
When Sòng Xiàowǔ pacified Jiànyè,
Mì was released and appointed Magistrate of Yúhú,
where he proved to be capable and diligent in his duties.
When Sòng Míngdì was Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
[一四]Mì devoted himself to serving him
and was favored by the emperor.
Upon ascending the throne,
the emperor made him Adjutant to the General of Agile Cavalry.
His younger brother Méng was ugly,
and the emperor often summoned and teased him.
Mì was twice promoted to Right Vice-Minister,
concurrently serving as Lang of the Bureau of Accounts.
In the fourth year of Tàishǐ (468 CE),
the fifteenth daughter of Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng died at the age of nineteen.
She had not yet had her hair pinned,
and the ritual officials discussed observing adult mourning rites,
with the princes wearing dágōng (heavy mourning) for her.
Left Vice-Minister Sūn Xiōng submitted a further memorial:
"The Lǐjì states, 'A girl has her hair pinned at fifteen,'
and Zhèng Xuán commented, 'This means she is old enough to be promised in marriage.
If not yet promised,
then she has her hair pinned at twenty.'"
Shè Cí said, 'Nineteen is still considered premature death.'
The ritual officials have violated classical texts,
and their reasoning has no basis."
The Grand Chamberlain and others were fined and allowed to redeem themselves.
Mì was punished with fifty strokes of the rod
and deprived of one hundred days' salary.
Mì then memorialized that Xiōng had not thoroughly researched the matter before,
and had mixed up his arguments with erroneous proposals,
so according to precedents,
he should also be held accountable.
Xiōng was again fined and allowed to redeem himself,
which was approved by imperial decree.
Mì was sent out to serve as Chief Clerk of the Champion Army for Jiànpíng Wáng Jǐngsù and Grand Administrator of Chángshā,
acting as the affairs of Xiāngzhōu.
His governance was harsh and strict.
Sēng Zūndào, who was on intimate terms with Mì,
accompanied Mì to the commandery.
When he committed a minor offense,
he was starved and imprisoned in the commandery jail.
Sēng Zūndào tore up his three robes and ate them all before he died.
This was reported by the competent authorities,
and Mì was recalled.
Upon Míngdì's death,
he was pardoned.
When Qí Gāodì was governor of Nán-Yānzhōu,
Mì served as the Administrator of the Zhenjūn Army and Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng.
Later, he entered service as the Yoují Jiāngjūn.
His nature was worldly,
〔一五〕and he was good at seizing opportune advantages.
At the end of Yuánhuī's reign,
the court and the populace alike fixed their hopes on Prince Jiànpíng, Jǐngsù.
Mì deeply committed himself to him.
When Jǐngsù's enterprise failed,
he barely escaped misfortune.
After Cāngwú Wáng was deposed,
public sentiment still harbored doubts and disloyalty.
Mì alone devoted his sincerity to Qí Gāodì.
In the first year of Shēngmíng,
he became Huángmén Shìláng
and concurrently held the position of Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
When Shěn Yōuzhī's affair arose,
the proposal to grant Gāodì the title of Huángyuè
was Mì's initiative.
After the situation settled,
he was promoted to Lìbù Láng.
In the first year of Qí Jiàn Yuán,
he held the position of Shìzhōng.
Soon after, when the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Prince Yùzhāng Yí, governed Xiāngzhōu,
he appointed Mì as his Administrator,
and Mì was enfeoffed as the Earl of Yǒngxīn County.
In the third year,
he became Zuǒhù Shàngshū.
When the imperial princes left the palace to establish their own residences,
requiring military and civil commanders,
all matters were entrusted to Mì.
Soon after, an imperial edict stated:
"Jiāng Mì is a humble scholar,
and indeed he cannot compete with those of noble lineage.
However, he possesses great talent and ability,
and can be promoted to oversee the Ministry of Personnel."
Mì excelled in literary and administrative skills
and was competent in every post.
When Gāodì passed away,
Mì feigned illness and did not enter the palace,
which made many suspect that he resented not being included in the dying instructions.
When Wǔdì ascended the throne,
Mì was again not promoted,
which caused him to harbor resentment and discontent.
At that time, Wǔdì was unwell.
Mì went to Prince Yùzhāng Yí
and privately asked:〔一六〕
"His Majesty's illness is not temporary,
and the Eastern Palace (the heir apparent) lacks talent.
What do you intend to do now?"
Wǔdì learned of this
and exiled Mì to be the Administrator of Zhènběi and Grand Administrator of Nán-Dōnghǎi.
Before he departed,
he was very worried,
so he had Yì divine by hexagrams, who said:
"A guest comes from the south,
with a golden bowl and jade cup."
The emperor ordered the Palace Censor-in-Chief Shěn Chōng to memorialize Mì's past and present misdeeds,
requesting his arrest and delivery to the Grand Judge.
An edict ordered him to commit suicide.
Indeed, he was poisoned with medicine contained in a golden flask.
His son, Jiè,
during the Jiànwǔ period, served as the Magistrate of Wú.
His administration was also deeply harsh.
People posted a skull of a dead person as Mì's head,
〔一七〕and Jiè abandoned his office and left.
A commentary says: Jìngyuán's simplicity earned him praise,
and Xuánbǎo's magnanimity gained him respect.
Their high regard in the world
was not an empty reputation.
However, Xuánbǎo, at that time, enjoyed the emperor's favor.
Although his destiny was decreed by heaven,
judging by his imperial grace,
it was also
"the assistance of a worthy person."
The Shěn family, generation after generation, passed down military prowess,
and Yǎn zhī's literary accomplishments were also recognized.
He meticulously planned strategies in the inner chambers
and thus participated in state affairs.
Chǔ Mò preserved his integrity and simplicity,
while Shúyuán maintained his principles in times of danger.
Their noble virtues and lofty character
are what one calls having worthy people in the world.
Mào Yuǎn, from the Jìn to the Chén dynasty,
had a lineage of refined conduct,
transmitting virtue for generations.
This is what is meant.
However, Zǒng was lost in imperial favor and intimacy,
and conversely, his literary elegance led to his downfall.
Thus, for a scholar to achieve fame,
what is valued is nothing but refinement.
Xuánshú's purity and integrity were renowned,
enough to emulate the ancient heroes.
As for Lìnghé, prying and spying became his nature,
and he ultimately stumbled on a dangerous path.
This was fitting.
Collations:
Biographies 27: Shěn Qìngzhī (Grandson Zhāo Luè, Son Wén Jì, Nephew Wén Xiù, Cousin Yōu Zhī, Yōu Zhī's Grandson Sēng Zhāo) Zōng (Cousin Jué)
Shěn Qìngzhī, courtesy name Hóngxiān,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
In his youth, he possessed ambition and strength.
At the end of the Jìn dynasty, when Sūn Ēn caused rebellion,
he led his followers to plunder Wǔkāng.
Qìngzhī, not yet crowned,
followed his clan to attack them,
winning repeatedly.
Because of this, he became known for his bravery.
After the period of chaos,
his hometown was scattered.
Qìngzhī personally tilled the fields,
working diligently to support himself.
At forty, he was still unknown.
His elder brother, Chǎngzhī, served as Zhào Lúnzhī's Zhēnglǔ Cānjūn
and supervised Nányáng Commandery.
He had merits in attacking the barbarians
and was subsequently appointed to a regular post.
Qìngzhī went to Xiāngyáng to visit his brother.
Lúnzhī saw him and appreciated him,
ordering his son, the Grand Administrator of Jìnglíng Bófú, to appoint him as Níngyuǎn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
The barbarians of Jìnglíng frequently raided.
Qìngzhī devised strategies for them,
defeating them repeatedly.
Bófú thereby earned the reputation of a general and commander.
In the second year of Yǒngchū,
Qìngzhī was appointed Diànzhōng Yuánwài Jiāngjūn.
He also followed Bófú to serve under Dào Yànzhī during the northern invasion.
When Bófú returned due to illness,
he then served under Tán Dàojì.
Dàojì reported to Wéndì, stating that Qìngzhī was loyal, cautious, and understood military affairs.
The emperor ordered him to lead a detachment to guard the Eastern Yè Gate,
and he gradually gained access
to the Forbidden Palace.
The Commander of the Imperial Guard, Liú Zhàn, noticed him
and wanted to promote him,
saying:
"You have been in the palace for many years;
it is time to discuss your promotion."
Qìngzhī, with a stern expression, said:
"I have been in the palace for ten years,
and I should naturally be transferred.
I do not wish to trouble Your Majesty with this."
Soon after, he was transferred to Zhèngyuán Jiāngjūn.
On the evening Zhàn was arrested,
the emperor opened the gate and summoned Qìngzhī.
Qìngzhī entered in military attire and bound trousers.
The emperor, seeing this, was surprised and said:
"Why are you dressed so urgently?"
Qìngzhī replied:
"When a squad leader is called in the middle of the night,
there is no time for leisurely dressing."
He was sent to arrest and kill Liú Bīn, the Grand Administrator of Wú Commandery.
In the nineteenth year of Yuánjiā,
when Liú Dàochǎn, the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, died,
the various barbarian tribes rose in great unrest.
The Western Expeditionary Cavalry Commander Zhū Xiūzhī suffered a defeat while suppressing the barbarians.
Qìngzhī was appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn
and led troops to assist Xiūzhī.
When Xiūzhī was imprisoned for failing to maintain discipline,
Qìngzhī took sole command of the army and advanced to suppress them,
greatly defeating the various barbarian tribes along the Miǎn River.
Later, he became the Fǔjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn under Xiàowǔ.
Xiàowǔ, with his original title, was appointed to Yōngzhōu.
Qìngzhī followed him westward with his administration,
achieving many successes in suppressing barbarian raids.
Upon returning to the capital,
he again served as Guǎnglíng Wáng Dàn's Běizhōngláng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
and was additionally appointed Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Nán-Jìyīn.
When the Yōngzhōu barbarians again raided,
Qìngzhī, as general and grand administrator, again entered the Miǎn River area with Prince Suí Dàn.
Upon arriving in Xiāngyáng,
he led the Rear Army's Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Liǔ Yuánjǐng and the Grand Administrator of Suí Commandery Zōng and others to attack the various mountain barbarians north of the Miǎn River,
greatly defeating them.
His prestige shook all the mountains,
and all the barbarian tribes bowed down.
Qìngzhī suffered from headaches
and liked to wear a fox fur cap.
The barbarians hated it
and called him "Lord Grey-head."
Whenever they saw Qìngzhī's army,
they would fearfully say:
"Lord Grey-head has come again!"
Yuè Shàn was skilled at setting up camps and battle formations.
Whenever tens of thousands of men halted,
he would ride his horse ahead,
leading his soldiers to follow him.
When his horse stopped, the camp was arrayed,
never in disarray.
When Shěn Yōuzhī replaced Yīn Xiàozǔ as the vanguard of the southern expedition,
Yīn Xiàozǔ had recently died,
and the troops were all fearful.
Shěn Yōuzhī sighed, saying:
"Zōng Gōng is a pity,
he indeed had his superior qualities."
However, his nature was severe and cruel,
and he enjoyed inflicting punishments and executions.
At that time, Wáng Xuánmó also showed little kindness to his subordinates.
The soldiers had a saying about them:
"Rather be a five-year convict,
than follow Wáng Xuánmó.
Wáng Xuánmó is still bearable,
Zōng Yuè will kill me even more."
When Tán Jīn was in Wèi,
he had an old acquaintance with Xuē Āndū.
Later, he moved to Niúméncūn in Xīnyě.
When Xuē Āndū returned to the country,
Tán Jīn often accompanied him on campaigns,
assisting Xuē Āndū,
breaking through strong defenses and charging into formations,
his strength and courage surpassed others.
In Xiàojiàn third year (456 CE),
he was appointed Túnqí Xiàowèi (Colonel of Cavalry) and Zhíhé (Palace Attendant),
and concurrently held the title of Nán Qīnghé Tàishǒu (Administrator of Southern Qīnghé Commandery).
In Jǐnghé first year (465 CE),
the Former Deposed Emperor executed the high officials,
and Tán Jīn and others were all used by him.
Tán Jīn was enfeoffed as Píngdū Xiànnán (Viscount of Píngdū County),
Tóng Tàiyī as Yíyáng Xiànnán (Viscount of Yíyáng County),
and Shěn Yōuzhī as Dōngxīng Xiànnán (Viscount of Dōngxīng County).
Among Zōng Yuè's fellow villagers, there were also Wǔ Niàn, Jiǎo Chángshēng, Cáo Xīnzhī, and Cài Nà, all of whom became prominent generals.
Wǔ Niàn rose to the position of Nányáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Nányáng Commandery),
Jiǎo Chángshēng to Níngmán Xiàowèi (Colonel for Pacifying Man Tribes),
Cáo Xīnzhī to Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (General of Swift Cavalry);
Cài Nà is seen in his son Dàogōng's biography.
Wú Xǐ,
was a native of Lín'ān in Wúxīng.
His original name was Xǐgōng,
but Emperor Míng reduced it to Xǐ.
He began his career as a Bái Yī Lì (clerk in plain clothes) in the Lǐngjūn Fǔ (Office of the Commander of the Imperial Guard).
He knew little of books in his youth,
but Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Imperial Guard) Shěn Yǎnzhī made him copy the Qǐjūzhù (Diaries of Activity and Repose).
After he finished copying,
he could recite most of it by heart.
Shěn Yǎnzhī once wrote a memorial declining a position,
but lost the original before it was submitted.
Wú Xǐ, having seen it once, immediately copied it,
without any omissions.
Shěn Yǎnzhī was very impressed with him.
Because of this, Wú Xǐ dabbled in history and the Hàn dynasty records,
and became quite knowledgeable about ancient and modern times.
Shěn Yǎnzhī's student Zhū Chóngrén entered the palace as Zhǔshū (Principal Scribe),
[一四]and recommended Wú Xǐ as Zhǔshū Lì (Principal Scribe's Clerk),
who was then promoted to Zhǔtú Lìngshǐ (Chief Clerk of Maps and Orders).
Emperor Wén once requested maps and books,
and Wú Xǐ presented them upside down.
The Emperor was angry and sent him out.
It so happened that Tàizǐ Bùbīng Xiàowèi (Colonel of Infantry for the Crown Prince) Shěn Qìngzhī was campaigning against the Man tribes,
and memorialized Emperor Wén to request Wú Xǐ to accompany him,
which brought him to the attention of Emperor Xiàowǔ.
He was gradually promoted to Hédōng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Hédōng Commandery) and Diànzhōng Yùshǐ (Palace Censor).
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
the four quarters rebelled.
Wú Xǐ requested three hundred elite soldiers to die in the east.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and immediately provisionally appointed him Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Establishes Martial Might),
and selected brave Yǔlín (Imperial Guards) to accompany him.
The deliberators considered Wú Xǐ a mere clerk,
who had never been a general,
and should not be sent.
Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretariat Gentleman) Cháo Shàngzhī said:
"Wú Xǐ has followed Shěn Qìngzhī through many military campaigns,
his nature is both brave and decisive,
and he is also skilled in battle formations.
If he can be entrusted with the task,
he will surely achieve success."
Thus, Wú Xǐ marched east.
Wú Xǐ had been employed by Emperor Xiàowǔ,
and his nature was generous and benevolent.
Wherever he went, people embraced him.
When he marched east,
the common people, hearing that Wú Hédōng was coming,
immediately surrendered and dispersed at the mere rumor.
Thus, Wú Xǐ was victorious wherever he went.
He was promoted to Bùbīng Xiàowèi (Colonel of Infantry)
and enfeoffed as Jìnglín Xiànhóu (Marquis of Jìnglín County).
After the eastern lands were pacified,
he again led his troops to campaign in the south,
and was promoted to Xúnyáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xúnyáng Commandery).
In Tàishǐ fourth year (468 CE),
he was re-enfeoffed as Dōngxīng Xiànhóu (Marquis of Dōngxīng County),
appointed Yòujūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Army) and Huáiyáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Huáiyáng Commandery),
and concurrently Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishuài (Leader of the Crown Prince's Left Guard).
In the fifth year (469 CE),
he was transferred to Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (General of Swift Cavalry),
with the titles of Tàishǒu and Lǜ (Leader) remaining as before.
In that same year,
he greatly defeated the Wèi army at Jīngtíng.
In the sixth year (470 CE),
he again led troops towards Yùzhōu to resist the Wèi army,
and was additionally appointed Dūdū Yùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yùzhōu).
The following year, he returned to Jiànyè.
Initially,
when Wú Xǐ campaigned in the east,
he reported to Emperor Míng that he would immediately behead Zǐfáng, Prince of Xúnyáng, and other rebel leaders in the east.
After the eastern lands were pacified,
Wú Xǐ saw that the southern rebels were still flourishing,
and feared that later reversals would bring disaster,
so he sent Zǐfáng alive back to the capital.
All the major rebel leaders, such as Gù Chēn and Wáng Tánshēng, were spared.
The Emperor, considering Wú Xǐ's recent great achievements,
did not question him, but resented it in his heart.
When Jīngzhōu was pacified,
he wantonly plundered,
amassing tens of thousands in ill-gotten gains.
He also once said to guests, "What kind of people were Hàn Gāo and Wèi Wǔ originally?"
The Emperor became even more displeased upon hearing this.
Later, after Shòu Jìzhī died,
Wú Xǐ became fearful internally,
and therefore requested the position of Zhōngsàn Dàfū (Grand Master of Remonstrance).
The Emperor became even more suspicious of him.
When the Emperor fell ill,
and worried about affairs after his death,
he suspected that Wú Xǐ would not be able to serve the young emperor in the future,
so he ordered him to commit suicide.
The Emperor summoned him into the inner hall,
chatted and joked with him very intimately,
and bestowed upon him famous delicacies and gold and silver imperial utensils.
He ordered the attendants not to allow the utensils to stay overnight at Wú Xǐ's house.
The Emperor was usually very superstitious and taboo,
not wanting the utensils to remain in a house of misfortune and disaster.
After Wú Xǐ died,
an imperial edict was issued to grant posthumous gifts,
and his son Wú Huīrén inherited his title.
[一五]
Huáng Huí,
was a soldier from the Jìnglín Commandery.
He began his career as a miscellaneous attendant in the commandery office,
and gradually rose to Chuánjiào (Messenger).
When Zāng Zhì was the Administrator of the Commandery,
Huáng Huí was transferred to Zhāishuài (Chief of the Fasting Hall).
When Zāng Zhì left office,
he took Huáng Huí with him.
When Zāng Zhì campaigned against the "Original Culprit" (Emperor Wén),
Huáng Huí rendered meritorious service by accompanying him,
and was exempted from military household status.
Later, he fled with Zāng Zhì after their defeat at Liángshān,
was arrested,
but met with an amnesty,
and thus went to the capital.
He got into a fight with someone at Xuānyáng Mén,
and falsely claimed to be a horseman for Yìgōng, Prince of Jiāngxià.
He was whipped two hundred times
and handed over to the Yòu Shàngfāng (Right Imperial Workshop).
It happened that Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretariat Gentleman) Dài Míngbǎo was imprisoned,
and Huáng Huí was assigned as Hùbó (House Steward).
He served Dài Míngbǎo with utmost devotion,
and exerted all his strength.
Dài Míngbǎo soon obtained a pardon,
[一六]and entrusted Huáng Huí as before,
memorializing to exempt Huáng Huí and appoint him to lead his personal guard unit,
and oversee his residence and the villa in the west of the river.
His nature was cunning,
and he was skilled in many things.
Dài Míngbǎo greatly favored and trusted him.
Huáng Huí was agile and powerful in combat,
his bravery and strength surpassed others.
In the west of the river, he formed alliances with various Chǔ people,
and frequently engaged in robbery.
When Emperor Míng first ascended the throne,
the four quarters rebelled.
Dài Míngbǎo memorialized the Emperor to have Huáng Huí recruit Chǔ people from west of the river.
He obtained eight hundred skilled fighters,
and they were assigned to Liú Miǎn for the western campaign.
He was repeatedly promoted to general and colonel,
and for his merits, was enfeoffed as Géyáng Xiànnán (Viscount of Géyáng County).
At the beginning of Yuánhuī (473 CE),
Xiūfàn, Prince of Guìyáng, rebelled.
Huáng Huí, as Túnqí Xiàowèi (Colonel of Cavalry), led troops attached to Qí Gāodì (Emperor Gāo of Qí),
and devised the false surrender plan at Xīntíng.
Huáng Huí saw that Xiūfàn was vulnerable,
and said to Zhāng Jìng'ér:
"You can take him,
I swear I will not kill any princes."
Zhāng Jìng'ér immediately beheaded Xiūfàn that day.
When the matter was settled,
he was advanced in noble rank to Marquis,
and re-enfeoffed as Wénxǐ County.
Zǐmín, courtesy name Yúnjú,
was the twentieth son of Emperor Wǔ.
Initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Yì'ān Commandery,
he was later changed to Yǒngyáng.
In the first year of Yǒngtài, he was murdered,
and Zǐtǎn, son of Yè, Prince Zhāo of Wǔlíng, was again appointed to succeed the former prince.
Dàoshēng, Prince Zhēn of Shǐ'ān, courtesy name Xiàobó,
was the second elder brother of Emperor Gāo.
He served the Sòng dynasty with the title Fèngcháoqǐng,
and then died.
When Emperor Gāo ascended the throne,
he posthumously granted him a封諡 (title and posthumous name).
He had three sons: the eldest was Fèng;
the second was Luán,
who became Emperor Míng;
the third was ●,
who became Prince Zhāo of Ānlù.
Fèng, courtesy name Jǐngcí,
served the Sòng dynasty with the title Zhèngyuánláng.
When he died,
Emperor Gāo ascended the throne
and posthumously named him Jìng Shìzǐ.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
Emperor Míng posthumously honored Dàoshēng as Jǐng Huáng,
and his consort, Lady Jiāng, as Empress.
A memorial temple was established for them west of the imperial road,
and his mausoleum was called Xiū'ān.
Fèng was posthumously enfeoffed as Prince Jìng of Shǐ'ān.
The Huálín Fèngzhuāng Gate was renamed Wàngxián Gate.
In the East Hall of Tàijí, phoenix birds were painted,
inscribed as "Divine Birds,"
and the luán bird was changed to "Divine Sparrow."
His son Yáoguāng succeeded him.
Yáoguāng, Prince of Shǐ'ān, courtesy name Yuánhuī,
was born lame.
Emperor Gāo thought he was unfit to perform offerings and sacrifices,
and intended to enfeoff his younger brother.
Emperor Wǔ remonstrated,
and so Yáoguāng inherited the peerage.
He held the position of Zhōngshūláng.
When Emperor Míng assisted in governance,
in all matters of punishment and reward,
he only consulted and deliberated with Yáoguāng,
who advised Emperor Míng to kill all the sons and younger brothers of Emperors Gāo and Wǔ,
which was adopted.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he became the Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu.
In the third year,
he was promoted to the title Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn.
He enjoyed administrative affairs,
and was quite cruel and harmful.
Due to his foot ailment, he could not attend court with the other officials,
and always entered through Wàngxián Gate in his carriage.
Whenever he had a long, private conversation with Emperor Míng,
after they finished speaking,
the Emperor would ask for incense and fire,
and the next day there would surely be an execution.
The Crown Prince disliked studying,
and only enjoyed wandering freely.
The court debated appointing Cài Zhòngxióng to lecture the rites to the Crown Prince.
Before he was halfway through,
Yáoguāng calmly said:
"Matters of literature and righteousness,
these are skills that scholars use to seek official positions.
What use is lecturing for His Imperial Highness, the Crown Prince?"
The Emperor thought he was right,
and so the lecturing was stopped.
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
he was granted his original title of Dàjiāngjūn,
and provided with an oil-lacquered carriage.
The Emperor was unwell,
and Yáoguāng frequently attended to his illness.
As the Emperor's illness worsened,
ten princes, including Xuàn, Prince of Hédōng, were killed in one night;
this was Yáoguāng's idea.
When the Emperor passed away,
his dying edict added the titles Shìzhōng and Zhōngshūlìng to Yáoguāng,
and granted him the privilege of being supported.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
he was granted twenty guards with ceremonial swords, and with his original title, he was given the privilege of establishing an office (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
Yáoguāng was very suspicious.
If someone presented him with shoes,
he would consider it an insult,
and they would be severely blamed and rebuked.
Liú Huì once wrote a memorial saying,
"His wisdom is inferior to a sunflower."
This also displeased him.
Having assisted the Marquis of Dōnghūn,
he secretly colluded with the Jiāng Shí brothers,
plotting to establish himself.
His younger brother Yáoxīn was in Jīngchǔ,
commanding troops in the upper reaches of the river,
and they secretly influenced each other.
Yáoguāng was to occupy the Eastern Palace and issue orders,
making Yáoxīn quickly descend.
Their secret plot was about to be launched,
but Yáoxīn died of illness.
When Jiāng Shí was executed,
the Marquis of Dōnghūn summoned Yáoguāng into the palace
to inform him of Shí's crime.
Yáoguāng was frightened,
returned to his residence, feigned madness, and cried loudly.
From then on, he claimed illness and no longer entered the palace.
Before this, when Yáoguāng was returning to the city from a journey,
the wind blew his ceremonial parasol out of the city.
Yáoguāng's younger brother Yáochāng had died earlier in Shòuchūn.
The troops from Yùzhōu
all came under Yáoguāng's command.
When Yáoxīn's coffin returned,
it was buried in Wǔjìn,
and stopped at the sandbank in front of the Eastern Palace.
The large number of troops from Jīngzhōu escorting it was very impressive.
After the Marquis of Dōnghūn executed Jiāng Shí,
fearing that Yáoguāng would not feel secure,
he wanted to transfer him to the position of Sītú and allow him to return home.
He summoned him to explain this intention.
Yáoguāng feared he would be killed,
and gathered the troops from Jīng and Yù prefectures at the gate of the Eastern Palace.
The crowd found this quite strange,
and no one knew his real intention.
Yáoguāng summoned his confidants, Dānyáng Chéng Liú Fēng, Chéngjú Cānjūn Liú Yàn, Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Cáo Shùshēng,
and others,
along with various commoners and Chu people,
intending to use "punishing Liú Xuān" as a pretext.
That night, he sent several hundred men to break into Dōngyě to release prisoners
and obtain weapons from the Imperial Armory.
He also summoned Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Yuán Lìshēng.
When Lìshēng arrived as summoned,
he immediately urged Yáoguāng to lead the city's troops,
attack the palace that night,
and burn the city gates with bundles of reeds.
He said,
"My lord, just follow in your carriage,
and victory will be as easy as turning your hand."
Yáoguāng hesitated and dared not go out.
As dawn approached,
Yáoguāng, in military attire, went to the office for deliberation.
He stopped his carriage to issue orders,
ascended the city wall with his weapons to distribute rewards.
Lìshēng again urged him to dispatch troops,
but Yáoguāng refused,
hoping for an internal change within the palace.
When the sun rose,
the palace troops gradually arrived.
Thereupon, emergency measures were announced
and a general amnesty was declared for the capital.
Lǐngjūn Xiāo Tánzhī was stationed at Xiānggōng Temple,
Zhènjūn Sīmǎ Cáo Wǔ was stationed at Qīngxī Great Bridge,
Tàizǐ Yòulǜ Zuǒ Xīngshèng was stationed at the East Gate of the Eastern Palace,
and the various armies surrounded the eastern city.
Yáoguāng sent Yuán Lìshēng to sally out from the west gate.
The palace troops were repeatedly defeated,
and the army commander Sāng Tiān'ài was killed.
Initially, Yáoguāng consulted with Cānjūn Xiāo Chàng.
Chàng, with a stern expression, refused to follow him.
Afterward, Chàng and Fǔjūn Chángshǐ Shěn Zhāolüè fled to the palace,
which greatly disheartened the morale of the people.
Then Yuán Lìshēng sallied out from the south gate,
and was captured by Cáo Wǔ.
He said to Wǔ,
"If you consider the Emperor to be wise and enlightened,
and Méi and Rú to be virtuous ministers,
then I deserve to die.
But even if I die today,
you too will die tomorrow."
Thereupon, he was killed.
When Yáoguāng heard that Lìshēng had been captured,
he was furious.
He leaped up from his bed
and ordered Lìshēng's son to be killed.
That evening, the palace troops shot fire arrows and burned the northeast corner tower.
By night, the city walls collapsed.
Yáoguāng returned to his small study,
ordering people to resist,
but his attendants all climbed over the roof and fled.
The palace army commanders Liú Guóbǎo and Shí Dāngbó were among the first to enter.
When Yáoguāng heard the external troops arriving,
he blew out the fire,
and stumbled down from his bed.
The soldiers pushed open the door and entered,
and beheaded him.
Yáoguāng died four days after launching his rebellion.
On the evening of the rebellion's launch, there was a lunar eclipse.
Those who understood omens said that the moon represents a high minister,
and an eclipse that fully covers it
foretells the path to ruin.
On the eve of his defeat,
everyone in the city dreamed of numerous snakes crawling out from the city walls in all directions.
They all discussed it among themselves,
and everyone found it strange.
The palace troops entered the city
and almost completely burned down the buildings.
When Chén Xiǎndá (陳顯達) started his rebellion,
Wáng Hóu (王侯) again entered the palace.
Zhāo Zhòu (昭冑), remembering his fear from the past,
fled to Jiāngxī (江西) with his younger brother, the Marquis of Yǒngxīn (永新), Zhāo Yǐng (昭穎),
disguised as Daoist priests.
When Cuī Huìjǐng (崔慧景) raised an army,
Zhāo Zhòu (昭冑) and his brother went to join him.
After Huìjǐng (慧景) was defeated,
Zhāo Zhòu (昭冑) and his brother were the first to surrender to the imperial army commander Hú Sōng (胡松).
Each returned to their residences as a prince and a marquis,
but they felt insecure
and plotted for their own future.
Sāng Yǎn (桑偃), a former personal guard of Zǐliáng (子良), who was now a deputy in Méi Chóng'ér's (梅蟲兒) army,
allied with the former Administrator of Bāxī (巴西), Xiāo Yín (蕭寅),
and planned to install Zhāo Zhòu (昭冑).
Zhāo Zhòu (昭冑) promised that if the plot succeeded, Yín (寅) would be made Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè (尚書左僕射) and Hùjūn (護軍).
Because Yín (寅) had his own troops,
all major matters were entrusted to him.
At that time, Hú Sōng (胡松) led his army at Xīntíng (新亭).
Yín (寅) sent someone to persuade him,
and Sōng (松) agreed.
Furthermore, Zhāng Xīntài (張欣泰) had once been the Administrator of Yōngzhōu (雍州)
and also had his own troops.
Zhāo Zhòu (昭冑) again sent Fáng Tiānbǎo (房天bǎo) to inform him of the plan,
and Xīntài (欣泰) immediately responded.
Huá Yǒngdá (華永達), a subordinate of Xiāo Yín (蕭寅), learned of the plot
and reported it to the imperial guard Zhū Guāngshàng (朱光尚).
Guāngshàng (光尚) used deviant Daoist practices to delude Dōng Hūn (東昏).
He then said to Dōng Hūn (東昏):
"Last night I saw Jiǎng Wáng (蔣王),
who said that Bālíng Wáng (巴陵王) is gathering a party outside and intends to rebel.
You must go out,
and then enter through Wànchūn Mén (萬春門).
The situation is unfathomable."
At that time, Dōng Hūn (東昏) was out roaming daily.
Hearing this, he was greatly alarmed
and did not go out for more than forty days.
Yǎn (偃) and his associates discussed recruiting over a hundred strong men
to enter through Wànchūn Mén (萬春門)
and seize him by surprise.
Zhāo Zhòu (昭冑) thought this was not advisable.
Wáng Shānshā (王山沙), a co-conspirator of Yǎn (偃), worried that the matter would take too long without success,
and reported it to the imperial guard Xú Sēngzhòng (徐僧重).
Yín (寅) sent someone to kill Shānshā (山沙) on the road.
Officials discovered the details of their plot among the musk.
Zhāo Zhòu (昭冑) and his brother, along with their co-conspirators, were all executed.
When Liáng (梁) received the abdication,
Zhāo Zhòu's (昭冑) son Tóng (同) was demoted and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jiānlì (監利).
Tóng's (同) younger brother Bēn (賁), courtesy name Wénhuàn (文奐),
was less than six feet tall,
but his spirit and intellect were resolute.
In his youth, he loved learning
and possessed literary talent,
being skilled in calligraphy and painting.
When he depicted landscapes on a fan,
within a mere foot,
one could sense the vast distance of ten thousand *lǐ*.
He was reserved and did not transmit his skills,
merely amusing himself.
He enjoyed writing
and once authored sixty volumes of the *Xījīng Zájì* (西京雜記).
He began his career as a Fǎcáo Cānjūn (法曹參軍) for Xiāngdōng Wáng (湘東王),
gaining the affection of the entire administration.
During the chaos,
the prince drafted a proclamation.
When Bēn (賁) read
"Looking south from Yǎnshī (偃師),
no longer are there storehouses cold with dew;
facing north from Héyáng (河陽),
perhaps there are felt tents of the nomads,"
he then said:
"This line, composed by His Majesty,
is not overly similar to the situation;
it seems to describe the imperial court,
not to delineate the rebels."
The prince heard this and was greatly enraged.
He had him arrested and imprisoned,
where he eventually starved to death.
Later, Bēn's (賁) corpse was pursued and mutilated,
and a *Huáijiù Chuán* (懷舊傳) was written to slander him,
with extreme defamation and calumny.
Lúlíng Wáng (廬陵王) Zǐqīng (子卿), courtesy name Yúncháng (雲長),
was the third son of Wǔ Dì (武帝).
In the first year of Jiàn'yuán (建元),
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Línrǔ Xiàn (臨汝縣).
[一四] When Wǔ Dì (武帝) ascended the throne,
he was made the Císhǐ (刺史) of Yǐngzhōu (郢州)
and additionally received the title of Dūdū (都督).
Zǐqīng (子卿) had no virtue among Wǔ Dì's (武帝) sons,
and he was born from the same mother as Yúfù Hóu (魚復侯) Zǐxiǎng (子響),
thus he was not favored.
He was transferred to be Dūdū (都督) and Císhǐ (刺史) of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
When Shǐxīng Wáng (始興王) became the Administrator of Yìzhōu (益州),
Zǐqīng (子卿) was relieved of his Dūdū (都督) post.
While at his post, Zǐqīng (子卿)
manufactured clothing and accessories
that often violated regulations.
He made tortoiseshell riding gear.
An imperial edict reprimanded him,
ordering him to send them immediately to the capital.
He also made silver stirrups and arrows wrapped in gold foil,
which were also ordered to be immediately destroyed.
It further stated that for all future clothing and insignias,
if not first reported and authorized,
the unauthorized maker would be severely punished with a杖 (rod).
The edict also said:
"I have recently ordered you to study,
and this year you have grown taller,
but your studies have not progressed.
Edicts are like wind passing your ear,
which disappoints me."
[一五]
In the tenth year of Yǒngmíng (永明),
he became Dūdū (都督) and Císhǐ (刺史) of Nányùzhōu (南豫州).
On his way to his post,
he playfully arranged his troops into a "water army" on the road.
The emperor heard of this and was greatly angered,
executing his Diǎnqiān (典籤).
Yídu Wáng (宜都王) Kēng (鏗) was sent to replace him.
Zǐqīng (子卿) returned to his residence,
and the emperor did not see him again until his death.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (隆昌),
he was made Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司),
and was assigned military assistants.
After Póyáng Wáng (鄱陽王) Qiāng (鏘) was killed,
Zǐqīng (子卿) was appointed to replace him as Sītú (司徒).
Blood oozed from the pillars and beams of his residence and flowed onto the ground,
and ten days later, he was killed.
Yúfù Hóu (魚復侯) Zǐxiǎng (子響), courtesy name Yúnyīn (雲音),
was the fourth son of Wǔ Dì (武帝).
Yùzhāng Wáng (豫章王) Yí (嶷) had no sons,
so he adopted Zǐxiǎng (子響).
Later, when Yí (嶷) had his own son,
he submitted a memorial to keep Zǐxiǎng (子響) as his heir.
When Wǔ Dì (武帝) ascended the throne,
he was made the Administrator of the two commanderies of Nánpéngchéng (南彭城) and Línhuái (臨淮).
Zǐxiǎng (子響) possessed extraordinary strength and courage.
He could draw a bow with a force of four *hú* (斛).
He often rode horses and galloped under bamboo groves in the imperial gardens,
without suffering any injury.
Since he was adopted as heir,
his carriages and attire differed from the other princes.
Whenever he entered the court, he would become indignant
and punch the walls of his carriage.
Wǔ Dì (武帝) learned of this
and ordered his carriages and attire to be the same as the imperial sons.
In the sixth year of Yǒngmíng (永明),
the officials proposed that Zǐxiǎng (子響) should return to his original lineage,
and he was then enfeoffed as the King of Bādōng (巴東) Commandery.
In the seventh year,
he became Dūdū (都督) and Císhǐ (刺史) of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
The Zhíhé Jiāngjūn (直閤將軍) Dǒng Mán (董蠻) was rough but strong,
and Zǐxiǎng (子響) wanted him to accompany him.
Mán (蠻) said:
"Your Highness is as mad as thunder; how dare I accompany you?"
Zǐxiǎng (子響) laughed and said:
"You dare to utter such words;
you are also wonderfully mad."
The emperor heard this and was displeased.
He said:
"His name is 'Mán' (蠻, barbarian);
how can he be expected to be refined?"
So he changed his name to Zhòngshū (仲舒).
He said to him:
"How is the Zhòngshū (仲舒) of today
compared to the Zhòngshū (仲舒) of yesteryear?"
He replied:
"The Zhòngshū (仲舒) of yesteryear
came from a private household;
the Zhòngshū (仲舒) of today
descends from the Heavenly Emperor.
Therefore,
he is far superior to his former self."
The emperor praised him.
Zǐxiǎng (子響) loved martial arts from a young age,
and had sixty armed guards by his side.
All of them were courageous and capable.
He often slaughtered cattle and served wine in his inner quarters,
enjoying himself with them.
He secretly ordered the making of brocade robes and crimson jackets,
intending to trade them with Mán (蠻) for weapons.
The Chángshǐ (長史) Liú Yín (劉寅) and others secretly reported this collectively.
The emperor ordered a thorough inspection.
Yín (寅) and the others, afraid,
wanted to keep it secret.
Zǐxiǎng (子響) heard that an imperial envoy had arrived,
but did not see the imperial edict.

[一六] He then summoned Yín (寅) and the Sīmǎ (司馬) Xí Gōngmù (席恭穆), the Zīyì Cānjūn (諮議參軍) Jiāng Yù (江悆), Yīn Táncàn (殷曇粲), the Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (中兵參軍) Zhōu Yàn (周彥), and the Diǎnqiān (典籤) Wú Xiūzhī (吳脩之), Wáng Xiánzōng (王賢宗), Wèi Jǐngshēn (魏景深) and others to enter together.
[一七] He had them all executed at Qíntái (琴臺).
The emperor heard of this and was enraged.

He sent the Wèi Wèi (衞尉) Hú Xiézhī (胡諧之), the Yóujī Jiāngjūn (游擊將軍) Yǐn Lüè (尹略), and the Zhōngshū Shèrén (中書舍人) Rú Fǎliàng (茹法亮) to lead three thousand Yǔlín (羽林) troops to arrest the various subordinates.
An edict stated:
"If Zǐxiǎng (子響) surrenders himself by binding his hands,
[一八] his life can be spared."
His mother, Ruǎn, was in the capital.
She sent a letter wanting to secretly welcome Shàng,
and Ruǎn reported the plan of her uterine brother, Yú Yáozhī.
Yáozhī galloped to inform Emperor Míng,
whereupon he immediately prepared his forces.
He dispatched the Central Protector of the Army, Wáng Xuánmiǎo, and the General Who Pacifies the West, Wáng Guǎngzhī, to campaign in the north and south.
He ordered Army Commander Péi Shūyè and Yáozhī to first attack Xúnyáng,
claiming they were the Sīmǎ of Yǐngfǔ.
Zǐmào, knowing this,
sent three hundred men to guard Pénchéng.
Shūyè sailed upstream directly,
and attacked Pénchéng.
Zǐmào had already prepared boats at Qíjīngzhǔ,
and hearing that Shūyè had taken Pénchéng,
he then occupied the prefecture to defend himself.
Many of Zǐmào's troops were from Yōngtǔ,
and they were all eager to fight.
Shūyè, fearing them,
sent Yú Yáozhī to persuade Zǐmào, saying:
"If you return to the capital now,
you will certainly have no great worries.
You will merely be given a scattered official position,
and will not lose your wealth and status."
Since Zǐmào did not send out troops to attack Shūyè,
the morale of his forces gradually diminished.
The Staff Officer of the Central Army, Yú Línzhī,
who was Yáozhī's brother,
persuaded Zǐmào to heavily bribe Shūyè.
Zǐmào sent Línzhī to go,
and Línzhī thereupon persuaded Shūyè to request Zǐmào's surrender.
Shūyè sent Army Commander Xú Xuánqìng with four hundred men to follow Línzhī into the city.
All the subordinate officials dispersed and fled,
only Zhōu Yīng and the Staff Officer of the Outer Army, Wáng Jiǎo, moved further into the inner city.
Zǐmào, hearing this, sighed and said:
"I did not expect that my administration would have two righteous gentlemen."
Línzhī, with two hundred armed men, personally entered the private quarters.
Zǐmào smiled and said to him:
"I did not expect that Wèiyáng [a metaphor for a maternal relative],
would instead become a '梟鏡' (an assassin)."
Línzhī covered his face with his sleeve
and had someone kill him.
His old acquaintances, fearing punishment, dared not come.
Only Yīng, Jiǎo, and Sēnghuì wailed with utmost sorrow
and arranged his funeral.
[二一]
Dǒng Sēnghuì,
a native of Gūshú, Dānyáng,
came from humble origins but was generous and possessed integrity.
He loved to read,
was very brave and fierce,
and could bend a five-hú bow with his hands behind his back,
a feat no one else of his time could accomplish.
Xuánmiǎo, knowing that he had participated in Zǐmào's plot,
arrested him.
Sēnghuì said:
"When Jìn'ān raised his righteous army,
I indeed participated in the discussions.
The ancients said, 'It is not difficult to die,
but it is difficult to find a worthy death.'
I have the fortune to die for my lord;
I have no regrets.
I wish to wait until my lord's grand interment is completed,
then withdraw and face the boiling cauldron.
Even dying then, it will be as if I live."
Xuánmiǎo admired his righteousness and granted his wish.
Upon returning, he fully reported to Emperor Míng,
who then assigned Sēnghuì to Dōngyě.
Whenever he spoke of the events at Jiǔjiāng,
he would be overcome with grief.
Zǐmào's son, Zhāojī,
nine years old,
wrote a letter on a two-inch square piece of silk,
inquiring about his condition,
and also sent five hundred coins,
disguising them as if from someone else,
and with difficulty managed to deliver them.
Sēnghuì, seeing the letter,
looked at the money and said:
"This is the young master's letter."
He died of grief.
Lù Chāozhī,
a native of Wú,
was known to Zǐmào for his integrity and refinement.
After Zǐmào's defeat,
Yú Línzhī advised him to flee.
He replied:
"All men must die;
this is nothing to fear.
If I were to flee,
not only would I abandon Jìn'ān's kindness,
but I would also fear being laughed at by Tián Héng's retainers."
Xuánmiǎo and others, recognizing his righteousness,
wished to imprison him and return to the capital,
while Chāozhī also sat upright, awaiting his fate.
A disciple of Chāozhī, surnamed Zhōu,
believed that killing Chāozhī would earn him a reward.
So he waited for Chāozhī to sit,
then decapitated him from behind.
His head fell, but his body did not stiffen.
Xuánmiǎo commended his integrity
and gave him a generous funeral.
Zhōu also helped carry the coffin,
but before it left the door,
the coffin fell,
directly crushing his head and breaking his neck, killing him instantly.
[二二] Those who heard of it all believed it to be the work of Heaven.
Xiāowáng Zǐlóng, courtesy name Yúnxīng,
was Emperor Wǔ's eighth son.
His nature was kind and beautiful,
and he possessed literary talent.
He married the daughter of the Grandee Secretary, Wáng Jiǎn, as his consort.
Emperor Wǔ, seeing Zǐlóng's literary ability,
said to Jiǎn:
"My family is like Dōng'ā [referring to Cáo Zhí, Prince of Dōng'ā, a famous literary figure]."
In the eighth year of Yǒngmíng (490 CE),
he became Area Commander-in-Chief and Governor of Jīngzhōu.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
he was made Attendant-in-Ordinary and General of the Household Army,
leading troops and establishing a staff.
In the first year of Yánxīng (494 CE),
he was transferred to be General-in-Chief of the Central Army,
with his position as Attendant-in-Ordinary remaining as before.
Zǐlóng was twenty-one years old,
but his physique was overly large and robust.
He often had Xú Sìbó prepare lú rú pills for him to take to reduce his weight,
but they were still ineffective.
Emperor Míng, upon assuming regency,
plotted to harm the various princes.
Among Emperor Wǔ's sons, Zǐlóng was most feared for his talent and appearance,
so he and Púyáng Wáng Qiāng were killed on the same night.
His collected works circulated in the world.
Jiàn'ān Wáng Zǐzhēn, courtesy name Yúnxiān,
was Emperor Wǔ's ninth son.
In the seventh year of Yǒngmíng (489 CE),
he was successively promoted to Governor of Yǐngzhōu,
with the added title of Area Commander-in-Chief.
In the first year of Lóngchāng (494 CE),
he was made Palace Attendant and General of the Protectorate Army.
In the first year of Yánxīng (494 CE),
Emperor Míng sent Péi Shūyè to have Kē Lìngsūn, the Palace Register, kill him.
Zǐzhēn ran and hid under the bed.
Lìngsūn pulled him out by hand,
and he knocked his head, begging to be a slave to atone for his death,
but it was not granted.
He was killed
at the age of nineteen.
Xīyáng Wáng Zǐmíng, courtesy name Yúnguāng,
was Emperor Wǔ's tenth son.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng (483 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Wǔchāng.
In the third year (485 CE),
he lost the national seal,
and was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Xīyáng.
In the tenth year (492 CE),
he became Administrator of Kuàijī,
and supervised the military affairs of five commanderies.
Zǐmíng had a clear and bright demeanor.
Men and women who saw him
all sighed in admiration.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (494 CE),
he was made General of the Household Army,
leading troops and establishing a staff.
In the second year (495 CE),
Xiāo Chén was executed.
Zǐmíng and his younger brothers Zǐhǎn and Zǐzhēn, who conspired with Chén, were also killed
at the age of seventeen.
Nánhǎi Wáng Zǐhǎn, courtesy name Yúnhuá,
was Emperor Wǔ's eleventh son,
and was quite learned.
His mother, Lè Rónghuá, was favored,
so Emperor Wǔ paid close attention to him.
His mother once suffered from a long illness.
Zǐhǎn prayed day and night.
At that time, bamboo was used for lamp wicks to illuminate the night.
These wicks, after a night, sprouted large branches and leaves.
His mother's illness also recovered.
Everyone believed it was due to his filial piety.
The Chief Clerk Liú Zōng and the Attendant Lecturer Hè Zǐqiáo composed odes for him,
which were considered beautiful stories at the time.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (494 CE),
he held the position of General of the Protectorate Army.
In the second year (495 CE),
he was killed
at the age of seventeen.
Bālíng Wáng Zǐlún, courtesy name Yúnzōng,
was Emperor Wǔ's thirteenth son.
In the tenth year of Yǒngmíng (492 CE),
he was made General of the Northern Central Army and Administrator of the two commanderies of Nán Lángyá and Péngchéng.
When Emperor Yùlín ascended the throne,
because Nán Péngchéng offered generous emoluments,
he took it from Zǐlún and gave it to Qímǔ Zhēnzhī, a Secretariat Drafter,
replacing it with Nán Lánlíng instead.
Yù Fèi Yùlín zhī xūn (豫廢鬱林之勳).
In the first year of Yánxīng (延興元年) [494 CE],
he was made Sīkōng (司空) [Minister of Works]
and promoted in rank to gōng (公) [duke].
When Míngdì (明帝) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Tàiwèi (太尉) [Grand Commandant]
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Póyáng Jùn (鄱陽郡公).
He was granted an additional two hundred soldiers
and provided with an oil-lacquered carriage.
Later, as Tàiwèi and Duke of Póyáng Jùn,
he was one of the Sāngōng (三公) [Three Ducal Ministers],
yet his office oversaw the command of the provincial military forces (liánshuài 典連率).
The emperor wished to eliminate all the descendants of Gāo (高) and Wǔ (武).
He replied:
"Are these people worth bothering about?"
The emperor then stopped.
During the Jiànwǔ (建武) era, Xiǎndá felt uneasy in his heart,
and deeply humbled himself and retreated.
His carriages and horses were decaying,
and his escort and guard of honor (lǔbù 鹵簿) all used weak and small men.
While attending a banquet,
after drinking, he asked the emperor for a pillow.
The emperor ordered it to be given to him.
Xiǎndá stroked the pillow and said:
"Your subject is already old,
and has enough wealth and honor.
I only lack a pillow to die on.
I specially beg it from Your Majesty."
The emperor's expression changed and he said:
"You are drunk, gōng (公) [duke]."
He requested to retire due to old age,
but it was not permitted.
In the first year of Yǒngtài (永泰) [498 CE],
Xiǎndá was sent to invade the north.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán (永元) [499 CE],
Xiǎndá, overseeing the commander of the Flat-North Army, Cuī Huìjǐng's (崔慧景) army of forty thousand men, besieged Mǎquān Chéng (馬圈城) in Nánxiāng (南鄉) district,
three hundred *lǐ* (里) from Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
After forty days of siege,
the Wèi (魏) army ran out of food,
eating the flesh of dead men and tree bark.
The outer siege tightened,
and the Wèi army broke out and fled.
Xiǎndá entered and occupied the city,
sending army commander Zhuāngqiū Hēi (莊丘黑) to take Nánxiāng Xiàn (南鄉縣).
Wèi Xiàowén Dì (魏孝文帝) personally led over a hundred thousand cavalry and arrived suddenly.
Army commanders Cuī Gōngzǔ (崔恭祖) and Hú Sōng (胡松) placed Xiǎndá in a black cloth curtain,
and several men carried him out.
They exited from Hūnjīnkǒu (汮水口).
with over thirty thousand killed.
Xiǎndá had always possessed great renown and prestige,
known in foreign territories,
but suffered a great loss this time.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) Fàn Xiù (范岫) memorialized for Xiǎndá to be dismissed from office,
and also presented a memorial to resign his own position,
but neither was permitted.
He was made Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (江州刺史) [Prefect of Jiāngzhōu],
and garrisoned at Pénchéng (盆城).
Originally,
when Wáng Jìngzé's (王敬則) affair broke out,
Shǐ'ān Wáng (始安王) Yáoguāng (遙光) memorialized Míngdì to be wary of Xiǎndá changing sides,
wishing to recall the army.
After the matter was settled, it was dropped.
Xiǎndá also harbored fear and unease.
When Dōnghūn (東昏) ascended,
he was even more reluctant to return to the capital,
and was very pleased to receive this appointment.
Soon after, he was granted the additional title of Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn (征南大將軍) [Grand General Who Conquers the South],
and provided with a sānwàngchē (三望車) [three-view carriage].
Xiǎndá heard that there was a great slaughter in the capital,
and that Xú Xiàosì (徐孝嗣) and others had all died.
Rumors circulated that troops would be sent to attack Jiāngzhōu.
Xiǎndá, fearing disaster,
raised troops on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month,
intending to attack Jiànyè (建鄴) directly,
to catch them unprepared.
He also remotely named Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ (郢州刺史) Jiàn'ān Wáng (建安王) Bǎoyín (寶寅) as his leader.
The imperial court sent Hòujūn Jiāngjūn (後軍將軍) Hú Sōng (胡松) and others to hold Liángshān (梁山).
Xiǎndá led several thousand men and departed from Xúnyáng (尋陽).
He fought against Sōng at Cǎishí (采石),
and greatly defeated him.
The capital was shaken with fear.
In the twelfth month,
he secretly led his army across the river, seized Shítóu (石頭), and advanced north to attack the city.
The palace was greatly alarmed,
and the gates were closed for defense.
Xiǎndá, mounted on his horse with his *shuò* (矟) [long spear], and several hundred infantry,
fought against the imperial army in front of Xīzhōu (西州).
They engaged twice and won a great victory.
His *shuò* broke,
but he still killed over ten men with his bare hands.
The government forces arrived in succession,
and Xiǎndá could not resist.
He retreated to Wūbǎng Cūn (烏榜村) behind Xīzhōu.
Cavalry officer Zhào Tán (趙潭) pierced him with his *shuò*, throwing him from his horse,
and beheaded him by a fence.
Blood gushed and splattered the fence,
similar to Chúnyú Bó (淳于伯) being executed.
He was seventy-three years old at the time.
Xiǎndá had contracted an illness in Jiāngzhōu,
but recovered without treatment,
which greatly displeased him.
At that time, there was heavy snow for the entire winter.
His head was displayed at Zhūquè (朱雀), but the snow did not gather on it.
All his sons were executed.
Zhāng Jìng'ér (張敬兒)
was a native of Guānjūn (冠軍), Nányáng (南陽).
His father, Chǒu (醜),
was a jùn jiāngjūn (郡將軍) [commander of a commandery],
and his highest office was jiéfǔ cānjūn (節府參軍) [staff officer in a general's headquarters].
Jìng'ér was skilled in archery and horsemanship from a young age and possessed courage.
He enjoyed shooting fierce beasts,
and never missed a shot.
The customs of Xīnyě (新野), Nányáng, were to excel in cavalry and archery,
and Jìng'ér was especially strong.
He gradually rose through offices to Níngmán Xíng Cānjūn (寧蠻行參軍) [Provisional Staff Officer to the General Who Pacifies the Barbarians].
He followed the commander of his commandery, Liú Hú (劉胡), to attack the various mountain barbarians in Xiāngyáng,
penetrating deep into dangerous terrain,
and conquering everywhere he went.
He also attacked the Húyáng (胡陽) barbarians.
The government army retreated,
but Jìng'ér remained behind alone on horseback,
and the bandits could not resist him.
When Shānyáng Wáng (山陽王) Xiūyòu (休祐) was garrisoned at Shòuyáng (壽陽),
he sought skilled archers and horsemen.
Jìng'ér and Yú Zhàn (俞湛) from Xiāngyáng were selected.
Jìng'ér was good at serving others,
and thus gained favor,
becoming a Chángjiān Xíng Cānjūn (長兼行參軍) [Permanent Provisional Staff Officer].
In the early Tàishǐ (泰始) era [465-472 CE],
he transferred with the headquarters to Piàojì Cānjūn (驃騎參軍) [Staff Officer to the General of Agile Cavalry],
and was appointed Zhōngbīng (中兵) [Head of Military Affairs].
He led troops to attack the Yìjiā (義嘉) rebels.
He and Liú Hú confronted each other at Quèwěi Zhōu (鵲尾洲).
He memorialized Míngdì to request his home commandery.
After the affair was settled,
he was appointed Nányáng Tàishǒu (南陽太守) [Administrator of Nányáng].
When Jìng'ér was a general in the Xiāngyáng (襄陽) headquarters,
his family was poor,
and whenever he had leave, he would work as a laborer to support himself.
He once carried water for Wú Tài's (吳泰) family in the east of the city,
and had an affair with Tài's favorite maid.
When the matter was discovered,
he was about to be killed by Tài,
but he fled and hid in a coffin for sale,
covering himself with the lid,
and thus escaped.
When he was at Quèwěi Zhōu,
he memorialized Míngdì, saying:
"Tài helped Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (雍州刺史) Yuán Yǐ (袁顗) by providing silk for bowstrings,
conspiring with him in rebellion.
I beg for his family's property."
The emperor permitted it.
At this point, Wú's (吳氏) property was confiscated.
Only his family members escaped naked.
The servants and wealth amounted to tens of millions,
all of which Jìng'ér acquired.
The maid with whom he previously had an affair
he immediately took as a concubine.
Later, he became Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉) [Commander of the Elite Cavalry].
When the affair of Guìyáng Wáng (桂陽王) broke out,
he was subordinate to Qí Gāodì (齊高帝) at Xīntíng (新亭).
When the rebels' arrows and stones were already exchanged,
Xiūfàn (休範), dressed in white, rode in his sedan chair to the tower below to inspect.
Jìng'ér and Huáng Huí (黃回) reported to Gāodì, requesting to feign surrender to capture him.
Gāodì said:
"If you accomplish this,
I will reward you with your home province."
Jìng'ér and Huí went out of the south gate of the city,
dropped their weapons and ran,
shouting that they surrendered.
Xiūfàn was pleased,
and summoned them to his sedan chair.
Huí pretended to convey a secret message from Gāodì,
and Xiūfàn believed him.
Huí signaled Jìng'ér.
Jìng'ér snatched Xiūfàn's personal dagger and beheaded him.
His hundred or so attendants all scattered.
Jìng'ér returned to Xīntíng with the head.
He was appointed Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍) [General of Gallant Cavalry],
and granted the additional title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍) [General Who Assists the State].
Gāodì held a banquet and said to Jìng'ér:
"Without your merit, there would be no today."
Zhāng Qí, courtesy name Zǐxiàng,
was a native of Fēngyì Commandery.
From a young age, he possessed courage and spirit.
Initially, he served Yuán Lìshēng, the Sīmǎ of Jīngzhōu.
Lìshēng was a heavy drinker,
treated his subordinates harshly,
and showed him no courtesy.
When Zhāng Jì of Wújùn became the Sīmǎ of the Jīngfu,
Qí followed him again,
and was greatly valued by him,
being regarded as a confidant.
Qí served Jì wholeheartedly.
When Jì became the governor of Nányǎnzhōu,
Qí was promoted to Bīng Cānjūn of the Fǔ.
When Liáng Wǔdì raised an army,
Dōnghūn summoned Jì back,
appointing him Dūdū Gōngchéng Zhūjūnshì.
Qí led Zhēn Guó to Jì at night.
Qí personally held a candle to set the plan.
The next morning, Qí, Jì, and Zhēn Guó executed Dōnghūn inside the palace hall.
Qí personally killed him.
After Wǔdì received the abdication,
Qí was enfeoffed as Ānchāng Hóu
and held the post of Lìyáng Tàishǒu.
Qí was illiterate,
unable to recognize characters,
but in the commandery, he was clear and orderly,
and administrative affairs were well managed.
In Tiānjiān fourth year (505 CE),
the Wèi general Wáng Zú attacked Shǔ,
besieging Bāxī.
The Emperor appointed Qí Fǔguó Jiāngjūn to relieve Shǔ.
Before he arrived,
Zú retreated.
Qí advanced to garrison Nán'ān,
and was transferred to Bāxī Tàishǒu.
[一六]
Initially,
Nánzhèng fell to Wèi,
so Nánliángzhōu was established to the west of Yìzhōu.
The provincial seat was newly founded,
and everything depended on Yìzhōu for supply.
Qí proposed a tax on the Yí and Láo barbarians,
obtaining 200,000 hú of rice.
In the eleventh year (512 CE),
he was promoted to Jiǎjié,
overseeing all forces outside Yìzhōu.
Qí stayed in the Yì region for several years,
campaigning against the Mán and Láo barbarians,
with no peaceful year for himself.
In his encampment,
he personally endured hardships and toil,
sharing difficulties with his soldiers and subordinates.
From the barracks to the city fortifications, everything was meticulously arranged for convenience.
When uniforms, rations, and supplies were distributed,
no one suffered from want.
As he gained the support of the people,
the Mán and Láo barbarians also dared not offend him,
hence his prestige spread throughout Yōngshǔ.
Bāxī Commandery occupied half of Yìzhōu,
and was also a vital thoroughfare on the eastern route.
When provincial governors passed through,
and military officials traveled long distances, they often faced destitution.
Qí gathered provisions along the road,
and planted vegetables,
so travelers could all obtain supplies.
He successively served as Nánliángzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was promoted to Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, Zhēngxī Póyáng Wáng Sīmǎ, and Tàishǒu of Xīnxīng and Yǒngníng Commanderies.
Before he could deploy troops,
he was posthumously given the title Zhuàng.
The encomium states: In the declining years of the Sòng dynasty,
chaos and separation were daily portents.
Every family harbored ambitions for the throne,
and individuals had different designs.
Gāo Dì observed the opportune moment with keen insight,
as if destined to initiate a new era.
Lǐ Ānrén, Dài Sēngjìng, Huán Kāng, Jiāo Dù, Cáo Wǔ, Lǚ Ānguó, Zhōu Shāntú, Zhōu Pánlóng, Wáng Guǎngzhī and others,
some showed their sincerity early,
some exhausted their efforts,
some were entrusted with regional commands,
some achieved merit under his banner.
The means by which they attained honor and favor
was certainly not in vain.
It verified that the hearts of the people had a destination,
and that their willingness to support him was not unfounded.
The saying goes:
"Courage without propriety leads to chaos."
Observing Fèngshú's path to advancement,
was it not close to chaos?
His eventual slaughter
was indeed fitting.
Although Zhēn Guó had his "bright mirror,"
his "cutting of gold" was not proven.
The righteousness of "retaliatory curses"
was logically appropriate.
As for his hope of becoming a minister,
how could it be realized?
Zhāng Qí's position was originally humble,
and his aspirations were easily satisfied.
His achievements were proclaimed wherever he served,
which was indeed excellent.
Collation Notes
Biographies Volume 37 Xún Bóyù Cuī Zǔsī (Zǔsī's paternal uncle Jǐngzhēn, Jǐngzhēn's son Yuánzǔ, Zǔsī's clansman Wénzhòng) Sū Kǎn Yú Cōng Hú Xiézhī (Fàn Bónián) Yú Wánzhī Liú Xiū Jiāng Shí (Liú Xuān)
Xún Bóyù, courtesy name Nòngzhāng,
was a native of Guǎnglíng.
His grandfather, Yǒng,
was Nánqiáo Tàishǒu.
His father, Chǎnzī,
was Gěishìzhōng.
Bóyù served the Sòng dynasty as Zhèn Jūn Xíng Cānjūn for Zǐxūn, the Prince of Jìn'ān.
In the early years of Tàishǐ,
he joined Zǐxūn's uprising.
After the defeat, he returned to the capital
and made a living by divination.
When Qí Gāo Dì was garrisoned in Huái'yīn,
Bóyù served Gāo Dì as Guānjūn Xíngyù Cānjūn.
Gāo Dì was suspected by Sòng Míngdì
and was summoned to be Huángmén Láng.
Deeply worried,
he saw a flock of cranes on the open marsh.
He then took up a brush and composed a poem, saying:
"The eight winds carry distant wings,
the nine wilds play clear notes.
Once the cloud-high ambition is shattered,
I become a bird in your garden."
He showed this to Bóyù, hinting at his deep concerns.
Bóyù advised Gāo Dì to send several dozen cavalry into Wèi territory
to set up markers.
Wèi indeed sent hundreds of light cavalry to patrol the border.
Gāo Dì reported this.
Still fearing he would not be allowed to stay,
he ordered Bóyù to divine.
Bóyù said he would not depart,
and the Emperor eventually returned to his original post.
From then on, he was trusted and favored.
Gāo Dì had an old subordinate, Zhú Jǐngxiù of Dōngguǎn, who was once assigned to forced labor due to a fault.
Gāo Dì said to Bóyù:
"Have you seen Jǐngxiù recently?"
He replied:
"I have visited him several times and severely reprimanded him,
telling him,
'If you promise to reform yourself,
you must swallow a knife to scrape your intestines and drink ash to wash your stomach.'"
The Emperor approved of his answer
and immediately released him.
He eventually became a loyal and trustworthy official.
Later, he followed Gāo Dì back to the capital
and was appointed Fèngcháoqǐng.
Gāo Dì made him manage family affairs.
When Wǔdì returned after being dismissed from Guǎngxīng,
he set up a separate residence.
