He sent people to dig up several trees from the main residence.
Bóyù did not allow it
and quickly reported it.
Gāo Dì approved of this.
When Gāo Dì was Nányǎnzhōu,
Bóyù followed him and was transferred to Zhèn Jūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
concurrently serving as Guǎnglíng Lìng.
Initially,
when Gāo Dì was in Huái'yīn,
Bóyù was on leave and returned to Guǎnglíng.
He dreamed of ascending the southern tower of Guǎnglíng City.
On it, two small boys in green clothes said to Bóyù:
"A solemn one in the grass,
the Nǐnwǔ pursue each other."
Bóyù looked, and all the people's heads below the city had grass on them.
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ (471 CE),
he again dreamed that Gāo Dì was on a boat at the northern islet of Guǎnglíng,
with wings under both armpits that were not spread.
Bóyù asked when they would spread.
The Emperor said:
"Three years from now."
In the dream, Bóyù considered himself a sorcerer
and spat six times to curse him.
Six dragons emerged,
and the wings under both armpits all spread,
then retracted again.
In the second year of Yuánhuī (474 CE),
Gāo Dì defeated Guìyáng,
and his prestige greatly shook the land.
Five years later, he deposed Cāngwú.
He said to Bóyù:
"Your dream is now coming true."
In the early days of Shēngmíng,
he continued to serve Gāo Dì as Piàojì Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
concurrently serving as Jìyáng Tàishǒu.
After the hegemon's enterprise was established,
Bóyù was loyal and diligent, giving his whole heart,
constantly guarding his side.
He was promoted to Qián Jiāngjūn
and was greatly entrusted and relied upon.
In the first year of Jiànjuán of Qí (479 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Nánfēng Xiànzǐ
and became Yùzhāng Wáng Sīkōng Zīyì,
retaining his post as Tàishǒu.
At that time, Wǔdì was in the Eastern Palace.
Believing himself to be advanced in years,
and having together with Gāodì founded the great enterprise,
he monopolized and decided all matters of the court, great and small,
often disregarding regulations.
His attendant Zhāng Jǐngzhēn was particularly favored and trusted,
and also often overstepped his bounds and was extravagant.
When Wǔdì returned from visiting the imperial tombs,
Jǐngzhēn, in plain clothes, rode in a painted *zéměng* boat,
sitting on a foreign couch.
Onlookers all suspected him to be the Crown Prince,
and officials both inside and outside the court were in awe and fear,
none daring to speak.
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Chén Yìnshú had already reported on the past and present transgressions of Jǐngzhēn and the Crown Prince.
Bóyù, taking advantage of Wǔdì’s return from visiting the imperial tombs,
secretly submitted a memorial about it.
The Emperor was greatly enraged.
Yùzhāngwáng Yí had always been favored.
Because Wǔdì was the eldest legitimate son,
and also because the Nánjùnwáng's brothers were all appointed,
Wǔdì had been made Crown Prince.
Now, however, there was an intention to change the succession.
When Wǔdì returned to the east,
Wén Huì Tàizǐ and Wénxǐ Gōngzǐ Liáng were dispatched to convey an imperial edict questioning and reproaching him,
and also to show him Jǐngzhēn's crimes,
ordering him, as Crown Prince, to arrest and execute Jǐngzhēn.
Yìnshú then informed Wǔdì,
saying that Bóyù had made it known.
Wǔdì was anxious and fearful,
feigning illness for over a month.
The Emperor’s anger did not subside.
As he was sleeping in the Tàiyáng Diàn during the day,
Wáng Jìngzé entered directly and kowtowed,
requesting permission to go to the Eastern Palace to console the Crown Prince.
Gāodì said nothing.
Jìngzé then loudly proclaimed an imperial edict to go to the Eastern Palace,
ordering preparations.
He also commanded the Tàiguān to prepare a feast,
and secretly sent someone to inform Wǔdì,
instructing him to receive the emperor.
He then called his attendants to fetch a sedan chair.
Gāodì showed no inclination to move.
Jìngzé fetched a robe and put it on Gāodì,
then pulled him into the sedan chair.
Thereupon, he proceeded to the Eastern Palace,
summoned the various princes for a feast,
and then toured the Xuánpǔ Yuán.
Chángshāwáng Huǎng held the imperial parasol,
Línchuānwáng Yìng held the pheasant-tail fan,
Wénxǐ Gōngzǐ Liáng held the wine pot,
Nánjùnwáng poured the wine,
and Wǔdì, Yùzhāngwáng Yí, and Jìngzé personally carried the dishes.
Gāodì drank heavily,
bestowed wine upon Wǔdì and those below him,
and all became greatly intoxicated, enjoying themselves to the fullest.
They departed at dusk.
On that day, had it not been for Jìngzé,
the Eastern Palace would have almost certainly been abolished.
Gāodì valued Bóyù’s devotion,
trusting him even more,
and made him responsible for confidential military and state affairs,
giving him immense power at court.
Whenever he rested briefly outside,
carriages and canopies filled the gate.
Once, when he suffered the sorrow of his mother’s passing,
on the day of donning mourning attire,
Zuǒshuài Xiāo Jǐngxiān and Shìzhōng Wáng Yàn rode together to condole him.
At the fifth watch, they got into their carriages.
Before they reached Bóyù’s residence by about two *lǐ*,
princes, marquises, and court officials already filled the alley.
Even when the drum sounded to mark the time, they could not advance.
Sītú Chǔ Yànhuí and Wèijūn Wáng Jiǎn, who followed closely behind, were only then able to advance,
and still had to wait for a long time in the reception hall.
An imperial edict was sent by the Zhōngshū Shèrén Xú Xīxiù, instructing them to cease weeping and dismiss the guests.
Only after a long while were they able to offer their condolences.
By the time they left,
both men were famished and exhausted,
their breath weak and failing,
gnashing their teeth with audible and visible frustration.
The next day, upon entering the palace,
they immediately said:
"The gates of the two palaces and the halls we have seen compared to Sún Bóyù's residence
could only have a birdnet set up."
They continued:
"Outside, people say,
'A thousand imperial edicts and ten thousand commands
are not as effective as a single word from Lord Xún.'"
Wǔdì deeply resented Bóyù.
When Gāodì was on his deathbed,
he pointed to Bóyù and entrusted him to Wǔdì.
When Wǔdì ascended the throne,
Bóyù was anxious and fearful.
The Emperor heard of this,
and knowing his friendship with Yuán Chóngzǔ,
whose landholdings were in Jiāngxī,
feared they might stir up rebellion.
He therefore took extra care to comfort him,
and Bóyù was at ease.
In Yǒngmíng First Year,
he and Chóngzǔ were both falsely accused and executed.
Yìnshú, however, became Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài.
Lǚ Wénxiǎn sighed, saying:
"Bóyù could plan for Tàizǔ but could not plan for himself;
is this not fate?"
Earlier,
when Bóyù was obscure,
a skilled geomancer of tombs told his father:
"Your tomb will produce someone who rises to power quickly but does not last long;
it will also produce a woman who deviates from proper conduct."
Bóyù heard this and said:
"If one hears the Way in the morning,
one may die content in the evening."
Shortly thereafter,
Bóyù’s elder sister was about to be married.
She was due to depart the next day,
but that evening she ran away with a man,
and the family searched for her without success.
Later, she became a nun.
Bóyù eventually met his downfall.
Cuī Zǔsī, courtesy name Jìngyuán,
was a native of Dōngwǔchéng, Qīnghé.
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Wèi Zhōngwèi Yǎn.
His grandfather, Yīn,
was Sòng Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
His father, Sēnghù, was a Zhōu Xiùcái.
Zǔsī had high aspirations in his youth
and loved to read.
At eighteen,
he served as Dūchāng Lìng.
He accompanied Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Hùzhī into the Yáo Miào.
In the temple, there was a statue of Sū Hóu sitting beside the main deity.
Hùzhī said:
"Emperor Yáo was a sage, yet he sits with the deity Sū Hóu.
What do you think of correcting this situation?"
Zǔsī replied:
"If you, Sir, clear this seat,
it would be like Yáo's temple again expelling the Four Felons."
Consequently, all other minor deities were removed.
When Qí Gāodì was in Huáinán,
Zǔsī, hearing of his reputation, allied himself with him.
He became the Emperor’s Fǔguó Zhǔbù,
and was highly trusted and favored,
participating in strategic discussions.
When the Sòng court first debated enfeoffing Gāodì as Liáng Gōng,
Zǔsī advised Gāodì:
"The prophecy says, 'A golden knife and sharp blade will simultaneously cut.'
It is now appropriate to claim the title of Qí,
truly conforming to the Mandate of Heaven."
Gāodì followed his advice.
From Xiàngguó Cóngshì Zhōngláng, he was promoted to Qíguó Nèishǐ.
After Gāodì became Qí Wáng,
he held a feast for entertainment.
When the soup and sliced raw fish arrived,
Zǔsī said:
"This flavor is indeed praised by both north and south."
Shìzhōng Shěn Wénjì said:
"Soup and sliced raw fish are Wú food,
not something Zǔsī understands."
Zǔsī responded:
"Stewed turtle and sliced raw carp
seem not to be poems of Gōuwú."
Wénjì retorted:
"Water shield soup from a thousand *lǐ* away,
how is it related to Lǔ or Wèi?"
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
saying:
"The water shield soup should indeed return to Shěn."
During the Tàijiàn reign, [Jìng] Qióng was made Attendant Yellow Gate Regular Mounted Attendant (Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng).
He was then transferred to be Middle Administrator (Zhōng Shùzǐ),
concurrently holding the title of Grand Author (Dà Zhùzuò),
and compiling the national history.
When Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
he served directly in the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shěng),
managing imperial edicts.
In the first year of Zhìdé (583),
he was appointed Minister of Finance (Dùzhī Shàngshū),
participated in selection affairs,
managed imperial proclamations,
and concurrently handled the cases of the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi) and Jiànkāng prisons.
Initially,
Qióng's father, Yún Gōng, by Imperial Edict of Liáng Wǔdì, compiled the *Jiāruì Jì* (Records of Auspicious Omens).
Qióng expounded on its principles and continued it,
from Yǒngdìng to Zhìdé,
completing it as a work of his own.
He was promoted to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
with his authorship duties remaining as before.
Qióng was thoroughly versed in genealogies and records,
and possessed excellent discernment.
Previously, when Minister of Personnel Zōng Yuánráo died,
the Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè) Yuán Xiàn recommended Qióng.
〔一六〕However, Xuāndì did not employ him until then,
when he was appointed to the position,
and was praised for being competent.
Qióng was humble and frugal by nature,
and did not promote himself.
Though his position and prestige grew daily,
his resolve remained modest.
His gardens, ponds, rooms, and dwellings
were not altered.
His carriages, horses, and clothes
were not extravagant or flamboyant.
His seasonal stipends
were all dispersed among his relatives,
leaving no surplus wealth in his home.
In his later years, he deeply cherished contentment,
wishing to avoid powerful officials,
and excused himself from duty due to illness.
Soon after, he suffered the loss of his mother.
Initially, when Qióng attended the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
his mother accompanied him to his official residence.
Upon her death, he returned to his hometown for mourning.
An imperial edict conferred additional funerary gifts.
〔一七〕Hòuzhǔ personally composed an epitaph for her,
which brought honor to him in court and countryside.
Qióng's grief and mourning were excessive, to the point of harming himself,
and he died in the fourth year of Zhìdé (586).
His collected works in twenty volumes circulated in the world.
His son, Cóngdiǎn,
courtesy name Yóuyí,
was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth.
At the age of eight,
he read Shěn Yuè's collected works.
Upon seeing a palindrome inkstone inscription (Huíwén Yánmíng),
he picked up a brush and imitated it,
immediately achieving fine results.
At twelve, he composed an ode to the willow (Liǔ Fù),
the words of which were exceptionally beautiful.
His paternal uncle, Yú, especially cherished and loved him.
When Yú was about to die,
he ordered all family funerary records to be entrusted to Cóngdiǎn.
Cóngdiǎn then compiled Yú's writings into ten volumes,
and also wrote a preface to the collection,
the prose of which was very skillful.
Cóngdiǎn was diligent and fond of scholarship,
extensively studying many books.
He held the positions of Prince's Grand Master of the Household (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ) and Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Xīyuàn) to the Minister of Education (Sītú).
When Chén fell, he entered Suí,
and became Junior Literary Editor (Zhùzuò Zuǒláng).
The Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè), Yáng Sù, recommended Cóngdiǎn to continue Sīmǎ Qiān's *Shǐjì* up to the Suí dynasty.
Before his book was finished,
he was dismissed from office because his younger brother accepted a position from Prince of Hàn, Liàng.
Later he died as Registrar (Zhǔbù) of Nányáng County.
Yǎn, courtesy name Wēnyù,
was Qióng's paternal cousin (from his father's brother).
His father, Líng Gōng,
was an Aide (Jìshì Cānjūn) to the Prince of Xuānchéng in the Central Army of Liáng.
Yǎn was orphaned young,
fond of learning,
and possessed integrity.
The province recommended him as a Cultivated Talent (Xiùcái).
He was successively promoted to Outer Military Assistant (Wàibīng Cānjūn) to the Prince of Shǐxīng, General Xuānhuì,
and Scholar (Xuéshì) of the Jiādé Palace.
Chén Wéndì, in his leisure time,
was quite interested in historical records.
Because Yǎn was erudite
and good at recitation,
he was invited to serve by the emperor's side.
Once, he was asked to compose an inscription for a sword.
Yǎn took up his brush and finished it immediately,
without any need for revision.
The emperor praised him for a long time,
and bestowed upon him a set of clothes.
Soon after, he concurrently served as Regular Mounted Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì),
and as Vice Envoy to Lángyá Wáng Hòu on a mission to Qí.
Hòu died upon reaching Yè,
and Yǎn became the chief envoy.
At that time, he was just over twenty years old.
His demeanor was bright and spirited,
and his answers were calm and quick-witted.
The scholars and high officials of Qí were deeply impressed by him.
In the early Tàijiàn reign,
he became Chief Clerk (Gōngcáo Shǐ) in the Residence of Prince Wǔlíng, Míngwēi,
and concurrently Palace Recorder (Guǎnjì) to the Eastern Palace.
He left office due to mourning his mother,
and then died.
In the second year of Zhìdé (584),
he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng).
Yǎn was of few desires,
rarely competing or boasting.
He devoted his mind to classics and books,
and was always tranquil.
Many of his literary compositions
were not preserved.
Hòuzhǔ sought his surviving writings,
and compiled them into two volumes.
His younger brother, Yú, courtesy name Gànyù,
was devoted to learning in his youth,
and excelled in literary composition.
The province recommended him as a Cultivated Talent (Xiùcái).
He was twice promoted to Outer Military Assistant (Wàibīng Cānjūn) to the Prince of Jìn'ān, General-in-Chief (Jūnshī),
and Scholar (Xuéshì) of the Eastern Palace.
His elder brother, Yǎn, was then Palace Recorder (Guǎnjì).
Both served by the emperor's side with their talent and scholarship,
and people at the time compared them to the "two Yìngs."
During the Tàijiàn reign,
he was successively promoted to Prince's Grand Master of the Household (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ)
and Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōng Shèrén).
Yú was intelligent and had a strong memory.
He often studied Zhuāngzi and Lǎozǐ under Zhōu Hóngzhèng of Rǔnán,
and studied the *Chéngshí Lùn* (Satya-siddhi Śāstra) under Dharma Master Sēngtāo,
grasping the main points of both.
At that time, the crown prince was fond of learning
and wished to extensively read many books.
As the *Zǐ Jí* (Collected Masters' Works) were numerous,
he ordered Yú to transcribe and compile them.
He died before completing it.
The crown prince shed tears for him,
and personally composed a lament,
then discussed his merits with the Grand Tutor (Zhànshì) Jiāng Zǒng,
with words of deep sorrow.
In the second year of Zhìdé (584),
he was posthumously granted the title of Minister of the Imperial Household (Guānglù Qīng).
He had ten volumes of collected works.
Yú had a paternal cousin (from his father's brother), Jiè,
and a paternal cousin (from his father's brother), Chēn.
Jiè, courtesy name Rùnyù,
was the son of Yànzǐ, Grand Supervisor of Works (Dà Jiàng Qīng) in Liáng.
He was refined and had a dignified bearing,
fond of learning and capable of literary composition.
When Hòuzhǔ was in the Eastern Palace,
he was summoned to be Palace Recorder (Guǎnjì),
and concurrently Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōng Shèrén).
Soon after, he lost his sight due to illness.
When he was about to return to his hometown,
the crown prince took off his clothes and presented them to him,
shedding tears for him.
He died in the eighth year of Tàijiàn (576).
In the second year of Zhìdé (584),
he was posthumously granted the title of Lesser Minister of the Household (Shǎofǔ Qīng).
He had ten volumes of collected works.
Chēn, courtesy name Jiéyù,
was the son of Qiū Gōng, Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ) to the Prince of Línchuān, General Xuānyì.
He was astute and outstanding in his youth,
and known for his filial piety towards his stepmother.
When Hòuzhǔ succeeded to the throne,
he was made Attendant Yellow Gate Regular Mounted Attendant (Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng) and Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén),
participating in confidential affairs.
Chēn was rather careless,
and was condemned for leaking palace secrets.
An imperial edict ordered him to commit suicide.
Língzhé (靈哲) spent his entire family fortune to ransom his嫡mǔ (嫡母) and Jǐnghuàn (景煥),
but for years he could not succeed.
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) pitied him,
and ordered an envoy to the North to request their return.
The Wèi (魏) people sent them back to the South,
and he inherited Huáizhēn's (懷珍) noble title.
Língzhé (靈哲) held the position of Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (兗州刺史)
and died in the first year of Lóngchāng (隆昌) (494 CE).
Jùn (峻), courtesy name Xiàobiāo (孝標),
originally named Fǎwǔ (法武),
was Huáizhēn's (懷珍) paternal cousin.
His father, Xuánzhī (琁之),
served Sòng (宋) as Shǐxīng Nèishǐ (始興內史).
Xuánzhī (琁之) died a month after Jùn's (峻) birth,
and his mother, Lady Xǔ (許氏), took Jùn (峻) and his elder brother Fǎfèng (法鳳) back to their hometown.
In the early Tàishǐ (泰始) era of Sòng (宋),
Wèi (魏) conquered Qīngzhōu (青州).
Jùn (峻) was eight years old at the time,
and was abducted and made a slave, taken to Zhōngshān (中山).
A wealthy man from Zhōngshān (中山), Liú Bǎo (劉寶), pitied Jùn (峻),
ransomed him with a bundle of silk,
and taught him literature.
When the Wèi (魏) people heard that he had relatives south of the Yangtze,
they relocated him to the capital of Dài (代).
He lived in poverty and could not support himself,
so he and his mother both became Buddhist nuns,
but later returned to secular life.
Jùn (峻) was fond of learning;
he lived in someone's side-chamber,
and diligently studied by himself,
often burning hemp torches,
from dusk till dawn.
Sometimes, when he dozed off,
he would singe his beard and hair,
and upon waking, he would resume reading;
such was his dedication.
At that time, Emperor Xiàowén (孝文) of Wèi (魏) selected all prominent figures;
talented scholars from the Jiangnan (江南) region
were all promoted.
However, Jùn (峻) and his brothers were not selected.
In the Yǒngmíng (永明) era of Qí (齊),
they both fled to Jiangnan (江南),
and Jùn (峻) changed his name and courtesy name to Jùn (峻) and Xiàobiāo (孝標) respectively.
He felt that he had not been enlightened in his youth,
but later he sharpened his intellect,
and became exceptionally intelligent.
He lamented that his knowledge was not extensive,
so whenever he heard of a rare book,
he would always go to beg for a loan.
Cuī Wèizǔ (崔慰祖) of Qīnghé (清河) called him
"the book fanatic."
Thus, he extensively read all sorts of books,
and his literary talent shone brightly.
Therefore, in his autobiography, he wrote:
"In the academy, many ascend the hall,
but there are also fools who disrobe."
This refers to his dullness in youth.
At that time, Prince Zǐliáng (子良) of Jìnglíng (竟陵) invited scholars,
and Jùn (峻) sought through someone to serve Zǐliáng (子良) in a state position.
Xú Xiàosì (徐孝嗣), the Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書), suppressed and refused him,
instead offering him the post of Shìláng (侍郎) to the Prince of Nánhǎi (南海),
which he did not accept.
During the time of Emperor Míng (明帝) of Qí (齊),
Xiāo Yáoxīn (蕭遙欣) was in Yùzhōu (豫州),
and appointed him as his Fǔ Xíngyù (府刑獄),
treating him with great courtesy.
Yáoxīn (遙欣) soon died,
and Jùn (峻) was not reassigned for a long time.
In the early Tiānjiān (天監) era of Liáng (梁),
he was summoned to the Xīshěng (西省),
and, with scholar Hè Zōng (賀蹤), was in charge of cataloging the Mìgé (祕閣).
Jùn's (峻) elder brother, Xiàoqìng (孝慶), was then the Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (青州刺ǐ);
Jùn (峻) took leave to visit him,
but was impeached for privately transporting contraband,
and was dismissed from office by the authorities.
Prince Ānchéng Xiùyǎ (安成王秀雅) greatly esteemed Jùn (峻).
When Prince Ānchéng (安成王) moved to Jīngzhōu (荊州),
he appointed Jùn (峻) as Hùcáo Cānjūn (戶曹參軍),
provided him with books,
and tasked him with compiling the Lèiyuàn (類苑).
Before it was completed,
he again left due to illness,
and then traveled to Zǐyán Shān (紫巖山) in Dōngyáng (東陽),
where he built a house to reside.
He wrote "Shān Qī Zhì" (山栖志),
which was very beautiful.
Initially,
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) of Liáng (梁) recruited literary scholars;
many highly talented individuals were brought in,
and promoted without regard for sequence.
Jùn (峻) acted according to his nature
and could not go along with the crowd.
Whenever Emperor Wǔ (武帝) gathered scholars to discuss historical affairs,
Fàn Yún (范雲) and Shěn Yuē (沈約) and their like would always downplay themselves and praise others,
which pleased the Emperor,
and he would bestow rewards upon them.
Once, during a discussion about embroidered quilts,
everyone said they had exhausted their ideas.
The Emperor then tried calling Jùn (峻) and asked him.
Jùn (峻) was poor, haggard, and jobless at the time,
but he suddenly requested paper and brush,
and listed over ten points.
All the guests were astonished,
and the Emperor could not help but turn pale.
From then on, he disliked Jùn (峻)
and no longer granted him audience.
When Jùn's (峻) Lèiyuàn (類苑) was completed,
totaling 120 volumes,
the Emperor immediately ordered various scholars to compile the Huálín Biànlüè (華林徧略) to surpass it,
and Jùn's (峻) work was ultimately not used.
Thereupon, he wrote "Biàn Mìng Lùn" (辯命論) to express his feelings.
After the treatise was finished,
Liú Zhǎo (劉沼) of Zhōngshān (中山) wrote to challenge it,
twice,
and Jùn (峻) expounded and answered both times.
Coincidentally, Zhǎo (沼) died,
and did not see Jùn's (峻) later replies.
Jùn (峻) then wrote a letter to narrate the events.
Many of his essays and treatises are not recorded.
Jùn (峻) also once wrote an autobiography,
which roughly says: "I compare myself to Féng Jìngtōng (馮敬通),
and there are three similarities and
four differences.
Why so?
Jìngtōng (敬通) possessed extraordinary talent that surpassed the world,
and his will was as strong as metal and stone;
though I
cannot match him,
my integrity is bright and spirited.
This is one similarity.
Jìngtōng (敬通) met an enlightened ruler during a restoration,
yet was never given an important position;
I met a heroic sovereign destined to rule,
yet was also rejected
in my prime.
This is the second similarity.
Jìngtōng (敬通) had a jealous wife,
to the point that he personally managed the well and mortar;
I have a fierce wife,
who also makes my household affairs difficult.
This is the third similarity.
Jìngtōng (敬通), in the Gēngshǐ (更始) era,
held military tallies,
galloped on horseback, and ate meat;
from my youth to old age,
I have been anxious and joyless.
This is one difference.
Jìngtōng (敬通) had
a son, Zhòngwén (仲文),
who achieved official position and established his name;
my misfortune is like Bódào's (伯道),
forever without descendants.
This is the second difference.
Jìngtōng (敬通) had great physical strength,
growing stronger with age;
I
suffer from constant ailments,
and could die at any moment.
This is the third difference.
Though Jìngtōng (敬通)'s (敬通) 'Ganoderma and orchids were destroyed by fire,'
and he eventually filled a ditch,
he was admired by famous sages,
and his
spirit remained vibrant and fragrant,
growing stronger over time;
my reputation is obscure and silent,
the world does not know me,
and once my soul departs,
I shall be like autumn grass.
This is the fourth difference.
Therefore,
I made this autobiography,
to leave it for those who appreciate such things."
Jùn (峻) was originally from a military family.
His elder brother, Fǎfèng (法鳳), returned from the North
and changed his name to Xiàoqìng (孝慶), courtesy name Zhòngchāng (仲昌).
He had leadership and strategy early on.
At the end of Qí (齊), he was Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (兗州刺史),
raised troops to support Emperor Wǔ (武帝) of Liáng (梁),
and was enfeoffed as Yúgān Nán (餘干男),
holding various prominent official positions.
Jùn (峻) alone was devoted to learning.
While living in Dōngyáng (東陽),
many scholars from Wú (吳) and Kuàijī (會稽) followed him to study.
He died in the third year of Pǔtōng (普通) (522 CE),
at the age of sixty.
His disciples posthumously honored him as Xuánjìng Xiānshēng (玄靖先生).
Liú Zhǎo (劉沼), courtesy name Míngxìn (明信),
was a native of Wèichāng (魏昌) in Zhōngshān (中山).
His sixth-generation ancestor, Yú (輿), was a Pàoxī Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍) of Jìn (晉).
Zhǎo (沼) was skilled at writing in his youth,
and as he grew older, he became widely learned,
eventually serving as Mòlíng Lìng (秣陵令).
Early in the Yǒngmíng reign,
Wáng Zǐliáng, Prince of Jìnglíng, invited him to be the Staff Officer of the General-in-chief of the North (Zhēngběi Sītú Jìshì).
Guǐ Huán wrote to Zhāng Róng and Wáng Sīyuǎn, saying: "I have received the respectful summons to report,
and I should indeed stop my public duties;
but I recall my lifelong aspirations
which are at odds with such gracious favors.
My nature is clumsy in the human world;
I am not accustomed to official advancement.
In the past,
I once served as a staff aide (xíngzuǒ),
but was dismissed for being unable to manage public affairs.
This is known by all who are familiar with me.
Estimating myself and discerning my place,
I dare not aspire to glory.
I have long been plagued by poverty,
and moreover, by idleness.
My clothes and appearance
are enough to shock people.
In the midst of this, for the sake of supporting my elderly parents,
I have pulled up my robes and walked on foot,
and it has been, from then until now,
two generations and twelve years.
The previous
dynasty urged me to reform myself,
and to strive for advancement through official ranks,
and seeing my threadbare clothes,
sometimes even bestowed garments upon me.
Yuán, Chǔ, and all the other gentlemen
strongly exhorted me,
but in the end, I could not change myself.
If I could not do it once,
how can I do it again?
There was a man of old who, after once removing his cap,
would not put it on his head again.
I always considered this to be a proper
ceremonial gesture of advance and retreat.
Furthermore, my elders are advanced in years,
and I am even less willing to occupy an official post and neglect my morning and evening filial duties.
For this reason, the previous court
graciously granted my request,
so I was able for several years
not to accept appointments.
Having become accustomed to this for many years,
and with increasing age and illness,
how can I manage the administration of Héjiān
or join the ranks of Dōngpíng's officials?
I originally have no ambition to withdraw from the world,
nor am I one who feigns arrogance to appear noble.
This, too, is something that those who listen and observe should deeply consider.
Recently, when I first received the instruction,
I immediately hoped to find a place among the guests and wanderers,
but resolutely
refused the glorious rank.
What is the reason for this?
Because ancient kings, marquises, and great men
sometimes used this method to attract scholars from all directions.
Some followed Shēn and Bái and entered Chǔ,
envying Zōu and Méi
and wandering in Liáng.
I dare not claim to be like those former worthies,
but I wish to follow in the footsteps of the 'Nine Nines' (jiǔjiǔ).
Since there is no difference in hearing the Way or gathering at the academy,
and fortunately I am not constrained by official duties,
I can serve my parents,
and carry out my private plans.
My aspiration is simply this."
He was appointed Cavalry Commandant (bùbīng xiàowèi),
but did not accept.
Guǐ Huán's physique was slender and small,
but his scholarship surpassed that of his contemporaries.
The gentry and noble youths in the capital
all sat below him to receive instruction,
and he was regarded by his generation as a great Confucian scholar,
compared to the ancient Cáo and Zhèng.
He was humble and unassuming by nature,
and did not presume upon his high reputation.
When he visited people,
only one student would follow him carrying a folding stool (húchuáng).
If the host had not yet been announced,
he would sit by the gate and wait for a response.
He lived in Tánqiáo,
in a few tiled houses,
all of which leaked.
His students, out of respect and admiration,
dared not openly point this out,
so they called it Qīngxī.
Wáng Zǐliáng, Prince of Jìnglíng, personally went to visit him.
In the seventh year,
he petitioned Emperor Wǔ to build a residence for Guǐ Huán,
granting him the former residence of Yáng Lièqiáo.
All the students congratulated him.
Guǐ Huán said:
"Is a beautiful house for me?
Is this grand dwelling my home?
It would be fortunate if I could be commanded to build a lecture hall,
but I am still afraid it might harm me."
Before he could move,
he fell ill.
Zǐliáng sent Péngchéng's Liú Huì and Shùnyáng's Fàn Zhěn, who had studied under Guǐ Huán, to his residence to prepare a fast (zhāi).
When he died,
all his disciples and students attended the funeral in mourning clothes.
Guǐ Huán had an utmost filial nature.
When his grandmother suffered from a carbuncle for a year,
he held the ointment by hand,
soaking his fingers until they festered.
His mother, Lady Kǒng, was very strict and discerning.
She said to her relatives:
"Āchēng is simply the Zēngzǐ of this generation."
Chēng
was Guǐ Huán's nickname.
He was over forty years old
and had not yet married.
During the Jiànyuán reign,
Emperor Gāo and Minister of Education (sītú) Chǔ Yànhuí arranged for Guǐ Huán to marry a daughter of the Wáng clan.
The Wáng woman bored a hole in the wall and hung her shoes there,
and dirt fell onto Lady Kǒng's bed.
Lady Kǒng was displeased.
Guǐ Huán immediately divorced his wife.
When he observed mourning for his mother,
he lived by the tomb and did not leave the mourning hut.
His feet became crippled,
and he could not rise without a staff.
There were always magpies (qúyù niǎo) on this mountain,
but while Guǐ Huán was on the mountain for three years, they dared not come.
After his mourning period ended and he returned home,
these birds reappeared.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng had studied under him in his youth.
In the first year of Tiānjiān, he issued an edict to erect a stele for Guǐ Huán,
posthumously conferring on him the title of Zhēnjiǎn Xiānshēng.
His collected writings circulated in the world.
Initially,
after Guǐ Huán finished lecturing on the "Yuelìng" (monthly ordinances),
he said to his student Yán Zhízhī:
"Since the time of the Eastern Jìn (Jiāngzuǒ),
the study of Yīn-Yáng and calendrical calculations has declined.
Although I am lecturing on this now,
I cannot even grasp its faint resemblance."
Scholars admired his humility.
At that time, Cài Zhòngxióng of Jìyáng, who was widely learned in ritual studies,
said to people:
"The five notes (wǔyīn) originally came from the central plains,
hence their harmonious resonance.
Now that the vital energy (tǔqì) of the southeast is partial and skewed,
it cannot move wood and stone."
Guǐ Huán also agreed with this.
Zhòngxióng discussed the Classics,
often disagreeing with the powerful officials of the time,
but he never changed his principles to seek conformity.
Therefore, he remained stagnant and did not advance,
only reaching the position of Left Vice-Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng) after many years.
People at the time regretted his misfortune.
Also, Lóu Yòuyú (courtesy name Jìyù) of Dōngyáng
compiled thirty volumes of "Lǐ Jùnshí" (Collected Rituals).
Guǐ Huán's younger brother, Guǐ Jìn (courtesy name Zǐjǐng),
was upright and followed a proper course.
His scholarly elegance was inferior to Guǐ Huán's, but his literary talent surpassed it.
In the Tàiyù reign of Sòng,
he served as a bier-puller for Emperor Míng.
Early in the Jiànyuán reign of Qí,
he served as a Champion General and Commandant (guānjūn zhēnglǔ cānjūn) for Wǔlíng Wáng Yè.
When Yè drank with his subordinates,
he personally carved roasted goose.
Guǐ Jìn said:
"The cutting and placing on the board
are the duties of the chef.
If Your Highness personally wields the imperial knife (luándāo),
your humble subordinate dares not remain seated."
He then rose and requested to withdraw.
Traveling east by boat with his friend Kǒng Dì from Kuàijī,
they encountered a woman on the bank.
Kǒng Dì gazed at her and said:
"Beautiful and alluring."
Guǐ Jìn said:
"How can this be fitting for a gentleman to say?
He is not my friend."
Thereupon, he untied his robe and separated himself.
Some say: He traveled east by boat with his friend Kǒng Chè.
Chè lingered his gaze on a woman on the bank.
Guǐ Jìn raised his mat to separate himself
and no longer sat with him.
His elder brother, Guǐ Huán, called Guǐ Jìn from beyond the wall at night,
but Guǐ Jìn did not answer.
He first got out of bed, put on his clothes, and stood up,
and only then responded.
Guǐ Huán was surprised by his delay.
Guǐ Jìn said:
"I had not yet finished fastening my belt."
Such was his firm character.
Crown Prince Wénhuì summoned Guǐ Jìn to serve in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng).
Each time he submitted a document, he would erase the draft.
Soon after, he was appointed Archer General (shèshēng xiàowèi)
and died in office.
At that time, Jiāng Chóngxīn of Jìyáng was also pure and upright.
Even when in a dark room,
he behaved as if facing an esteemed guest,
but he was not as good as Guǐ Jìn.
Chóngxīn's highest position was Archer General (shèshēng xiàowèi).
Thus, skill should not be
emulated, nor should simplicity be admired.
Therefore, those who make impulsive and arbitrary judgments,
who prioritize reputation over substance,
like Jué Yǔ and Xiè Shēng,
how can they compare to
Sān Qiān?
Those who commit themselves to the Pèi clan,
fear that the two Tángs will not be transmitted.
Thus, fine jade and precious metal,
are instead ridiculed by clumsy eyes;
while rustic country songs,
are more suited to the ears in Yǐngzhōng.
The "Yángchūn" melody is too high to be harmonious,
and its exquisite sound is so unique that it is not sought after.
Ultimately, failing to carefully examine every detail,
and to weigh substance against refinement,
leads to an unskillful mind,
and ultimately disgraces the refined hand.
This is why
scholars with hidden talent,
seeing Zhèngbāng, know to retreat;
and those wearing grand hats and fine shoes,
looking towards Mǐnxiāng, sigh.
If poetry is like this,
then prose is also the same.
It is merely that ink and paper do not speak,
and are subject to being used and stained;
paper and scrolls are without feeling,
and are allowed to be unfolded and folded.
How dire it is!
The current state of literature,
has come to this.
As for the poems of Xiè Tiǎo and Shěn Yuē of recent times,
and the prose of Rèn Fǎng and Lù Chuí,
these are the pinnacles of literature,
models of composition.
Zhāng Shìjiǎn's
rhapsodies,
and Zhōu Shēngyì's debates,
are also fine works,
difficult to encounter again.
Literature has not fallen into decline,
there must be exceptional talents;
and the leader among them,
who else but you, my brother?
Every time I wish to discuss these matters,
there is no one with whom to speak,
I think of my Zǐjiàn,
to discuss and deliberate together.
To distinguish the clear from the turbid,
like the Jīng and Wèi rivers;
to comment on merits and flaws,
like those in Rǔ
nán.
Once black and white are determined,
and right and wrong are distinguished,
it will make the petty feel ashamed,
and those who pretend talent feel disgraced.
I yearn for you but cannot see you,
how can I bear this sorrow!
When Emperor Jiǎnwén ascended the throne,
he appointed Jiānwú as Dùzhī Shàngshū.
At that time, the powerful border garrisons upstream
all occupied provinces and resisted Hóu Jǐng.
Hóu Jǐng forged an imperial edict and sent Jiānwú as an envoy to Jiāngzhōu to persuade Dāngyáng Gōng Dàxīn.
Dàxīn then surrendered to the rebel,
and Jiānwú consequently fled eastward.
Later, the rebel Sòng Zǐxiān captured Kuàijī,
and having apprehended Jiānwú, wished to kill him.
Sòng Zǐxiān first said to him:
"I hear you can compose poetry.
Compose one now;
if you can,
I will spare your life."
Jiānwú immediately took up a brush and completed it,
the diction and style were very beautiful.
Zǐxiān then released him and made him Jiànchāng Lìng.
He then made his way by a secret route to Jiānglíng,
served successively as Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and concurrently as Yìyáng Tàishǒu,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Wǔkāng County.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì and Zhōngshū Lìng.
His son was Xìn.
Liú Qiú, courtesy name Língyù,
also known as Démíng,
was from Nièyáng, Nányáng,
and a seventh-generation descendant of Qí Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Jiáo.
He moved to reside in Jiānglíng.
From a young age, Qiú was principled and fond of learning,
and would seclude himself once he obtained a salary.
During the Tàishǐ era of the Sòng dynasty,
he served as Jìshì to Pǐngwáng Piàojì and Dāngyáng Lìng.
He resigned his official post and returned home to a quiet life,
often wearing a deerskin lined robe,
abstaining from grains,
and taking atractylodes and sesame as medicine.
At the beginning of the Jiàn Yuán era of Qí,
when Yùzhāng Wáng Yì was in Jīngzhōu,
he instructed that Qiú be appointed Biéjià,
and sent letters and courtesies to invite him, along with Zōng Cè and Yǔ Yì of the same commandery.
Qiú and the others each wrote a reply declining the offer.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng,
Cìshǐ Lúlíng Wáng Zǐqīng memorialized that Qiú and Zōng Cè, Zōng Shàngzhī, Yǔ Yì, and Liú Zhāo, five people from the same commandery,
be granted the honor of a plain carriage and silk.
An imperial edict summoned him as Tōngzhíláng,
but he did not accept.
Jìnglíng Wáng sent a letter conveying his intent,
to which Qiú replied:
"I, Qiú, have been ill for four seasons,
and spent three seasons cultivating and planting,
enjoying the lingering shade in the mountains and wetlands,
entrusting my twilight affections to fish and birds.
How can this not be the profound grace of Táng and Yú,
and the grand generosity of Zhōu and Shào?"
Qiú was a devout believer in Buddhism,
wore coarse cloth,
performed Buddhist rites, and observed a permanent vegetarian diet.
He annotated the Fǎhuá Jīng,
and lectured on Buddhist doctrines himself.
As Xīshāzhōu in Jiānglíng was far from people,
he moved his residence there.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
an imperial edict summoned him as Guózǐ Bóshì,
but he did not accept.
In the winter of that year, Qiú fell ill,
and at midday, white clouds lingered within the eaves and doorways,
accompanied by a fragrant aroma and the sound of chimes.
He passed away that day,
at the age of fifty-eight.
Qiú's son was Zhīlín.
Zhīlín, courtesy name Sīzhēn,
could compose prose at the age of eight.
Qiú said:
"This child will surely revive our clan through his literary talent."
He often told his sons:
"If compared to the Yán clan,
Zhīlín has inherited my literary talent."
Because of this, he was praised by the local community.
At that time, there was a Buddhist monk, Huì Yǒu, who had extraordinary insight.
Whenever he visited Qiú, he would call Zhīlín by his infant name, saying:
"Sēngqié's blessed child."
And he would grasp his hand and encourage him.
At fifteen,
he was recommended as a Màocái,
and excelled in the classical examinations and policy discussions.
Shěn Yuē and Rèn Fǎng were amazed to see him.
Lìbù Shàngshū Wáng Zhān once visited Rèn Fǎng,
and happened to find Zhīlín seated there.
Fǎng said to Zhān:
"This is Liú Zhīlín from Nányáng, he is highly learned but not yet in official service,
someone the 'Water Mirror' should select and promote."
He was immediately appointed Tàixué Bóshì.
"To speak highly of him is not as good as a personal interview."
At that time, Zhāng Jì had just been appointed Shàngshū Púshè,
and entrusted Fǎng to write a memorial declining the post.
Fǎng asked Zhīlín to compose it for him,
and he took up the brush and completed it instantly.
Fǎng said:
"The talent from Jīngnán
indeed possesses extraordinary ability;
in future official service, he will surely surpass me."
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Yuè Ài was Zhīlín's maternal uncle.
All the impeachment memorials from the Céntái
were drafted by Zhīlín.
Later, he served as Jīngzhōu Zhōng Cóngshì.
When Liáng Jiǎnwén governed Jīngzhōu,
he was then promoted to Xuānhuì Jìshì.
Zhīlín was assiduous in his studies and discerning,
with a broad knowledge of many books.
At that time, Liú Xiǎn and Wéi Léng were both known for their strong memories,
but whenever Zhīlín discussed with them,
they could never surpass him.
Liú Zhīhēng’s courtesy name was Jiāhuì.
When he was four years old,
he was adopted by his paternal uncle Sōng.
When he grew up, he loved learning.
He had a handsome appearance
and was skilled at conversation.
When Emperor Wǔ was in charge of Jīngzhōu,
he only conversed with Liú Qiú.
When Liú Qiú introduced Liú Zhīlún and Liú Zhīhēng to him,
the Emperor said:
“Zhīlún will certainly become prominent through his writings,
and Zhīhēng will achieve renown through his accomplishments.”
Later, the province nominated him as a Xiùcái,
and he was appointed Professor of the Imperial Academy (Dàxué Bóshì).
He then replaced his elder brother Zhīlún as Palace Aide to the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén).
He was successively promoted to Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi),
and Aide-de-camp to Yì, the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì Zīyì Cānjūn).
By imperial decree, he was granted a golden staff and bestowed with a poem.
In the sixth year of Dàtōng,
an army was dispatched to Nánzhèng.
An imperial edict ordered Yì, the Prince of Xiāngdōng, to command all the armies.
Zhīhēng, as Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng), was made acting Imperial Commissioner (Xíngtái Chéngzhì).
He traveled through the northern border of his home province,
commanding all the troops,
bearing his staff of authority as he marched west.
The many multi-decked ships and armaments were an impressive sight.
Old and young lined the banks to watch, saying:
“This is the former Xiùcái.”
His local community admired him.
On this campaign,
he largely achieved victory and recovery.
All soldiers who performed meritorious service were recorded.
However, Zhīhēng was impeached by Lán Qīn.
The authorities then implicated him,
and so his promotions and rewards were not carried out.
He merely returned to his original position.
After a long time,
the Emperor read the biography of Chén Tāng
and regretted that Chén Tāng, having achieved great feats in distant lands, was obstructed by civil officials.
The eunuch Zhāng Sēngyìn said:
“I have heard some outsiders say
that Liú Zhīhēng resembles him.”
The Emperor was enlightened and moved,
and thus enfeoffed him as Viscount of Línjiāng (Línjiāng Zǐ).
He firmly declined the appointment.
Zhīhēng's excellent achievements and good reputation
were superior to those of Zhū Yì.
However, since they were not on good terms,
he feared being harmed by Zhū Yì.
Therefore, Zhū Yì arranged for him to leave,
making him Chief Clerk to Yì, the Prince of Ānxī and Dōngxiāng (Ānxī Dōngxiāng Wáng Yì Zhǎngshǐ) and Governor of Nánjùn (Nánjùn Tàishǒu), replacing Zhīlún.
The Emperor asked Zhū Yì:
“Is Zhīhēng happy to replace his brother?
The relationship between these brothers
is not merely like that of the ‘Elder Fēng’ and ‘Younger Fēng’.”
He also said to the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng) Hé Jìngróng:
“The Chief Clerk of Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu Zhǎngshǐ) and the Governor of Nánjùn (Nánjùn Tàishǒu)
are both positions that my Grand Councilor (Púshè) has held.
Now Zhīhēng has already achieved the highest ranks.”
He performed exceptionally well in the commandery,
and officials and common people praised him.
Upon his death,
the people of Jīngzhōu mourned him,
no longer calling him by his name,
but referring to him as “Grand Governor of Nánjùn” and “Younger Governor of Nánjùn” (Dà Nánjùn Xiǎo Nánjùn).
His son, Guǎngdé,
was also fond of learning,
and possessed talent and spirit.
During the Chéngshèng era,
he held the position of Governor of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Tàishǒu).
When Wèi pacified Jīngzhōu,
he sought refuge with Wáng Lín.
After Wáng Lín was defeated,
during the Tàijiàn era of Chén,
he successively held the post of Governor of Hédōng (Hédōng Tàishǒu),
and died in office.
〔二二〕
Zhīhēng’s younger brother, Zhīchí,
held the position of Attendant to the Prefectural Administrator of Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu Zhōng Cóngshìshǐ).
His son, Zhòngwēi,
had great ambition in his youth
and was well-versed in literature and history.
During the Liáng Chéngshèng era,
he was a Middle Imperial Secretary (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
When Xiāo Zhuāng declared himself Emperor,
he was appointed Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
and followed Xiāo Zhuāng until his end in Yèzhōng.
Liú Tǎn, whose courtesy name was Déduó,
was Liú Qiú's younger cousin.
During his service in Qí, he successively held the positions of Magistrate of Cànlíng (Cànlíng Lìng)
and Registrar and Aide-de-camp to the Southern General of the Household (Nán Zhōngláng Lùshì Cānjūn).
Wherever he served, he was known for his administrative competence.
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng raised his army,
Yáng Gōngzé, then General of the Auxiliary State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn), was Governor of Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ),
and led his troops to Xiàkǒu.
The Western Court deliberated on who should act as Governor of the province,
and Liú Tǎn requested to do so.
He was then appointed Chief Clerk to the General of the Auxiliary State (Fǔguó Zhǎngshǐ) and Governor of Chángshā (Chángshā Tàishǒu),
acting as Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
Liú Tǎn had previously served in Xiāngzhōu
and had many old favors, so
many people welcomed him on the road.
Liú Xīzǔ, the Governor of Ānchéng (Ānchéng Tàishǒu), sent by Emperor Dōnghūn of Qí, defeated Fàn Sēngjiǎn, the governor selected by the Western Terrace, at Píngdū.
Liú Xīzǔ then sent a proclamation to the Xiāng region.
Consequently, Wáng Sēngcàn, the Administrator of Shǐxīng (Shǐxīng Nèishǐ), responded to it,
and all the commanderies in the Xiāng region
rose in revolt.
The provincial people all wanted to escape by boat,
but Liú Tǎn gathered all the boats and burned them.
Zhōng Xuánshào, the former Garrison Commander of Xiāngzhōu (Xiāngzhōu Zhènjūn), secretly conspired with Wáng Sēngcàn.
〔二三〕When Liú Tǎn heard of his plot,
he feigned ignorance.
He deliberately handled a lawsuit until nightfall,
leaving the city gates open to mislead Zhōng Xuánshào.
Zhōng Xuánshào had not yet launched his plot.
The next morning, he went to Liú Tǎn to ask why.
Liú Tǎn detained him for a long conversation,
while secretly sending trusted soldiers to raid his home.
Zhōng Xuánshào was still sitting and had not yet left,
when the soldiers returned, reporting that they had found all his documents and their full details.
Zhōng Xuánshào immediately confessed,
and was executed on the spot.
His documents were burned,
and no questions were asked of his remaining associates.
In the early Tiānjiān era of Liáng,
his merits were discussed, and he was enfeoffed as Viscount of Lìpǔ (Lìpǔ Zǐ).
In the third year,
he was promoted to Chief Clerk to the General of the Western Household (Xī Zhōngláng Zhǎngshǐ) and Governor of Shǔjùn (Shǔjùn Tàishǒu),
acting as Administrator of Yìzhōu.
He died on the way before reaching Shǔ.
The论 (Commentary) says: The Liú Huán brothers
and the Sēngshào father and son
all prospered in their specialized fields,
adorned with scholarly conduct,
and maintained personal integrity,
differing from those who are eager to gain and anxious about loss.
Yǔ Yì and Liú Qiú achieved high standing in their generation.
Their conduct
also included hidden virtues.
The excellence of their sons’ scholarship
each established their family’s reputation.
Xiǎn and Zhīlún were envied by the ruler of their time,
some were dismissed for no fault of their own,
others died not from illness.
This differs from the way wise kings of old humbled themselves to employ the worthy.
From this, one can know the lack of magnanimity of Emperor Wǔ
and the excessive jealousy of Empress Yuán.
The short lifespan of the Liáng dynasty,
was it not fitting?
〔校勘記〕 (Collation Notes)

Biographies, Chapter 41, Imperial Clan of Liáng, Part One: Hóu Jǐng, Marquis of Wúpíng (son of Máihé, Quàn, Miǎn, Bó; brother of Chāng, Áng, Yù); Yì, Prince Xuānwǔ of Chángshā (son of Yè; grandson of Xiàoyǎn; Yè's brothers Zǎo, Yóu; Yóu's sons Sháo, Jùn; Yóu's brothers Lǎng, Míng); Fū, Prince Zhāozhāo of Yǒngyáng; Chàng, Prince Xuān of Héngyáng; Róng, Prince Jiǎn of Guìyáng (son of Xiàng; Xiàng's son Zào); Hóng, Prince Jìnghuì of Línchuān (Hóng's sons Zhèngré, Zhèngyì, Zhèngdé; Zhèngdé's son Jiànlǐ; Zhèngdé's brothers Zhèngzé, Zhèngdé's brother Zhènglì; Zhènglì's son Bēn; Zhènglì's brothers Zhèngbiǎo, Zhèngxìn).
Hóu Jǐng, Marquis of Wúpíng (Wúpíng Hóu Jǐng), whose courtesy name was Zǐzhāo,
was a paternal cousin of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
His grandfather, Dàocì, was known for his courtesy and deference.
When there were disputes in the countryside,
he was relied upon to settle them.
He also provided for those in need,
and the villagers called him
“King of the Market” (Xū Wáng).
They all secretly said,
“His descendants will surely become great.”
He served Sòng, ending his career as Aide to the Imperial Censor (Shū Shìyùshǐ).
At the end of Qí, he was posthumously granted the title of Grand Master of the Palace with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū).
He had three sons: the eldest was Shàngzhī,
the second was Wéndì,
and the third was Chóngzhī.
Shàngzhī was honest and magnanimous, possessing great talent.
He served as Middle Staff Officer (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn) to Jiàn'ān Wáng, the Minister of Education (Sītú Jiàn'ān Wáng).
The entire administration referred to him as an elder of integrity.
He was promoted to Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi)
and died in office.
In the early Tiānjiān era of Liáng,
he was posthumously given the posthumous title of Marquis Wénxuān (Wénxuān Hóu).
His son, Língjūn,
served Qí as Magistrate of Guǎngdé (Guǎngdé Lìng).
When Emperor Wǔ raised his army,
he acted as Administrator of Kuàijī Commandery (Kuàijī Jùnshì).
Soon after,
he died.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngchāng County (Dōngchāng Xiàn Hóu).
His son Jiǎn inherited.
Chóngzhī served Qí, rising to the official position of Governor of Dōngyáng (Dōngyáng Tàishǒu).
He distinguished himself by his competence,
and his administration was notably strict and severe.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
when Táng Yùzhī of Qiántáng revolted,
his separate forces broke through Dōngyáng,
and Chóngzhī was killed.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
he was posthumously given the posthumous title of Marquis Zhōngjiǎn (Zhōngjiǎn Hóu).
In the ninth year,
he was summoned to be the Crown Prince's Middle Palace Attendant (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ).
Initially,
when Dèng Yuánqǐ was in Shǔ,
he was fond of accumulating wealth,
and his goods and money piled up like mountains.
Gold, jade, precious silks were kept in one room,
named the Inner Treasury (Nèicáng);
fine silks, brocades, and felts were kept in another room,
called the Outer Treasury (Wàifǔ).
Zǎo gave the contents of the Outer Treasury to his generals,
and returned the Inner Treasury to the royal coffers,
keeping nothing for himself.
When he returned to court at this time,
he traveled light.
He was promoted twice to Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng).
Zǎo was by nature humble and reserved,
not seeking fame or advancement.
He was skilled in writing,
and particularly fond of ancient styles.
Unless it was for a public banquet,
he never wrote indiscriminately.
Even if he wrote a short piece,
he would discard the original once finished.
He successively served as Provincial Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yōng and Yǎn prefectures.
He frequently governed prefectures and garrisons,
and all the people and officials praised him.
He attributed good deeds to others and always humbled himself,
as if always falling short.
In the sixth year of Pǔtōng,
he was made General of the Army Adviser (Jūnshī Jiāngjūn),
and with the Marquis of Xīfēng, Zhèngdé, he invaded Wōyáng to the north.
However, they withdrew their troops,
which led to an impeachment by the relevant authorities (Yǒusī),
resulting in his dismissal from office and the stripping of his title and fiefdom.
In the eighth year,
his title and fiefdom were restored.
In the third year of Zhōngdàtōng,
he was made General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn),
and Household Supervisor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì),
then went out to serve as Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
The Emperor often called him by his childhood name,
and sighed, saying:
"If all my sons and nephews were like Jiāyè,
what more worries would I have?"
He entered court as Minister of the Left (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè),
and was given the additional post of Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng),
but he firmly declined,
which was not permitted.
In the fifth year of Dàtóng,

he was promoted to General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn), Minister without Portfolio with the Privileges of the Three Grandees (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng),
with Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng) as before.
Zǎo was tranquil by nature,
living alone in a room,
where his bed bore knee marks.
Members of the imperial clan and high officials all took him as an example.
He always considered his rank and emolument excessive,
and often contemplated retiring.
His gate and courtyard were quiet,
and guests rarely visited.
Emperor Jiǎnwén particularly respected and loved him.
Since suffering family misfortune,
he wore plain clothes and sat on rush mats,
eating no fresh poultry,
and listening to no music except at official court functions.
Emperor Wǔ frequently praised him for this.
He went out to serve as Provincial Governor (Cìshǐ) of Nánxú Prefecture.
When Hóu Jǐng revolted,
Zǎo dispatched his heir, Yù, to lead troops to reinforce the capital.
After the city fell,
he was given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì).
Hóu Jǐng sent his Minister without Portfolio (Yítóng) Xiāo Yōng to replace him in defending Jīngkǒu.
Zǎo then fell ill with a qi disorder.
Someone advised him to flee north of the Jiāng River,
but Zǎo said:
"I am a pillar of the state,
entrusted with a particularly heavy responsibility.
Since I cannot exterminate the rebel,
I should simply die with the court."
He then refused food and died.
Zǎo's younger brother, Yóu,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Línrú,
and served as Grand Administrator (Jùnshǒu) of Wúxīng.
He was unconventional by nature,
and consorted with the spirit of the King of Chǔ Temple,
drinking up to one hú (a measure of volume) of wine.
Whenever he offered libations,
he would drink to his heart's content and to extreme drunkenness.
The divine image also showed signs of being tipsy,
and his prayers were always answered.
Later, he served as Provincial Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yì Prefecture,
Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng),
and Central Protector of the Army (Zhōnghùjūn).
At that time, Qí Gǒu'ér, a man from Jiāngyáng, rebelled,
and with a force of one hundred thousand, attacked the prefectural city.
Yóu's troops and provisions were both exhausted,
and the people harbored disloyal thoughts.
He then prayed remotely for rescue.
On that day, an old man named Tián met a cavalryman bathing his iron steed, coming from the east.
He asked how far it was to the city,
and the cavalryman replied,
"One hundred and forty lǐ."
It was already late in the day.
The cavalryman raised his spear and said:
"Tell those who come after
to ride quickly,
as they wish to defeat the rebels by daybreak."
Soon, several hundred cavalrymen arrived like the wind.
One cavalryman passed by and asked for a drink.
Old man Tián asked who he was,
and he replied:
"The King of Chǔ from Wúxīng has come to rescue the Marquis of Línrú."
At this time,
prayers at the temple had no effect.
More than ten days later,
the clay figures of the guards and attendants in the temple were found to be wet with mud as if sweating.
On that day,
Yóu utterly defeated Gǒu'ér.
〔一六〕While in the prefecture, Yóu was rather presumptuous and extravagant.
At guest banquets, there were even fragrant oranges,
and no paired sleeping mats were provided.
〔一七〕Emperor Wǔ eventually learned of this,
and considered it an offense.
When he returned to the capital,
he fell ill from worry and shame,
and died.
His posthumous name was Líng,
because of his consorting with spirits.
Yóu's son, Sháo, styled Démào,
was initially enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng of Shàngjiǎ County.
In the early Tàiqīng era, he was a Palace Gentleman (Shèrén).
When the city fell, he received an imperial decree to flee west.
Upon reaching Jiānglíng,
many literati came to seek him out,
asking Sháo to recount the events inside the city.
Sháo could not tell each person individually,
so he compiled a scroll of notes,
which he would show to inquiring guests.
The Prince of Xiāngdōng heard of it and took it to read,
saying:
"In the past, Wáng Sháozhī wrote the Lóng'ān Jì in ten scrolls,
recounting the chaos and separation at the end of the Jìn Dynasty.
Now, Xiāo Sháo can also write the Tàiqīng Jì in ten scrolls."
Sháo then revised it into the Tàiqīng Jì.
Many of his discussions
were based on Xie Wú's writings.
Since Sháo received the imperial command to compile and write,
much of it was not an accurate record.
The Prince of Xiāngdōng valued him,
and posthumously changed his lineage to that of Xuānwǔ Wáng,
enfeoffing him as Prince of Chángshā,
and he eventually became Provincial Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǐng Prefecture.
When Sháo was a young boy,
Yǔ Xìn loved him,
and they shared the 'severed sleeve' affection.
All his provisions for clothing and food
were supplied by Yǔ Xìn.
When guests came,
Sháo would also serve wine for Yǔ Xìn.
Later, when he was in Yǐng Prefecture,
Yǔ Xìn traveled west to Jiānglíng,
passing through Jiāngxià.
Sháo treated Yǔ Xìn very coldly.
He sat under a dark green canopy,
invited Yǔ Xìn to the banquet,
but seated him on a separate mat,
with a look of self-importance.
Yǔ Xìn gradually became intolerant.
During the revelry,
he directly climbed onto Sháo's bed,
trampling the dishes and delicacies,
and looking directly at Sháo's face,
he said:
"Your Excellency's appearance today is quite different from recent days."
At that time, guests filled the seats,
and Sháo was greatly ashamed.
Sháo's younger brother, Jùn, styled Dékuǎn,
was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts,
and adept at writing essays.
Later in life, he took up military training,
and his physical strength surpassed that of others,
similar to the Marquis of Yǒng'ān, Què.
He held the positions of Palace Gentleman of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng) and General of Striking Awe (Chāowǔ Jiāngjūn),
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Nán'ān.
〔一八〕When the city fell,
he was treated with respect by the rebel Rèn Yuē.
He plotted to summon the heir of the Prince of Póyáng, Fàn, to attack Rèn Yuē,
but was instead harmed by him.
In the seventh year,
he suffered the sorrow of his beloved mother, Concubine Chén Tàifēi.
An imperial edict ordered him to resume his duties.
Soon after, he was transferred to the position of Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the added title of Dūdū.
He established schools
and invited recluses.
He engaged recluses Hán Huáimíng of Hédōng, Hán Wàng of Nánpíng, Yǔ Chéngxiān of Nánjùn, and Guō Má of Hédōng, among others.
That year,
people from Hùchéng in Wèi Prefecture rebelled,
killing the Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Sīmǎ Yuè.
They invited the Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Mǎ Xiānpín,
who then sought assistance from Jīngzhōu.
The multitude all said that they should wait for a report from the court.
Xiù said:
“They await me as a helper;
help should be swift.
Waiting for an imperial decree is not suitable for an emergency.”
He immediately dispatched troops to their aid.
When the Jǔ Shuǐ (river) suddenly rose,
it damaged people's fields.
Xiù provided them with 20,000 hú of grain.
He instructed the Chángshǐ Xiāo Chēn to select poor, elderly, and single male officials in the province,
and in one day, he dismissed over a hundred people,
which greatly pleased the common folk.
Jīngzhōu had often suffered from drought.
Everyone wanted to move the market and dig canals.
Xiù, however, blamed himself
and personally prayed at Chǔwàng.
Soon after, sweet rain immediately fell,
and they achieved a prosperous year.
Furthermore, the Tàishǒu of Wǔníng was murdered by his younger brother,
who then falsely claimed that the locals had rebelled.
Xiù exposed his treachery and wickedness.
He surrendered at the mere prospect of investigation,
and everyone called Xiù divine.
He built Tiānjū Temple in Jīngzhōu,
because Emperor Wǔ had once toured Liángguǎn there.
When he left his post,
his journey reached Dàléi.
A storm with high waves suddenly arose,
and the bow of his ship sank.
Xiù's only concern was for the safety of others.
In the thirteenth year,
he was appointed Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ,
with the added title of Dūdū.
Yǐngzhōu was a crucial strategic location,
and taxes and levies were excessively burdensome,
beyond what the people could endure,
even to the extent of employing women for labor.
Xiù made it his priority to be frugal himself
and eliminated unnecessary expenses.
The common folk lived in peace,
and the region was tranquil.
Xiàkǒu was often a battlefield,
and many skeletons were exposed.
Xiù offered sacrifices and buried them below Huánghè Lóu.
One night, he dreamt that hundreds of people bowed in gratitude and left.
Every winter month,
he would make padded jackets and trousers to give to those who were cold.
At that time, the rebellious "蠻" (Mán) from Sīzhōu, Tián Lǔshēng, Lǔ Xián, and Chāo Xiù, who occupied Ménglóng, surrendered.
Emperor Wǔ appointed Lǔshēng as Běi Sīzhōu Cìshǐ,
Lǔ Xián as Běi Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Chāo Xiù as Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
to serve as a defense for the northern border.
However, Lǔshēng and Chāo Xiù slandered each other,
and had intentions of leaving or defecting.
Xiù comforted them, embraced them, and brought them into his fold,
allowing each to be utilized,
which was relied upon at the time.
He was transferred to Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
but died en route.
Emperor Wǔ, upon hearing of it,
was deeply grieved and mourned.
He dispatched Nánkāng Wáng Jì to meet the coffin along the road.
Initially,
when Xiù traveled west,
the people of Yǐngzhōu escorted him out of the border.
When they heard of his illness,
the common folk and merchants alike all prayed for his life.
When he died,
people from the four provinces tore their clothes to make white caps and wept as they welcomed and sent off his coffin.
The Mán from Yōngzhōu were awaiting Xiù,
but upon hearing of his death,
they offered sacrifices, wept, and departed.
When the coffin arrived at the capital,
he was posthumously granted the title Sīkōng,
and given the posthumous name Kāng.
Xiù possessed a beautiful appearance and dignified demeanor.
Whenever he was at court,
all officials would fix their eyes upon him.
He was by nature benevolent and lenient,
and his joys and angers were not displayed on his countenance.
His attendants once accidentally threw a stone and killed a swan he kept.
The Zhāishuài (head of the attendants) requested to punish them for their crime.
Xiù said:
“How could I harm people over a bird?”
While at the capital, one morning when he was attending to public affairs,
someone brought him food
and accidentally overturned it.
He then left and boarded his carriage,
going the entire morning without eating,
yet he did not reprimand them either.
At that time, all the princes hosted scholars.
Jiàn'ān and Ānchéng, the two princes, were especially fond of talented individuals.
The world spoke of the two Ān princes for their high regard for scholars,
comparing them to
the "Four Nobles."
Xiù dedicated himself to scholarship
and collected classics and records.
He invited the scholar Liú Xiàobiāo of Píngyuán to compile the Lèiyuàn.
Although the book was not yet finished,
it was already circulating in the world.
Xiù and Emperor Wǔ were commoner brothers (relatives before the emperor ascended the throne).
After becoming sovereign and minister,
he was exceedingly cautious and reverent,
more so than those of humble origins,
which made the Emperor esteem him even more.
He lost his parents early and was an orphan,
and was especially devoted to Shǐxīng Wáng Dàn.
Dàn had long been Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and always divided whatever he received equally with Xiù.
Xiù accepted it contentedly,
not declining even large amounts.
The harmony between the brothers
was praised by contemporary opinion.
His subordinates Xiàhóu Dǎn and others petitioned to erect a tombstone and epitaph,
which the emperor granted by edict.
The highly talented individuals of the era who frequented the prince's gate
included Wáng Sēngrú of Dōnghǎi, Lù Chuí of Wúqùn, Liú Xiàochuò of Péngchéng, and Péi Zǐyě of Hédōng.
Each composed a text for the epitaph,
intending to choose one for use,
but all were praised as faithful records,
so four steles were erected simultaneously.
His heir, Jī, succeeded him.
Jī, courtesy name Zhìtōng,
held the position of Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and died in the province.
Jī had a beautiful appearance and demeanor,
and was skilled in breathing exercises (or literary composition).
His family had many books,
and he was widely read and had a strong memory.
However, he enjoyed frivolous activities and favored strength,
keeping scholars at a distance
and associating with petty people.
As governor of the province, he focused solely on accumulating wealth,
had no administrative achievements,
and was frequently impeached.
When he was about to be buried,
the relevant authorities requested a posthumous name.
An edict stated:
“The Prince was fond of internal affairs (i.e., personal pleasure) and negligent in governance;
he should be posthumously named Yáng.”
He authored several thousand words of poetry and prose.
Emperor Yuán collected and prefaced them.
His son Cāo succeeded him.
Jī's younger brother Tuī, courtesy name Zhìjìn,
was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
and fond of literary composition,
deeply appreciated and admired by Jiǎnwén.
In the sixth year of Pǔtōng,
as a prince, he was enfeoffed as Nánpǔ Hóu.
He successively served as Tàishǒu of Huáinán, Jìnlíng, and Wúqùn.
Wherever he served, there was bound to be severe drought that devastated the land.
The people of Wú called him
“Drought Mother.”
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he defended Dōngfǔ.
When the city fell,
Tuī grasped his staff and died.
Nánpíng Yuánxiāng Wáng Wěi, courtesy name Wéndá,
was the eighth son of Emperor Wén.
He was intelligent, alert, and fond of learning in his youth.
He served Qí as the Pìqí Wàibīng Cānjūn of Jìn'ān Wáng.
When Emperor Wǔ was in Yōngzhōu,
he feared that chaos would soon erupt in the world,
and sought to welcome Wěi and Shǐxīng Wáng Dàn.
Soon after, he heard they had entered Miǎn.
The Emperor joyfully said to his subordinates:
“Ā Bā and Shíyī are arriving soon,
and I shall have no worries.”
When he raised an army,
he left Wěi to manage the affairs of Yōngzhōu.
When the Emperor conquered Yǐng and Lǔ,
descended upon Xúnyáng,
and besieged Jiànyè,
the son of Bādōng Tàishǒu Xiāo Huìxùn, named Guī, and the Bāxī Tàishǒu Lǔ Xiūliè raised armies and threatened Jīngzhōu.
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu died suddenly from grief and indignation.
The western court was terrified,
and levied troops from Wěi.
Wěi then allocated his provincial officials and officers to Shǐxīng Wáng Dàn to go and confront them.
When Dàn arrived,
Guī and the others all surrendered.
Emperor Hé of Qí issued an edict appointing Wěi as Dūdū and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Fàn's courtesy name was Shìyí.
He was gentle and had sagacity.
When he served as Wèiwèi Qīng,
he personally patrolled every night.
Wǔdì praised his hard work.
He was dispatched as Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
He traveled to Jīngzhōu when Zhōngliè Wáng passed away,
so he stopped and resigned.
Wǔdì did not permit it,
and issued an edict for him to temporarily supervise Jīngzhōu.
When Xiāngdōng Wáng arrived,
Fàn resumed his duties as before,
and sent his younger brother, Xiāngtán Hóu Tuì, to follow the funeral procession south.
In Dàtóng元年,
for opening the Jiàndào road
and recovering Huáyáng, his fief was increased.
Soon after, he was summoned to be Lǐngjūn Jiàngjūn and Shìzhōng.
Although Fàn was not learned,
he prided himself on his strategic planning.
He loved rare curiosities and ancient artifacts,
gathered talented writers,
and composed verses on impulse;
sometimes, they even had extraordinary charm.
He once obtained an old pípa,
on which was inscribed
"Qí Jìnglíng Shìzǐ."
Fàn sighed over how people pass but objects remain,
took up his brush and composed a poem,
which he showed to Xiāngdōng Wáng.
The King recited its verses
and wrote a pípa rhapsody to match it.
Later, he became Dūdū and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Fàn governed the people,
and gained great contemporary renown.
He appeased and comforted his officers and soldiers,
winning their complete devotion.
Thus, he kept soldiers and horses,
repaired city walls,
and stored military provisions in his private residence.
At that time, Lúlíng Wáng was in Jīngzhōu,
which was the Dūdū Fǔ,
and they had always been incompatible.
So he submitted a memorial accusing Fàn of plotting rebellion.
Fàn also swiftly submitted a memorial to defend himself,
and Wǔdì pardoned him.
Contemporary commentators still believed Fàn intended to become a rebel.
There was also a children's rhyme that said:
"Don't rush,
be patient, Duke.
Who will become the Son of Heaven?
Grass covers the side of the carriage already."
At that time, Wǔdì was old,
and none of the princes were willing to submit to each other.
Jiǎnwén, though the heir apparent,
was also uneasy,
and had particular suspicion and animosity towards Sīkōng Shàolíng Wáng Lún.
Lún was then Dānyáng Yǐn,
and his power shook the capital.
Jiǎnwén then selected elite troops to guard the palace.
The brothers were at odds,
and this news spread everywhere.
Fàn, whose name matched the rumor, sought to become a Gōng.
Soon after,
he was granted the title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Fàn was secretly delighted,
believing the prophecy to be true.
He thought that if Wǔdì were to die,
the princes would surely rebel.
Since Fàn had the support of the populace
and a distinguished reputation,
he believed he could seize the opportunity to pacify the empire.
So he again gathered soldiers and commoners,
hoping for an extraordinary outcome.
In Tàiqīng元年,
a major northern invasion was launched.
Initially, for the commander-in-chief,
the Emperor wanted to use Fàn.
At that time, Zhū Yì, having rushed back from outside,
heard of this and hastily entered, saying:
"Sìwáng is exceptionally heroic and powerful,
and gains the ultimate loyalty of people,
however, wherever he goes, he is extraordinarily cruel and tyrannical,
not the material for one who brings comfort to the people.
Previously, Your Majesty ascended the Běigù Tíng to gaze northward,
and said that there was an aura of rebellion south of the Jiāng,
and that kinsmen would become leaders of strife.
Today's situation
especially requires careful selection."
The Emperor was silent and said:
"How about Kuàilǐ?"
He replied:
"If Your Majesty chooses him,
your servant will have no regrets."
Kuàilǐ was timid and lacked strategy.
His palanquin had a plank roof
covered with oxhide.
The Emperor heard this and was displeased.
When they reached Sùyù,
Zhēnyáng Hóu Míng requested to go,
and Míng was then substituted,
while Fàn was made Zhēngběi Dàjiàngjūn,
overall supervisor of all military affairs for the northern campaign in Hènběi.
Soon after, he was promoted to Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Hóu Jǐng was defeated at Wōyáng,
and retreated to defend Shòuyáng.
So Fàn was reassigned as Hézhōu Cìshǐ,
stationed at Héfèi.
At that time, Jǐng's disloyal actions were evident,
and Fàn repeatedly submitted memorials about it,
but Zhū Yì always suppressed them and did not report them.
When Jǐng besieged the capital,
Fàn sent his heir apparent Sì and Péi Zhī Gāo and others to assist.
He was promoted to Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
When Táichéng fell,
Fàn abandoned Héfèi,
moved to defend Dōngguān,
requested troops from Wèi,
and sent his two sons as hostages.
The Wèi people occupied Héfèi,
but ultimately did not assist Fàn.
Fàn, with no strategy for advance or retreat,
then sailed upstream westward,
stationing his army at Cóngyáng,
〔一四〕and sent a message to Xúnyáng Wáng Dàxīn.
Dàxīn urged him to return to Jiǔjiāng,
intending to join forces and head westward.
Fàn was greatly pleased to receive the letter,
and thus led his army to Pénchéng,
making Jìnxī into Jìnzhōu.
He sent his son Sì to be the Cìshǐ,
and arbitrarily changed
the prefectures and counties of Jiāngzhōu.
Consequently, the jurisdiction of Xúnyáng
was reduced to just one prefecture.
Moreover, fearing Fàn,
market trade was cut off.
Fàn then again sent his younger brother, Guānníng Hóu Yǒng, to lead troops to open up Nánchuān,
to assist Zhuāng Tiě.
At that time, the two commanders suspected each other,
and no longer had the will to defeat the rebels.
Fàn's tens of thousands of troops
all ran out of food,
and many starved to death.
Fàn eventually developed a carbuncle on his back and died.
The masses secretly kept his death a secret,
and honored his younger brother, Nán'ān Hóu Tián, as their leader,
who had several thousand troops.
Fàn's general, Hóu Tián, attacked Zhuāng Tiě at Yùzhāng,
killed him,
and absorbed all his troops.
They then welcomed the coffin to the prefecture,
and encountered a storm at Sōngmén.
The coffin sank into the water,
but was retrieved by hooks.
When Yú Qìng Zhī pressed upon Yùzhāng,
Hóu Tián surrendered Fàn's sixteen sons to the rebels.
The rebels killed them all in Shítóu Pítkēng.
The heir apparent Sì, courtesy name Chángyìn,
had a robust and imposing appearance,
with a waist ten spans in circumference.
He was brave and decisive by nature,
and had courage and resourcefulness.
He was uninhibited and did not bother with minor conduct,
yet he devoted himself to nurturing warriors,
all of whom rendered him ultimate loyalty.
When Fàn died,
Sì still occupied Jìnxī.
Food in the city was exhausted,
and the soldiers were all in dire need.
Hóu Jǐng sent Rèn Yuē to attack Sì.
At that time, the rebels were flourishing,
and everyone advised him to stop for now.
Sì drew his sword and shouted at them, saying:
"Today's battle
is the moment for Xiāo Sì to dedicate his life and die for his principles!"
During the battle,
he was struck in the neck by a stray arrow.
He did not permit it to be pulled out,
and with the arrow still in him, personally killed several people.
Only when the rebels retreated did he order it to be pulled out,
and he immediately gasped his last.
His wife and children were captured by Rèn Yuē.
Initially,
Fàn had been in a standoff with Xúnyáng Wáng Dàxīn,
and even after Sì's death,
they still did not dare to announce Fàn's death.
Fàn Dí Zī [範弟諮], courtesy name Shìgōng [世恭],
held the position of Wèiwèi Qīng [衞尉卿],
and was enfeoffed as Wǔlín Hóu [武林侯].
After Jiǎnwén [簡文] ascended the throne,
the imperial guard became stricter around Jǐngzhōu [景周],
and outsiders were largely unable to see him.
Only Zī [諮], along with Wáng Kè [王克] and Yīn Bùhài [殷不害], due to their gentle and cultivated nature, were able to enter and exit the emperor's private chambers.
They attended him morning and evening.
The Son of Heaven discussed and lectured on the Six Arts with them,
never ceasing in their time together.
When the affair of Nánkāng Wáng Huìlǐ [南康王會理事] failed,
Kè [克] and Bùhài [不害], fearing disaster, distanced themselves.
Zī [諮], however, could not bear to leave the emperor,
and continued his court attendance without interruption.
The rebels hated this,
and ordered his enemy Diāo Xù [刁戌] to assassinate Zī [諮] outside the Guǎngmòmén [廣莫門].
Zī's [諮] younger brother Xiū [脩], courtesy name Shìhé [世和],
〔一五〕was enfeoffed as Yífēng Hóu [宜豐侯].
He had a resolute character and was steadfast,
with a dignified and impeccable demeanor.
At nine, he mastered the Lúnyǔ [論語],
and at eleven, he could compose essays.
Hónglú Qīng [鴻臚卿] Péi Zǐyě [裴子野] saw and admired him.
He was exceptionally filial.
At the age of twelve,
he mourned the death of his birth mother, Lady Xú [徐氏].
He returned from Jīngzhōu [荊州] to bury her.
While crossing the middle of the river, they encountered a storm.
Many of the forward and rear detachments sank.
Xiū [脩] held the coffin and wailed loudly,
blood and tears flowing,
tossing and turning with the waves,
but ultimately, they suffered no further harm.
After the burial,
he built a hut and lived by the tomb.
Before this, the mountains had many fierce beasts,
but from then on, they vanished.
Wild birds became tame and familiar,
perching and roosting on the eaves.
Wǔdì [武帝] praised him for this,
and announced it to the imperial clan.
He served concurrently as Wèiwèi Qīng [衞尉卿].
He had a handsome appearance.
Whenever the imperial guard was stationed around the palace,
Wǔdì [武帝] would shift his carriage to look at him.
Initially,
the heir apparent Fàn [範] served as Wèiwèi [衞尉].
When patrolling the city at night,
he often used the excuse of the wind to whip and flog the guards,
wishing the emperor to know of his diligence.
When Xiū [脩] was in office,
he would patrol twice a night,
but did not wish anyone to know.
Someone asked him the reason,
and he replied,
"Nighttime patrols are indeed arduous,
a truly laborious task.
If the benevolent emperor
were to hear of it, he might perhaps order us to stop.
To defy an edict is unacceptable,
but to obey an edict would mean neglecting duty.
Moreover, even Hú Zhì's [胡質] integrity
still feared being known by others.
This is merely a regular duty of the office;
why should one seek to make oneself known for it?"
Those who heard him sighed in admiration.
At that time, many imperial princes and marquises served in small counties near the capital.
After demonstrating achievements in these probationary roles,
they were then allowed to serve as governors of frontier prefectures.
The emperor, recognizing Xiū's [脩] broad vision and magnanimity,
appointed him from Wèiwèi [衞尉] to guard Zhōnglí [鍾離],
and later transferred him to be the Cìshǐ [刺史] of Liáng [梁] and Qín [秦] prefectures.
He served in Hànzhōng [漢中] for seven years,
transforming customs and traditions.
People called him "Kind Father."
His Zhǎngshǐ [長史] Fàn Hóngzhòu [范洪冑] had a field of one qǐng.
Just before autumn, it was afflicted by locusts.
Xiū [脩] personally went to the field,
deeply blaming himself.
Gōngcáo Shǐ [功曹史] Lángxié Wáng Lián [琅邪王廉] advised Xiū [脩] to catch the locusts.
Xiū [脩] said,
"This is due to the lack of virtue of the Cìshǐ [刺史];
what good will catching them do?"
As soon as he finished speaking,
suddenly, thousands of birds flew in, obscuring the sun.
In an instant,
they ate all the insects and left.
No one knew what kind of birds they were.
Coincidentally, an imperial envoy saw it
〔一六〕and fully reported it to the emperor.
