A sealed imperial letter arrived, expressing commendation and inquiry,
and a handwritten edict stated:
"When 'dog's teeth' do not enter,
there is nothing to surpass this."
The people of the prefecture petitioned to erect a stele to praise his virtue.
The heir apparent Fàn [範] was in Pénchéng [盆城],
and there were some dissenting opinions.
Wǔlíng Wáng Dàshēng [武陵王大生] grew suspicious and wary,
and rumors circulated.
Xiū [脩] earnestly explained himself,
requested to send a hostage son,
and also offered to assist in defense.
Wǔlíng Wáng [武陵王] then sent his Cóngshì Zhōngláng [從事中郎] Xiāo Gù [蕭固] to consult on current affairs,
to fully understand Xiū's [脩] intentions.
Xiū [脩] tearfully spoke of the principles of loyal officials and filial sons.
The king respectfully accepted his words.
Thus, throughout Xiū's [脩] lifetime,
he did not act unrighteously.
One night,
a dog suddenly lay down on Xiū's [脩] bed.
Xiū [脩] said,
"Could this be a sign of invasion?"
Consequently, he greatly repaired the city walls and fortresses.
In the first year of Chéngshèng [承聖] (552 CE),
the Wèi [魏] general Dáxī Wǔ [達奚武] came to attack.
Xiū [脩] dispatched his Jìshì Cānjūn [記室參軍] Liú Fán [劉璠] to Yìzhōu [益州],
seeking aid from Wǔlíng Wáng Jì [武陵王紀].
He sent General Yáng Gānyùn [楊乾運] to reinforce him,
and enfeoffed Xiū [脩] as Suí Jùnwáng [隨郡王].
When Fán [璠] returned to Bōzhǒng [嶓冢],
he surrendered to Wèi [魏],
and Gānyùn [乾運] withdrew his troops.
Fán [璠] arrived at the city walls,
persuading those within the city to surrender to Wèi [魏].
Xiū [脩] rebuked him, saying,
"You could not die for your loyalty,
but instead became a persuader?!"
He ordered him to be shot.
Secret messengers were sent to Jīngzhōu [荊州].
Yuándì [元帝] sent a messenger to communicate with him.
Xiū's [脩] Zhōngzhíbīng Cānjūn [中直兵參軍] Chén Guǐ [陳晷] was very brave and eloquent.
〔一七〕He volunteered to be a scout.
He was captured,
and killed due to his resolute words.
Then Yú Xīn [虞馨], a Zīyì [諮議], was sent to Dáxī Wǔ [達奚武] with cattle and wine.
Wǔ [武] said to him,
"Liáng [梁] has already been defeated by Hóu Jǐng [侯景];
why does the King defend this isolated city?"
Xiū [脩] replied that he would defend it to the death,
vowing to be a general who would sacrifice his head.
Wèi Xiāng [魏相] Āndìng Gōng [安定公] Yǔwén Tài [宇文泰] sent a letter to reason with him.
Overwhelmed by force, he surrendered.
Āndìng Gōng [安定公] treated him with great respect.
Soon after, he ordered him to return to Jiānglíng [江陵],
providing him with generous provisions,
and giving him a thousand households of civil and military personnel as his staff.
Yuándì [元帝] feared he might cause trouble,
and imperial envoys watched him,
never ceasing on the road.
On the night of his arrival,
he ordered him to be robbed.
By dawn,
Xiū [脩] submitted a memorial surrendering his horses and weapons, only then did the emperor feel at ease.
When Xiū [脩] entered for an audience,
he looked at the imperial gate and was overcome with sorrow.
Yuándì [元帝] also wept,
and the entire court cried.
Soon after, he was appointed Cìshǐ [刺史] of Xiāngzhōu [湘州].
Chángshā [長沙] had frequently suffered from warfare and famine,
and its households were devastated.
Xiū [脩] encouraged agricultural efforts,
and within a year,
over three thousand displaced families had arrived.
Yuándì [元帝] was very suspicious,
often executing people.
Xiū [脩] quietly and respectfully guarded himself,
concealing his reputation and traces.
Yuándì [元帝], also because he was an elder of the imperial clan,
deeply respected and honored him.
When news of the siege of Jiānglíng [江陵] arrived,
he immediately boarded a boat to go to its rescue.
When he reached west of Bālíng [巴陵],
Jiānglíng [江陵] had already fallen.
When Jìngdì [敬帝] ascended the throne,
he remotely appointed Xiū [脩] as Tàiwèi [太尉],
and later promoted him to Tàibǎo [太保].
At that time, the imperial house was increasingly weakened.
Although Xiū [脩] planned a righteous uprising,
his strength was insufficient to accomplish it.
He then developed a back ailment and vomited blood, dying at the age of fifty-two.
Yuánzhào (圓照), courtesy name Míngzhōu (明周),
in the early days of Zhōngdàtóng (中大同) era,
served as Yìzhōu (益州) Dōngzhāi Láng (東齋郎) and the Grand Administrator of Sòngníng (宋寧) and Sòngxìng (宋興) commanderies.
The crown princes of the distant princely states were all held as hostages in Jiànyè (建鄴).
The Emperor especially loved Jì (紀),
and therefore sent Yuánzhào (圓照) to assist Jì (紀).
Jì’s (紀) instigation of conflict
was entirely Yuánzhào’s (圓照) doing.
His younger brother, Yuánzhèng (圓正), had already been seen imprisoned in Jiānglíng (江陵).
When Jì (紀) eventually died by military means,
Emperor Yuán (元帝) sent a message to Yuánzhèng (圓正) saying:
"The western army has been defeated,
and the fate of your father is unknown."
The intention was to make him commit suicide.
However, when Yuánzhèng (圓正) received this message,
he wailed and cried with utmost sorrow.
Believing that the calamity and disaster were all caused by Yuánzhào (圓照),
he only wept for the crown prince,
speaking without interruption.
The Emperor thought that Yuánzhèng (圓正) would be saddened by the news
and surely commit suicide.
After repeatedly observing that he could not bring himself to die,
he was again handed over to the Tíngwèi (廷尉) prison.
When he saw Yuánzhào (圓照), he said:
"Elder brother,
how could you sow discord among family members,
causing such cruel pain?"
Yuánzhào (圓照) said nothing more,
only stating that his calculations were mistaken.
He then starved himself to death in prison,
biting and consuming his own arm.
He died after thirteen days,
and the world heard of it and mourned him.
Yuánzhèng (圓正), courtesy name Míngyǔn (明允),
was Jì’s (紀) second son.
He had a handsome demeanor,
was skilled in conversation,
generous and benevolent,
and enjoyed associating with scholars.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jiāng'ān (江安).
He served as the Grand Administrator of Xīyáng (西陽),
where he had benevolent governance.
Being located upstream,
many people attached themselves to him.
When Hóu Jǐng (侯景) rebelled,
Yuánzhèng (圓正) gathered nearly ten thousand soldiers.
Later, he became unruly in the middle reaches of the river,
not obeying the imperial commands.
After Hóu Jǐng (侯景) was defeated,
he again planned to enter Shǔ (蜀).
Emperor Yuán (元帝) intended to eliminate him
and appointed him as General Píngnán (平南將軍).
When he arrived, he was not seen.
Emperor Yuán (元帝) had the heir of Nánpíng (南平) Prince, Kè (恪), and others intoxicate him and imprison him.
At that time, Jì (紀) proclaimed himself King of Liáng (梁王).
After Jì (紀) was defeated and died,
the relevant authorities formally requested to remove Jì (紀) from the imperial genealogy.
Emperor Yuán (元帝) granted it,
and bestowed upon him the surname Tāotièshì (饕餮氏).
Jì (紀) was most beloved by Emperor Wǔ (武帝).
Few of Emperor Wǔ’s (武帝) sons attained high official positions;
only Jì (紀) distinguished himself through accomplishments,
being the first to serve in the imperial secretariat.
His elder brother, Shàolíng (邵陵) Prince Lún (綸), was repeatedly demoted for offenses,
and always felt aggrieved.
When he heard that Jì (紀) was appointed General Zhēngxī (征西),
Lún (綸) sighed, leaning on his pillow, saying:
"What achievements does Wǔlíng (武陵) have
that his position precedes mine?
The court is muddled,
it seems they do not know people."
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) heard of this
and angrily said:
"Wǔlíng (武陵) has the merit of caring for people and expanding territory.
What accomplishments do you have?"
In the early days of Tàiqīng (太清) era,
the Emperor missed him,
and sent Zhāng Sēngyóu (張僧繇), a skilled painter, to Shǔ (蜀) to paint his likeness.
He was in Shǔ (蜀) for seventeen years,
opening up Níngzhōu (寧州) and Yuèsuī (越嶲) to the south,
and connecting with Zīlíng (資陵) and Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) to the west.
Internally, he promoted agriculture, sericulture, salt, and iron industries,
externally, he facilitated trade and distant commerce,
thus enabling him to accumulate wealth and resources,
and amass abundant armaments.
He had eight thousand horses,
and the finest ones were kept indoors,
with his sleeping quarters opened to allow them passage.
At sunset,
he would always take the horses out for a walk.
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery,
and particularly adept at spear dancing.
On the ninth day of the month, he would review military exercises,
personally leading the banner formations.
When he heard of the national crisis,
he said to his aides:
"Can these civil officials of the seven departments
really save the country?"
When he moved east,
he made gold into one-jin (斤) cakes,
and a hundred cakes constituted one 'zuò' (簉), having as many as a hundred 'zuò' (簉);
silver was five times that amount,
and other brocades, woolens, silks, and colorful fabrics were likewise abundant.
Every battle, he would display gold and silk to his generals and soldiers,
but never actually distributed rewards.
Chén Zhīzǔ (陳知祖), the Cǐshǐ (刺史) of Níngzhōu (寧州), requested to distribute gold and silver to recruit brave warriors,
but Jì (紀) refused,
and Chén Zhīzǔ (陳知祖) wept and left.
From then on, people became disaffected,
and no one was willing to serve him.
Jì (紀) had studied divination and observation,
was good at geomancy (wind patterns),
and also knew that he could no longer succeed.
Looking at the celestial phenomena,
he sighed at the ways of Heaven,
and the sound of him pounding his bed could be heard outside.
If anyone requested an audience,
he would refuse, citing illness.
After his death,
he was buried on a sandbar,
without a mound or a coffin.
Emperor Yuán (元帝) handed Liú Xiàoshèng (劉孝勝) over to the Tíngwèi (廷尉),
but soon released him.
Initially,
when Jì (紀) was about to usurp the throne,
various strange omens appeared.
In his private sleeping quarters, a cypress palace pillar sprouted flowers around its joints,
with forty-six stems.
They were delicate and lovely,
resembling lotus flowers.
Those who understood said:
"Wáng Dùn’s (王敦) ominous flowers are
not a good sign."
At that time, a star-gazer in Shǔ (蜀) told Jì (紀):
"If your Excellency moves east,
it should be in the Shēn (申) year.
When Tàibái (太白) appears in the west,
following it will be advantageous.
Depart from Shǔ (蜀) in the Shēn (申) year,
and enter Jīng (荊) in the Yǒu (酉) year;
this opportunity must not be missed."
In the year he departed from Shǔ (蜀),
Tàibái (太白) was in the west.
By the next year,
it had already moved east.
The commentary says: How profound
is the cunning of slander and flattery!
For their words attach to righteousness,
their actions appear respectful,
pleasing to the eye and agreeable to the mind,
applicable everywhere.
To the extent that they separate fathers and sons,
create discord between brothers,
depose the legitimate heir of Chǔ (楚),
and estrange the successor of Hàn (漢),
one can only sigh deeply,
for it is truly not a single path.
With Zhāomíng (昭明)’s intimacy and virtue,
and Emperor Wǔ’s (武帝) love and trust,
once slander reached him,
he could not clear his name until death,
let alone those of lower status.
Zōng (綜) was entangled in Qín Zhèng’s (秦政) suspicions,
harbored the ambition of a 'fùchǐ' (負尺),
acted with unbridled recklessness,
and ultimately met with defeat and flight.
Lúlíng (廬陵)’s great wealth became a burden,
and his ambitious spirit was self-serving.
It was fortunate that he perished early,
before he could unleash his tyranny.
Nánkāng (南康) governed effectively
and observed mourning rituals properly.
It is a pity he died young,
unable to rescue the empire in its critical final years.
Shàolíng (邵陵) was reckless and impetuous in his youth,
and lost his human decency.
His later efforts to serve the emperor
were perhaps commendable.
Wǔlíng (武陵), with his advantageous geographical position,
ultimately met with ruin.
His talent was shallow, but his ambition was great;
how could he avoid such a fate?
[Textual Notes]
Biography 44: Sons of Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文帝) of Liáng (梁) - Sons of Emperor Yuán (元帝).
In the sixteenth year,
he was again appointed governor of Yùzhōu.
As he was about to depart,
Emperor Wǔ invited his court officials to a farewell banquet for Fèng Dàogēn in Wǔdé Diàn,
and summoned a painter to create his portrait.
Dàogēn prostrated himself and said gratefully:
"The only way I can repay the state
is with my death.
However, with peace reigning throughout the land,
I lament that there is no place for me to die."
When Yùbù again received Dàogēn,
everyone rejoiced.
Emperor Wǔ often praised him, saying:
"Wherever Fèng Dàogēn is,
he can make the court forget about having another province."
After residing in the province for a short time, he fell ill
and requested to return.
The court recalled him to serve as Sànqí Chángshì and Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn.
He died in office.
On that day,
the imperial carriage was performing the spring sacrifice at the two ancestral temples.
When the emperor exited the palace,
the officials reported the news.
The emperor asked Zhū Jiào, the Zhōngshū Shèrén:
"A propitious day and a day of misfortune coincide;
should I proceed now?"
He replied:
"In the past, when Liǔ Zhuāng was gravely ill,
Duke Xiàn of Wèi was about to offer a sacrifice.
He requested the attendant of the deceased, saying: 'There is my minister Liǔ Zhuāng,
who is not merely my minister,
but a minister of the state.
Hearing of his death,
I request to visit him.'
He went without removing his sacrificial robes
and subsequently offered condolences.
Although Dàogēn was not yet a minister of the state,
he also rendered services to the royal house.
It is proper to visit him."
The emperor immediately rode to his residence
and wept with great sorrow.
His posthumous title was Wēi.
His son Huái succeeded him.
Kāng Xuàn, courtesy name Chángmíng,
was a native of Lántián, Huàshān.
His ancestors originated from Kāngjū.
Initially,
when the Hàn dynasty established the Dūhù,
subjugating all of the Western Regions,
Kāngjū also sent a侍子 (shìzǐ) to serve in Héxī.
They then remained there and did not leave,
and later adopted their surname from the place.
During the Jìn dynasty, due to chaos in Lǒngyòu,
they relocated to Lántián.
Xuàn's great-grandfather, Yǐn, served as the Tàizǐ Zhānshì for Fú Jiān,
and gave birth to Mù.
Mù served Yáo Cháng as Hénán Yǐn.
During the Yǒngchū reign of the Sòng dynasty,
Mù led over three thousand households of his clan into Xiàngyáng's Xiànnán.
The Sòng dynasty established Huàshān Jùn and Lántián Xiàn for them,
provisionally located in Xiàngyáng,
and appointed Mù as the Cìshǐ of Qín and Liáng provinces.
He died
before taking office.
Xuàn's elder paternal cousin Yuánlóng and father Yuánfǔ
were both supported by the displaced people
and successively served as the Tàishǒu of Huàshān.
In his youth, Xuàn was ambitious and resolute.
He served the Qí dynasty as the Tàishǒu of Huàshān,
and won the trust and obedience of the neglected and uncultivated population.
When Liáng Wǔ Dì raised an army,
Xuàn led his commandery to respond.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
he was enfeoffed as Nányáng Xiàn Nán,
He was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ,
and, together with Lǐngjūn Xiāo Jǐng,
was in charge of security within the palace.
Xuàn was eight feet tall
and had an unparalleled appearance.
Although he held a prominent position,
he still practiced martial arts.
When the Emperor visited Déyáng Diàn to watch horse games,
he ordered Xuàn to perform horse archery.
Xuàn drew his bowstring and hit the target,
delighting the spectators.
On that day,
the Emperor had a painter create Xuàn's portrait,
and sent an imperial envoy to hold it and ask Xuàn:
"Do you recognize this portrait?"
Such was the intimacy he enjoyed.
At that time, Wèi defector Wáng Zú proposed a plan,
suggesting the construction of a dam on the Huái River to flood Shòuyáng.
Zú cited a northern children's rhyme:
"Jīngshān is the upper gate,
Fúshān is the lower gate,
Tóngtuó is the rushing canal,
together they flood the Jùyě Zé."
The Emperor agreed,
and sent water engineer Chén Chéngbó and staff officer Jiāngjūn Zǔ [⿰耳幾] to inspect the terrain.
They all said that the sand and soil within the Huái River were light and easily swept away,
not firm,
and the project could not be completed.
The Emperor did not accept their advice
and mobilized people from Xú and Yáng provinces, requiring five able-bodied men from every twenty households to construct it.
He granted Xuàn the Imperial Insignia and made him Dūdu Huáishàng Zhūjūnshì,
also overseeing the laborers and soldiers for the dam construction,
with a force of 200,000 men.
They started from Fúshān south of Zhōnglí
and extended north to Chánshí,
building earthworks along the banks,
joining in the middle of the river.
In the fourth month of the fourteenth year,
as the dam was about to be completed,
the Huái River's swift current
caused it to break again.
The multitude suffered from this.
Some said that the Jiāng and Huái rivers had many flood dragons,
which could ride the wind and rain to break cliffs and banks,
and that their nature abhorred iron.
Because of this, they brought ironware from the two eastern and western foundries,
large items like cauldrons and tripods,
small items like sickles and hoes,
tens of millions of catties were sunk at the dam site,
but it still could not be closed.
Then they cut down trees to make well-frames,
and added earth on top.
Within a hundred *lǐ* along the Huái River, all hills and ridges, trees and stones, large or small, were completely used up,
and the shoulders of the porters were worn through.
In summer, there was widespread disease,
and the dead lay piled up,
with flies and insects buzzing day and night.
Emperor Wǔ pitied them,
and sent Shàngshū Yòupúyè Yuán Áng and Shìzhōng Xiè Jǔ, bearing imperial insignias, to offer comfort and relief,
and also to grant exemptions and remissions.
That winter was extremely cold,
the Huái and Sì rivers were completely frozen,
and seventeen or eighteen out of every ten soldiers died.
The Emperor sent clothes and trousers as gifts.
In the eleventh month,
Wèi general Yáng Dàyǎn announced he would break the dam.
Xuàn ordered his troops to dismantle their camps and set up temporary shelters to await him.
He sent his son Yuè to challenge the enemy,
and Yuè beheaded Xú Fāngxīng, the Sīmǎ of the Wèi Xiányáng King's residence,
causing the Wèi army to retreat slightly.
In the fourth month of the fifteenth year,
the dam was completed.
It was nine *lǐ* long,
one hundred and forty *zhàng* wide at the bottom,
forty-five *zhàng* wide at the top,
twenty *zhàng* high,
and nineteen *zhàng* and five *chǐ* deep.
It was flanked by embankments,
and willows were planted.
The soldiers settled in safely,
lining up on top of it.
The water was clear;
looking down, the towns, residences, and tombs
were clearly visible beneath it.
Someone said to Xuàn:
"The Four Great Rivers are how Heaven regulates the *qì*;
they cannot be blocked for long.
If a deep channel is dug to flow eastward,
then the flowing waves will be calm and gentle,
and the dam will not break."
Xuàn agreed,
and opened a deep channel to flow eastward.
He also spread a counter-espionage message to Wèi, saying:
"Liáng fears the opening of the deep channel."
The Wèi people believed it
and indeed dug five *zhàng* deep into the mountain,
opening a deep channel to flow northward.
The water flowed day and night,
but the deep channel did not diminish.
In that month,
the Wèi army finally collapsed and returned.
The area affected by the water covered several hundred square *lǐ* along the Huái River.
The Wèi garrisons in Shòuyáng city gradually moved to Bāgōng Shān.
The residents south of this area dispersed to the hills and ridges.
Initially,
when the dam started in Xúzhōu,
the Cìshǐ Zhāng Bàozǐ thought he would definitely be in charge of the project.
But then Xuàn came as an official from elsewhere to supervise the work,
and Bàozǐ was greatly ashamed.
Because of this, he slandered Xuàn, accusing him of communicating with Wèi.
Although the Emperor did not accept the slander,
he still recalled Xuàn when the project was completed.
Soon after, he was appointed Cìshǐ of Sīzhōu
and concurrently Tàishǒu of Ānlù.

Lièzhuàn Dìsìshíbā Wéi Ruì (xiōng Zuǎn chǎn Ruì zǐ Fàng sūn Càn Fàng dì Zhèng Zhèng zǐ Zài Dǐng Zhèng dì Léng Léng dì Àn) Péi Suì (Suì zǐ Zhīlǐ xiōng zǐ Zhīgāo Zhīgāo dì Zhīpíng zǐ Jì Zhīgāo dì Zhīhéng)
Wéi Ruì, zì Huáiwén,
was a native of Jīngzhào Dùlíng.
For generations, his family was a prominent clan in the Sānfǔ region.
His grandfather, Xuán,
avoided official duties and lived in seclusion in the Southern Mountains of Cháng'ān.
When Sòng Wǔdì entered Guānzhōng,
he was summoned as a clerk in the Grand Commandant's office,
but he did not go.
His paternal uncle, Zǔzhēng,
served as Guānglùxūn at the end of the Sòng dynasty.
His father, Zǔguī,
was the Níngyuǎn Zhǎngshǐ.
Ruì was known for his filial piety towards his stepmother.
Zǔzhēng repeatedly served as a commandery administrator;
each time he took Ruì to his post,
treating him like a son.
At that time, Ruì's maternal cousin, Wáng Chéng, and his maternal aunt's son, Dù Yùn, both had great reputations in their hometown.
Zǔzhēng said to Ruì:
"How do you rate yourself compared to Chéng and Yùn?"
Ruì was too modest to reply.
Zǔzhēng said:
"Your literary skill might be slightly less,
but your learning and knowledge surely surpass theirs.
However, in managing the state
and achieving great deeds,
none can match you."
His maternal cousin, Dù Yòuwén, served as the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu
and invited Ruì to go with him.
The land of Liángzhōu was rich and abundant,
and many who went there were ruined by bribery.
Though Ruì was young,
he alone was known for his integrity.
In the early Yǒngguāng era of the Sòng dynasty,
Yuán Yǐ became the Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu.
He saw Ruì and was impressed,
appointing him as his Principal Clerk (zhǔbù).
When Yǐ arrived at the province,
he raised troops with Dèng Wǎn.
Ruì requested to be sent out as the Yìchéng Jùnshǒu,
thus escaping Yǐ's disaster.
He was successively promoted to Qíxīng Tàishǒu,
then Biejia of his home province,
Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
and Yòujūn Jiàngjūn.
At the end of the Qí dynasty, there were many troubles,
and he wished to return to his hometown,
requesting to be appointed as Shàngyōng Tàishǒu.
Soon after, Tàiwèi Chén Xiǎndá and Hùjūn Jiàngjūn Cuī Huìjǐng repeatedly pressed Jianyè,
causing panic among the people.
The people of Xītǔ deliberated,
and Ruì said:
"Although Chén is an old general,
he is not a man of great talent.
Cuī has indeed seen more action,
but he is cowardly and not martial.
The true lord of the empire
will likely rise in our province."
He then sent his two sons to pledge allegiance to Liáng Wǔdì.
When the army was raised and the summons arrived,
Ruì led the people of the commandery to cut bamboos for rafts,
traveling day and night to answer the call,
with two thousand men
and two hundred horses.
The Emperor was very pleased to see Ruì,
patting his desk and saying:
"I have seen your face on other days;
today I see your heart.
My endeavor is accomplished!"
When the army conquered Yǐng and Lǔ,
and pacified Gāhú,
Ruì offered many strategies,
all of which were adopted.
When the main army departed from Yǐng,
a general to stay behind and guard was deliberated,
and the Emperor found it difficult to choose.
After a long time,
he looked at Ruì and said:
"To abandon a qíjì and not ride it,
why fuss and search elsewhere?"
On that very day, he was appointed Jiāngxià Tàishǒu,
and concurrently managed the affairs of Yǐngzhōu province.
Initially,
when Yǐngchéng was defended,
nearly one hundred thousand men and women
were confined within the walls for a year.
Seventy or eighty percent died from illness and plague,
their bodies piled up below,
while the living slept above them,
filling every house.
Ruì carefully investigated and provided relief,
managing all arrangements,
and the common people relied on him.
When the Liáng dynasty was established,
he was summoned to be Dàlǐ.
Upon Wǔdì's ascension,
he was promoted to Tíngwèi
and enfeoffed as the Zǐ of Dūliáng.
In the second year of Tiānjiān,
he was re-enfeoffed as Yǒngchāng,
and then promoted again to Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently serving as Lìyáng Tàishǒu.
The Wèi sent troops to attack,
and Ruì led his provincial forces to repel them.
In the fourth year, he invaded Wèi territory,
and an imperial edict appointed Ruì as the general supervisor of all armies.
Ruì sent Zhǎngshǐ Wáng Chāozōng and Liángjùn Tàishǒu Féng Dàogēn to attack the Wèi city of Xiǎoxiàn,
but they could not take it.
Ruì inspected the siege works,
when suddenly several hundred Wèi soldiers emerged from the city and formed a line outside the gate.
Ruì wanted to attack them.
All the generals said:
"We came lightly just now;
please let us return to arm ourselves before fighting."
Ruì said:
"There are more than two thousand Wèi soldiers in the city,
holding fast behind closed gates,
enough to defend themselves.
Now they suddenly send men outside without cause;
these must be their bravest and most skilled.
If we can defeat them,
their city will fall by itself."
The multitude still hesitated,
so Ruì pointed to his marshal's staff and said:
"The court has granted this,
not for decoration.
The rules of Wéi Ruì
are not to be violated."
Thereupon, he advanced his troops,
the Wèi army was defeated,
and he then pressed the attack,
taking the city during the night.
He then advanced to attack Héféi.
Earlier, Yòujūn Sīmǎ Hú Jǐnglüè had reached Héféi,
but had been unable to take it for a long time.
Ruì surveyed the mountains and rivers,
saying:
"I have heard that 'the Fén River can irrigate Píngyáng' —
this is exactly it."
He then dammed the Féi River.
Soon the dam was completed and the water flowed,
and boats and ships arrived continuously.
The Wèi initially divided their forces to build small eastern and western cities,
flanking Héféi.
Ruì first attacked these two cities.
Presently, Wèi reinforcements led by Yáng Língyìn, with an army of fifty thousand, arrived unexpectedly.
The troops feared they were outnumbered
and requested to send a memorial asking for more soldiers.
Ruì said:
"The enemy has already reached the city walls;
are we still going to seek more troops?
Moreover, while we seek reinforcements,
they will also summon more forces.
'Victory in battle depends on harmony'
is an ancient teaching."
He then engaged in battle,
defeating them,
and the soldiers felt a little relieved.
Initially,
when the Féi River dam was built,
he ordered the army commander Wáng Huáijìng to build a city on the bank to guard it.
The Wèi attacked and captured the city,
then, emboldened by victory, reached Ruì's dike.
The army supervisor Pān Língyòu advised Ruì to retreat to Cáohú,
and the other generals also requested to flee and secure Sānyì.
Ruì angrily said:
"Generals die in defense,
they only advance, never retreat."
Thereupon, he ordered umbrellas, fans, banners, and streamers to be set up below the dike,
to show his unwavering resolve.
Ruì was naturally frail;
in every battle, he never rode a horse,
but was carried in a palanquin,
supervising and encouraging all the troops.
When the Wèi soldiers dug into the dike,
Ruì personally contended with them.
The Wèi army retreated,
and he then built a rampart on the dike to secure it.
He constructed fighting ships as tall as Héféi city,
surrounding it on all four sides.
The city fell,
and more than ten thousand were captured.
He kept none of the captured military supplies for himself.
Initially,
Hú Jǐnglüè and the vanguard Zhao Zǔyuè were in the same army but harbored ill will towards each other,
intending to bring harm to one another.
Jǐnglüè, in a fit of rage,
bit his own teeth,
making them all bleed.
Ruì, seeing the discord among the generals,
which could lead to disaster,
poured wine and personally offered it to Jǐnglüè, saying:
"I only wish for the two valiant ones not to engage in private quarrels again."
Thus, throughout this campaign, they managed to avoid harm.
During the Zhìdé reign,
the Crown Prince entered school for the Dì ritual (to Confucius),
and all officials attended in rows.
Xiàokè delivered a lecture on the topic of the Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety).
The Latter Lord commanded the Crown Prince to face north and pay his respects.
In the first year of Zhēnmíng (587 CE),
he was appointed Dūguān Shàngshū.
Since the Jìn dynasty,
the officials of the Shàngshū (department)
all brought their families to reside in the department offices (shěng).
The shěng was located within the Tái Chéng, inside the Xiàshè Gate.
There was a covered walkway (gédào) spanning the road east to west,
connecting to the imperial court hall (cháotáng).
The first one was the Dūguān Shěng,
reaching the gédào to the west.
Due to its ancient age,
it was often haunted by ghosts.
Every evening at dusk,
there would be inexplicable sounds and lights,
or people wearing official robes and hats would be seen emerging from the well,
only to disappear again moments later;
or doors would open and close by themselves.
Many residents died there.
Shàngshū Zhōu Què died in this shěng.
Xiàokè replaced Què,
and immediately took up residence there.
After two years,
all the strange occurrences ceased.
People at the time all attributed it to his integrity and uprightness (zhēnzhèng).
Xiàokè was of a pure and simple nature,
and loved to bestow favors,
thus he often suffered from hunger and cold.
The Latter Lord commanded that he be given the tax revenue from Shítou Jīn.
Xiàokè used it all to organize vegetarian feasts and transcribe sutras,
spending it as soon as he received it.
In the second year (588 CE),
he became Sànqí Chángshì,
serving the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng).
When Chén fell,
he was transferred to Cháng'ān as per the usual practice.
His family was utterly destitute.
His birth mother was ill,
and he wanted to make her rice porridge,
but could not always manage to obtain it.
After his mother's death,
Xiàokè thereafter ate only wheat.
If anyone offered him polished rice,
Xiàokè would weep sadly at the sight of it,
and never ate it again for the rest of his life.
In the twelfth year of Kāihuáng (592 CE),
Cháng'ān suffered from a plague.
Emperor Wén of Suí, hearing of his reputation and conduct,
summoned him to lecture on the Jīngāng Bānruò Jīng (Diamond Sūtra) in the Shàngshū Dūtáng.
Soon after, he was appointed Guózǐ Bóshì,
and later served the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
lecturing on Rites and Commentaries.
In the nineteenth year (599 CE),
he died of illness,
aged seventy-three.
At the time of his death, he sat upright, chanting the Buddha's name.
An extraordinary fragrance filled the room,
astonishing all his neighbors.
His son, Wànzǎi,
held the position of Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ.
Bào Quán, courtesy name Rùnyuè,
was a native of Dōnghǎi.
His father, Jǐ, courtesy name Jǐngxuán,
[二六]was poor.
Because his mother was old, he went to the Lìbù Shàngshū Wáng Liàng to seek an official position.
Liàng was greatly impressed at their first meeting,
and appointed him Chōnglíng Lìng.
Later, he was recommended by Míng Shānbīn,
and became Tàicháng Chéng.
Because his maternal cousin Fù Zhāo was Tàicháng,
and according to regulations, officials in mourning (sīfú) could not serve under a relative,
he was reappointed Shàngshū Láng,
and finally ended his career as Xiāngdōng Wáng Zīyì Cānjūn.
Quán had a handsome beard,
and was skilled in deportment.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
and extremely intelligent and perceptive.
He was extensively versed in history and commentaries,
and also possessed literary talent.
He served Emperor Yuán in his youth as Guócháng Shì.
He was promoted early,
and Emperor Yuán said to him:
"Among my literati, none surpasses you."
Later, he became Tōngzhí Shìláng.
He often rode in a high-canopied carriage,
accompanied by dozens of attendants,
with exquisite parasols and accoutrements.
On the road, he encountered Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Wáng Chéng.
Chéng, suspecting he was not of the old nobility,
sent someone to inquire.
Quán's attendant replied,
"Bào Tōngzhí."
Chéng was surprised,
and, wishing to humiliate him,
sent someone to approach his carriage and ask:
"What kind of person is Bào Tōngzhí to be so extravagant!"
The young men in the capital city then made this a common saying.
Seeing ostentatious people,
they would jokingly ask,
"What kind of person is Bào Tōngzhí to be so extravagant?"
using it as a jest.
When Emperor Yuán took control,
he was successively promoted to Xìnzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Fāngděng's rebellion failed,
Emperor Yuán was furious.
Quán and Wáng Sēngbiàn were dispatched to suppress it.
Sēngbiàn said:
"What is our plan?"
Quán replied:
"The matter is as easy as melting snow,
why worry so much?"
Sēngbiàn said:
"Your words are merely the common talk of a literatus.
Hédōng has few skilled warriors.
[二七]We cannot go without a strong force of ten thousand elite soldiers.
The crack troops from Jìnglíng will arrive soon,
and we can still reiterate our request.
I wish to go and speak to the Emperor with you."
Quán agreed.
However, when Sēngbiàn made his proposal as he had said,
Quán remained silent and did not support him.
Emperor Yuán was greatly angered,
and so he put Sēngbiàn in shackles.
People at the time compared Quán to Lì Jì.
Quán then exclusively led the campaign against Chángshā,
but failed to conquer it for a long time.
Emperor Yuán then enumerated Quán's twenty offenses,
and wrote to reprimand him, saying:
"Your face is like a jade crown,
yet you are suspected of being a wooden dummy.
Your beard is like hedgehog quills,
only wasting space around your mouth."
Then he released Wáng Sēngbiàn from prison to replace Quán as Dūdū,
and sent Shèrén Luó Chónghuān with three hundred imperial guards to accompany Sēngbiàn.
Upon reaching Chángshā,
he sent a message to Quán saying:
"Shèrén Luó has been ordered to deliver Wáng Jìnglíng here."
Quán was startled,
and looked around at his attendants, saying:
"With Wáng Jìnglíng assisting me in my strategy,
the rebels will not be difficult to pacify!"
Then he dusted off a mat and sat down to await him.
When Sēngbiàn entered,
he sat with his back to Quán and said:
"Bào Láng,
you are guilty.
The imperial decree orders me to shackle you.
Do not judge me by our old acquaintance."
He commanded Chónghuān to show the decree to Quán,
and had him shackled under the bed.
Quán's expression remained composed,
showing no fear whatsoever.
He said:
"Delaying the imperial army is a crime I willingly accept.
However, I only fear that future generations will miss the muddle-headed Bào Quán."
Sēngbiàn's expression was very displeased.
Quán then confessed his crime of prolonged delay.
Emperor Yuán soon reinstated him to his position,
ordering him and Sēngbiàn to jointly press east against Shàolíng Wáng at Yǐngzhōu.
When Yǐngzhōu was pacified,
Emperor Yuán made his heir apparent, Fāngzhū, the Cìshǐ,
and Quán the Chángshǐ,
managing the affairs of the prefecture.
Fāngzhū found Quán gentle and weak,
and never adopted his advice.
He made Quán lie on the bed and rode on his back as a horse,
writing his name on his clothes.
Consequently, the entire prefecture took advantage of him.
Hóu Jǐng secretly sent his generals Sòng Zǐxiān and Rèn Yuē to attack them.
Fāngzhū and Quán paid no attention to military administration,
only indulging in dice and wine, saying,
"How could the rebels possibly reach us?"
Soon, however, many messengers arrived,
and only then did they order the gates closed.
The city fell,
and the rebels seized Fāngzhū and Quán and sent them to Jǐng.
Later, Jǐng attacked Wáng Sēngbiàn at Bālíng but failed,
and retreated in defeat.
He then killed Quán at Jiāngxià,
and sank his body at Huánghè Jī.
Earlier,
Quán dreamt of wearing a crimson robe and walking on water.
When he died,
his entire body was covered in blood as he sank into the river, just as in his dream.
Quán was especially learned in rites and ceremonies,
and compiled "Xīnyí," thirty scrolls which circulated in the world.
In the second year of Tàiqīng [548 CE],
Xu Wénshèng heard of the national crisis,
so he recruited several tens of thousands of men and came to assist.
Yuán Dì appointed him as the Cìshǐ of Qínzhōu,
added the title Dūdū,
and entrusted him with the strategy for an eastern expedition.
He descended eastward to Wǔchāng,
where he encountered Rèn Yuē, a general of Hóu Jǐng,
and they engaged in a standoff.
Yuán Dì also ordered Hùjūn Jiāngjūn Yǐn Yuè, Píngdōng Jiāngjūn Dù Yòu’ān, Bāzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Xún, and others to join him,
all under Wénshèng’s command.
They greatly defeated Yuē at Bèijī.
Yuē retreated to defend Xīyáng,
and Wénshèng advanced to occupy Lúzhōu,
where they again engaged in a standoff.
Jǐng heard of this,
and led a large army westward to relieve Yuē,
reaching Xīyáng.
All the generals said:
“Jǐng’s naval forces advanced lightly,
and are also very hungry and tired;
attacking them will surely result in a great victory.”
Wénshèng did not permit it.
Wénshèng’s wife, Shí Shì, was previously in Jiànyè,
and at this time,
Jǐng transported her back to him.
Wénshèng was deeply grateful to Jǐng,
and so he secretly communicated with his envoys,
having no fighting spirit at all.
The troops were all indignant and resentful.
Dù Yòu’ān, Sòng Zào, and others then led their divisions to advance independently,
greatly defeating Jǐng,
and capturing his boats and ships to return.
It happened that Jǐng secretly dispatched cavalry to attack and capture Yǐngzhōu via a hidden path.
The army was terrified,
and subsequently suffered a great rout,
Wénshèng fled back to Jīngzhōu.
Yuán Dì still appointed him as the Dàdūdū of the northern side of the city.
He also accumulated a great deal of ill-gotten gains.
Yuán Dì was greatly enraged,
and issued an order enumerating his ten crimes,
removing his official title and rank.
Wénshèng secretly harbored resentment and discontent.
The Emperor heard of this,
and so had him imprisoned.
At that time, Rèn Yuē was captured,
and was imprisoned with Wénshèng.
Wénshèng said to Yuē:
“Why did you not surrender earlier,
causing me to come to this?”
Yuē replied:
“I did not see your horse’s tracks outside the gate,
how could I have surrendered?”
Wénshèng had no reply,
and subsequently died in prison.
Yīn Zǐchūn, courtesy name Yòuwén,
was a native of Gūzāng in Wǔwēi.
At the end of Jìn Yìxī [418 CE],
his great-grandfather followed Sòng Wǔdì in his southward migration,
reaching Nánpíng,
and settled there.
His father, Zhìbó, was a neighbor of Liáng Wǔdì,
and they were very close in their youth.
He once entered the Emperor’s private chambers,
and saw an unusual five-colored light.
He then clasped the Emperor’s hand and said:
“You will certainly become greatly noble later,
and will not be a mere subject.
The world is in chaos,
will it be you who brings peace to the common people?”
The Emperor said:
“Fortunately, do not speak too much.”
Thereupon, their affection grew even closer,
and whenever the Emperor had a request,
it was as if it were from an external treasury.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Zhìbó’s official position reached Cìshǐ of Liáng and Qín prefectures.
Zǐchūn’s career included positions such as Shùzhǔ of Qúshān and Tàishǒu of Dōngguǎn.
At that time, Shílùshān in Qīngzhōu bordered the sea,
and there was an ancient shrine there.
Cìshǐ Wáng Shénniàn, seeing that the people’s prayers were costly,
destroyed the divine image
and damaged the buildings.
On a crossbeam above the seat, there was a large snake over a *zhàng* [approx. 3 meters] long.
The laborers beat it but could not capture it,
and it managed to enter the seawater.
That night,
Zǐchūn dreamed of a person announcing his name and coming to Zǐchūn, saying:
“Someone has caused suffering,
destroying my dwelling.
Having nowhere to stay,
I admire your profound virtue
and wish to reside in this area.”
Zǐchūn secretly remembered this in his heart.
Two days later, he realized it,
and was very surprised,
thinking it was the god from his previous dream.
So he prepared sacrificial animals and wine and invited the god,
settling it in one place.
A few days later,
he again dreamed of a person in red robes who sent a message,
expressing thanks and saying:
“Having received your great kindness,
I shall repay you with a prefecture.”
Zǐchūn was delighted in his heart,
and served even more diligently.
After more than a month,
Wèi wanted to attack Qúshān.
Spies had previously informed him,
so Zǐchūn set an ambush and destroyed them.
An imperial edict appointed him Cìshǐ of Nánqīngzhōu,
stationed at Qúshān.
He was further promoted to Dūdū and Cìshǐ of Liáng and Qín prefectures.
Although Zǐchūn had no other talents,
he was known for his integrity when governing people.
His household was mixed,
but he himself wore dirty clothes,
and washed his feet only once every few years,
saying that each washing would cause loss of wealth and ruin of affairs,
and claimed that when he was in Liángzhōu,
washing his feet led to the downfall of Liángzhōu.
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
he was summoned to be Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
then promoted to Shìzhōng.
During Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion,
Yuán Dì ordered Zǐchūn to follow Wáng Sēngbiàn in attacking and subduing Shàolíng Wáng.
He also joined Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Xú Wénshèng in an eastern campaign against Jǐng.
Upon reaching Bèijī, they encountered Jǐng,
and Zǐchūn fought bravely,
excelling above all the armies.
When Yǐngzhōu fell,
the army retreated,
and he died in Jiānglíng.
Zǐkēng.
Yīn Kēng, courtesy name Zǐjiān,
was broadly versed in historical records,
and especially skilled in five-character poetry,
which was highly regarded at the time.
He served as Fǎcáo Cānjūn for Xiāngdōng Wáng of Liáng.
Initially, Kēng once hosted a banquet with guests and friends.
Seeing the cup-bearer,
he turned the wine and roasted meat to give to him.
All the seated guests laughed.
Kēng said:
“We drink wine all day,
but the one holding the cups does not know its taste,
which is not humane.”
When Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion occurred,
Kēng was once captured by the rebels.
Someone rescued him, and he escaped.
Kēng asked who it was,
and it was the former cup-bearer.
During the Tiānjiā period of Chén [560-566 CE],
he served as Zhōnglùshì Cānjūn for Shǐxīng Wáng.
Wén Dì once hosted a banquet for his officials to compose poetry.
Xú Líng mentioned Kēng,
and the Emperor immediately summoned Kēng to join the banquet,
and had him compose a poem about the newly completed Ānlègōng.
Kēng took up his brush and finished it immediately,
and the Emperor greatly admired it.
He was successively promoted to Jìnlíng Tàishǒu,
Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì,
and passed away shortly after.
A collection of his writings in three volumes circulated in the world.
Dù Zè,
was a native of Dùlíng in Jīngzhào.
His ancestors moved south from the north,
residing in Xiāngyáng of Yōngzhōu,
and his descendants settled there.
His father, Huáibǎo, had great ambition and integrity from a young age.
During the Tiānjiān period of Liáng [502-519 CE], he repeatedly achieved military merits.
Later, he again rendered meritorious service in Nánzhèng,
reaching the position of Cìshǐ of Liáng and Qín prefectures.
At the beginning of Dàtóng [535 CE],
the Wèi army again besieged Nánzhèng.
Huáibǎo ordered his third son, Ní, to lead two hundred men to fight the Wèi vanguard at Guāngdàosì.
A stray arrow hit his eye,
and he lost his horse.
The enemy’s spears were about to reach him,
but Ní cut down one of their cavalrymen, mounted his horse,
and galloped back.
Ní had extraordinary physical strength,
was skilled with horses and excellent at archery.
In one day, he fought seven or eight engagements.
The "Frost Bright Vermillion Bow" he carried required over four *shí* [approx. 480 kg] of force,
and his "Striped Silk Spear" was twenty-five *chǐ* [approx. 6 meters] long.
He had one hundred and seventy "one-heart, dare-to-die" warriors.
Each time he sallied forth, he killed and wounded several hundred people.
The enemy feared him,
calling him Dù Biāo.
Huáibǎo died in the prefecture,
and was given the posthumous title Huán Hóu.
At that time, the various armies were all guarding along the river,
the palace was empty.
Chén Shújiān (陳叔堅) reported to the Empress Dowager,
asking her to order Crown Prince's Retainer Sīmǎ Shēn (司馬申) to urgently summon Right General of the Guards Xiāo Móhē (蕭摩訶),
and bring troops to the west gate of the palace.
As Chén Shúlíng's (陳叔陵) situation became urgent,
he dispatched his Secretary Wéi Liàng (韋諒) to send musical instruments to Móhē (摩訶),
saying:
"If the matter is successful, I will make you a Grand Chancellor."
Móhē (摩訶) deceptively replied:
"I must wait until a trusted general of the King's inner circle comes personally,
only then will I dare to obey."
Shúlíng (叔陵) immediately sent Dài Xù (戴洫) and Tán Qíyín (譚騏驎) to Móhē (摩訶).
〔一八〕Móhē (摩訶) seized them and sent them to the palace,
where they were executed beneath the elevated corridor.
Their heads were displayed through the eastern city,
and then hung at the Zhūquèmén (朱雀門) gate.
Shúlíng (叔陵) knew he could not succeed,
so he went and drowned his consort Zhāng (張) and seven favored concubines in a well.
Shúlíng (叔陵) had some subordinate soldiers previously stationed in Xīnlín (新林).
Thereupon, he led several hundred men and horses,
crossed a small ferry,
intending to head to Xīnlín (新林),
and then enter the north by boat.
When he reached Báiyánglù (白楊路),
he was intercepted by the palace army.
When Bógù (伯固) saw the troops approaching,
he quickly fled into an alley.
Shúlíng (叔陵) drew his sword and pursued him,
but Bógù (伯固) turned back.
Most of Shúlíng's (叔陵) subordinates abandoned their armor and scattered.
Móhē's (摩訶) horse attendant Chén Zhìshēn (陳智深) rode up and stabbed Shúlíng (叔陵),
the eunuch Wáng Fēiqín (王飛禽) hacked at him dozens of times,
and the horse attendant Chén Zhònghuá (陳仲華) then decapitated him and sent the head to the palace.
From the hour of Yín (寅) to Sǐ (巳), peace was restored.
The Eight Secretaries of the Department of State Affairs memorialized:
"We request to follow the precedents of the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
to float the corpse in the river,
and to defile and inundate his residence;
and to also destroy the tomb and temple of his mother, the Páng (彭) clan,
and return the Xie (謝) clan's burial ground."
The Last Emperor followed their memorial.
All of Shúlíng's (叔陵) sons
were granted death on the same day.
Yùzhāng Wáng Shúyīng (豫章王叔英), courtesy name Zǐliè (子烈),
was the third son of Emperor Xuān (宣帝).
He was broad-minded and benevolent.
He was enfeoffed in the first year of Tàijiàn (太建).
Later, he held the position of Sīkōng (司空).
During the Dàyè (大業) reign of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
he was Fúlíng Tàishǒu (涪陵太守),
and died.
Chángshā Wáng Shújiān (長沙王叔堅), courtesy name Zǐchéng (子成),
was the fourth son of Emperor Xuān (宣ān).
His mother was originally a maid from a wine shop in Wúzhōng (吳中),
and a physiognomist said she would bear a noble son.
When Emperor Xuān (宣帝) was still humble,
he had relations with her while drinking,
and Shújiān (叔堅) was born.
When he became noble,
she was summoned and appointed Shúyí (淑儀).
Shújiān (叔堅) was strict and orderly from a young age,
and also somewhat indulged in drink,
so his brothers feared him.
He was fond of numerology,
and excelled in divination, geomancy, metallurgy, and jade carving,
mastering their subtleties.
Initially, he was enfeoffed as Fēngchéng Hóu (豐城侯).
He was enfeoffed in the first year of Tàijiàn (太建).
He successively rose to Dānyáng Yǐn (丹陽尹).
Initially,
Shújiān (叔堅) and Shǐxīng Wáng Shúlíng (始興王叔陵) both recruited retainers,
each vying for power and favor,
and were very displeased with each other.
At every court assembly and procession,
they would not concede precedence,
but would insist on taking separate paths,
and their attendants would sometimes fight over the road,
even to the point of death.
When Emperor Xuān (宣帝) fell ill,
Shújiān (叔堅) and Shúlíng (叔陵) both attended to the Last Emperor during his illness.
Shúlíng (叔陵) secretly harbored evil intentions,
and Shújiān (叔堅) suspected him,
secretly observing his actions.
When the rebellion occurred,
it was thanks to Shújiān (叔堅) that he was saved.
For his meritorious service, he was promoted to Piāoqí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (揚州刺史).
Soon after, he was transferred to Sīkōng (司空),
with his General and Inspector titles remaining as before.
At that time, the Last Emperor suffered from a wound
and could not attend to state affairs.
All matters, great or small,
were decided by Shújiān (叔堅),
whose power overshadowed the court.
The Last Emperor thus became estranged from and wary of him.
Kǒng Fàn (孔範), Guǎn Bīn (管斌), Shī Wénqìng (施文慶), and others,
who were former officials of the Eastern Palace,
secretly undermined him day and night.
In the first year of Zhìdé (至德),
an edict was issued ordering him to retain his original title but adopt the formalities of the Three Ministers,
and to be sent out as Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (江州刺史).
Before he departed,
he was soon made Sīkōng (司空),
though this was actually to seize his power.
Moreover, people were secretly ordered to create charms to bewitch him,
carving wooden effigies,
dressing them in Daoist robes,
and installing mechanisms
that allowed them to bow and kneel.
Day and night, sacrifices were offered under the stars and moon,
and curses were uttered against him.
Furthermore, people were ordered to submit memorials accusing him,
and investigations were made to confirm the facts.
The Last Emperor summoned Shújiān (叔堅) and imprisoned him in the Western Palace,
intending to depose him,
and ordered a close attendant to proclaim an imperial decree enumerating his faults.
Shújiān (叔堅) pleaded that he had been framed by sycophants,
and that he would be ashamed to face Shúlíng (叔陵) on the day of his death.
The Last Emperor was moved by his past achievements,
and so pardoned him,
relieving him of his official duties,
and allowing him to return to his residence as a prince.
Later, he held the position of Zhōngjūn Dàjiāngjūn (中軍大將軍), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司), and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史).
When his term was complete, he returned to the capital.
After Chén (陳) fell and entered Suí (隋) rule,
he was relocated to Guāzhōu (瓜州).
Shújiān (叔堅) had always been noble,
and did not know how his family managed their livelihood.
At this point, he and his consort Shěn (沈) indulged in heavy drinking,
and did not concern themselves with farming.
During the Dàyè (大業) period,
he was Suìníng Jùnshǒu (遂寧郡守),
and died.
Jiàn'ān Wáng Shúqīng (建安王叔卿), courtesy name Zǐbì (子弼),
was the fifth son of Emperor Xuān (宣帝).
His nature was straightforward,
he possessed talent and ability,
and his appearance was very imposing.
He was established in the fourth year of Tàijiàn (太建).
He held the position of Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監).
After Chén (陳) fell, he entered Suí (隋) rule.
During the Dàyè (大業) period,
he was Dūguān Láng (都官郎),
and Shàngdǎng Tōngshǒu (上黨通守).
Yídū Wáng Shúmíng (宜都王叔明), courtesy name Zǐzhāo (子昭),
was the sixth son of Emperor Xuān (宣帝).
His demeanor was beautiful,
and his bearing gentle and soft,
resembling a woman.
He was established in the fifth year of Tàijiàn (太建).
He held the position of Shìzhōng (侍中).
After Chén (陳) fell, he entered Suí (隋) rule.
During the Dàyè (大業) period,
he was Hónglú Shàopīng (鴻臚少卿).
Hédōng Wáng Shúxiàn (河東王叔獻), courtesy name Zǐgōng (子恭),
was the ninth son of Emperor Xuān (宣帝).
His nature was respectful and diligent,
intelligent and fond of learning.
He was established in the fifth year of Tàijiàn (太建).
He held the position of Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ (南徐州刺史).
He died,
and was posthumously granted Sīkōng (司空),
with the posthumous name Kāngjiǎn (康簡).
His son Xiàokuān (孝寬) succeeded him.
During the Dàyè (大業) period of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
he was Wènchéng Lìng (汶城令).
Xīncài Wáng Shúqí (新蔡王叔齊), courtesy name Zǐsù (子肅),
was the eleventh son of Emperor Xuān (宣帝).
His demeanor was bright and elegant,
he was extensively read in classics and histories,
and was good at writing.
He was established in the seventh year of Tàijiàn (太建).
He held the position of Shìzhōng (侍中).
After Chén (陳) fell, he entered Suí (隋) rule.
During the Dàyè (大業) period,
he was Shàngshū Zhǔkè Láng (尚書主客郎).
In the second year of Tàijiàn (570 CE),
[Chén Zhāodá] was sent to conquer Jiānglíng.
At that time, Emperor Míng of Liáng and the Zhōu army had amassed a large number of boats and ships in Qīngní.
Zhāodá dispatched his auxiliary generals Qián Dàojí and Chéng Wénjì to burn them with light boats.
The Zhōu also built a fort on the south bank of the gorge entrance,
named Ānshǔ Chéng.
They strung a large rope across the river,
wove reeds into a bridge,
and used it to transport military provisions.
Zhāodá then ordered his soldiers to make long halberds,
placed them on the tower ships,
and cut the rope from below.
With the rope broken and provisions cut off,
he then led his troops to attack the city,
and it surrendered.
In the third year (571 CE),
he died of illness in the army,
and was posthumously granted the title of Dà Jiāngjūn.
Zhāodá was strict and harsh by nature.
Whenever he was ordered to go on an expedition,
he would travel twice the normal speed day and night.
However, for any victories he achieved,
he would always attribute the credit to his generals and commanders.
His meals and drinks
were the same as those of his subordinates,
and the officers and soldiers were attached to him for this reason.
At every feast,
he would arrange for a grand display of female entertainers and various music,
including Qiāng and Hú sounds.
Their music, postures, and appearances
were all among the finest of the time.
He would not abandon this even when facing the enemy.
In the fourth year (572 CE),
he was granted the honor of being enshrined in Emperor Wén's ancestral temple.
His son, Dàbǎo,
inherited the title of Shàolíng Jùn Gōng,
and held the position of Fēngzhōu Cìshǐ.
While in the province, he was greedy and unrestrained,
causing the common people to resent him bitterly.
The Later Emperor replaced him with the Tàipú Qīng Lǐ Yūn.
Dàbǎo then ambushed and killed Yūn and rebelled.
He was soon captured,
his head was impaled at Zhūquè Háng,
and his three familial exterminations were carried out.
Wú Míngchè, courtesy name Tōngzhào,
was a native of Qínjùn.
His father, Shù,
was a Yòujūn Jiāngjūn of Liáng.
Míngchè was orphaned young
and was extremely filial by nature.
At the age of fourteen,
he was distressed that his ancestral tomb had not been repaired.
As his family was poor and had no means to provide for it,
he diligently engaged in farming.
At that time, the world suffered from a severe drought,
and the crops withered.
Míngchè was grieved and indignant,
and would often go to the fields and cry aloud,
appealing to Heaven.
A few days later,
someone returning from the fields
said that the seedlings had revived.
Míngchè suspected he was being deceived,
but when he went, it was as reported.
In autumn, he had a great harvest,
sufficient to cover the funeral expenses.
At that time, there was a man named Yī,
skilled in geomancy for graves,
who said to Míngchè's elder brother:
"On the day of your burial,
there will surely be someone riding a white horse chasing deer passing by the tomb.
This is a sign that the youngest filial son will achieve great nobility."
At the appointed time, it indeed came to pass.
Míngchè was indeed Shù's youngest son.
When Hóu Jǐng attacked the capital,
Míngchè had over three thousand hú of grain and wheat.
As his neighbors were starving,
he said to his elder brothers:
"People today do not expect to live long;
how can we not share this with our fellow villagers?"
Thereupon, he divided it equally by household,
sharing their abundance and scarcity.
Bandits heard of this and avoided them,
and many relied on him to survive.
When Emperor Wǔ of Chén was garrisoned at Jīngkǒu,
he cultivated a deep bond with Míngchè.
Míngchè then went to see Emperor Wǔ,
who descended the steps for him,
took his hand, and immediately seated him.
Míngchè also had a slight understanding of historical records and classics.
He studied astronomy, gūxū (auspicious/inauspicious times), and dùnjiǎ (esoteric divination) with Zhōu Hóngzhèng of Rǔnán,
gaining a general mastery of these arts.
He somewhat considered himself a hero,
and Emperor Wǔ also held him in high regard.
Upon receiving the imperial abdication,
he was appointed Ānnán Jiāngjūn.
He, Hóu Āndū, and Zhōu Wényù led troops to suppress Wáng Lín.
When the armies were defeated and annihilated,
Míngchè extricated himself and returned to the capital.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he was promoted from his original position to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
When Zhōu Dí rebelled,
an edict appointed Míngchè as Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
concurrently Yùzhāng Tàishǒu,
to command all armies to suppress Dí.
Míngchè was by nature upright and inflexible,
and his administration was not very harmonious.
Emperor Wén heard of this
and sent Ānchéng Wáng Xū to replace Míngchè,
ordering him to return to court with his original title.
In the fifth year of Tiānjiā (566 CE),
he was transferred to Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
When he took his leave to depart for the commandery,
the Emperor said to him:
"Although Wúxīng is a commandery, it is the venerable homeland of the Emperor,
and thus I bestow it upon you."
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
and soon thereafter promoted to Dānyáng Yǐn.
He was also granted an edict allowing forty armed guards to accompany him in and out of the palace.
When Dào Zhòngjǔ fabricated an edict to bring out Emperor Xuān,
Máo Xǐ knew it was a deception.
Emperor Xuān was fearful
and sent Xǐ to consult with Míngchè.
Míngchè said:
"The successor ruler is in mourning,
and there are many shortcomings in the affairs of state.
Your Highness is truly a Zhōu or Shào [of antiquity],
your virtue surpasses that of Yī or Huò.
I wish you would stay inside and plan deeply;
be careful not to harbor doubts."
When Huá Jiǎo, the Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ, secretly harbored rebellious intentions,
an edict appointed Míngchè as Dūdū and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and he was ordered to suppress Jiǎo with Zhēngnán Dà Jiāngjūn Chúnyú Liàng and others.
After Jiǎo was pacified,
he was granted the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī
and elevated to the rank of Gōng.
In the fifth year of Tàijiàn (573 CE),
the court debated a northern expedition.
While the high officials had differing opinions,
Míngchè resolutely requested to go.
An edict added the titles of Shìzhōng and Dūdū Zhēngtǎo Zhūjūnsì to him.
He commanded over one hundred thousand troops and departed from the capital.
Along the river, cities and towns
successively surrendered.
When the army reached Qínjùn,
the Qí Dà Jiāngjūn Wèi Pòhú led troops to reinforce them,
but Míngchè defeated and drove them away,
and Qínjùn surrendered.
Emperor Xuān, considering Qínjùn Míngchè's old hometown,
ordered a grand sacrificial feast (Tàiláo) to be prepared,
and allowed him to worship at the shrine and sweep the tombs.
The civil and military ceremony was very grand,
and the local people honored him.
He then captured Rénzhōu.
He was appointed Zhēngběi Dà Jiāngjūn
and promoted to the title of Nánpíng Jùn Gōng.
He then pressed on to Shòuyáng.
Qí sent Wáng Lín to defend it,
but Míngchè attacked at night,
and by midnight, the defenders collapsed.
The Qí army retreated to the Xiàngguó Chéng and Jīn Chéng.
Míngchè ordered his army to improve their siege equipment,
and also blocked the Féishuǐ river to flood the city.
The city suffered from dampness,
many had abdominal illnesses,
their hands and feet were swollen,
and sixteen or seventeen out of ten died.
At this time, Qí sent Dà Jiāng Pí Jǐnghé to lead several hundred thousand troops to reinforce them.
They stopped thirty lǐ from Shòuchūn
and did not advance.
All the generals asked:
"What is our plan?"
Míngchè said:
"Speed is paramount in warfare,
but they have set up camp and are not advancing,
blunting their own vanguard.
I know they dare not fight, this is clear."
Thereupon, he personally donned his armor,
and attacked fiercely from all four sides.
The city was terrified,
and with one drumbeat, Wáng Lín and others were captured and sent to Jiànyè.
Jǐnghé, in fear, fled.
An edict appointed him Chējì Dà Jiāngjūn and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ,
increasing his feudal household to three thousand five hundred households including the previous ones.
An emissary, Xiāo Chún, was sent to Shòuyáng to convey the decree.
Míngchè set up an altar south of the city.
Two hundred thousand soldiers,
arrayed with flags, drums, spears, and armor,
ascended the altar to receive the decree.
The ceremony completed, they withdrew.
Jìngchéng 幼聰慧,
好讀書.
起家著作佐郎.
永定元年,
領度所部士卒,
隨周文育, 侯安都征王琳,
於沌口敗績,
為琳所縶.
二年,
隨文育, 安都得歸.
父度為吳郡太守,
以敬成監郡.
光大元年,
為巴州刺史.
尋為水軍,
隨吳明徹平華皎.
二年,
以父憂去職.
尋起為南豫州刺史,
襲爵湘東郡公.
太建五年,
除吳興太守.
隨都督吳明徹北討,
出秦郡,
別遣敬成為都督,
乘金翅自歐陽引埭泝江,
由廣陵,
齊人皆城守,
弗敢出.
自繁梁湖下淮,
剋淮陰, 山陽, 鹽城三郡,
仍進剋鬱洲.
進號壯武將軍,
鎮朐山.
坐於軍中輒科訂,
并誅新附者,
免官.
尋除安州刺史,
鎮宿預.
卒,
諡曰思.
子敞嗣.
Dù Léng 字雄盛,
吳郡錢唐人也.
少落泊,
不為時知.
頗涉書傳.
游嶺南,
事梁廣州刺史新渝侯蕭映.
映卒,
從陳武帝,
平蔡路養, 李遷仕皆有功.
梁元帝承制,
授石州刺史, 上陌縣侯.
侯景平後,
武帝鎮朱方,
以稜監義興, 琅邪二郡.
武帝謀誅王僧辯,
引稜與侯安都等共議,
稜難之.
武帝懼其泄己,
乃以手巾絞稜,
稜悶絕於地,
因閉於別室.
軍發,
召與同行.
及僧辯平後,
武帝東征杜龕等,
留稜與安都居守.
徐嗣徽, 任約引齊師濟江,
攻臺城,
安都與稜隨方抗拒,
未嘗解帶.
賊平,
以功除右衞將軍, 丹陽尹.
永定元年,
位侍中, 中領軍.
武帝崩,
文帝在南皖.
時內無嫡嗣,
外有強敵,
侯瑱, 侯安都, 徐度等並在軍中,
朝廷宿將,
唯稜在都,
獨典禁兵,
乃與蔡景歷等祕不發喪,
奉迎文帝.
文帝即位,
遷領軍將軍,
以預建立功,
改封永城縣侯,
位丹陽尹.
廢帝即位,
加特進, 侍中.
光大元年,
解尹,
量置佐史,
給扶.
太建元年,
出為吳興太守.
二年,
徵為侍中.
尋加特進, 護軍將軍.
三年,
以公事免侍中, 護軍.
四年,
復為侍中, 右光祿大夫,
將軍, 佐史, 扶並如故.
稜歷事三帝,
並見恩寵.
末年不預征役,
優游都下.
頃之,
卒于官.
贈開府儀同三司,
諡曰成,
配享武帝廟庭.
子安世嗣.
Zhōu Tiěwǔ,
不知何許人也.
語音傖重,
膂力過人,
便馬槊.
事梁河東王蕭譽,
以勇敢聞.
譽為湘州,
以為臨蒸令.
侯景之亂,
梁元帝遣世子方等伐譽,
譽拒戰,
大捷,
方等死,
鐵武功最.
及王僧辯討譽,
於陣獲之,
將烹焉,
鐵武呼曰:
「侯景未滅,
奈何殺壯士! 」
僧辯奇其言,
宥之,
還其麾下.
及侯景西上,
鐵武從僧辯剋任約,
獲宋子仙,
每戰有功.
元帝承制,
授潼州刺史,
封沌陽縣子.
又從僧辯定建鄴,
降謝答仁,
平陸納於湘州,
錄前後功,
進爵為侯.
陳武帝誅僧辯,
鐵武率所部降,
因復其本職.
徐嗣徽引齊寇度江,
鐵武破其水軍.
嗣徽平,
遷太子左衞率.
尋隨周文育拒蕭勃,
文育命鐵武偏軍襲勃,
禽勃前軍歐陽頠.
又隨文育西征王琳於沌口,
敗績,
與文育, 侯安都並為琳所禽.
琳見諸將與語,
唯鐵武辭氣不屈,
故琳盡宥文育之徒,
獨鐵武見害.
贈侍中, 護軍.
天嘉五年,
文帝又詔配食武帝廟庭.
子瑜嗣.
Chéng Língxǐ 字玄滌,
新安海寧人也.
少以勇力聞,
步行日二百里,
便騎善游,
素為鄉里畏伏.
侯景之亂,
據黟, 歙聚徒以拒景.
景軍據有新安,
新安太守湘西鄉侯蕭隱奔依靈洗,
靈洗奉以主盟.
梁元帝授靈洗譙州刺史資,
領新安太守,
封巴丘縣侯.
後助王僧辯鎮防.
He was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and was in charge of the affairs of the Five Rites.
At that time, Chén Bāo, the Cìshǐ of Hézhōu, was notoriously corrupt,
sending envoys to the island to collect fish,
and also ordering people to beg for rice in the six commanderies.
The common people suffered greatly from this.
Yuán Ráo impeached him and had him dismissed.
Wǔlíng Wáng Bólǐ, the Tàishǒu of Wúxīng, and Nánkāng Sì Wáng Fāngtài, the Nèishǐ of Yùzhāng,
were arrogant and lawless.
Yuán Ráo investigated and impeached them,
and they were all cashiered and dismissed.
Yuán Ráo was fair-minded by nature,
skilled in upholding the law,
well-versed in precedents,
and clear and experienced in administrative principles.
When officials broke the law,
when policies were inconvenient,
or when they fell short of the requirements of Confucian ethics,
he would correct them as appropriate,
contributing greatly.
He was promoted to Nánkāng Nèishǐ.
He used over three thousand hù of his official rice salary to assist the people with their taxes,
visited and inquired about the elderly,
and rescued the destitute.
The common people relied on him greatly.
Due to his excellent administration, he was recalled to court,
and an imperial edict added the title Sànqí Chángshì.
Later, he served as Lìbù Shàngshū,
and then died.
Hán Zǐgāo was
a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His family was originally humble.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he lived in the capital.
When Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Chén Wéndì went out to govern Wúxīng.
Zǐgāo was sixteen years old,
with his hair still in topknots.
His appearance was beautiful,
resembling a woman.
He joined a unit at the Huái River bank, hitching a ride to return to his hometown.
Wéndì saw him and asked:
"Can you serve me?"
Zǐgāo agreed.
Zǐgāo's original name was Mánzǐ;
the Emperor changed his name.
He was respectful and cautious by nature,
carrying the Emperor's personal knife and serving wine and roasted meat.
The Emperor was impatient,
but Zǐgāo understood his wishes.
As he grew older,
he practiced riding and archery,
and had considerable courage and decisiveness,
wishing to become a general.
When Dù Kān was pacified,
he was allotted soldiers.
Wéndì loved him very much,
and he was never far from his side.
The Emperor once dreamed of riding a horse up a mountain;
the path was dangerous, and he was about to fall,
but Zǐgāo pushed and supported him, allowing him to ascend.
When Wéndì was campaigning against Zhāng Biāo,
Shěn Tài and others had already surrendered.
The Emperor occupied the prefectural city,
and Zhōu Wényù was stationed at Xiāngyán Sì in the northern suburbs.
Zhāng Biāo returned from Shànxiàn at night to raid the city.
Wéndì exited from the North Gate.
In the chaos and darkness of the evening,
the soldiers were in disarray,
and only Zǐgāo was by his side.
Wéndì then sent Zǐgāo through the chaotic troops to see Wényù,
and to report back and convey messages.
In the darkness, he also went to comfort the various armies.
As Wéndì's scattered soldiers gradually gathered,
Zǐgāo led them into Wényù's camp,
and together they erected a palisade.
The next day, Biāo was defeated;
Biāo fled to Sōngshān,
and Zhèdōng was pacified.
Wéndì then assigned many of his subordinates to Zǐgāo.
Zǐgāo also spent money lightly and treated scholars with respect,
so many people came to him.
When Wéndì ascended the throne,
he appointed Zǐgāo as Yòujūn Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed him as the Earl of Wénzhāo Xiàn.
When Wáng Lín was pacified,
Zǐgāo's command grew even larger.
Generals and soldiers attached themselves to him,
and whatever he recommended,
the Emperor would employ.
In the sixth year of Tiānjiā (565),
he was made Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
When Wéndì was ill,
he attended him with medicine.
When the Deposed Emperor (Fèi Dì) ascended the throne,
he was given the additional title of Sànqí Chángshì.
When Xuāndì entered to assist in governance,
Zǐgāo's military power became too great,
and he felt deeply insecure.
He frequently visited the imperial secretariat and chancellery for advice,
and also sought to be dispatched as a governor to Hēngzhōu and Guǎngzhōu.
In the eighth month of the first year of Guāngdà (567),
Lù Fāng, the former magistrate of Shàngyú Xiàn, and Zǐgāo's military commander accused him of rebellion.
Xuāndì was in the Shàngshū Shěng,
and he summoned civil and military officials to discuss establishing an imperial heir apparent.
Zǐgāo was present.
He was seized and sent to the Tíngwèi (Court of the Imperial Clan).
That evening, along with Dào Zhòngjǔ, he was granted death.
His father Yánqìng and his sons and younger brothers were all pardoned.
Huà Jiǎo was
a native of Jìyáng, Jìnlíng.
His family had been minor officials for generations.
Jiǎo served as Shàngshū Bǐbù Lìshǐ in the Liáng dynasty.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
he served Wáng Wěi, one of Jǐng's partisans.
When Chén Wǔdì marched south,
Wéndì was imprisoned by Jǐng,
and Jiǎo treated Wéndì very kindly.
When Jǐng was pacified,
Wéndì became Tàishǒu of Wúxīng,
and appointed Jiǎo as Dū Lùshì,
trusting him deeply.
When Wéndì pacified Dù Kān,
he further assigned armored troops to Jiǎo.
He was clear in his management of subordinates
and good at comforting and receiving them,
giving his clothes and sharing his food,
always distributing fairly, whether little or much.
In the first year of Tiānjiā (560),
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Huáirén Xiàn.
When Wáng Lín marched east,
Jiǎo followed Hóu Tián to resist him.
After Lín was pacified,
he was put in charge of Jiāngzhōu affairs.
Later, he followed Dūdū Wú Míngchè to campaign against Zhōu Dí.
After Dí was pacified,
he was promoted to the rank of Marquis for his merits,
and also appointed Dūdū and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Jiǎo rose from a lowly official,
was good at managing property,
and also campaigned in the mountain caves,
obtaining many bronze drums and captured people,
all of whom he sent to the capital.
When the Deposed Emperor ascended the throne,
he was re-enfeoffed as the Duke of Chóng'ān Xiàn.
After Hán Zǐgāo was executed,
Jiǎo felt insecure internally.
In the first year of Guāngdà (567),
he secretly requested Guǎngzhōu
to observe the emperor's intentions.
Xuāndì falsely agreed to this,
but the imperial edict was not issued.
Jiǎo also sent envoys to invite Zhōu troops,
and furthermore honored Liáng Míngdì.
His forces were very strong.
The imperial edict then appointed Wú Míngchè as Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
intending to attack Jiǎo with light troops.
Fearing Jiǎo might strike first,
he sent Míngchè ahead with thirty thousand troops,
to ride the Jīnchì directly to Yǐngzhōu,
and also sent Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn Chúnyú Liàng with fifty thousand troops,
to follow on large ships.
At that time, Liáng Míngdì sent a naval force to support Jiǎo.
Zhōu Wǔdì sent Wèi Gōng Yǔwén Zhí to camp at Lǔshān,
and also sent Zhùguó Chánghú Gōng Yuán Dìng to besiege Yǐngzhōu.
Liáng Míngdì appointed Jiǎo as Sīkōng.
Dài Sēngshuò, the Bāzhōu Cìshǐ; Rèn Mánnú, the Héngyáng Nèishǐ; Pān Zhìqián, the Bālíng Nèishǐ; Zhāng Zhāoyù, the Yuèyáng Tàishǒu; Cáo Xuān, the Guìyáng Tàishǒu; and Qián Míng, the Xiāngdōng Tàishǒu,
were all subordinate to Jiǎo.
Additionally, Cáo Qìng, the Chángshā Tàishǒu, and others who were originally under Jiǎo,
were used by him.
The Emperor feared that the governors and administrators of the upstream regions would all be incited and misled by Jiǎo,
so he issued an edict granting a partial amnesty to Xiāngzhōu and Bāzhōu,
promising clemency to the rebel chief commanders and generals
who would surrender.
Jiǎo loaded firewood onto large ships,
and set them on fire with the wind.
Soon the wind shifted, and his own ships caught fire.
Jiǎo was utterly defeated,
and fled with Dài Sēngshuò to Jiānglíng.
Yuán Dìng and others had no boats to cross the river,
so they marched on foot to Bālíng.
The city of Bālíng had already been occupied by Chén forces,
so they surrendered
and were sent to Jiànyè.
Jiǎo eventually died in Jiānglíng.
His partisans were all executed,
with only Rèn Mánnú, Zhāng Zhāoyù, Cáo Xuān, and Liú Guǎngyè being spared.
Liú Shīzhī was
a native of Xiāngrén, Pèiguó.
His family was originally of noble lineage.
His grandfather, Xīzhī,
was the Qí Huáinán Tàishǒu,
known for his good governance.
His father, Jǐngyàn,
was the Liáng Sīnóng Qīng.
In the old customs of the northern lands,
when someone was ill, it was essential to send a son or younger brother to inquire.
Jì was thirteen years old,
when his father sent him to visit Wéi Huá of the same commandery.
Huá's son, Xuán, had a great reputation,
and when he saw Jì, he was impressed,
and gave his daughter to him in marriage.
He was successively promoted to the Rear Army Registrar and Aide-de-camp for Liú Yìxīn, the Prince of Chángshā.
In the seventh year of Yuánjiā (430 CE),
he followed Dào Yànzhī into Hénán,
and was made Jiànwǔ General.
When the Wèi withdrew all their Hénán garrisons and returned to Héběi,
Yànzhī ordered Jì to defend Luòyáng.
The city of Luòyáng had been in ruins for a long time,
and there were no provisions.
When Yànzhī was defeated and retreated,
Jì wanted to abandon the city and flee,
but feared being executed by Emperor Wén.
Earlier,
when Emperor Wǔ pacified Guān and Luò,
he had brought the old bronze bells and stands back south.
A large bell had fallen into the Luò River,
and at this time, the Emperor sent General Yáo Sǒngfū to lead 1,500 men to retrieve it.
At that time, Sǒngfū was leading his troops to pull the bell from the Luò River,
when Jì sent an envoy to deceive him, saying:
"Since the barbarians have crossed south,
Luòchéng is strategically weak.
We have now repaired the city walls and moats,
and they are all firm and strong.
Our military provisions are also sufficient;
what we lack is men.
If you lead your troops to join us,
and we defend this city together,
once a great achievement is established,
retrieving the bell will not be too late."
Sǒngfū believed him,
and led his troops to Jì.
When they arrived, the city was indefensible,
and there were no provisions.
Thereupon, Sǒngfū led his troops away,
and Jì also abandoned the city and fled south.
He reported to Emperor Wén:
"I originally intended to defend to the death,
but Yáo Sǒngfū entered the city and immediately fled,
causing morale to collapse,
and it could no longer be restrained."
The Emperor was enraged,
and ordered Jiànwēi General Zhèng Shùnzhī to kill Sǒngfū in Shòuyáng.
Sǒngfū was
a man from Wǔkāng, Wúxīng,
courageous and strong,
and no lesser general of Sòng could compare.
In the seventeenth year (440 CE),
Jì became the Inspector of Qīng and Jì provinces.
He served for eight years,
and his benevolent governance was evident throughout the Qí region.
From Yìxī to the end of Sòng,
only Yáng Mùzhī and Jì among the Inspectors were praised by officials and common people.
Later, he was summoned to be the Left Army General.
His elder brother, Tǎn, replaced him as Inspector,
and the people of the northern lands considered this an honor.
Tǎn's eldest son, Wǎn, was Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
Emperor Wén once sent a sealed imperial edict to Tǎn,
which Wǎn would invariably open and read.
Before a letter could be dispatched,
it would sometimes be recalled.
One time, after an imperial edict had been sent,
a major investigation was conducted.
The Emperor sent his Chief Scribe to interrogate and reprimand Jì,
and to investigate who opened the letter.
Jì replied:
"The one who opened the letter is my fourth son, Jìwén.
I await punishment."
The Emperor specially pardoned him and did not question further.
He died in office.
His fifth son, Yòuwén, was lacking in conduct.
At the beginning of Emperor Míng's reign,
he was enfeoffed as the County Baron of Shàoyáng for his military achievements,
but was soon stripped of his title for cunning and deceit.
Later, by exposing the rebellion plot of Grand Commandant Lújiāng Wáng Huī,
he was appointed Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng.
During the Yuánhuī era of the Deposed Emperor, he became Sànqí Chángshì.
Wherever Yòuwén governed, he was greedy and oppressive,
accumulating thousands of gold coins for his family.
He resided close to Shěn Bó and Sūn Chāozhī,
and was also on very good terms with Ruǎn Diànfū.
After Diànfū died,
the Deposed Emperor deeply resented Yòuwén.
The Emperor would make incognito trips,
often listening to string and wind instruments outside Yòuwén's gate at night.
Over time, his resentment grew unbearable,
so he personally led his imperial guards to execute Yòuwén, Bó, Chāozhī, and others.
His elder brother, Shúwén, who was Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
was also executed.
Shēn Tián, courtesy name Gōngxiū,
was a native of Wèi County, Wèi Commandery.
His great-grandfather, Zhōng,
was Sītú for Shí Jìlóng.
When Sòng Wǔdì pacified Guǎnggù,
Tián's father, Xuān, and Xuān's paternal cousin, Yǒng, were all able to return to Jìn,
and both were recognized for their competence and utility.
When Emperor Wǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Xuān as Tàizhōng Dàfū.
In the early Yuánjiā era, Xuān
served successively as Inspector of Yǎn and Qīng provinces.
Tián's elder brother, Mó, defended Huátái with Zhū Xiūzhī.
The Wèi captured Huátái and took Mó captive.
Later, he was able to return
and became the Grand Administrator of Jìnglíng.
Tián initially served as a concurrent Aide-de-camp for Piàojì Liú Dàolián.
When Sòng was established,
he was invited to be the Palace General of the Eastern Palace.
After returning to the imperial court,
he served at the palace for ten years,
never asking for leave for rest or urgent matters.
He successively served as Grand Administrator of Xiàpéi and Běihǎi commanderies,
achieving administrative success wherever he went.
He also served as Grand Administrator of Běiqiáo and Liáng commanderies.
The border of the commanderies was adjacent to areas of dense thorns and brigands,
and was frequently subjected to raids.
Upon Tián's arrival,
he secretly learned of an approaching bandit attack.
He then ambushed them at a strategic point,
catching them by surprise,
and completely captured and annihilated them.
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā (435 CE),
he was promoted to Supervisor of Military Affairs for Lǔ, Dōngpíng, and Jìběi commanderies, and Grand Administrator of Tàishān,
where his authority and benevolence were equally renowned,
benefiting both officials and common people.
In the twenty-first year (444 CE),
Jì Province's seat was moved to Lìxià,
and Tián was made Inspector of Jì Province,
with additional supervisory duties.
The following year,
he was made Grand Administrator of Jìnán.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ ascended the throne,
he became Inspector of Qīng Province,
soon with additional supervisory duties.
The Qí region had been constantly involved in warfare for years,
and the people were suffering.
Tián defended the border,
and encouraged farming and sericulture.
Within two or three years,
the region became prosperous and abundant.
He was by nature incorruptible and frugal.
Though he frequently held provincial and commandery posts,
his wife and children still suffered from hunger and cold,
and the world praised him for this.
Later, he was appointed Inspector of Yù Province,
but was recalled due to illness,
and died on the way.
On the day of his death,
his family had no remaining assets.
His son, Shí,
was Grand Administrator of Nánqiáo.
Mó's son, Yuánsì,
was Grand Administrator of Hǎilíng.
Yuánsì's younger brother, Qiān,
was Internal Administrator of Línchuān.
Yǒng's son, Tǎn,
in the early Xiàojiàn era, was the Right Imperial Guard Commander of the Crown Prince,
and Inspector of Xú Province.
In the first year of Dàmíng (457 CE),
the Wèi attacked Yǎn Province.
Emperor Xiàowǔ sent the Left Imperial Guard Commander of the Crown Prince, Xuē Āndū, and the Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng, Shěn Fǎxì, to defend the north.
By the time they reached Yǎn Province,
the Wèi army had already departed.
Tǎn suggested that since the brigands and fugitives
frequently harassed the border people,
and the army had been dispatched without achieving anything,
it would be appropriate to use this opportunity to suppress them.
The Emperor agreed.
However, the brigands and fugitives had already heard the news,
and their entire villages fled.
Āndū and Fǎxì were dismissed from their posts but retained their duties as commoners,
while Tǎn was to be executed in the marketplace.
The numerous officials pleaded on his behalf, but to no avail.
Just as the execution was about to be carried out,
Shǐxīng Gōng Shěn Qìngzhī entered the marketplace, embraced Tǎn, and wept bitterly, saying:
"You are innocent,
wrongfully executed by the imperial court.
I too will not last long after entering this market."
The market official reported this to the Emperor,
who then pardoned Tǎn's life
and imprisoned him in the Imperial Arsenal.
Soon after, he was pardoned,
and reinstated as Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
He died of illness.
Farmers
are exempted from compulsory labor, and allowed to raise daughters;
they are permitted to keep bondservants.
Maids may only wear blue cloth garments.
Monks and nuns are all required to eat vegetarian food.
If this is done,
then the Dharma will flourish and customs will thrive,
the country will be rich
and its people prosperous.
Otherwise,
it is feared that in the future, temples will be built everywhere,
and every household will shave their heads (become monks/nuns).
With every foot of land and every person,
it will no longer belong to the state.
The imperial court promoted and appointed veterans
to govern the prefectures and commanderies on the three borders,
disregarding the principles of governing people,
and solely focusing on greed and cruelty.
They oppressed the good and the innocent,
causing harm worse than jackals
and wolves.
The people of Jiāng and Xiāng especially suffered from this malpractice.
Beyond the three passes,
evil was encountered everywhere.
These meritorious individuals, at the beginning of their defection,
had only themselves;
but when they were
appointed,
they all recruited their private retainers (bùqǔ).
And the people of Yáng and Xú,
