oppressed by numerous corvée duties,
many joined their recruitment,
coveting their wealth.
They all put down empty names in the registers,
only sending them out to
the three ferries (sānjīn),
their names recorded for distant service,
while their bodies returned to their hometowns.
Furthermore, fearing scrutiny from their original jurisdictions,
they then fled to other territories.
The rise of "migrant households" (qiáo hù)
is precisely due to this reason.
Moreover,
since the rise of the Liáng dynasty,
people have been conscripted for military service,
known as "three-fives" (sānwǔ).
When people joined as recruited soldiers,
the commanding generals showed no grace,
and their care and support were unreasonable,
many died.
They were then falsely branded as traitors
or deserters.
Some died on the battlefield,
but their names were on the list of rebels.
The supervisory warrants were issued for their apprehension,
calling them "fugitive rebels,"
and their family members were recorded as bondservants.
If the whole family then rebelled,
then those of the same
registry were seized.
If those of the same registry then rebelled,
then those of the same vicinage were seized.
If those of the same vicinage then rebelled,
then people were seized from the entire village.
If one person committed an offense,
the entire village would be emptied.
Even during periods of amnesty
and grace,
when past offenses were supposed to be completely wiped clean,
the supervisory warrants still followed the old dates,
with strict deadlines.
Superiors did not trust their subordinates,
〔三四〕who in turn pressured each other.
When the imperial envoy arrived at the prefecture,
the prefecture
then dispatched an escorting envoy to the commandery.
Prefectures and commanderies competed in their urgency,
all heading down to the cities.
Most magistrates were mediocre talents,
and became submissive out of fear.
Thus, they collected household taxes,
presenting their baskets
and hampers,
making people pay heavy bribes,
and promising to issue empty documents.
If any local official attempted even slightly to reform these customs,
severe penalties would immediately follow.
Consequently, officials everywhere indulged in avarice,
in order to serve
their superiors.
He also said,
"I request that the entry of "living mouths" (shēngkǒu) into the North from the border garrisons be stopped,
and that the abandoned passes and ferries be strictly investigated and exposed."
He also said,
"The young man from Lúlíng
is not suitable to guard Xiāngyáng;
Zuǒ Púshè Wáng Jiǎn,
while in mourning,
was appointed to Wújùn,
without any refusal or modesty."
His words were sharp and critical.
He also
"requested the restoration of the four stars in the suburban sacrifice."
Although the Emperor could not adopt all his suggestions,
he praised his uprightness
and promoted him to be the Magistrate of Yùzhāng Zhōnglíng and
Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì.
In the seventh year of Pǔtōng,
Nánzhōu Jīn was renamed Nánjīn Xiàowèi,
with Zǔ Shēn appointed to the post.
He was granted the title Yúnqí Jiāngjūn,
with a salary of two thousand measures of grain.
He was ordered to recruit two thousand bùqǔ.
When he arrived at Nánzhōu,
he was publicly strict and incorruptible.
For a long time, royal princes and powerful families passed through the ferry,
〔三五〕disregarding laws and regulations,
and harboring fugitives.
Zǔ Shēn searched for and investigated evildoers,
without fear of the powerful,
and brought them to justice.
He impeached Shàolíng Wáng, the Governor of Jiāngzhōu, and Zhōu Shě, the Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince, for corruption.
People far and near stood on tiptoe (in awe),
none daring to be reckless.
The Administrator of Huáinán feared him as if he were a superior official.
He always wore a simple cloth jacket,
used a plain wooden desk,
and his meals never exceeded one meat dish.
When an old woman presented him with an early green cucumber,
Zǔ Shēn repaid her with a bolt of silk.
Later, a rich man tried to bribe him with goods,
and Zǔ Shēn had him whipped and paraded before the public.
The court and the populace dreaded him,
and all requests for favors ceased.
His subordinates were all elite soldiers;
his orders were obeyed and prohibitions enforced.
When pursuing criminals,
he would cross borders to capture them.
There were once bandits on the Jiāng River;
Zǔ Shēn personally led the campaign to suppress them.
When the battle lines were formed, he did not dare to advance immediately,
but ordered his trusted men to lead the charge.
If they did not advance in time,
he would execute them.
Consequently, he thoroughly defeated the bandits,
his prestige shook far and near,
and the Chángjiāng River became peaceful and clear.
Commentary: Good governance for the people
is like a skilled craftsman with clay:
little effort is expended, but many vessels are made.
In the Hàn dynasty, the population was prosperous,
and legal affairs were simple and lenient.
The duties of commanderies and prefectures
were free from external disturbances.
Rewards and punishments were enforced,
and officials often made their own decisions.
Imperial edicts were rarely
sent to the states and cities.
Officials who held office sometimes did so for their descendants,
all promoting virtuous governance to maximize harmony among people,
and fostering righteousness and humility to maintain simplicity and longevity.
Thus, the transformations brought about by Gōng and Huáng
were easily achieved.
Later generations saw
the proliferation of deceit and falsehood,
the population dwindled compared to former times,
and affairs were more numerous than in previous eras.
Achieving accomplishments and establishing good customs
became a hundred times more difficult.
If one were to govern the people of this age
with the transformative power of antiquity,
or if a good official of today
were to manage the customs of previous eras,
then the "string music in Wǔchéng"
would be too slow,
and "lying down to govern Huáinán"
would barely be possible.
It is not necessarily that today's talents are inferior to those of old,
but rather that the quality of governance has become purer or baser.

Fú Zhēng was appointed Guózǐ Bóshì,
and concurrently served as Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi.
At that time, Shǐxīng Nèishǐ Hé Yuǎn had repeatedly achieved a reputation for integrity.
Emperor Wǔ promoted him to Huángmén Shìláng,
and soon after, transferred him to Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn and Jiān Wú Jùnshì.
Fú Zhēng, considering his social standing had always been superior to Hé Yuǎn’s,
and both were praised for being incorruptible as officials,
was displeased that Hé Yuǎn was repeatedly promoted
while he himself only advanced step by step.
His expectations were not met,
so he often feigned illness and stayed at home.
He soon requested leave to go to Dōngyáng to attend his sister’s funeral,
then stayed in Kuàijī to build a residence,
and formally requested to be relieved of his duties.
An imperial edict appointed him Yùzhāng Nèishǐ,
whereupon he accepted the appointment.
Shū Shìyùshǐ Yú Mìng played, saying:
“I have heard rumors that Yùzhāng Nèishǐ Fú Zhēng,
last year, requested leave
under the pretext of attending his sister’s funeral,
and then remained in Kuàijī without leaving.
At the beginning of his journey eastward,
he bought a house and sold his carriage.
From this, it can be inferred
that he originally had no intention of returning.
Fú Zhēng has successively governed two states,
and largely avoided avarice and corruption.
This is, by itself, a fundamental principle of governance;
how can it be considered an achievement?
He always believed his talent and reputation surpassed Hé Yuǎn’s,
yet Hé Yuǎn was promoted for his integrity,
and his position grew more distinguished.
Fú Zhēng harbored deep resentment and complaints,
which manifested in his words and demeanor.
Heaven is high, but it hears the low;
no private matter goes unilluminated.
On the twenty-first day of the twelfth month of last year, an edict stated: ‘Guózǐ Bóshì, concurrently Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi Fú Zhēng, has been honest and fair in his governance.
He should be nurtured and cared for,
and not be allowed to harbor resentment,
lest it diminish the spirit of scholars.
He may be appointed Yùzhāng Nèishǐ.’
How can a subject, upon receiving such an edict,
not be utterly terrified,
and confess his guilt to the proper authorities?
Instead, he presumptuously accepted the favor without declining,
and begrudged this petty gain.
Consequently, the morale of scholars has collapsed,
and public opinion is agitated.
Investigating his actions and examining his intentions,
there is nothing that can be excused.
I request that Fú Zhēng be impeached for great disrespect.”
An imperial edict ordered no deliberation on the matter,
and Fú Zhēng was thus able to proceed to his commandery.
Fú Zhēng was appointed Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng
and concurrently Guózǐ Bóshì,
but died before taking up the post.
Initially,
Fú Zhēng’s father Fú Mánróng and Rèn Yáo of Lè’ān were both close to Qí Tàiwèi Wáng Jiǎn.
Rèn Yáo’s son Rèn Fǎng and Fú Zhēng were both recognized.
After a while,
Rèn Fǎng’s talent and fortune gradually flourished;
by the end of Qí, he was already Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ.
Fú Zhēng, however, remained stalled at Cānjūnshì,
and by the time they died, their official positions were roughly equal.
Fú Zhēng was frugal and simple by nature,
with plain carriages and clothing.
Although outwardly reclusive and quiet,
he could not avoid inner competitiveness,
and thus was ridiculed at the time.
Nevertheless, he was able to recommend later generations,
always appearing as if he himself was not as good,
and young scholars sometimes relied on him for this reason.
His son was Fú Tǐng.
Fú Tǐng, courtesy name Shìbiāo,
was intelligent and perceptive as a child,
and at seven, he had mastered the Xiàojīng and Lúnyǔ.
As he grew older,
he was widely learned and talented in thought,
writing five-character-line poems,
and was skilled at imitating the style of Xiè Kānglè.
His father’s friend Rèn Fǎng of Lè’ān greatly admired and praised him,
often saying:
“This child is peerless under heaven.”
At the end of Qí, when the province selected Xiùcái,
his policy proposals were considered the best of the time.
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's army arrived,
Fú Tǐng went to pay respects at Xīnlín.
The Emperor was very pleased to see him,
likened him to Yán Zǐ,
and appointed him Zhēngdōng Xíng Cānjūn.
He was eighteen years old at the time.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
he was appointed Zhōngjūn Cānjūnshì.
His residence was in Cháogōu,
where he lectured on the Lúnyǔ from his home;
those who listened filled the court.
For three generations, Fú Tǐng’s family simultaneously gathered disciples and taught,
a rare occurrence.
He successively served as Magistrate of Jìnlíng and Wǔkāng.
After his tenure in the counties, he returned
and built a house in the eastern suburbs,
no longer pursuing an official career.
Fú Tǐng had a great reputation from a young age,
and was also good at navigating contemporary society.
Many powerful figures in the court associated with him,
so he could not long remain reclusive.
Later, he re-entered official service,
appointed Nántái Shū Shìyùshǐ.
He was impeached for accepting bribes due to an incident,
and fearing punishment,
he changed his clothes and became a monk, adopting the name Sēngtǐng.
He remained in hiding for a long time,
and later, upon receiving an amnesty,
he emerged at Tiānxīn Temple.
When Shàolíng Wáng became governor of Jiāngzhōu,
Fú Tǐng was drawn to his post.
The Prince enjoyed literature and scholarship,
and Fú Tǐng received great favor and courtesy.
Fú Tǐng could not endure a vegetarian diet,
and so returned to secular life.
He died during the Hóu Jǐng Rebellion.
He authored ten volumes of Ěrshuō
and twenty volumes of collected works.
His son, Fú Zhīmìng,
resented the court
because his father did not advance in his official career,
and later devoted himself entirely to Hóu Jǐng.
He attacked Yǐngzhōu
and besieged Bālíng;
all military dispatches and proclamations were his writings.
When Xītái was mentioned,
all wrote furiously.
When Hóu Jǐng usurped the throne,
Fú Zhīmìng became Zhōngshū Shèrén,
wielding great power both inside and outside the court.
When Hóu Jǐng was defeated,
Fú Zhīmìng was sent to Jiānglíng,
and died in prison.
Fú Tǐng’s younger brother Fú Chuí also had a talent for writing
and served as Shàolíng Wáng’s Jìshì Cānjūn.
Hé Tóngzhī, courtesy name Shìwēi,
was a native of Qián, Lújiāng,
and a sixth-generation descendant of Jìn Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Hé Yùn.
His grandfather, Hé Shàozhī,
was Sòng Yuánwài Sǎnjì Chángshì.
His father, Hé Xīn,
was Qí Fèngcháoqǐng.
Hé Tóngzhī was fond of the Sānlǐ from a young age,
learning independently and mastering them through intense, focused effort,
never ceasing to read.
He read over three hundred chapters of ritual discussions,
almost all of which he could recite from memory.
Tàiwèi Wáng Jiǎn greatly esteemed him.
He began his career as Yángzhōu Cóngshì,
and then became Zǒngmíngguǎn Xuéshì.
During the Qí dynasty,
he first served as Guózǐ Zhùjiào,
lecturing to students on mourning rites,
tying grass into mourning sashes
and folding handkerchiefs into caps.
For students who did not understand,
he patiently and thoroughly guided them,
and the capital praised him as a pure Confucian scholar.
In the Jiànwǔ era,
he served as Zhèn Běi Jìshì Cānjūn
and attended to the Crown Prince’s lectures.
At that time, Bùbīng Xiàowèi Liú Huán and Zhēngshì Wú Bāo had already passed away,
and Hé Tóngzhī was the only great scholar left in the capital.
At that time, the state’s auspicious and inauspicious ritual protocols
were all decided by him.
Later, he became Piàojì Sīmǎ.
At the end of the Yǒngyuán era,
when the capital was in military chaos,
Hé Tóngzhī regularly gathered students to lecture,
tirelessly and diligently.
He loved cleanliness by nature;
he would wash over ten times a day,
yet still felt it was insufficient,
and people at the time called him "water-obsessed."
He had a profound filial nature;
after his parents' deaths,
he always set up a room
where he would prostrate himself and weep on the first and fifteenth days of each month,
doing so for over twenty years.
People of his time admired his filial conduct.
At that time, there was also Liú Chéng, Magistrate of Suí'ān,
who was even more obsessed with cleanliness.
While in office, he swept and cleaned the city and its environs,
leaving no stray grass on the roads,
and removing insects and dirt from the water.
The common people could not endure his demands,
and he was dismissed from office.
However, he was very upright and honest,
and skilled in medicine,
renowned alongside Xú Sìbó.
His son, Liú Cōng, was able to inherit his family profession.
Tóng Zhī, after Dōnghūn's
accession to the throne, seeing his
cruelty and tyranny, excused himself
on account of illness, and for the rest of his life
did not involve himself in state affairs. When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
At that time, all institutions were being established
from scratch, and Tóng Zhī, basing his proposals on ritual,
made many beneficial contributions.
He died in office in Tiānjiān 2 (503 CE).
According to custom,
a Zuǒchéng received no posthumous official rank,
but the Emperor specially decreed him posthumously granted Huángmén Shìláng,
which scholars considered a great honor.
His collected works on essays and ritual discussions amounted to about a hundred chapters.
His sons were Cháoyǐn and Cháohuì.
Yán Zhízhī, courtesy name Xiàoyuán,
was a native of Zǐguī, Jiànpíng.
In his youth, he was skilled in Zhuāng and Lǎo,
and capable in xuányán discussions,
with a profound understanding of Sāngfú, Xiàojīng, and Lúnyǔ.
As he grew older,
he thoroughly studied Zhèng Shì's Rítual, Zhōuyì, Máoshī, and Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū.
He was by nature pure, filial, cautious, and sincere,
and did not boast of his strengths to others.
When young, he suffered the sorrow of his father's death,
and consequently ate vegetarian for twenty-three years.
He served Qí as Yòuchángshì of the Guǎnghàn King's Kingdom,
and also attended the king during his studies.
When the king was executed,
none of the people of the kingdom dared to look,
but Zhízhī alone rushed forward crying,
personally arranged the funeral and burial,
and barefoot followed the funeral procession to the burial ground,
where he erected a mound for him.
Only after the burial did he return.
At the time, people admired his righteousness.
Later, he became the Magistrate of Kānglè.
Zhízhī was incorruptible in the county,
and was praised by both people and officials.
In Tiānjiān 2 (503 CE) of Liáng,
an imperial edict sought learned scholars to revise the Five Rites.
The officials proposed Zhízhī to preside over the Mourning Rites.
In Tiānjiān 4 (505 CE),
the positions of Five Classics Academicians (Wǔjīng Bóshì) were first established,
each opening a hall for teaching.
Zhízhī was concurrently appointed Wǔjīng Bóshì.
Zhízhī's hall was in Cháogōu,
and his students numbered constantly in the hundreds.
His lectures were well-structured and methodical,
and his analysis of principles was clear.
Whenever he ascended the podium to lecture,
students from all five halls would arrive,
and listeners numbered over a thousand.
He was promoted to Zhōngfǔ Jìshì Cānjūn,
still concurrently holding the title of Bóshì.
He died in the hall.
Zhízhī, after becoming ill, refused to accept emoluments,
causing his wife and children to suffer hardship.
When he died,
there was no place to hold the funeral.
His students purchased a house for him,
and only then was the funeral successfully carried out.
Zhízhī was by nature benevolent
and fond of performing good deeds secretly;
he never slackened even in private.
Once, when he was young and traveling in the mountains,
he saw a sick person.
When asked his name, he could not answer.
Zhízhī carried him home,
arranged for medicine and care,
but he died after six days.
He provided a coffin, shroud, and funeral for him,
and never knew where the person was from.
Another time, he was walking along Zhàntáng [a pond],
and saw a sick person lying by the side of the pond.
When asked,
he said,
"My surname is Huáng,
my family is originally from Jīngzhōu,
and I was working as a hired laborer.
I fell seriously ill,
and the boat owner, about to depart,
abandoned me on the bank."
Zhízhī felt pity,
carried him back and treated him,
and after a year, he recovered.
The man asked to serve as Zhízhī's slave for life to repay his great kindness.
Zhízhī did not accept,
but gave him provisions and sent him away.
He compiled 479 scrolls of notes on mourning rites.
Sīmǎ Jūn, courtesy name Zhēnsù,
was a native of Wēn, Hénèi.
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Prince Qió of Jìn, Chéng.
His grandfather, Liàng,
was Sòng Sīkōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
His father, Duān, courtesy name Jìngwén,
served Qí as Fèngcháoqǐng,
and was appointed by Prince Shǐ'ān, Yáoguāng, to manage his literary records.
When Yáoguāng was defeated,
Cáo Wǔ entered the city and saw Duān.
Duān said,
"I have received great kindness from Shǐ'ān.
You ought to kill me."
Cáo Wǔ shouted at him to leave quickly.
Duān replied,
"Life and death are determined by fate.
If you fail in your endeavor,
you will consider the righteous army as bandits."
Cáo Wǔ left him and departed.
Soon after, soldiers arrived and killed him.
Jūn was orphaned in his youth, poor but fond of learning.
He studied under Liú Huán of Pèiguó,
and with strong effort and dedication, was highly regarded by Huán.
As he grew older,
he was broadly knowledgeable in classical studies,
and especially clear on the Three Rites.
In the early Tiānjiān era of Liáng, he became Magistrate of Jìyáng,
and had a reputation for clean governance.
He entered court and was appointed Shàngshū Cíbù Láng.
In the first year of Shàotài,
he was again summoned to be a Guózǐ Bóshì.
During the Tiānjiā reign of the Chén dynasty,
an imperial edict appointed him to attend the Eastern Palace as a lecturer.
He was appointed Zhōngláng for the King of Póyáng’s household and Cānjūn for Consultations,
and was treated with great courtesy and respect.
Soon after, he was appointed Yǔlín Jiān,
and then promoted to Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng,
〔二九〕with his former positions as Guózǐ Bóshì and Shìdú remaining unchanged.
At that time, the imperial court was newly established,
and many debates and proposals were settled
and applied.
Whenever he lectured at the Eastern Palace,
the Crown Prince would always humble himself and treat him with deference.
Yuè believed that the palace officials were not all the most talented individuals of the time,
and that the Crown Prince was kind and gentle,
while Xuāndì showed signs of usurping the succession.
Harboring deep indignation,
he submitted a memorial saying:
“During the Liáng dynasty, I served as a minor official,
my salary not enough to replace farming.
In the final chaotic years,
I hid myself in remote valleys.
Fortunately, I encountered a sagely era,
and was able to participate in the prosperous reign.
The imperial court, believing me to have a slight understanding of the arts and learning,
graciously extended an invitation,
promoting me to a noble position,
and providing me with a generous stipend.
The favor shown by the Two Palaces
is different from that shown to ordinary people.
Even wood and stone know gratitude,
and dogs and horses recognize their upkeep.
Who am I then,
not to harbor thoughts of repaying this kindness?
I respectfully reflect that the Crown Prince is the foundation of the empire.
He cultivates goodness in the spring palace.
I have attended him in the classics
for five years now.
As far as this fool can see,
there are many vacant positions,
and the輔弼 (fǔbì, imperial assistants) who address doubts
are not yet the best selections of the time.
As for the literary academies,
upright and incorruptible individuals
should attend the imperial court,
discussing matters from morning till evening,
hearing the sagely maxims of ancient saints,
and the political doctrines of past worthies.
If this were the case,
then perverse words
would have no way to enter.
My years are pressing,
and I have no personal ambitions.
It is simply that to harbor this thought and not speak,
would be to betray the enlightened sage.
I dare to present my humble and foolish words,
and wish for them to be kept private and not divulged.”
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor was deeply moved,
but in the end, he was unable to implement reforms.
When the deposed emperor ascended the throne,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
concurrently Zhōngshū Shèrén,
and Huángmén Shìláng as before.
He held the position of Tiānbǎo Bóshì,
was in charge of ceremonies,
and still served as the Emperor's teacher.
He entered the palace to lecture,
and was greatly respected and favored.
At that time, Xuāndì was assisting in governance,
and Huá Jiǎo raised troops and refused to comply.
Yuè then requested leave to return east.
Someone slandered him to Xuāndì,
saying that Yuè intended to incite the border garrisons.
Consequently, he was dismissed from office.
In the first year of Tàijiàn,
he died at home,
aged seventy-seven.
His writings, including commentaries on the Sāngfú, Máoshī, Lǎozǐ, Xiàojīng, Lúnyǔ, etc., totaled over forty volumes,
and his poems, odes, epitaphs, memorials, and tables amounted to over two hundred pieces.
At that time, there was a man from Dōngyáng named Gōng Mèngshū,
who was also proficient in the Máoshī
and skilled in discussing names and principles.
He served in the Liáng dynasty, holding the position of Xúnyáng Jùnchéng.
When Yuándì was in Jiāngzhōu,
he held him in high regard,
and personally studied under him.
During the Tiānjiā reign,
he held the position of Tàizhōng Dàfū.
Shěn Bùhài, courtesy name Xiàohé,
was a native of Wúxīng Wǔkāng.
He was orphaned young,
but was well-behaved and fond of learning.
In the early Tiānjiā reign of the Chén dynasty,
he was appointed Jìshì Cānjūn for the King of Héngyáng’s household,
and concurrently Xuéshì for the Jiādé Palace.
Since the chaos and destruction of the late Liáng dynasty,
the national academy had not yet been established.
Bùhài submitted a memorial requesting the establishment of a Confucian academy,
and the Emperor replied with a gracious edict.
He also submitted a memorial requesting the revision of musical pieces,
and an imperial edict instructed him to compose eight songs for the music of the three courts,
totaling twenty tunes,
〔三０〕which were then performed in the music bureau.
Later, he became Guózǐ Bóshì,
and concurrently Yǔlín Jiān.
He was commanded to revise the Five Rites,
and was in charge of composing ceremonial documents, posthumous titles, and other matters.
During the Tàijiàn reign,
he held the position of Guānglù Qīng,
Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì,
and concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
then he died.
Bùhài was well-versed in classical scholarship
and skilled in writing.
Although he had a comprehensive understanding of the classics,
his home contained no scrolls.
Whenever he composed,
he would pick up a brush and finish it immediately,
without ever needing to look things up.
Zhōu Hóngzhèng of Rǔnán often praised him, saying:
“Shěn Shēng can be called a sage of ideas!”
He authored one hundred volumes of Wǔlǐ Yí and
fourteen volumes of collected writings.
His son Zhìdào, courtesy name Chóngjī,
was famous from a young age.
He served as Àndōng Xīncài Wáng Jìshì Cānjūn.
After the fall of Chén, he entered Suí,
and then died.
Wáng Yuánguī, courtesy name Zhèngfàn,
was a native of Tàiyuán Jìnyáng.
His grandfather Dàoshí
was the Qí Jìn’ān Jùnshǒu.
〔三一〕His father Wěi
was the Liáng Wǔlíng Wáng Fǔ Jìshì Cānjūn.
Yuánguī was orphaned at the age of eight.
He and his two brothers
followed their mother to rely on their maternal uncle in Línhǎi Commandery,
when he was twelve years old.
A local magnate of the commandery, Liú Tián,
who possessed immense wealth,
wished to marry his daughter to him.
His mother, seeing her sons were young and weak,
wanted to form a strong alliance.
Yuánguī tearfully pleaded, saying:
“To maintain kinship without losing one’s principles
was highly valued by the ancients.
How can we seek temporary peace in a foreign land
and casually marry into an unsuitable family?”
His mother was moved by his words and stopped.
Yuánguī was filial by nature and served his mother with great diligence,
never leaving her side morning or evening.
During the Liáng dynasty, there was a violent flood in Shānyīn County,
which swept away homes.
Yuánguī only had a small boat.
In a rush, he helped his mother, sister, aunt, and nieces into the boat.
〔三二〕Yuánguī himself rowed the boat away,
leaving his three sons and daughters
perched in treetops.
When the water receded,
all were saved,
and people at the time praised his ultimate filial conduct.
When young, he studied under Shěn Wén'ē of Wúxīng.
At eighteen,
he was proficient in the Chūnqiū Zuǒshì, Xiàojīng, Lúnyǔ, and Sāngfú.
He served in the Liáng dynasty as Zhōngjūn Xuānchéng Wáng Jìshì Cānjūn.
During the Tiānjiā reign of the Chén dynasty,
he became Zhèndōng Póyáng Wáng Fǔ Jìshì Cānjūn,
and concurrently Guózǐ Zhùjiào.
When the Later Emperor was in the Eastern Palace,
he was invited to be a scholar,
and received instruction on the Lǐjì, Zuǒzhuàn, Sāngfú, and other texts.
He was promoted to Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
〔三三〕Xīn'ān Wáng Bó Gù once entered the palace,
just as Yuánguī was about to lecture.
He then requested to hold the classic for him,
which was considered an honor at the time.
Soon after, he was appointed Shàngshū Cíbù Láng.
Since the Liáng dynasty, various scholars who passed down the study of the Zuǒshì
all used the interpretations of Jiǎ Kuí and Fú Qián to refute Dù Yù,
totaling one hundred and eighty points.
Yuánguī, citing evidence and offering clear analysis,
left no room for doubt or ambiguity.
Whenever the state deliberated on major auspicious or inauspicious rites,
he was always among the participants.
Later, he became Nánpíng Wáng Fǔ Xiànnèi Cānjūn.
When the King served as Jiāngzhōu,
Yuánguī accompanied the household to the post.
Scholars from all directions,
traveling thousands of miles to seek his teachings,
often numbered in the tens or hundreds.
After the fall of Chén, he entered Suí,
and died as Qín Wáng Fǔ Dōnggé Jìjiǔ.
Yuánguī authored eleven volumes of Chūnqiū Fātí Cí and Yìjì,
〔三四〕fourteen volumes of Xù Jīngdiǎn Dàyì,
two volumes of Xiàojīng Yìjì,
three volumes of Zuǒzhuàn Yīn,
and two volumes of Lǐjì Yīn.
Whenever he sold goods,
he would only ask for half price.
The people of the town all knew and understood this,
so they would invariably add to the original price when offering it to him.
Both parties would yield to each other,
insisting that it be sold at a humble price,
only then would he accept payment.
He planted bamboo on his homestead,
and at night, someone stole the bamboo shoots.
Yuánpíng
encountered him, and the thief fled and fell into a ditch.
Yuánpíng then built a small bridge over the ditch at the spot where he had planted bamboo, making it passable,
and also gathered bamboo shoots and placed them outside his fence.
His neighbors felt ashamed,
and no one took them again.
When Emperor Wén of Sòng
passed away, Yuánpíng
wailed in grief, eating only one wheat bun a day,
for five days.
People asked,
"Who among us is not a subject of the Emperor?
Why are you doing this exclusively?"
Yuánpíng wept and replied,
"My family was highly regarded by the previous dynasty,
and received praise and commendation.
Unable to repay this kindness,
my private heart is deeply moved."
He also made a living by growing melons.
In the seventh year of Dàmíng, there was a great drought,
and the melon canal was no longer navigable by boat.
The county magistrate, Liú Sēngxiù,
pitying his poverty and old age, diverted water from the canal to him.
Yuánpíng said,
"There is a great drought across the entire land,
and all the people are suffering.
How can we reduce the water for irrigating fields
to allow boats to transport melons?"
So he walked along another path to Qiántáng to sell his goods.
Whenever he traveled and saw people pulling a weir but unable to pass,
he would swiftly help them with his oar.
He would tow his own boat
without relying on others.
If his own boat had already passed,
but others had not yet caught up,
he would often stop and wait,
making this his regular practice.
Once, south of the county at Guōfèng weir, he was helping someone pull a boat
when he encountered brawlers who were being arrested by officials.
The brawlers scattered and fled,
but only Yuánpíng remained.
The officials seized him and sent him to the county office.
The county magistrate was new
and not yet familiar with him,
and was about to impose a severe punishment.
Yuánpíng removed his clothes and submitted to the penalty,
not uttering a single word of protest.
Everyone around him, great and small, bowed their heads and pleaded for his rescue,
only then was he spared.
He had never previously visited officials,
but from then on, he began to show respect.
When the Grand Administrator Cài Xīngzōng
assumed his post in the commandery, he greatly esteemed and admired him.
He privately sent one hundred *hú* of rice each to Yuánpíng and Zhū Bǎinián's wife from Shānyīn.
Yuánpíng vowed he would rather die than accept,
and Bǎinián's wife also firmly declined.
In Kuàijī Commandery, the respected "Wàngjì" (Illustrious Counsel) and "Wàngxiào" (Illustrious Filial Piety) positions,
for those from prominent families,
were no less significant than those for secretaries or authors.
In the seventh year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Míng,
Xīngzōng wished to recommend Kǒng Zhòngzhì's son from Shānyīn for "Wàngjì",
and Yuánpíng's second son for "Wàngxiào".
Zhòngzhì was from a high-status family in Huì;
Yuánpíng possessed exemplary conduct across the land.
He wished to match them against each other.
However, Emperor Míng issued a separate imperial decree for personnel appointments,
so both selections were shelved.
Xīngzōng was summoned back to the capital
and memorialized his exceptional conduct,
recommending him as a Grand Academy Scholar.
However, Xīngzōng passed away,
and the matter did not proceed.
He died at home.
His three sons and one younger brother
all had good family conduct.
Yán Shìqī
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
He was by nature generous.
The wives of Zhāng Mài and two other men in his village each gave birth to children.
Due to famine,
they intended to abandon them and not raise them.
Shìqī shared his food and gave his clothes to relieve their destitution,
and all three children were able to grow up.
In the same county, Yú Yáng's wife, Zhuāng, was ninety years old,
and Zhuāng's daughter, Lán, was seventy.
Both were old and ill, without support.
Shìqī provided them with food for twenty years,
and when they died, he personally buried them.
His relatives, Yán Hóng, and fifteen villagers, including Pān Bó,
all starved to death during a famine year,
their bones exposed and uncollected.
Shìqī bought coffins, buried them,
and raised their orphaned children.
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā of Sòng,
the appropriate authorities posted a sign at his door saying,
"Gate of Yán, the Righteous."
His personal corvée duties were remitted,
and his land taxes were exempted for ten years.
Wú Kuí
was a native of Wūchéng, Wúxīng.
Having endured famine
and then epidemic disease,
thirteen people in his family—parents, elder brother and sister-in-law, and many younger relatives within the "small mourning" degree, both male and female—died.
Kuí himself was gravely ill at the time;
his neighbors wrapped him in a rush mat
and buried him by the village.
Afterwards, all his relatives were gone,
only Kuí and his wife survived.
His house was utterly bare;
in winter, he had no quilt or trousers.
By day, he worked as a laborer;
by night, he cut wood and burned bricks.
His wife also shared Kuí's sincere efforts,
without any slackening.
When Kuí traveled at night and encountered fierce beasts,
the beasts would invariably move off the road to avoid him.
Within a year, he completed seven graves
and buried thirteen coffins,
which his neighbors praised.
On the day of the funerals,
everyone came out to help,
and the burial rites, though frugal, were meticulously performed.
At that time, Kuí had previously borrowed labor fees from his neighbors.
After the burials,
everyone forgave him all the debts.
Kuí accepted nothing,
instead repaying them all with his own labor.
Grand Administrator Zhāng Chóngzhī
thrice offered him official appointments with courtesy.
Grand Administrator Wáng Sháozhī
promoted him to Staff Officer in charge of meritorious deeds.
Kuí, due to his humble family background,
firmly declined to take the post.
He was recommended as a Xiaolián.
Pān Zōng
was a native of Wūchéng, Wúxīng.
During Sūn Ēn's rebellion,
the rebel faction attacked and destroyed villages.
Zōng and his father, Biāo, fled from the bandits together.
Biāo was old and walked slowly;
the bandits were closing in on Biāo.
Biāo said to Zōng,
"I cannot go on.
If you run, you can escape.
Please do not let us both die."
Biāo, exhausted, sat on the ground.
Zōng went forward to the bandits and kowtowed, saying,
"My father is old;
I beg you to spare his life."
When the bandits arrived,
Biāo also pleaded with them, saying,
"My son is young and can run on his own,
but now he won't leave because of his old father.
I do not fear death;
I beg you to spare this child."
The bandits then hacked at Biāo.
Zōng embraced his father beneath his abdomen.
The bandits struck Zōng's head and face four times in all,
and Zōng immediately fainted.
One bandit came from the side and said to the others,
"You want to achieve great things;
this child is dying to save his father.
How can you kill him?
Killing a filial son is inauspicious."
The bandits then stopped,
and both father and son were spared.
The village's Secretariat Supervisor Qiū Xìzǔ and Court Steward Shěn Chìqián,
seeing Zōng's extraordinary conduct, recommended him for appointment as Left Household Clerk,
and he was appointed Prefect of Suíchāng.
After his term was complete, he returned home.
When Grand Administrator Wáng Sháozhī
assumed his post in the commandery, he issued an instruction to list his deeds for the provincial and capital authorities,
detailing his conduct.
When Zōng was about to depart,
Sháozhī held a farewell banquet
and presented him with a four-character poem.
In the fourth year of Yuánjiā,
the appropriate authorities petitioned to change his village's name to Chúnxiàolǐ (Village of Pure Filial Piety),
and his land taxes and cloth taxes were exempted for three generations.
There was also a Lady Zhào, wife of Wú Kāng from Jìnlíng.
Her father died, and her younger brother was young.
They encountered a famine year.
Her mother was old and critically ill.
Lady Zhào went to the village to beg for food.
Her words were mournful and pitiable.
The villagers took pity on her,
each sharing a *shēng* of rice,
and thus they were spared.
When she married Kāngzhī,
her husband died a short while later.
Her family wished to remarry her,
but she swore an oath not to be unfaithful.
There was also a Lady Huáng, wife of Jiǎng Jùn from Yìxīng.
Her husband died, and she refused to remarry.
Her family pressured her.
She wished to commit suicide,
and only then did they stop.
In the third year of Jiànyuán,
an imperial edict exempted and honored her household.
There was also Lady Dīng, mother of Wú Yì from Yǒngxīng, Kuàijī.
[(22)] She lost her husband when she was young.
Her nature was benevolent and loving.
When a famine year struck,
she shared her clothes and food to feed the hungry in the village.
She never refused her neighbors when they asked to borrow from her.
When Chén Rǎng from the same village lost his parents,
being an orphan without relatives,
Lady Dīng took him in.
When he grew up, she arranged his marriage.
There was also Lady Xú, wife of Wáng Lǐ from the same village.
During a famine year, she died as a traveler in Shānyīn.
Lady Dīng bought a coffin and burial items for her,
[(23)] and personally went to lay her out and bury her.
At the end of Yuánhuī,
there was heavy snow.
Merchants and travelers ceased their journeys.
Villages and households were starving.
Lady Dīng personally took out salt and rice,
and distributed it according to the number of mouths.
When Zuǒ Qiáo from the same village had four deaths and no means for burial,
Lady Dīng provided the coffin and outer coffin.
For those who failed to pay their three levies,
she paid on their behalf.
[(24)] Lady Wáng, Lady Dīng's eldest son's wife, became a widow,
and firmly resolved not to remarry.
The prefecture and commandery reported this.
An imperial edict honored her household and
exempted her from rent and taxes.
There was also a commoner, Lady Chén, from Kuàijī.
She had three daughters,
but no sons.
Her grandparents were eighty or ninety years old,
and senile.
Her father suffered from a severe chronic illness.
Her mother was restless in her home.
When a famine year struck,
the three daughters together went to Xīhú to gather water caltrops and water oats.
They took turns going to the market to sell them every day,
never slacking.
The villagers called them the "Righteous Household,"
and many wished to marry them.
The eldest daughter, grieving her solitary state,
swore she would not leave.
Her grandparents soon died one after another.
The three daughters personally arranged their funerals and burials,
and built a hermitage to live by the tomb.
There was also a daughter of the Wáng family from Gàizhōnglǐ, Yǒngxīng, who, at the age of five,
contracted a poisonous illness and became blind in both eyes.
She was extremely filial by nature.
At twenty, her father died.
She cried out once before the corpse,
and blood flowed from both her eyes.
Her younger sister, É, licked the blood,
and her left eye immediately opened.
People at the time called this "Filial Piety's Response."
There was also a daughter of the Tú family from Dōngwūlǐ, Zhūjì.
Her father was blind,
her mother had a chronic illness.
Her relatives abandoned them,
and the villagers would not tolerate them.
The daughter moved her parents far away to Zhùluó,
[(25)] chopping firewood by day
and spinning by night
to support them.
When both parents died,
she personally arranged their funerals and burials,
and carried earth to build their grave.
Suddenly, a voice from the sky said:
"Your extreme filial piety is commendable.
The mountain god wishes to command you.
You can heal people's illnesses,
and will surely achieve great wealth and honor."
The daughter thought it was an evil spirit
and dared not obey.
Consequently, she fell ill for a long time.
A neighbor was poisoned by a *xīyù* from Zhōngxī.
[(26)] The daughter tried to heal him,
and felt her own illness immediately improve.
She then practiced shamanism to heal people's illnesses,
and none were not cured.
Her family's wealth grew daily,
and many villagers wished to marry her.
Because she had no brothers,
the daughter vowed to guard the grave and not marry,
and was killed by mountain bandits.
There was also Lady Yáo, wife of Chéng Gōngjì from Wúxīng.
She had two sons,
but Gōngjì and his elder brothers Gōngyuàn and Qiánbó all died,
each leaving one son.
Lady Yáo raised them,
sold fields and houses to arrange wives for them,
and she and her two sons lived as lodgers in a neighbor's house.
Emperor Míng issued an edict to arrange marriages for her two sons
and exempted her household from corvée labor.
There was also Lady Chǔ, wife of Fàn Fǎxún from Wújùn,
who also diligently performed her wifely duties.
During the Shēngmíng era of Sòng,
Sūn Tán'guàn plotted rebellion and fled.
Lady Chǔ said to her son Sēngjiǎn:
"Sūn Yuèzhōu is the son of your late maternal aunt's sister.
In kinship, he is your father's maternal cousin.
In friendship, his righteousness surpasses that of ancient people.
If he flees and cannot escape,
you should take him in."
Tán'guàn was soon executed.
Lady Chǔ ordered Sēngjiǎn to go and collect his body for burial.
She was over seventy years old
when she died in the Yǒngmíng era.
Sēngjiǎn, hearing of her illness while in the capital, rushed back.
Before he arrived,
Lady Chǔ had already died.
When they tried to move her body for the funeral, it would not budge.
Soon after, Sēngjiǎn arrived.
Gōngsūn Sēngyuǎn was from Shàn, Kuàijī.
He was extremely filial during his father's mourning
and served his mother and paternal uncle with great care.
During a famine year,
Sēngyuǎn reduced his own food to feed his mother and paternal uncle.
When his younger brother died,
being poor and unable to afford a burial,
[(27)] he personally sold himself as a bondservant to his neighbors
to provide for the expenses of the funeral and burial,
and personally carried earth
and planted pines and cypresses by hand.
His elder siblings were not yet married,
so he sold himself again to arrange their weddings.
His reputation spread throughout the commandery and prefecture.
When Emperor Gāo of Qí ascended the throne,
he dispatched Yu Yán and twelve other envoys, all Palace Attendants, to tour the realm.
[(28)] They reported Sēngyuǎn and twenty-two others,
and an imperial edict honored all their households
and exempted them from rent and taxes.
Wú Xīnzhī was from Lìchéng, Jìnlíng.
[(29)] At the end of the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
his younger brother Wèizhī was an official in Wǔjìn County.
He joined Wáng Dàn in raising an uprising.
Yuánxiōng sent the army commander Huá Qīn to suppress them.
[(30)] All the officials and people scattered,
but Wèizhī alone remained and was captured.
As he was about to die,
Xīnzhī went to Qīn to beg to substitute his own life for his brother's.
His words and tears were profoundly sorrowful,
and both brothers were pardoned.
In the third year of Jiànyuán of Qí,
an imperial edict exempted and honored him.
In the early Yǒngmíng era,
Tóng Chāozhī's two sons from Guǎnglíng committed crimes and contended for death.
[(31)] The Grand Administrator Liú Qùn reported this.
Hán Xìbó, from Xiāngyáng,
served his parents with utmost filial piety.
A neighbor in Xiāngyáng planted a mulberry tree on the boundary as a marker.
Xìbó felt that the mulberry branches shaded and hindered the neighbor's land,
so he moved the boundary marker back several *chǐ*.
The neighbor then encroached again.
Xìbó would always re-plant.
After a long time,
the neighbor felt ashamed
and returned the encroached land,
personally going to apologize to him.
In the third year of Jiànyuán of Qí,
his household was exempted and honored,
and he died of old age.
At that time, there was Wénrén Xiǒng from Wúxīng,
who, at seventeen,
gathered followers to avenge his father.
He was admired by Emperor Gāo
and rose to the position of Commandant of Chángshuǐ.
Gǎo was intelligent and alert in his youth,
possessing an utmost nature.
At the age of twelve,
he suffered a maternal loss.
His mourning and grief exceeded the prescribed rites,
and he did not take water or gruel
for almost ten days.
Whenever he wailed with sorrow,
he would faint.
His father often tried to persuade him
to take some porridge,
but he remained gaunt and emaciated, a mere skeleton.
After the mourning period ended,
his relatives' children came to inquire after him.
Liáng Wǔdì saw how frail and ill he was,
and sighed for a long time.
He called him by his pet name and said to his father:
“Yesterday I saw Luó’ér’s face, haggard and wan,
which made me feel sad.
This shows he does not disgrace the family tradition;
you have a worthy son.”
Later, he was repeatedly promoted to Zhèngyuán Láng.
When he suffered his paternal loss,
his grief and debilitation were even more severe.
He built a hut by the tomb,
eating only one sheng of thin barley porridge daily.
The tomb was in Xīnlín,
connected to hills and mounds,
which historically had many fierce beasts.
Gǎo lived in his hut for several years,
and jackals and wolves disappeared from the area.
There were often two doves nesting and roosting by his hut,
unusually tame and familiar.
During the Chéngshèng era,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shùzǐ.
When Wèi conquered Jiānglíng,
he entered Cháng’ān with the other officials.
As the Liáng imperial clan was massacred,
the Crown Prince’s burial was misplaced.
When the Zhōu received the abdication,
Gǎo, as an imperial official,
presented a memorial requesting to return to Jiānglíng to rebury the prince.
His words were very poignant and earnest.
The Zhōu court replied with a gracious edict,
immediately ordering Jīngzhōu to inter him with full rites.
In the eighth year of Tài jiàn of Chén,
he returned from Zhōu.
Xuāndì specially bestowed extraordinary rites upon him.
He successively held the positions of Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì and Tàizhōng Dàfū,
and then died.
His collected works comprised ten juan.
His son, Yányì, courtesy name Xīzhōng,
was intelligent, quick-witted, and fond of learning in his youth.
Initially, he followed his father into the pass.
Upon suffering his maternal loss,
his mourning exceeded the rites.
When Gǎo returned to the capital,
Yányì personally carried the funeral bier,
hiding by day and traveling by night,
braving ice and frost,
his hands and feet chapped and frostbitten.
Upon reaching the capital,
he became crippled and disabled,
and only recovered after several years.
He served as Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Zhāng Zhāo, courtesy name Dé Míng,
was a native of Wú County, Wú Commandery.
As a child, he possessed filial piety.
His father, Yǎn, often suffered from xuēkě and
craved fresh fish.
Zhāo would personally weave nets and catch fish
to provide for him day and night.
His younger brother, Gān, courtesy name Xuánmíng,
was intelligent, keen, and fond of learning,
and also possessed an utmost nature.
When their father died,
neither brother wore cotton or silk,
nor ate salt or vinegar,
subsisting on only one sheng of barley meal porridge daily.
Every time they were overcome with grief,
they would vomit blood.
When neighbors heard of this,
they all shed tears.
Before the mourning period for their father was over,
their mother, Lady Lù, also died.
The brothers then grieved and debilitated for six years,
their appearance reduced to skin and bones.
Being poor,
they could not afford a grand burial.
Thus, they wore coarse clothes and ate vegetables,
for more than ten years,
shutting their doors and staying indoors,
completely withdrawing from human affairs.
At that time, Héngyáng Wáng Bóxìn presided over the province.
[一五]He nominated Gān as Xiàolián,
but Gān firmly declined.
Both brothers became ill due to their debilitation.
Zhāo lost sight in one eye,
and Gān also suffered from a chronic illness of internal cold.
Neither reached fifty years of age
before dying at home,
and both lines of descent ended.
During Xuāndì’s reign,
there was a man named Wáng Zhīxuán from Tàiyuán,
who resided in Shàn County, Kuàijī.
He was known for his filial piety at home.
When he suffered his paternal loss,
[一六]he died from grief and debilitation.
The Emperor praised him
and issued an edict to rename his residential Qīngkǔ Lǐ to Xiàojīa Lǐ.
[一七]
The论 (Lùn) states: Since the decline in moral customs began,
human ethics have deteriorated.
The teaching of restraint and guidance
is what guides customs first.
Changing villages and honoring gateways
serves the purpose of encouragement and commendation.
Thus, during the Hàn dynasty, scholars dedicated themselves to self-cultivation,
and loyalty and filial piety became common customs.
Attaining high office and wearing official attire
was impossible without this.
Since the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
this custom has waned and virtue has been lacking.
Those who disciplined themselves and practiced strict conduct
were considered to have little regard for comfort and luxury.
If filial piety is established in the family courtyard
and loyalty recorded in historical annals,
most often it arises from humble origins,
not from those of high official standing.
Considering this in terms of moral education,
is it not a shame for the ministers and high officials?
Collated Notes

Biographies, Volume Sixty-Five: Hermits, Part One: Táo Qián, Zōng Shǎowén (Sūn Cè, his cousin Yùzhī), Shěn Dàoqián, Kǒng Chúnzhī, Zhōu Xùzhī, Dài Yōng, Zhái Fǎcì, Léi Cìzōng, Liú Níngzhī, Gōng Qí, Zhū Bǎinián, Guān Kāngzhī (Xīn Pǔmíng, Lóu Huìmíng), the Fisherman, Chǔ Bóyù, Gù Huān (Lú Dù), Dù Jīngchǎn (Kǒng Dàohuī, Jīngchǎn’s son Qī, the children of Shàn County).
The Yì Jīng says: The Way of the junzǐ has four aspects,
which refers to speech and silence.
Therefore, some enter the imperial court and do not leave,
while others seek the rivers and lakes and return forever.
Avoiding worldly turmoil,
their dispositions and actions are myriad.
If one is internally sufficient in dao and yi,
and forgets both the subtle and the obvious,
hiding their presence in remote cliffs,
and concealing their name in foolish valleys,
freeing themselves from the shackles of benevolence and righteousness,
and manifesting their form and spirit between heaven and earth,
then beyond the conventional teachings, there is another kind of conduct.
Thus, in Yáo’s domain, there were people who were not considered sages,
and Confucius’s school mistakenly welcomed the guests of jīshǔ.
Secondly, there are those who highly value their independent integrity,
and cherish the empty fame of leaving or staying.
Some consider forestalling future regret,
their actions leading to awareness of danger.
Others, whose Way is not upheld,
sing their laments in mountains and marshes.
All use the universe to form their minds,
borrowing wind and clouds as their spirit.
To seek one's aspirations and realize the Way
is never wrong;
therefore, one must preserve integrity and cultivate simplicity,
adorned by arts and professions.
Otherwise,
what difference is there
between them and the woodcutters in the mountains?
As for the likes of Táo Qián,
some served without seeking fame,
and retired without criticizing customs;
some preserved themselves in secluded paths,
following the Dao within the Confucian school;
some hid their traces by rivers and lakes,
others concealed their names beneath rocks.
These are all among those who lived in seclusion at that time.
Now, they are all compiled
to form the chapter on recluses.
Furthermore, during the Qí and Liáng periods,
there was a Buddhist monk named Shì Bǎozhì.
Although he lived neither openly nor obscurely,
his Dao accorded with the subtle and profound.
Examining his deeds,
he was also one of those beyond worldly conventions.
Therefore, he is appended here.
Táo Qián, courtesy name Yuānmíng,
or sometimes Shēnmíng,
given name Yuánliàng.
A native of Cháisāng, Xúnyáng.
He was the great-grandson of Jìn Dàsīmǎ Kǎn.
He possessed noble aspirations in his youth.
By his dwelling were five willow trees,
hence he often wrote the "Biography of Mr. Five Willows," which says: "The gentleman does not know from where he came,
nor is his surname or given name known.
He is tranquil and speaks little,
and does not covet glory or profit.
He is fond of reading,
but does not seek a thorough understanding.
Whenever there is a gathering..."
ideas,
happily forgetting to eat.
By nature, he loved wine,
but his family was poor and he could not obtain it.
His relatives and old friends, knowing this about him,
would sometimes prepare wine and invite him over.
When he arrived for a drink, he would always finish it,
expecting
to get completely drunk.
Once drunk, he would leave,
never holding back his feelings, whether staying or going.
His house, enclosed by bare walls, was
exposed to wind and sun.
His coarse clothes were patched and mended;
his bamboo basket and gourd ladle were often empty,
yet he was
at ease.
He often wrote essays to entertain himself,
mostly expressing his aspirations,
forgetting about gains and losses,
and thus he lived out his life.
This is how he described himself.
Indeed, it was a self-portrait,
and people of his time called it a truthful record.
With elderly parents and a poor family,
he took office as the Libationer of a Prefecture (zhōu jìjiǔ).
Unable to endure official duties,
he resigned after a short time and returned home.
The Prefecture summoned him to be a Chief Clerk (zhǔbù),
but he did not accept.
He farmed himself to support himself,
and consequently suffered from a debilitating illness (léijí).
Tán Dàojì, the Inspector (cìshǐ) of Jiāngzhōu, went to visit him.
He had been lying down emaciated and hungry for many days.
Tán Dàojì said to him:
"Indeed, a worthy person living in the world,
when the world is without the Way, withdraws;
when the world has the Way, he enters office.
Now you live in an enlightened age,
why do you inflict such hardship on yourself?"
He replied:
"How would Táo Qián dare to aspire to be worthy?
My ambition does not reach that far."
Tán Dàojì offered him millet and meat,
and he waved him away.
Later, he served as a Staff Officer (cānjūn) to the General Who Guards the Army (zhèn jūn) and the General Who Builds Awe (jiàn wēi).
He said to his relatives and friends:
"I merely wish to play the zither and sing,
to earn money for the three paths (sānjìng).
Is that acceptable?"
Those in charge heard of this
and appointed him Magistrate (lìng) of Péngzé.
He did not bring his family with him,
but sent a servant to his son,
writing:
"Your daily expenses,
it is difficult for you to provide for yourself.
Now I send this servant
to help you with the labor of firewood and water.
This is also someone's child,
so you should treat him well."
He ordered his clerks to plant glutinous rice (shú) in all the public fields.
His wife and children earnestly requested to plant non-glutinous rice (jīng),
so he had two qǐng and fifty mù planted with glutinous rice,
and fifty mù with non-glutinous rice.
The Commandery (jùn) sent a supervising official (dūyóu) to the county.
His clerks reported that he should don his official sash to receive him.
Táo Qián sighed and said:
"I cannot bend my waist for five measures of rice (wǔ dòu mǐ) to a petty person from the countryside."
That very day, he resigned his seal and sash and left his post,
composing "Gūi Qù Lái Xī" (歸去來兮) to fulfill his aspirations,
saying: Return home, oh!
My fields and gardens are about to become overgrown, why not return?
Since I have allowed my mind to be enslaved by my body,
why should I be distraught and grieve alone?
I realize that what is past cannot be
remedied,
but what is to come can still be pursued.
Indeed, I have not strayed far down the wrong path;
I realize that today is right and yesterday was wrong.
My boat bobs gently along,
the wind wafts softly, blowing my clothes.
I ask
a traveler about the road ahead,
lamenting the faintness of the morning light.
Then I gaze upon my humble abode,
filled with joy and running quickly.
My servants welcome me,
my young children wait at the gate.
The three paths (sānjìng) are becoming
overgrown,
but the pines and chrysanthemums remain.
I lead my children into the house,
where there is wine filling the goblet.
I take up the pot and cup to pour for myself,
gazing at the trees in the courtyard with a happy face.
Leaning against the south window, I express my pride,
content
with the small space I occupy.
Daily wandering in the garden becomes a delight;
though a gate is there, it is usually closed.
I lean on my staff to rest as I wander,
from time to time raising my head to gaze afar.
The clouds emerge from the ravines
without purpose;
tired birds know to return to their nests.
The sun sets, its light growing dim;
I lean on a lone pine tree and linger.
Return home, oh!
I beg to cease all social interactions and abandon travel.
The world and I have abandoned each other;
why should I seek anything more by riding forth?
I enjoy the heartfelt conversations of my relatives,
and delight in music and books
to dispel my worries.
Farmers inform me that spring has arrived,
and there will be work in the western fields.
Sometimes I order a covered cart,
sometimes I paddle a small boat.
I traverse deep and winding valleys,
and also
rugged and hilly terrain.
The trees are verdant and thriving,
the springs trickle and begin to flow.
I admire all things for seizing their opportune moment,
and feel that my own life is nearing its end.
Enough!
How long can this form reside in the universe?
Why not let my heart follow its own course, whether to stay or go?
Why should I rush about, wondering where to go?
Wealth and high position are not my desire;
the Heavenly Realm (dìxiāng)
cannot be hoped for.
I cherish good times and wander alone,
sometimes planting my staff and weeding young plants.
I ascend the eastern hill (dōnggāo) and let out a long cry,
I face the clear stream and compose poetry.
Let me simply follow the transformations of nature and return
to dust.
I delight in Heaven's decree, what more doubt could there be?
At the end of the Yìxī (義熙) era,
he was summoned to be Assistant Recorder (zhùzuò zuǒláng),
but he did not accept.
Wáng Hóng, the Inspector (cìshǐ) of Jiāngzhōu, wished to meet him,
but could not summon him.
Táo Qián once went to Lúshān (廬山).
Wáng Hóng instructed Táo Qián's old friend, Páng Tōngzhī, to bring wine and utensils to meet him halfway at Lìlǐ (栗里).
Táo Qián had a leg ailment,
so he had a student and two boys carry him in a wicker palanquin (lán yǔ).
When they arrived,
he happily drank with them.
Soon Wáng Hóng arrived,
and Táo Qián showed no displeasure.
Before this,
Yán Yánzhī served as a Meritorious Officer (gōngcáo) in the Rear Army (hòujūn) under Liú Liǔ,
and formed a deep friendship (qíngfā) with Táo Qián in Xúnyáng (尋陽).
Later, when Yán Yánzhī was the Administrator (jùn) of Shǐ'ān,
he passed by Táo Qián's home.
Each time he went, he would drink heavily until he was drunk.
Wáng Hóng wished to invite Yán Yánzhī to a gathering,
but failed for a whole day.
When Yán Yánzhī left,
he left twenty thousand coins for Táo Qián.
Táo Qián sent all of it to the wine shop and gradually retrieved wine from it.
Once, on the ninth day of the ninth month (Jiǔyuè Jiǔrì), he had no wine.
He went out and sat for a long time among the chrysanthemum bushes by his house.
He happened to meet Wáng Hóng, who brought him wine.
He immediately began to drink,
and returned home only after he was drunk.
Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì (衡陽王義季) was appointed governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
He personally went to his residence,
and they enjoyed a feast together.
He was appointed Cányì Cānjūn (諮議參軍),
but did not take up the post.
He loved mountains and rivers,
and enjoyed traveling far.
He ascended Jīng (荊) and Wū (巫) in the west,
and climbed Héngyuè (衡岳) in the south.
He then built a dwelling on Héngshān (衡山),
wishing to embrace the ambition of Shàng Píng (尚平).
When he fell ill and returned to Jiānglíng (江陵),
he sighed, saying:
"Old age and illness have both arrived.
I fear it will be difficult to see all the famous mountains.
I can only clear my mind and observe the Way,
and travel to them in my dreams as I lie down."
All the places he had visited and walked,
he had them painted in his room,
saying
"When I play the qín and move its strings,
I wish all the mountains to resonate."
In ancient times, there was a tune called Jīnshí Nòng (金石弄),
which was highly valued by the various Huán (桓) clans.
When the Huán (桓) clan fell,
its sound was lost,
and only Shǎo Wén (少文) preserved it.
Wén Dì (文帝) sent the music master Yáng Guān (楊觀) to learn it from him.
Shǎo Wén's (少文) grandson Cè (測)
also possessed his grandfather's style.
Cè (測), courtesy name Jìngwēi (敬微),
also named Màoshēn (茂深),
lived in Jiānglíng (江陵).
In his youth, he was quiet and reclusive,
and did not enjoy human society.
He sighed, saying:
"My family is poor and my parents are old;
one serves without choosing an office.
The former sages considered this a beautiful tale,
but I secretly have doubts.
If one truly cannot secretly move the earth to produce gold,
or mysteriously summon carp from the river,
one should merely use the way of Heaven
and share the benefits of the earth.
Who could eat people's generous salaries
and worry about people's heavy affairs?"
Qí Piàojì Yùzhāng Wáng Yí (齊驃騎豫章王嶷) summoned him as a Cānjūn (參軍),
but he did not take up the post.
Cè (測) replied to the government, saying:
"Why should one wrongly injure the seabirds,
or wield an axe against the mountain trees?"
When his mother died,
he personally carried earth
and planted pines and cypresses.
Yí (嶷) again sent a letter inviting him,
appointing him as a Cānjūn (參軍).
Cè (測) replied:
"My nature is like that of fish and birds;
I love to dwell in mountains and valleys,
fond of pines and clouds,
and easily lost to human paths.
Wandering freely among rocks and streams,
I am like a madman,
suddenly unaware that old age is approaching.
But now my temples are white,
how can I be expected to be assessed for emptiness and held accountable for existence,
or to limit the longing of fish and birds?"
In the third year of Yǒngmíng (永明),
an imperial edict summoned him to be a Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人),
but he did not accept.
Wishing to travel to famous mountains,
he then copied his grandfather Shǎo Wén's (少文) portrait of Shàng Zǐpíng (尚子平) onto his wall.
Cè's (測) eldest son, Bīn (賓), was an official in the capital.
Knowing his father's intention,
he immediately sought a position and returned as Nánjùn Chéng (南郡丞).
Cè (測) then entrusted him with family affairs.
[一０] Cǐshǐ Ānlù Wáng Zǐjìng (刺史安陸王子敬), Chángshǐ Liú Yín (長史劉寅), and others all sent him gifts,
but Cè (測) accepted none.
He took the two books, Lǎozi (老子)
and Zhuāngzi (莊子), with him.
His children and grandchildren bowed and tearfully bid him farewell.
Cè (測) let out a long whistle and did not look back,
then went to Lúshān (廬山),
and resided in his grandfather Shǎo Wén's (少文) old dwelling.
Yúfù Hóu Zǐxiǎng (魚復侯子響), as governor of Jiāngzhōu (江州),
generously sent him gifts.
Cè (測) said:
"When I was young, I had a wild illness,
so I sought mountains to gather herbs,
and traveled far to reach this place.
I consume pine and atractylodes according to my hunger,
and wear kudzu and vines according to my body shape.
This plain life is enough;
how could I accept such unexpected generosity?"
Zǐxiǎng (子響) ordered his carriage to visit him,
but Cè (測) refused to see him.
Later, Zǐxiǎng (子響) arrived unannounced,
suddenly appearing at his residence.
Cè (測), having no choice,
put on a headscarf and coarse garment to face him,
but did not exchange a single word.
Zǐxiǎng (子響) retreated, displeased.
Shìzhōng Wáng Xiùzhī (侍中王秀之) admired him greatly,
and ordered Lù Tànwēi (陸探微) to paint his likeness facing himself,
and also sent a letter saying:
"The ancients had paintings of Qiáo (僑) and Zhá (札),
but lightly compared themselves to them."
Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) also highly esteemed him,
and presented him with a rush mat and bamboo shoot mat.
Soon after,
Cè (測) returned west for his brother's funeral,
and then remained in the old dwelling at Yǒngyè Sì (永業寺).
He cut off contact with guests and friends,
only communicating with like-minded individuals such as Yǔ Yì (庾易), Liú Qiú (劉虬), and his relative Shàng Zhī (尚之).
Jīngzhōu Cǐshǐ Suí Wáng Zǐlóng (荊州刺史隨王子隆) arrived at his post.
[一一] He sent Biéjià Zōng Xīn (別駕宗忻) to convey greetings.
Cè (測) laughed, saying:
"The noble and the humble are naturally separated,
how can this reach me?"
He ultimately did not reply.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ (建武),
he was summoned as Sītú Zhǔbù (司徒主簿),
but did not accept,
and died.
Cè (測) was skilled in painting.
He painted Ruan Jí (阮籍) meeting Sūmén (蘇門) on an imperial banner,
and sat and slept facing it.
He also painted the Fóyǐng Tái (佛影臺) at Yǒngyè (永業),
all of which were masterpieces.
He loved music,
was skilled in Yì (易) and Lǎo (老),
and continued Huángfǔ Mì's (皇甫謐) Gāoshì Zhuàn (高士傳) in three volumes.
He once traveled to the seven peaks of Héngshān (衡山),
and wrote the Héngshān Lúshān Jì (衡山、廬山記).
Shàng Zhī (尚之), courtesy name Jìngwén (敬文),
[一二] also loved mountains and wetlands.
He accepted none of the summons or appointments,
and died of old age.
Yù zhī (彧之), courtesy name Shúcàn (叔粲),
was Shǎo Wén's (少文) cousin.
He was orphaned young,
and served his elder brother with reverence and diligence.
His family was poor, but he loved learning.
Although his literary style did not match Shǎo Wén's (少文),
his genuine simplicity surpassed it.
He accepted none of the summons or appointments.
In the early Yuánjiā (元嘉) era of Sòng (宋),
the envoy Lù Zǐzhēn (陸子真) visited to observe local customs,
and called on Yù zhī (彧之) three times.
Each time he excused himself with illness and refused to see him,
telling others:
"I am a commoner, a man of the fields,
who has lived in the countryside since childhood.
How can I be suitable for high-ranking guests?"
When Zǐzhēn (子真) returned,
he submitted a memorial recommending him,
but he still did not accept the summons.
He died at home.
Shěn Dàolán (沈道虔) was a native of Wǔkāng (武康), Wúxīng (吳興).
In his youth, he was benevolent and loving,
fond of Lǎo (老) and Yì (易),
and lived at the foot of Shíshān (石山) north of the county.
After the famine following Sūn Ēn's (孫恩) rebellion,
the county magistrate Yǔ Sùzhī (庾肅之) invited him out to the abandoned Tóutóu Lǐ (廢頭里) south of the county,
and built a house for him by the stream,
where he could enjoy the mountains and waters.
Sometimes he would return to the quiet studio on Shíshān (石山),
sharing food with his orphaned nephews,
not changing his principles even in hardship.
He learned to play the qín from Dài Kuí (戴逵),
and Wáng Jìnghóng (王敬弘) deeply respected him.
He was invited by the prefecture, province, and government a total of twelve times,
but never accepted.
When someone secretly stole vegetables from his garden,
he saw it upon returning from outside,
and hid himself,
waiting for the thief to leave before coming out.
Another person pulled up a large bamboo shoot behind his house.
When someone told him to stop them,
he said:
"I regret that this shoot cannot grow into a forest,
but there are better ones to share."
Then he had someone buy large bamboo shoots and send them to the person.
The thief was ashamed and did not take them.
Dàolán (道虔) had them placed inside his gate and then returned.
He often supported himself by gleaning.
When fellow gleaners sometimes fought over grains,
Dàolán (道虔) advised them but they did not stop,
so he gave them all that he had gathered.
The disputants were ashamed,
and thereafter, whenever they disputed, they would say,
"Don't let the lay scholar know."
[一三] In winter, he had no extra clothes.
Dài Yōng (戴顒) heard of this and invited him,
made clothes for him,
and also gave him ten thousand cash.
When he returned,
he distributed the clothes he was wearing and the money to his brothers' children who had no clothes.
The Fisherman:
his name is unknown,
nor is it known where he was from.
Sūn Miǎn 孫緬 of Tàikāng 太康 was the Grand Administrator of Xúnyáng 尋陽.
At sunset, he was strolling by the riverbank
when he saw a small boat appear and disappear as it rode the waves.
Soon, the Fisherman arrived.
His spirit and bearing were unrestrained.
He cast his line and whistled long.
Miǎn 緬 found him very unusual.
So he asked,
"Do you have fish to sell?"
The Fisherman smiled and replied,
"My fishing is not fishing;
how could I be one who sells fish?"
Miǎn 緬 was even more puzzled.
Thereupon, he lifted his clothes and waded into the water,
saying,
"I observe, sir, that you are a man of the Way.
Plying the oars all day,
you must be truly weary.
I have heard that gold and white jade
are great riches;
four-horse carriages and high canopies
are glorious power.
Now the kingly Way is enlightened,
and its authority extends overseas.
Scholars who have been hidden
are all eagerly flocking to it.
Why do you not assist in this splendid prosperity?
Why do you conceal yourself so?"
The Fisherman said,
"I am a madman of the mountains and seas,
unfamiliar with worldly affairs.
I cannot distinguish between the humble and the poor,
let alone the glorious and the noble."
Then he sang:
"Bamboo pole, slender and long,
River water, flowing softly.
Forgetting one another is joy;
greedy for bait, they swallow the hook.
Neither Bóyí 伯夷 nor Liǔxià Huì 柳下惠,
Just enough to forget worries."
Thereupon, he serenely rowed away.
Miǎn's 緬 courtesy name was Bóxù 伯緒.
He was the son of Tàizǐ Pú Xīng Zēng 太子僕興曾.
He was learned in righteousness.
Sòng Míngdì 宋明帝 knew him very well.
He held the positions of Shàngshū Zuǒchéng 尚書左丞
and Dōng Zhōngláng Sīmǎ 東中郎司馬.
Chǔ Bóyù 褚伯玉, courtesy name Yuánqú 元璩,
was a native of Qiántáng 錢唐 in Wújùn 吳郡.
His great-grandfather, Hán 含,
was the Grand Administrator of Shǐpíng 始平.
His father, Dàng 逿,
was a Cónglǔ Cānjūn 征虜參軍.
Bóyù 伯玉 was reclusive and upright from a young age,
with few desires.
At the age of eighteen,
his father arranged a marriage for him.
As the bride entered the front gate,
Bóyù 伯玉 exited through the back gate.
He then went to Shàn 剡
and lived on Pùbùshān 瀑布山 (Waterfall Mountain).
He was naturally tolerant of cold and heat;
people of his time compared him to Wáng Zhòngdū 王仲都.
He lived in the mountains for over thirty years,
isolated from people.
When Wáng Sēngdá 王僧達 became the Administrator of Wújùn 吳郡,
he earnestly invited him.
Bóyù 伯玉 had no choice but
to stay at the commandery residence for a night or two,
exchanging only a few words before departing.
Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍 Qiū Zhēnsūn 丘珍孫 wrote to Sēngdá 僧達, saying:
"I heard that Mr. Chǔ 褚 is staying at your esteemed guest house.
This man has lived a hidden life, dwelling among clouds,
not serving kings or nobles,
maintaining a lofty detachment and living on wild food,
for many years now.
If not for your humble and virtuous nature,
how could you have attracted him?
In the past, Kǒng Wénjǔ 孔文舉 dwelled in Yěchéng 冶城,
and Xiè Āndào 謝安道 entered Chāngmén 昌門;
this is the third such instance.
Such a man who abstains from grain,
a person who feeds on the mist and clouds,
can only be temporarily attracted;
it is not proper to detain him for long.
You should consider fulfilling his lofty ambition
and enabling his transformation into an immortal.
When he plans to return,
I wish to briefly trouble your pure presence,
and I also wish to assist in persuading him."
Sēngdá 僧達 replied:
"Mr. Chǔ 褚 has long been a companion of the white clouds.
Ancient recluses
sometimes worried about their children,
or caused Huáyīn 華陰 to become a marketplace;
but this man is utterly detached,
befriending only pines and rocks,
isolated on solitary peaks and sheer cliffs
for several decades.
Recently, I earnestly invited him to come here,
hoping to comfort him day and night.
Currently, we discuss *zhī* 芝 (reishi mushrooms) and *guì* 桂 (cassia),
and inquire about *lì* 荔 (lychee) and *luó* 蘿 (vines),
as if we have already peered into the misty elixir
and gazed upon the azure islet.
Knowing that you wish to see him,
I will certainly arrange an introduction."
In the second year of Sòng Xiàojiàn 宋孝建 (455 CE),
Sànqí Chángshì Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 Yuè Xún 樂詢, when inspecting local customs,
memorialized to recommend Bóyù 伯玉,
who was offered the position of Běnzhōu Yìcáo Cóngshì 本州議曹從事 (Consultant to the Prefectural Deliberative Bureau),
but he did not accept.
When Qí Gāodì 齊高帝 ascended the throne,
he personally issued an edict to the two commanderies of Wú 吳 and Kuàijī 會稽 to greet and send him with proper rites,
but he again declined due to illness.
The Emperor did not wish to go against his will,
and decreed that the Tàipíngguǎn 太平館 (Hall of Great Peace) be built for him to reside in on Báishíshān 白石山 (White Stone Mountain) in Shàn 剡.
He died in the first year of Jiànyuán 建元 (479 CE),
at the age of eighty-six.
Bóyù 伯玉 always lived on the upper floor of a building,
and was buried at the location of that building.
Kǒng Guī 孔珪 received Taoist methods from him,
and erected a stele for him beside the hall.
Gù Huān 顧歡, courtesy name Jǐngyí 景怡,
also named Xuánpíng 玄平,
was a native of Yánguān 鹽官 in Wújùn 吳郡.
his father and grandfather were both farmers.
Huān 歡 alone loved learning.
At the age of six or seven,
he knew how to calculate the *liùjiǎ* 六甲.
His family was poor.
His father sent him to the fields to scare away sparrows.
Huān 歡 wrote the *Huángquè Fù* 黃雀賦 (Rhapsody on Yellow Sparrows) and returned home,
with the sparrows having eaten more than half of the rice.
His father was angry and intended to beat him,
but stopped upon seeing the rhapsody.
There was a schoolhouse in his village.
Being poor, Huān 歡 could not afford to attend,
so he listened while leaning against the back wall of the schoolhouse,
forgetting nothing.
In the evenings, he would burn pine knots to read,
or illuminate himself with chaff.
When he grew up,
he was dedicated and tireless in his studies.
He heard that Shào Xuánzhī 邵玄之 of Wúxīng 吳興 could transmit the texts and commentaries of the Five Classics,
so he pretended to be a scribe's apprentice
and studied under him.
Gù Yǐzhī 顧顗之 of the same commandery, who was a county magistrate,
saw him and found him remarkable,
sending his sons to associate with him,
and his grandson Xiànzhī 憲之 also studied the classics under him.
When he was over twenty,
he further consulted Léi Cìzōng 雷次宗 of Yùzhāng 豫章 on various principles of Daoism and Confucianism.
When his mother died,
he did not take water or food for six or seven days.
He built a hut by her grave
and subsequently lived as a recluse, not entering officialdom.
He established a school on Tiāntáishān 天台山 in Shàn 剡 and gathered disciples;
those who studied under him often numbered nearly a hundred.
Huān 歡 was orphaned early.
When he read the *Shī* 詩 to
"Alas, my parents!"
he would always hold the book and weep uncontrollably.
Because of this, his students stopped studying the *Liáo'é Piān* 蓼莪篇 (Ode to the蓼莪),
and it was no longer lectured on.
In his later years, he practiced dietary restrictions (taking elixirs),
and did not communicate with people.
Every morning when he went out,
mountain birds would gather on his palm to take food.
He loved Huáng-Lǎo 黃老 (Huang-Lao Daoism),
and thoroughly understood *Yīnyáng Shū* 陰陽書 (Yin-Yang texts),
and his numerological predictions were often effective.
and stayed temporarily at Dōngfǔ 東府.
Suddenly, he inscribed on a pillar,
"Thirty years, second month, twenty-first day,"
and then returned east.
Later, the Prime Villain (Emperor Wén of Liu Song's assassin) committed regicide,
which was exactly that year, month, and day.
Míng Sēngshào wrote "Zhèng Èr Jiào Lùn" (Treatise on Correcting the Two Teachings),
holding
that "the Buddha illuminates his ultimate principle,
while Lǎozi perfects his life.
Those who cling to life are deluded;
those who understand the ultimate principle are enlightened.
Now, the Daoists claim longevity and immortality,
and say they are registered in the Celestial Bureaucracy,
which greatly deviates from the original principles of Lǎozi and Zhuāngzi's writings."
Crown Prince Wénhuì and Prince Jìnglíng Zǐliáng both favored Buddhist teachings.
Mèng Jǐngyì of Wúxīng was a Daoist,
and the Crown Prince summoned him to Xuánpǔ,
where a great assembly of monks was present.
Zǐliáng had Jǐngyì prostrate before the Buddha,
but Jǐngyì refused.
Zǐliáng sent him the Shídì Jīng (Ten Stages Sūtra).
Jǐngyì then composed "Zhèng Yī Lùn" (Treatise on the Correct One),
which roughly states:
"Bǎojī (Ratnakūṭa) said,
'The Buddha proclaims the Dharma extensively with a single sound.'
Lǎozi said,
'The sage embraces the One as the model for all under heaven.'
The wonder of the One
is that it is empty and profound, transcending the realm of being,
while its divine transformation abundantly supplies the boundless.
It acts for all things without acting,
abides in a single number yet is numberless.
None can name it,
so it is provisionally called the One.
In Buddhism, it is called 'true reality' (實相, shíxiàng);
in Daoism, it is called 'the Dark Female' (玄牝, xuánpìn).
The Great Image of Dao
is the Buddha's Dharmakāya.
One guards the Dharmakāya with a non-guarding guard,
and holds the Great Image with a non-clinging hold.
However, as there are 84,000 kinds of things,
there are 84,000 Dharma teachings.
The Dharma is even countless,
and practices are also boundless.
[三四]Levels depend on circumstances,
but all must be guided back to the One.
Returning to the One is called 'dedication' (回向, huíxiàng);
turning towards the correct means there is no evil.
Once evil views are dispelled,
countless good deeds are renewed daily.
The 'Three, Five, Four, Six'
are applied as needed,
but the independent and unchanging
is beyond learning and free from worry.
Saints of countless eons
all follow this One.
Lǎozi and Shìjiā (Buddha) were never divided;
it is the deluded who divide them and fail to unite them.
When countless good deeds are fully cultivated,
and cultivation is perfected, one becomes a sage.
Though there are ten titles and a thousand appellations,
they can never fully express it.
Since it can never be fully expressed,
how can it be conceived or discussed?"
Zhāng Róng, Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng, wrote "Ménlǜ" (Rules for the Gate), saying:
"Dao and Buddha,
when reaching the ultimate, are not two.
[三五]I have seen Daoists and Buddhists debate Confucianism and Mohism,
and Buddhists and Daoists distinguish right from wrong.
Once, a swan (鴻, hóng) flew high in the sky,
so distant it was hard to discern.
The Yuè people thought it was a wild duck (鳧, fú),
while the Chǔ people thought it was a mythical bird (乙, yǐ).
People are from Chǔ or Yuè,
but the swan is always one."
He showed this to Crown Prince's Retainer Zhōu Yǒng.
Yǒng challenged him, saying:
"The ultimate nature of emptiness,
though its stillness is the same,
the methods to reach that stillness,
their principles differ.
The treatise's 'when reaching the ultimate, not two'
is it reaching the ultimate in emptiness,
or is it not two in the ultimate nature?
The single thing your reverence relies on is 'swan' or 'mythical bird,'
but in driving forth Buddhism and Daoism,
one cannot avoid two extremes.
I do not know your lofty insight;
how do you identify the origin?
