To lightly adhere to it, does that have a principle?"
The back-and-forth exchange was lengthy and is not recorded here.
Huān was not eloquent verbally,
but good at writing treatises.
He also annotated Wáng Bì's "Yì Èr Xì" (Two Appendices to the Book of Changes),
which scholars propagated.
Knowing his end was near,
he composed a poem to express his aspirations, saying:
"There is no abode in the five paths of rebirth,
but the Three Pure Ones have an eternal home.
The pure qi follows the course of Heaven,
the wandering soul transforms with things.
The great bird Kūn (鵬鵾, Péngkūn) goes to the great sea,
the cicada and dove (蜩鳩, tiáoqiū) to the mulberry and ramie.
Those who understand life let go and stay,
those who die well equalize day and night.
Entrusting destiny, what can one ride?
What direction cannot be traversed?
I lift my heart, aspiring to the ancient enlightened ones,
and thus, gently, depart."
He predicted his day of death,
and chose his burial time,
passing away in Shànshān,
at the age of sixty-four.
His body was fragrant and soft,
which Daoists called "cadaver liberation and immortal transformation" (屍解仙化, shījiě xiānhuà).
He was reburied in his old tomb,
and entwined trees grew by the side of the grave.
The county magistrate, Jiāng Shāntú, memorialized the emperor,
and Emperor Wǔ (武帝) ordered Huān's sons to compile "Huān Wényì" (Discussions of Huān's Writings) in thirty volumes.
Also, Lú Dù, courtesy name Xiàozhāng, from Shǐxīng,
also possessed Daoist arts.
In his youth, he followed Zhāng Yǒng in the northern invasion against Wèi.
When Yǒng was defeated,
and the Wèi forces pursued them relentlessly,
they were blocked by the Huái River and could not cross.
Dù made a vow in his heart, saying:
"If I can escape death,
from now on I will never again kill a living being."
In a moment, he saw two shields floating,
grabbed them, and was able to cross.
Later, he retired to Sāngù Shān in Xīchāng, Lúlíng,
[三六]where birds and beasts followed him.
One night, a deer bumped his wall.
Dù said:
"Do not damage my wall."
The deer immediately left.
[三七]In front of his house was a pond where he kept fish,
all of whom he called by name,
and they would come in order to take food before leaving.
He foreknew the year and month of his death,
and bade farewell to his friends and family.
At the end of Yǒngmíng,
he died of old age.
Dù Jīngchǎn, courtesy name Jǐngqí,
was from Qiántáng, Wú Jùn.
His grandfather, Yùn,
was a staff officer for Liú Yì's Wèijūn.
His father, Dàoqú,
was a provincial official and skilled at playing the zither.
Jīngchǎn was quiet and tranquil in his youth,
not interested in fame or officialdom,
and although somewhat learned in literature and meaning,
he devoted himself to cultivating Huáng-Lǎo Daoism.
Kǒng Jì of Kuàijī,
[三八]who was pure, firm, and had lofty principles,
became his close friend after their first meeting.
The commandery appointed him principal clerk,
and the province summoned him as an official,
but he claimed illness and left.
He shared a close bond with Gù Huān from the same commandery.
He opened a dwelling on Dōngshān in Shǐníng to teach.
[三九]During the JiànYuán reign of Qí,
when Wǔlíng Wáng Yè was governor of Kuàijī,
Emperor Gāo of Qí sent the scholar Liú Huán to the east to lecture for Yè.
Huán specially went to visit and associate with him,
saying:
"Master Dù
is the Tái and Shàng of today."
Jīngchǎn invited Huán to his mountain dwelling to lecture on books,
spending all his resources to host him.
His son, Qī, personally wore straw sandals
to serve meals to Huán's students.
Kǒng Guī, Zhōu Yǒng, and Xiè Zhāng (𦵩) all wrote letters to convey their cordial regards.
In the tenth year of Yǒngmíng,
Guī, along with Guānglù Dàfū Lù Chéng, Cíbù Shàngshū Yú Cóng, Tàizǐ Yòushuài Shěn Yuē, and Sītú Yòuchángshǐ Zhāng Róng, memorialized to recommend Jīngchǎn,
who was summoned to be Fèng Cháoqǐng,
but he did not go.
He gathered disciples and taught on Rìmén Shān in Kuàijī.
At the beginning of Jiànwǔ,
he was summoned as Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
Jīngchǎn said:
"Did Zhuāngzi, holding his fishing rod,
ever turn back for a white jade disc?"
He declined due to illness and then died.
Cài Huì, courtesy name Xiūmíng,
was a native of Chénliú.
He was upright and did not associate with common people.
Lǐ Huī said to Jiāng Xiào:
“The ancients referred to those who were content in poverty and pure as ‘yí’ (夷),
and those who are stained but not defiled as ‘bái’ (白).
As for Cài Xiūmíng,
can he not be called ‘yíbái’ (夷白)?”
There was also Kǒng Sìzhī, courtesy name Jìngbó, from Lǔguó.
During the Sòng dynasty, he served as a Zhongshū Shèrén alongside Qí Gāodì,
but this was not his preference.
After resigning from his post as the Administrator of Lújiāng Commandery,
he retired to Zhōngshān.
The imperial court appointed him Tàizhōng Dàfū.
He died in office.
Xú Bózhēn, courtesy name Wénchǔ,
was a native of Tàimò, Dōngyáng.
His grandfather and father were both commandery clerks.
Bózhēn was orphaned and poor in his youth.
Without paper for writing,
he often practiced writing on bamboo arrows, ruò leaves, banana leaves, and the ground.
When a mountain flood suddenly occurred,
sweeping away homes and dwellings,
and all the villagers fled,
Bózhēn piled up beds and sat,
reciting books without ceasing.
His uncle Fánzhī was a close friend of Yán Yánzhī.
He returned to Qūméngshān to establish a hermitage and lectured there,
and Bózhēn went to study with him.
After accumulating ten years,
he thoroughly studied the classics and histories,
and many scholars on their travels relied on him.
The Administrator Wáng Tánshēng of Lángyá and Zhāng Yān of Wújùn both treated him with courtesy and invited him,
but Bózhēn would respond to the summons and then withdraw.
This happened a total of twelve times.
The recluse Shěn Yǎn engaged him in close conversation,
establishing a pure friendship.
Gù Huān of Wújùn singled out difficult meanings in the Shàngshū,
and Bózhēn responded,
very systematically,
which scholars honored.
He was fond of Buddhism, Lǎo, and Zhuāng,
and also mastered Daoist arts.
Once, during a drought,
Bózhēn divined,
and rain came as predicted.
His every action was礼 (lǐ)-compliant.
Passing beneath a crooked tree,
he would hurry to avoid it.
He lost his wife early
and did not remarry in later life,
likening himself to Zēng Cān.
Nine *lǐ* south of his residence was a high mountain,
which Bān Gù called Jiǔyánshān.
It was where Lóngqiū Cháng of the Later Hàn dynasty had retired.
The mountain had many *lóngxūchēngbǎi* (龍鬚檉柏) trees,
appearing in five colors when viewed from afar.
People called it Fùrén Yán.
Two years later,
Bózhēn moved there.
Between the steps and the door,
the trees all grew with intertwined branches.
A *zǐ* tree grew in front of his gate,
and in one year it became too large to be embraced.
On the stone wall east of his lodge,
a red light suddenly shone brightly at night,
then quickly vanished.
A pair of white sparrows nested in his window and door,
which commentators regarded as a sign of his hidden virtue.
The Inspector, Wáng, of Yùzhāng, invited him to be a Cánjūn Yìcáo,
but he did not accept.
His family was very poor,
and his four brothers all grew old together with white hair,
so people called them
“the Four Hoary Ones.”
He died in the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
aged eighty-four.
He had over a thousand disciples.
Lóu Yòuyú, courtesy name Jìyù, from the same commandery as Bózhēn,
also gathered students and lectured,
and did not respond to invitations for official service.
He was greatly admired and uniquely appreciated by Línchuān Wáng Yìng,
and authored thirty volumes of *Lǐ Jùnshí*.
Shěn Línschì, courtesy name Yúnzhēn,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His grandfather, Yīngqí,
was a Jìn Tàizhōng Dàfū.
His father, Qiánzhī,
was the Sòng Lè'ān Magistrate.
Línschì was intelligent and quick-witted as a child.
At the age of seven,
he listened to his uncle, Yuè, speak on metaphysics.
After the guests dispersed,
he recalled everything without missing a word.
Yuè patted his shoulder and said:
“If this culture is not to perish,
it will be through you!”
When he grew up,
he was widely versed in the classics and histories,
and possessed lofty aspirations.
When his parents died,
he observed mourning rites with utmost devotion.
After the mourning period,
he would shed tears for more than ten days on their death anniversaries.
Living in poverty, he wove curtains and recited books,
his hands and mouth never idle.
Locals called him “the Curtain-Weaving Gentleman.”
Once, while making bamboo objects for someone, he accidentally cut his hand,
and immediately returned home weeping.
His fellow workers said to him:
“This is not enough to be harmed by,
why shed tears?”
He replied:
“This doesn’t hurt,
but to damage the body given by my parents
fills me with sorrow.”
Once, walking on the road,
a neighbor recognized his clogs.
Línschì said:
“Are these your clogs?”
He immediately went home barefoot.
When the neighbor found his clogs, he sent the previous pair back to him.
Línschì said:
“Are these not your clogs?”
He laughed and accepted them.
In the late Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
Emperor Wén ordered the Púyè Hé Shàngzhī to compile the Five Classics,
and sought out scholars.
The county nominated Línschì.
He reluctantly went to the capital,
and Shàngzhī treated him with great respect.
Upon his arrival,
Shàngzhī said to his son Yǎn:
“Mountains and forests indeed contain many extraordinary individuals.
Shěn Línschì is
of the same caliber as Huáng Shūdù.
How can he be used to clarify the turbid?
You should make him your teacher.”
Línschì once suffered from a lack of books.
While traveling in the capital,
he reviewed all four sections [of the library]
and then sighed:
“The ancients, what kind of people were they?”
Soon after, he feigned illness and returned to his hometown,
avoiding contact with others.
He raised his orphaned nephew,
his righteousness well-known in the local community.
Someone advised him to take office,
to which he replied:
“Fish are confined in nets, beasts in cages;
the whole world is one such trap.
The sages, with their profound enlightenment,
always tread the path of good first.
I truly cannot yet practice ‘sitting in oblivion’ with virtuous conduct,
so why should I not aspire to ‘daily decrease’?”
He then composed the *Xuánsàn Fù* to cut himself off from the world.
The Administrator Kǒng Shānshì invited him, but he did not accept.
His relatives, Xúzhōu Inspector Tánqìng, Shìzhōng Huáiwén, and Zuǒlǜ Bó, came to visit him,
but Línschì never responded.
He retired to Wúchāshān in Yúbù,
lecturing on the classics and teaching.
Tens to hundreds of scholars studied with him,
each building their own dwelling
and settling near him.
At the time, a saying went:
“On Wúchāshān lives a virtuous scholar;
opening his door to teach has made it a marketplace.”
Línschì greatly valued Lù Jī’s *Liánzhū*,
and often lectured on it to his students.
Zhāng Yǒng, the Zhēngběi, became the Administrator of Wúxīng,
and invited Línschì to the commandery.
Línschì heard that there were beautiful mountains and waters behind the commandery office.
This was where Dài Āndào had traveled in Wúxīng,
and had created a mountain pond from an ancient tomb.
Wishing to see it,
he went and stayed for several months.
Yǒng wanted to appoint him as a Gōngcáo.
Línschì said:
“Your Excellency’s virtue and conduct are pure and unadorned.
You cherish the mountains and valleys,
which is why I, in humble attire and leaning on my staff,
have forgotten my weariness and illness.
But if you must adorn chaos with beautiful eyebrows,
and crown a Yùe commoner with an official’s cap,
though I am not clever,
I beg to adhere to lofty principles.
I would rather leap into the Eastern Sea and die,
than endure this tattooing and nose-cutting.”
Yǒng then desisted.
Liáng Wǔdì was on good terms with Shēn when young.
When he raised an army,
he appointed Shēn as Registrar and Adjutant in the Pingxī Mansion,
but Shēn refused to submit.
Throughout his life, he rarely socialized.
When Liǔ Yùn of Hédōng wanted to associate with him,
he refused and did not accept.
During the Pǔtōng era,
an imperial edict summoned him to be a Huángmén Shìláng,
but he claimed illness and did not rise.
In his later years, he particularly adhered to Buddhism,
establishing a dào chǎng within his residence,
performing circumambulations and repentance rituals,
six times a day without ceasing.
He recited the Fǎhuá Jīng,
once daily.
Later, in the middle of the night, he suddenly saw a dào rén who called himself Yuàn Gōng.
His demeanor and bearing were very unusual.
He addressed Shēn as Shàngxíng Xiānshēng,
gave him incense, and left.
In the fourth year of Dàtōng in the Zhōng era,
he suddenly awoke from sleep,
saying:
"Yuàn Gōng has come again.
I cannot stay long."
His complexion did not change.
As soon as he finished speaking, he passed away,
aged seventy-eight.
The entire household heard a voice chanting in the air:
"Shàngxíng Xiānshēng has already been reborn in the Pure Land of Mí."
Wǔdì heard this and issued an edict,
posthumously honoring him as Zhēnjié Chǔshì,
to display his noble character.
Shēn authored Dìlì in twenty volumes,
Yìlín in twenty volumes,
Xù Wǔ Duānxiū Jiānglíng Jì in one volume,
Jìncháo Záshì in five volumes,
and Zǒngchāo in eighty volumes,
which circulated in the world.
His son Mànqiàn, courtesy name Shìhuá,
also had an early excellent reputation.
When Yuán Dì was in Jīngzhōu,
he served as Zhōng Lùshì.
Whenever he went out,
the Emperor would often watch him depart,
saying to Liú Zhīlìn:
"Jīngnán indeed has many noble men."
Later, he was transferred to Cányì Cānjūn.
His works include Sāngfú Yí,
Wénzì Tǐlì,
Lǎozǐ Yìshū,
Suànjīng, and Qīyào Lìshù,
along with his compiled writings,
totaling ninety-five volumes.
His son Jìcái possessed learning and conduct.
During the Chéngshèng era,
he held the position of Zhōngshū Shìláng.
When Jiānglíng fell,
he entered Cháng'ān with the others.
Zhāng Xiàoxiù, courtesy name Wényì,
was a native of Wǎn in Nányáng.
He moved to Xúnyáng.
His great-grandfather was Xūwú,
his grandfather Sēngjiān,
and his father Xī,
all serving as Biéjià Cóngshì.
Xiàoxiù was over six chǐ tall,
with a fair complexion and beautiful beard and eyebrows.
He served as a Cóngshì Shǐ in the prefecture.
When the Inspector Chén Bózhī rebelled,
Xiàoxiù conspired with the local gentry to attack him,
but the plot was discovered,
and he fled to the side of the Pén Shuǐ.
A merchant hid him in a chǔ,
and he eventually made his way to Dōnglín.
Bózhī captured his mother, Guō,
and killed her by pouring wax over her.
Xiàoxiù sent away his wife and concubines
and entered Kuāng Shān to practice the Dao.
After the mourning period, King Jiàn'ān summoned him to be a Biéjià.
He then resigned his post and returned to the mountains,
residing in Dōnglín Sì.
He owned several tens of qǐng of land
and several hundred retainers,
whom he directed to cultivate the land diligently,
providing entirely for the mountain community.
People from far and near came to admire him,
flocking to him like to a marketplace.
Xiàoxiù was naturally straightforward and
disliked superficiality.
He always wore a gu pí jīn
and straw sandals,
holding a bīnglǘ pí zhǔwěi in his hand.
He consumed hánshí sǎn
and slept on a stone in the depth of winter.
He widely studied various books
and specialized in Buddhist scriptures.
If monks violated the precepts,
he would gather the assembly before the Buddha,
perform a karma ritual and flog them,
and many were able to correct their faults.
He was skilled in debate
and adept at clerical script.
Indeed, there was no art or skill
that he did not thoroughly master.
He died in the third year of Pǔtōng.
Everyone in the room smelled an extraordinary fragrance.
Liáng Jiǎnwén grieved deeply for him
and wrote a letter to Liú Huìfěi,
describing his integrity and purity.
Yǔ Chéngxiān, courtesy name Zǐtōng,
was a native of Yānlíng in Yǐngchuān.
From a young age, he was calm and composed with high aspirations and principles.
Right and wrong were not uttered in his words,
and joy or anger did not show on his face,
so people could not fathom him.
In his youth, he studied under Liú Qiú of Nányáng.
He had a powerful memory and keen perception,
surpassing his peers.
There was no profound classic or Buddhist scripture
that he did not thoroughly comprehend;
the Nine Streams and Seven Summaries
were all areas in which he was proficient.
He was appointed Gōngcáo but did not take the position,
instead traveling with the Daoist Wáng Sēngzhèn to Héng Yuè.
Later, due to his brother's illness, he returned to his hometown
and consequently resided on Tǔtái Shān.
When Liáng Póyáng Zhōngliè Wáng was in the prefecture,
he admired his character
and invited him to associate and stay with him,
asking him to lecture on Lǎozǐ.
Renowned monks from far and near
all came to attend.
Discussions and challenges arose sharply,
and various heterodox views were presented.
Chéngxiān calmly responded to each,
and all heard things they had never heard before.
Zhōngliè Wáng particularly revered him.
In the third year of Dàtōng in the Zhōng era,
Liú Huìfěi of Lú Shān came to Jīngzhōu.
Chéngxiān, having an old acquaintance with him,
went to visit him.
Students from Jīng and Shǎn then invited Chéngxiān to lecture on Lǎozǐ.
debating throughout the day,
and lingering for over a month
before returning to the mountain.
The King personally saw him off
and also presented him with poems,
which the recluses praised.
He died that year,
and the Inspector offered generous funeral gifts.
His disciple Huáng Shìlóng respectfully declined, saying:
"Our late teacher usually did not seek satiety in food
or lightness in clothing.
Whatever gifts he received,
he never accepted.
On his dying day,
he instructed his household
to use a thin coffin barely covering his form
and simple cloth for burial.
Although we are honored by the bestowal,
we dare not lightly accept the imperial command
to violate his lifelong principles.
The money and cloth have been returned to the envoy."
The public opinion at the time held him in high esteem.
Mǎ Shū, courtesy name Yàolǐ,
was a native of Méi in Fúfēng.
His grandfather Língqìng
was a Registrar and Adjutant for King Jìnglíng of Qí.
Shū was orphaned at a few years old
and raised by his aunt.
At six,
he could recite the Xiàojīng, Lúnyǔ, and Lǎozǐ.
As he grew,
he extensively studied classics and histories,
particularly excelling in Buddhist scriptures and the commentaries on Zhōuyì and Lǎozǐ.
When King Shàolíng Lún of Liáng was the Inspector of Nánxúzhōu,
having long heard of his reputation,
he invited him to be a scholar.
Lún himself lectured on the Dàpǐn Jīng at the time,
and instructed Shū to lecture on Wéimó, Lǎozǐ, and Zhōuyì,
all commencing on the same day.
Two thousand people, both clergy and laity, came to listen.
The King, wishing to observe their strengths and weaknesses,
then said to the assembly:
"When debating with Scholar Mǎ,
you must make him concede;
there should be no empty establishment of host and guest."
Thereupon, scholars from several schools
each raised questions.
Shū then sequentially analyzed and explained,
unfolding their main points,
and then branching out into infinite transformations,
such that the debaters merely listened in silence and accepted.
Lún greatly praised him.
Xú Yuán
had the courtesy name Chángyù, and was a native of Kāiyáng, Southern Lángxié.
His original name was Yuàn.
Later, because it was the same name as Fù Liàng's father,
Liàng requested it be changed to Yuán.
He first served as Dianjūn in the Dàsīmǎ's residence of the Prince of Lángxié during the Jìn dynasty.
He accompanied the northern campaigns,
and his subtle and meticulous approach to affairs
was recognized by Emperor Wǔ.
When the young emperor (Shàodì) was in the Eastern Palace,
he entered to serve at his side.
In the early years of Emperor Wén,
he was again trusted and employed,
eventually reaching the position of Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ.
In Yuánjiā twelve,
he was transferred to Nántái Yùshǐ,
and then served as Hòujūn Xíng Cānjūn for Prince Shǐxīng, Jùn.
He again attended the Crown Prince in the Eastern Palace,
and was promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
Whenever Emperor Wén went on a military expedition,
he would often delegate military strategies to him in advance.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Wáng Xuánmó and others were again dispatched to invade the north.
Yuán was allocated five hundred men
to accompany the army to Quèqiáo,
bearing confidential imperial decrees to be announced as needed.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ reached Xīntíng,
Prince Jiāngxià, Yìgōng, fled south.
Yuán was in the palace at the time,
and feigned encouragement to pursue Yìgōng,
thus managing to escape south himself.
At that time, Emperor Xiàowǔ was about to ascend the throne.
The military headquarters were in a rush
and unfamiliar with court protocols.
Yuán was well-versed in these matters,
and upon his arrival,
everyone was delighted.
He was concurrently appointed Tàicháng Chéng to compile the ritual regulations.
Later, he was concurrently Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
then promoted to Zuǒchéng.
Previously,
during the Yuánjiā era, Zhuòzuò Láng Hé Chéngtiān was tasked with compiling the national history.
In the early years of Emperor Xiàowǔ, Fèng Cháoqǐng Shān Qiānzhī and Nántái Yùshǐ Sū Bǎoshēng were again ordered to complete it.
In Xiàojiàn six,
Yuán was again appointed Lǐng Zhuòzuò Láng
to finish the work.
Although Yuán based it on previous works,
he entirely made it a book of his own family's perspective.
He submitted a memorial stating,
"Starting from Yìxī
as the beginning of the imperial enterprise,
recording and enumerating the efforts
as the conclusion of the meritorious ministers."
Thereupon, there was broad debate both inside and outside the court.
Tàizǎi Prince Jiāngxià, Yìgōng, and thirty-five others agreed with Yuán
that the first year of Yìxī should be the demarcation.
Sànqí Chángshì Prince Bālíng, Xiūruò, and Shàngshū Jīnbù Láng Tán Dàoluán both argued that the third year of Yuánxīng should be the beginning.
Tàixué Bóshì Yú Hé argued that the founding of the state should be taken as the first year of Sònggōng.
The imperial edict stated:
"Xiàng Jí and Shèng Gōng,
in compiling the two Hàn histories,
there are precedents in previous histories.
Huán Xuán's biography should be included in the Sòng code,
the rest shall be as Yuán suggested."
When Emperor Xiàowǔ died,
and Jǐngníng Líng was constructed,
he was concurrently Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng while retaining his original office.
Yuán was adaptable and good at serving people,
capable of grasping the subtle intentions of the ruler.
He was somewhat learned in books and traditions,
and particularly familiar with court ceremonies.
In the early years of Yuánjiā,
he entered to serve at the emperor's side,
participating in consultations.
He was skilled at flattery
and embellished his words with classical texts,
thus he was favored and employed by Emperor Wén.
During the Dàmíng era,
he was entrusted with especially heavy responsibilities.
No major court ceremony
could proceed without Yuán's deliberations.
Even if there were scholars of the time whose understanding surpassed his,
they dared not voice differing opinions,
and what they said was not adopted.
When Emperor Xiàowǔ died,
after the period of public mourning,
the Shìdú Bóshì of Prince Jìn'ān, Zǐxūn, consulted Yuán on whether it was appropriate to continue studying.
Yuán replied:
"During mourning, one studies mourning rites;
what objection is there to continuing studies?"
A few days later,
the Bóshì of Prince Shǐ'ān, Zǐzhēn, consulted Yuán.
Yuán said:
"Minor mourning requires suspending studies;
how can one read during three years of mourning?"
His arbitrary and contradictory judgments were all like this.
The former deposed emperor (Qián Fèidì) was violent and lawless,
and many old palace officials were punished and dismissed.
Only Yuán was skillful in adapting and welcoming,
remaining unscathed from beginning to end.
After the execution of the various dukes,
Yuán was appointed Huángmén Shìláng,
concurrently Lǐng Shèshēng Xiàowèi,
with his Zhuòzuò duties remaining as before,
and was enfeoffed as the Viscount of Wúpíng County.
The favor and trust he received were immense,
unmatched by any other minister.
Whenever the emperor traveled,
Yuán often shared a carriage with Shěn Qìngzhī and Princess Shānyīn.
Emperor Míng
ascended the throne,
and as Huángmén Shìláng,
he was transferred to Lǐng Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
The following year,
he was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū,
with his Zhuòzuò duties remaining as before.
Yuán had held power for a long time,
and the emperor (Míngdì) had disliked him when he was still a prince.
During the Jǐnghé era,
when the emperor was humiliated and constrained,
Yuán's treatment of him was very disrespectful,
which increased his resentment.
In Tàishǐ three,
an imperial edict exposed his crimes,
and he was exiled to Jiāozhōu.
As he was departing,
another edict removed him to a prefecture within Guǎngzhōu.
The relevant authorities proposed that he be made Sònglóng Tàishǒu.
By the time the appointment order arrived,
Yuán had already reached Jiāozhōu.
After a long time, he was permitted to return,
and was appointed Nánkāng Jùn Chéng.
When Emperor Míng died,
he returned to the capital.
Yuán was appointed Jǐnán Tàishǒu,
and again appointed Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
In Yuánhuī three, he died
at the age of eighty-two.
Yuán's son, Xīxiù,
was very learned and knowledgeable,
and also skilled in zhuàn and lì scripts.
The steles of Zhèngjué and Chánlíng monasteries
were written by Xīxiù.
When Yuán was exiled to Jiāozhōu,
Emperor Míng summoned Xīxiù and said:
"Soon I will allow your father to return."
Xīxiù bowed twice and replied:
"My father is old;
I fear he may not live to receive your future grace."
The emperor greatly praised him,
and immediately summoned Yuán back.
Xīxiù held the positions of Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn and Huáinán Tàishǒu.
His son, Hóng, was very skilled in official duties,
but was harsh in his work
and showed little kindness to others.
In the Qí dynasty, he held successive positions as Táiláng,
Mòlíng and Jiànkāng Ling,
and Xiāngdōng Tàishǒu.
Ruǎn Diànfū
was a native of Zhūjì, Kuàijī.
In the early years when Emperor Míng left his residence,
he was chosen as Zhǔyī.
Later, he was again requested to be the Crown Prince's teacher,
and was greatly trusted and favored.
Towards the end of the Jǐnghé era,
Emperor Míng was confined in the palace,
residing in the Bìshū Shěng,
and was suspected by the (deposed) emperor,
with great disaster imminent.
Diànfū, together with Wáng Dàolóng, Lǐ Dào'ér, and the emperor's attendants Lángxié Chúnyú Wénzǔ, conspired to depose and establish a new emperor.
At that time, Zhíge Jiāngjūn Liǔ Guāngshì also had a secret plot with the emperor's attendants Lánlíng Miáo Fāngshèng and Dānyáng Zhōu Dēngzhī,
but did not know whom to support.
Dēngzhī had a previous acquaintance with Emperor Míng,
so Fāngshèng and others had Dēngzhī establish a connection with Diànfū.
Diànfū was greatly pleased.
Previously,
when the (deposed) emperor established his empress,
all eunuchs of the various princes were temporarily removed.
Qián Lánshēng, an attendant of Emperor Míng, was also among them.
After the event, he had not yet been dismissed.
Diànfū secretly sent Lánshēng to monitor the (deposed) emperor.
Fearing exposure,
Lánshēng did not wish to come forward himself.
He would report the emperor's every move
to Chúnyú Wénzǔ, who would then inform Diànfū.
After the Emperor executed the various dukes,
he no longer had any scruples or fears.
There was no day he didn't go out to roam.
His favorite Concubine Pān (潘) originally had the surname Yú (俞) and the given name Nízǐ (尼子);
she was a courtesan of Wáng Jìngzé (王敬則).
Some say that Emperor Wén (文) of Sòng (宋) had a Concubine Pān (潘),
who was on the throne for thirty years,
and so he changed her surname to Pān (潘).
Her father, Bǎoqìng (寶慶), also changed his surname accordingly.
The Emperor called Bǎoqìng (寶慶) and Rú Fǎzhēn (茹法珍) "Āzhàng" (阿丈) (maternal uncles),
and Chóng'ér (蟲兒) and Yú Língyùn (俞靈韻), a soldier from the Dōngyě (東冶) camp, "Āxiōng" (阿兄) (elder brothers).
The Emperor, along with Fǎzhēn (法珍) and others, went to see Bǎoqìng (寶慶).
The Emperor personally drew water,
helped people cook,
and joked around with market gossip.
The Emperor also rode lightly armored in military attire to the homes of his trusted guards to feast,
and always went to celebrate or mourn for joyful or sorrowful occasions.
The eunuch Wáng Bǎosūn (王寶孫), thirteen or fourteen years old,
was called Chāngzǐ (倀子) (familiar ghost),
and was the most favored.
He participated in court politics,
and even Wáng Xuānzhī (王咺之) and Chóng'ér (蟲兒) deferred to him.
He controlled ministers,
altered imperial edicts,
and even rode his horse into the palace
to criticize the Son of Heaven.
When the dukes and ministers saw him,
none dared to breathe.

Those who helped him in his corrupt and chaotic rule were: Rú Fǎzhēn (茹法珍), Chóng'ér (蟲兒), Wáng Xuānzhī (王咺之), Yú Bǎoqìng (俞寶慶), Yú Língyùn (俞靈韻), Zhù Língyǒng (祝靈勇), Fàn Liàngzhī (范亮之), Xú Sēngzhòng (徐僧重), Shí Chóngjì (時崇濟), Ruì Āntài (芮安泰), Liú Wéntài (劉文泰), Lǚ Wénqìng (呂文慶), Hú Huīguāng (胡輝guāng), Miào Mǎiyǎng (繆買養), Zhāng Dàozhī (章道之), Yáng Jìngzǐ (楊敬子), Lǐ Cànzhī (李粲之), Zhōu Guǎanzhī (周管之), Fàn Tánjì (范曇濟), Shí Tányuè (石曇悅), Zhāng Ènǔ (張惡奴), Wáng Shènggōng (王勝公), Wáng Huáizǎo (王懷藻), Méi Shīzhì (梅師濟), Zōu Bó'ér (鄒伯兒), Shǐ Yuányì (史元益), Wáng Língfàn (王靈範), Xí Xiūwén (席休文), Xiè Pāng (解滂), and Grand Astrologer Luò Wénshū (駱文叔), Great Sorcerer Zhū Guāngshàng (朱光尚),
totaling thirty-one people.

There were also ten eunuchs: Wáng Bǎosūn (王寶孫), Wáng Fǎzhāo (王法昭), Xǔ Lǎngzhī (許朗之), Xǔ BóSūn (許伯孫), Fāng Fóniàn (方佛念), Mǎ Sēngměng (馬僧猛), Shèng Shào (盛劭), Wáng Zhú'ér (王竺兒), Suí Yào (隨要), Yuán Xìshì (袁係世) and others.
When Liáng Wǔ (梁武) pacified Jiànyè (建鄴),
all were executed.
Furthermore, Zhū Xīngguāng (朱興光) was resented by Rú Fǎzhēn (茹法珍),
and was found guilty and imprisoned.
Fēng Yǒngzhī (豐勇之) and Wáng Zhēnguó (王珍國) were on good terms,
and their executions were both averted.
Initially,
all the trusted guards and their ilk were called "ghosts."
A rumor circulated in the palace:
"The Zhào (趙) ghost eats 'yā juān' (鴨●),
and all the ghosts are put in order."
At the time, no one understood it.
When Liáng Wǔ (梁武) pacified Jiànyè (建鄴),
and Dōnghūn (東昏) died,
the group of petty individuals were all exterminated at once,
hence they were referred to as "the various ghosts."
In common parlance, finely chopped meat mixed with ginger and cinnamon was called "juān" (●),
implying that the wicked faction would all be finely chopped and cooked.
Zhōu Shízhēn (周石珍) was a servant from Jiànkāng (建康),
whose family had for generations made a living by selling silk.
During Emperor Tiānjiān's (天監) reign of Liáng (梁),
he gradually rose to be a left and right messenger.
He was seven *chǐ* tall
and quite skilled in discourse.
Later, he became the Director of the Imperial Workshop,
and concurrently served as the Magistrate of Kāiyáng (開陽).
He successively held the position of General of the Imperial Guards.
In the third year of Tàiqīng (太清),
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Nánfēng (南豐) County,
still leading the Imperial Workshop.
Before the Imperial City fell,
he had already secretly corresponded with Hóu Jǐng (侯景) and allied with him.
When the gate first opened,
Shízhēn (石珍) was still attending the Emperor.
At that time, the rebels sent their followers into the palace,
some driving donkeys and horses in and out of the palace courtyard.
Emperor Wǔ (武) was then seated in the Wéndé (文德) Hall,
and asked in surprise,
Shízhēn (石珍) said:
"They are all Prime Minister's armored soldiers."
The Emperor said:
"What kind of Prime Minister?"
He replied:
"Prime Minister Hóu (侯)."
The Emperor angrily rebuked him:
"His name is Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
why call him Prime Minister!"
Shízhēn (石珍) sought to curry favor with the rebels,
and so adopted their partisan Tián Qiān (田遷) as his own son,
and Qiān (遷) also served him as a father.
When Jǐng (景) usurped the throne,
the systems and regalia were all devised by Shízhēn (石珍).
After Jǐng (景) was suppressed,
he, along with Yán Dàn (嚴亶), the Scribe of the Central Secretariat, and others, were sent to Jiānglíng (江陵).
Dàn (亶) was originally a Supervisor of Religious Affairs,
and had resided in the palace offices for a long time,
being familiar with many historical facts.
He held an important position among the rebels,
second only to Shízhēn (石珍).
When Jiǎnwén (簡文) was installed,
Dàn (亶) imitated the northern people by wearing boots into the hall,
without observing proper reverence.
When someone found this strange,
Dàn (亶) said:
"Why should I fear Liú Chán (劉禪)?"
He followed Jǐng (景) to besiege Bālíng (巴陵) Commandery,
and shouted:
"Why does Jīngzhōu (荊州) not surrender!"
When they arrived in Jiānglíng (江陵),
and were about to be executed in the market,
he wept and said to Shízhēn (石珍):
"Our deaths are also due to our accumulated sins."
Shízhēn (石珍) and his son Shēng (昇) embraced and cried.
Dàn (亶) said to the executioner:
"Please tell the Prince of Xiāngdōng (湘東),
'If there had been no overthrow,
how would you have risen?'"
They were both cut in half at the waist.
Thereafter, other rebel partisans were killed,
their tongues clamped with planks
and nailed down,
so they could no longer speak.
Lù Yàn (陸驗) and Xú Lín (徐驎)
were both from Wú (吳) County, Wú (吳).
Yàn (驗) was poor in his youth,
and was dissolute and ill-behaved.
A local named Yù Jíqīng (郁吉卿) was very wealthy,
and Yàn (驗) devoted himself to serving him.
Jíqīng (吉卿) lent him money and rice,
and Yàn (驗) borrowed it for trading,
thus accumulating a thousand pieces of gold.
Consequently, he went to the capital,
and spent his wealth to serve the powerful.
Zhū Jiǎo (朱䌇),
a fellow townsman of his,
had once shown him kindness,
and so spoke to Emperor Wǔ (武) to promote him.
He and Xú Lín (徐驎) successively served as Assistant Ministers of the Privy Treasury and Prefects of the Grand Market.
Yàn (驗) originally had no talents,
and his appearance was particularly ugly.
Previously,
a foreign country had presented a live rhinoceros,
whose form was very uncouth,
so the local people all called Yàn (驗) "the live rhinoceros."
Yàn (驗) and Lín (驎) both made strictness and harshness their business,
and all merchants feared them.
Jiǎo (䌇) was especially close to them,
and people of the time called them "the three pests."
Fù Qí (傅岐), the Minister of Agriculture,
was an upright scholar.
He once said to Jiǎo (䌇):
"You participate in governing the state,
and enjoy such honor and favor.
What I have heard recently
is so filthy and messy.
If the sagely ruler were to awaken,
could you escape?"
Jiǎo (䌇) said:
"I have long known the slanders from outside.
If my conscience is clear,
why worry about what people say?"
Qí (岐) said to others:
"Zhū Yànhé (朱彥和) is about to die.
He relies on flattery to gain favor,
and uses sophistry to reject remonstrance.
He hears of danger but is not afraid,
and knows evil but does not change.
Heaven has taken away his discernment;
how can he last long?"
Yàn (驗) indeed used extortion as his skill,
and within a few years, he reached high office,
wearing jade pendants and sable tails,
ranking alongside the distinguished.
He rose to be Right General of the Crown Prince's Guards,
and upon his death,
was posthumously granted the title of Right General of the Guards.
When people near and far heard of his death,
none were not delighted.
Lín (驎) had long been resented by Luán (綸), the Prince of Shàolíng (邵陵),
and in the second year of Tàiqīng (太清),
he was killed by Luán (綸).
Sīmǎ Shēn (司馬申), courtesy name Jìhé (季和),
was from Wēn (溫), Hénèi (河內).
His grandfather, Huìyuǎn (慧遠),
was the Liáng (梁) Commissioner of Waterways.
His father, Xuántōng (玄通),
was the Liáng (梁) Left Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Revenue.
Shēn (申) showed early sagacity,
and was good at *yì* (弈) (Go) by fourteen.
He once accompanied his father to visit Dào Gài (到溉), the Minister of Personnel.
At that time, Yīn Zǐchūn (陰子春), the Inspector of Liángzhōu (梁州), and Zhū Jiǎo (朱䌇), the General of the Imperial Guards, were present.
They called him to play.
Shēn (申) often had brilliant ideas.
Jiǎo (䌇) observed him and was impressed,
and subsequently invited Shēn (申) to accompany him.
During the calamity of Tàiqīng (太清),
both his parents died.
Because of this, he swore an oath
to carry earth and eat vegetarian food for the rest of his life.
Liáng Yuándì 承制,
he was repeatedly promoted to Zhenxi Waibing Jìshì Cānjūn.
When Hóu Jǐng attacked Yǐngzhōu,
Shēn followed Dudū Wáng Sēngbiàn to hold Bālíng.
Each time he offered a strategy,
it was adopted and implemented.
Sēngbiàn sighed,
"This man's skill in personally leading a charge on horseback
might not be his forte,
but if he were to manage troops and defend a city,
he would certainly achieve extraordinary feats."
When Sēngbiàn was campaigning against Lù Nà,
the enemy troops suddenly arrived at that time,
and those around them were scattered.
Shēn personally shielded Sēngbiàn,
advancing with a shield,
when Pèi Zhīhéng's rescue arrived,
and the enemy then retreated.
Sēngbiàn looked back and laughed,
"The benevolent must be courageous;
how could that be an empty saying!"
During the Tàijiàn era of Chén,
he was appointed Mòlíng Lìng.
In office, he was noted for his uprightness and competence,
and white sparrows gathered in the county court.
He was again made Dōnggōng Tōngshì Shèrén.
When Shūlíng committed his rebellion,
the plot did not succeed,
so he went out to hold Dōngfǔ.
Shēn urgently summoned Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Xiāo Móhē to lead troops to arrive first,
pursued and beheaded him.
Hòuzhǔ greatly commended this.
For his merit, he was appointed Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ,
enfeoffed as Wénzhāo Xiàn Bó,
and concurrently served as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
He was promoted to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
He served three emperors successively,
managing confidential affairs internally,
and somewhat wielding power and influence.
His nature was cruel and harmful,
and he was fond of writing anonymous letters to slander and ruin others.
The upright gentlemen of the court
all suffered from his malice.
He participated in deliberations,
but then publicly spread the news outside,
attributing it to his own efforts.
Secret affairs within the imperial secretariat
were often leaked.
He was also resolute and daring by nature,
good at responding,
and able to observe the emperor's demeanor.
If anyone offended him,
he would certainly use subtle words to slander them;
if someone attached themselves to him,
he would seize the opportunity to promote them.
Thus, within and outside the court,
everyone followed his lead.
Initially,
when Shàngshū Yòupúyè Shěn Jūnlǐ died,
the court deliberated appointing Máo Xǐ as his successor.
Shēn feared that Xǐ would become involved in state affairs,
so he disparaged Xǐ to the Hòuzhǔ, saying:
"Xǐ, your subject's brother-in-law,
during Gāodì's time, praised Your Majesty for having 'wine virtue,'
and requested the dismissal of palace officials.
Has Your Majesty forgotten this?"
Xǐ was consequently dismissed and forbidden from office.
He also colluded with Shī Wénqìng and Lǐ Tuō'ér,
slandered and killed Fù Zǎi,
and seized Rèn Zhōng's troops to assign them to Cài Zhēng and Kǒng Fàn.
This caused the military and civil officials to become demoralized,
leading to the downfall.
Shēn once napped during the day in the lower department of the Ministry of Personnel;
a crow pecked his mouth,
and blood flowed to the ground.
Contemporary opinion regarded this as the consequence of slandering worthy people.
Later, he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
with Yòuwèi and Shèrén as before.
He died in the fourth year of Zhìdé.
Hòuzhǔ mourned him for a long time.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
his noble rank was elevated to Hóu,
and he was given the posthumous name Zhōng.
At his burial,
Hòuzhǔ personally composed his tomb inscription.
His son Xiù succeeded him,
and his official position reached Tàizǐ Shèrén.
Shī Wénqìng's
origin is unknown.
[一六]His family was originally a family of officials,
and Wénqìng was fond of learning,
having read widely in books and historical records.
When Chén Hòuzhǔ was in the Eastern Palace,
Wénqìng served him.
When he ascended the throne,
Wénqìng was promoted to Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Following Shūlíng's rebellion,
and the Sui army's approach to the border,
many military and state affairs
arose suddenly.
Wénqìng was intelligent and had a strong memory,
and was proficient in official duties.
He could calculate mentally and dictate orally,
arranging matters promptly.
Because of this, he was greatly favored and trusted.
Moreover, since the Tàijiàn era,
official administration had become lax and simple,
and all departments were undisciplined.
Wénqìng exerted all his efforts,
showing no leniency or omission.
He meticulously arranged official positions and linked affairs,
and none failed to be awe-struck.
He also brought in Shěn Kèqīng, Yáng Huìlǎng, Xú Zhé, Jì Huìjǐng, and others,
claiming they possessed administrative ability.
Hòuzhǔ believed him.
However, they generally lacked a broad understanding of affairs,
and their supervision was harsh and petty,
their accumulation of wealth insatiable.
The princes and high-ranking officials
all detested them.
Hòuzhǔ increasingly regarded Wénqìng as capable,
and particularly trusted and valued him.
All matters, internal and external,
were entrusted to him.
He was repeatedly promoted to Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ,
with Shèrén as before.
In the third year of Zhēnmíng,
Jìn Xīwáng Shūwén, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, had been in office for a long time
and had gained great popular support.
Hòuzhǔ, because he controlled the upper reaches of the river,
secretly harbored jealousy towards him.
He judged that he himself had shown little kindness to his officials,
feared they would not be loyal,
and had no one suitable to entrust with the task.
Therefore, he promoted Wénqìng to Dudū, Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
assigned him elite troops,
intending to send him west upstream,
and then summon Shūwén back to court.
Wénqìng was deeply pleased with this arrangement,
but feared being outside
and that later officials might find fault with him.
Therefore, he recommended his partisan Shěn Kèqīng to take his place.
Before they departed,
the two jointly managed confidential affairs.
At that time, the Sui army launched a large-scale invasion,
advancing by multiple routes.
Shàngshū Púyè Yuán Xiàn, Piàojì Jiāngjūn Xiāo Móhē, and other civil and military officials deliberated together,
requesting to station five thousand troops each at Jīngkǒu and Cǎishí,
and also dispatch two hundred golden-winged boats,
to patrol up and down the river
as a defense.
Wénqìng feared that he would have no troops to command,
which would impede his execution of duties,
and Kèqīng also benefited from Wénqìng entrusting him with special authority.
Both spoke to the court, saying:
"If there are discussions or deliberations,
there is no need for a face-to-face presentation;
just write a memorial,
and it will be submitted as a general report."
Xiàn and others thought this was acceptable.
The two brought a memorial and reported to Hòuzhǔ, saying:
"This is a normal matter;
the generals at the border cities
are sufficient to handle it.
If we dispatch men and boats,
we fear it will cause alarm."
When the Sui army approached the river,
spies arrived frequently.
Xiàn and others earnestly submitted requests,
even two or three times.
Wénqìng and others said:
"The New Year's grand assembly is approaching,
and on the day of the southern sacrifice,
the Crown Prince will have many attendants.
If we dispatch troops now,
the event will be disrupted and incomplete."
Hòuzhǔ said:
"Let's dispatch troops now.
If there's no trouble in the north,
we can then have the navy participate in the sacrifice.
Why not?"
They replied again:
"If we do that,
the news will reach neighboring states,
and they will think our country is weak."
Later, they also bribed Jiāng Zǒng,
and Zǒng internally spoke on their behalf.
Hòuzhǔ was reluctant to go against his wishes,
but pressed by the requests of the officials,
he ordered the matter to be referred for external detailed discussion.
He also suppressed Xiàn and others,
thus the decision was not made,
and the Sui army crossed the river.
During the reign of Emperor Ān of the Jìn,
King Zàn of Wō sent envoys to pay tribute.
Then, in the second year of Yǒngchū of Emperor Wǔ of Sòng,
an imperial edict stated:
"Wō Zàn's distant sincerity is truly deserving of recognition;
he may be granted an appointment."
In the second year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Wén,
Zàn again dispatched Sīmǎ Cáo Dá to present a memorial and local products.
When Zàn died,
his brother Zhēn was enthroned.
He sent envoys to offer tribute,

claiming himself to be Administrator with Imperial Authority, Grand Superintendent of Military Affairs of Wō, Báijì, Xīnluó, Rènnà, Qínhán, and Mùhán (six states), General-in-Chief Pacifying the East, and King of Wō.
He submitted a memorial requesting official appointments.
An imperial edict appointed him General Pacifying the East and King of Wō.

Zhēn further requested official appointments for thirteen individuals, including Wōwěi, as General Pacifying the West, General Quelling the Barbarians, General Champion, and General of the Auxiliary State.
〔一二〕The imperial edict approved all of these.
Twenty years later,
King Jì of Wō sent envoys with offerings,
and he was again appointed General Pacifying the East and King of Wō.
In the twenty-eighth year,
he was granted the additional title of Administrator with Imperial Authority, Grand Superintendent of Military Affairs of Wō, Xīnluó, Rènnà, Jiāluó, Qínhán, and Mùhán (six states).
His title of General Pacifying the East remained as before;
and the twenty-three individuals he had recommended were also granted appointments.
When Jì died,
his heir apparent Xìng sent envoys with offerings.
In the sixth year of Dàmíng of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
an imperial edict appointed Xìng General Pacifying the East and King of Wō.
When Xìng died,
his brother Wǔ was enthroned.

He claimed himself to be Administrator with Imperial Authority, Grand Superintendent of Military Affairs of Wō, Báijì, Xīnluó, Rènnà, Jiāluó, Qínhán, and Mùhán (seven states), General-in-Chief Pacifying the East, and King of Wō.
In the second year of Shēngmíng of Emperor Shùn,
he sent envoys to present a memorial,
stating:
"From ancient times, our ancestors
personally donned armor,
traversed mountains and rivers,
and found no time for peace.
They campaigned eastward against fifty-five kingdoms of the Màorén,
subdued sixty-six kingdoms of various Yí to the west,
and leveled ninety-five kingdoms north of the sea.
The kingly way flourished and prospered,
the territory expanded to distant frontiers,
and for generations, tribute was paid to the court
without fail each year.
We traveled through Báijì,
decorating our ships and boats.
However, Gōulí acted without principle,
plotting to swallow us.
My deceased father Jì was about to launch a major expedition
when he suddenly lost his father and elder brother,
causing the almost completed task
to lack but one basketful [of earth].
Now I wish to train troops to fulfill the aspirations of my father and elder brother.
I presumptuously grant myself the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
and all others are likewise presumptuously granted appointments
to encourage their loyalty and integrity."

An imperial edict appointed Wǔ Administrator with Imperial Authority, Grand Superintendent of Military Affairs of Wō, Xīnluó, Rènnà, Jiāluó, Qínhán, and Mùhán (six states), 〔一三〕General-in-Chief Pacifying the East, and King of Wō.
During the JiànYuán era of Qí,
Wǔ was appointed Administrator with Imperial Authority, Grand Superintendent of Military Affairs of Wō, Xīnluó, Rènnà, Jiāluó, Qínhán, and Mùhán (six states), and General-in-Chief Guarding the East.
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng ascended the throne,
Wǔ's title was advanced to General-in-Chief Quelling the East.
To its south is the Land of Dwarfs (Zhūrú Guó),
whose people are four feet tall.
Further south are the Land of Black Teeth (Hēichǐ Guó) and the Land of Nudity (Luǒ Guó),
over four thousand *lǐ* from Wō,
reachable by boat in about a year.
Ten thousand *lǐ* to the southwest are the Sea People,
whose bodies are black and eyes white,
naked and ugly.
Their flesh is delicious,
and travelers sometimes shoot and eat them.
The Land of Tattooed Bodies (Wénshēn Guó) is over seven thousand *lǐ* northeast of Wō.
The people's bodies are tattooed like beasts.
On their foreheads are three tattoos.
Those with straight tattoos are noble,
and those with small tattoos are lowly.
〔一四〕The local customs are joyful,
goods are abundant and cheap,
and travelers do not carry provisions.
They have houses,
but no walled cities.
Where the king resides,
it is decorated with gold, silver, and precious jewels,
and a moat is dug around the house,
ten feet wide,
filled with mercury.
When it rains, the water flows over the mercury.
They use precious treasures as currency in the markets.
Those who commit minor crimes are flogged with whips and sticks.
Those who commit capital crimes are placed for ferocious beasts to eat.
If there is an injustice, the beast avoids eating them,
and after a night, they are pardoned.
The Great Hàn Country (Dàhàn Guó) is over five thousand *lǐ* east of the Land of Tattooed Bodies.
They have no weapons [like spears and shields],
do not engage in warfare,
and their customs are generally the same as the Land of Tattooed Bodies, but their language is different.
Regarding Fúsāng Guó:
In the first year of Yǒngyuán of Qí,
a śramaṇa named Huìshēn came from that country to Jīngzhōu,
and said:
"Fúsāng is over twenty thousand *lǐ* east of the Great Hàn Country,
its land is east of the Middle Kingdom.
Its soil has many *fúsāng* trees,
hence its name.
The leaves of the *fúsāng* resemble those of the *tóng* tree,
and when they first sprout, they are like bamboo shoots;
the people of the country eat them.
Its fruits are like pears and red.
Their bark is spun into cloth,
which is used for clothing,
and also for brocade.
〔一五〕They build plank houses,
without walled cities.
They have writing,
using *fúsāng* bark for paper.
They have no weapons or armor,
and do not engage in warfare.
The laws of their country include northern and southern prisons.
If someone commits a crime,
those with minor offenses enter the southern prison,
and those with serious offenses enter the northern prison.
If there is a general amnesty, those in the southern prison are released,
but not those in the northern prison.
In the northern prison, men and women are paired together;
if a boy is born, he becomes a slave at eight years old,
and if a girl is born, she becomes a maidservant at nine years old.
Those who commit crimes [and are in the northern prison] do not leave until death.
If a noble person commits a crime,
the people of the country gather in a large assembly,
seat the criminal in a pit,
and hold a banquet and bid farewell as if they were parting for death.
They draw circles of ash around the pit.
If there is one circle, only the criminal is banished.
If there are two circles, it extends to the children and grandchildren.
If there are three circles, it extends to seven generations.
The king is called Yǐqí.
The highest noble is called Duìlú,
〔一六〕the second highest is Xiǎoduìlú,
and the third highest is Nàduōshā.
When the king travels, he is accompanied by drums, horns, and attendants.
The color of their clothes changes with the year.
In *jiǎ-yǐ* years, it is blue;
in *bǐng-dīng* years, it is red;
in *wù-jǐ* years, it is yellow;
in *gēng-xīn* years, it is white;
and in *rén-guǐ* years, it is black.
They have oxen with very long horns,
which they use to carry objects,
up to twenty *hú*.
They have chariots, ox-carts, and deer-carts.
The people of the country raise deer like the Chinese raise cattle,
using their milk for cheese.
They have red pears that
do not spoil for a year.
〔一七〕There are many grapes.
Their land has no iron but has copper,
and they do not value gold or silver.
There are no taxes or tariffs in their markets.
Regarding their marriage customs:
The groom builds a house outside the bride's family gate,
sweeping and cleaning morning and evening.
If, after a year, the girl is not pleased, he is driven away.
If they are pleased with each other, the marriage is concluded.
Marriage rites are generally similar to those in China.
For the death of parents, they do not eat for seven days.
For the death of grandparents, they do not eat for five days.
For the death of siblings, paternal uncles, paternal aunts, or sisters, they do not eat for three days.
They set up seats for divine images,
and bow and make offerings morning and evening,
but do not wear mourning clothes.
When a successor king is enthroned,
he does not attend to state affairs for three years.
In the past, their customs had no Buddhist teachings.
In the second year of Dàmíng of Sòng,
five bhikkhus from Jìbīn Guó once traveled through their country,
spreading Buddhist dharma, scriptures, and images,
and teaching them to become monastics.
Thus, their customs changed."
Jǐng went out
and attacked Gūshú in separate groups,
capturing Wénchénghóu Níng (淮南太守文成侯寧), the Grand Administrator of Huáinán.
They then reached Cíhú.
Jiāng Zǐyī (江子一), the Commandant of Nánjīn, fled back to Jiànyè.
The Crown Prince, seeing the urgency of the situation,
went in to respectfully address Emperor Wǔ:
"Please entrust this matter to me;
I hope not to trouble Your Majesty's mind."
The Emperor said:
"This is your own affair;
why ask again?"
The Crown Prince then remained in the Zhōngshūshěng (中書省) to give instructions,
but inside and outside, chaos reigned, with people seizing each other, and communication was cut off.
Thereupon, an edict appointed Xuānchéngwáng Dàqì (宣城王大器), the Inspector of Yángzhōu, as the Grand Commander of All Internal and External Military Affairs (都督內外諸軍事),
and Yáng Kǎn (羊侃), the Dūguānshàngshū (都官尚書), as the Army Advisor General (軍師將軍) to assist him.
Nánpǔhóu Tuī (南浦侯推) was dispatched to defend the Eastern Palace City (東府城),
Xīfēnggōng Dàchūn (西豐公大春) to defend Shítóu,
and Qīngchēzhǎngshǐ Xiè Xǐ (輕車長史謝禧) to defend Báixià.
Soon after, Jǐng arrived at Zhūquèháng,
and sent Xú Sīyù (徐思玉) in to present a petition,
requesting to enter the court wearing armor
to eliminate the wicked elements surrounding the emperor,
and asking for reliable shèrén (舍人) to be sent out to discuss and explain,
in reality wishing to observe the city's defenses.
The Emperor sent Zhōngshūshèrén Hè Jì (中書舍人賀季) and Zhǔshū Guō Bǎoliàng (主書郭寶亮) with Sīyù to comfort Jǐng at Bǎnqiáo.
Jǐng, facing north, received the imperial command.
Jì asked:
"What is the name [or justification] for this action
you are taking today?"
Jǐng said:
"I want to be Emperor."
Wáng Wěi (王偉) stepped forward and said:
"Zhū Chài (朱䌇) and Xú Lín (徐驎) are flattering and corrupt, disturbing the government;
we wish only to eliminate treacherous officials."
Jǐng, having spoken such harsh words,
detained Jì and did not send him back;
Bǎoliàng returned to the palace.
Earlier,
a children's rhyme in the Dàtóng era said:
"Blue silk, white horse from Shòuyáng comes."
After Jǐng's defeat at Wōyáng,
he requested brocade,
but the court supplied blue cloth.
By this time, it was all used for robes,
and the color was still blue.
Jǐng rode a white horse,
with blue silk for the reins,
intending to fulfill the prophecy.
Xiāo Zhèngdé (蕭正德), who was previously stationed in Dānyáng Commandery,
now led his troops to join Jǐng.
Yǔ Xìn (庾信), the Magistrate of Jiànkāng, led over a thousand soldiers to camp north of the bridge.
When Jǐng arrived and reached the bridge,
they only removed one boat.
Seeing that the enemy soldiers all wore iron masks,
Yǔ Xìn then abandoned his army and fled.
The patrolling troops at Nántáng then closed the bridge again to allow Jǐng to cross.
The Crown Prince gave his own horse to Wáng Zhì (王質),
assigned him three thousand elite soldiers,
and sent him to reinforce Yǔ Xìn.
Zhì encountered the rebels at the Commander's Residence (領軍府)
and fled before even forming ranks.
Jǐng, capitalizing on his victory, reached the palace gate.
Xīfēnggōng Dàchūn abandoned Shítóu City and fled;
Jǐng sent his Yítóng Yú Zǐyuè (儀同于子悅) to occupy it.
Xiè Xǐ also abandoned Báixià City and fled.
Jǐng sent a hundred detachments to attack the city,
setting fire to the Dàsīmǎ, Dōnghuá, and Xīhuá Gates.
The city was unprepared in its haste,
so they dug through the gate towers,
poured water down to extinguish the fire,
which eventually died out after a long time.
The rebels also chopped at the Dōngyè Gate, about to enter.
Yáng Kǎn chopped through the gate door and stabbed several people to death,
whereupon the rebels retreated.
They also climbed the Eastern Palace wall and shot into the city.
By night,
Jiǎnwén recruited people to go out and burn the Eastern Palace halls and pavilions, which were utterly destroyed.
The hundreds of collected maps and records
all turned to ashes.
Earlier, Jiǎnwén dreamed of someone drawing Qín Shǐhuáng,
saying,
"This person will again burn books,"
which was now proven true.
Jǐng also burned the city's western horse stables, Shìlín Guǎn (士林館), and Tàifǔ Sì (太府寺).
The next day,
Jǐng again made hundreds of wooden donkeys to attack the city.
Those on the city wall threw stones,
smashing them all to pieces.
The rebels then made pointed wooden donkeys,
shaped like coffins (槥),
which stones could not break.
So, they made pheasant-tail torches,
filled them with grease and wax,
and piled them under to burn them.
As the rebels could not succeed,
and many soldiers died,
they stopped the attack
and built a long siege-wall to cut off inside and outside.
They also petitioned to execute Zhū Chài, Lù Yàn (陸驗), Xú Lín, Zhōu Shízhēn (周石珍), and others.
Inside the city, reward notices were also shot out,
stating that anyone who could cut off Jǐng's head
would be given Jǐng's position,
along with one hundred million coins,
ten thousand bolts each of cloth and silk,
and two troupes of female musicians.
Zhuāng Tiě (莊鐵) then fled to Lìyáng,
falsely claiming that Jǐng had been beheaded.
Guō Luò (郭駱), who was defending Jǐng's city, was terrified
and abandoned the city, fleeing to Shòuyáng.
Tiě was able to enter the city,
then fled to Xúnyáng.
In the eleventh month,
Jǐng enthroned Xiāo Zhèngdé as Emperor,
who assumed the false imperial position,
residing in Yíxiántáng (儀賢堂),
and changed the year name to Zhèngpíng.
Originally, there was a children's rhyme containing the words
"Zhèngpíng,"
so this name was adopted to match it.
Those who understood believed that Zhèngdé would eventually be completely annihilated.
Jǐng made himself Xiàngguó (相國) and Tiānzhù Jiāngjūn (天柱將軍).
Zhèngdé married his daughter to him.
Jǐng again attacked the Eastern Palace City,
setting up hundred-foot high siege towers (樓車),
whose hooks caused all the city battlements to fall.
When the city fell,
Jǐng sent his Yítóng Lú Huīlüè (儀同盧暉略) to lead several thousand men with long swords to line the city gates,
driving all the civil and military officials inside the city out naked,
and making soldiers kill them;
over three thousand people died.
Nánpǔhóu Tuī was killed that day.
Jǐng made Zhèngdé's son Jiànlǐ (見理) and Huīlüè guard the Eastern Palace City.
Initially,
when Jǐng arrived at the capital,
he spread the rumor that
"Emperor Wǔ has already died."
Even inside the city, people believed it.
Jiǎnwén, fearing a change in public sentiment,
requested that the Emperor's carriage tour the city.
When the Emperor was about to ascend the city wall,
Lù Yàn remonstrated:
"Your Majesty is of immense importance;
how can you act so lightly?"
He then wept.
The Emperor was deeply moved by his words,
and so went to the Dàsīmǎ Gate.
Those on the city wall, hearing the ceremonial shouts, all beat drums and cheered.
No soldier failed to wipe away tears,
and the common people were then reassured.
Jǐng also erected earthen mountains to the east and west of the city, overlooking it.
Inside the city, two similar mountains were also built to counter them.
Jiǎnwén and all below him personally carried earth with shovels.
Initially,
when Jǐng arrived,
he hoped to conquer Jiànyè quickly,
issuing very clear commands
and not harming the populace.
But since he failed to capture the city,
people's morale declined and wavered.
Also fearing that all the reinforcement armies would gather
and his troops would disintegrate,
he unleashed his soldiers to kill and plunder,
so that corpses blocked the roads.
Wealthy families and powerful households
were plundered at will;
daughters, wives, and concubines
were all taken into the army camps.
He also recruited northerners who had previously been slaves,
ordering them all to emancipate themselves,
and rewarded them beyond normal ranks.
Zhū Chài's household slave, who had been tattooed, then, with his fellows, climbed over the city wall and defected to the rebels.
Jǐng made him an Yítóng
and had him ride to the palace gate to entice those inside the city,
mounted on a horse and wearing a brocade robe, shouting abuse:
"Zhū Chài served as an official for fifty years
before he became a Zhōnglǐngjūn (中領軍).
I have only just begun serving my lord,
and I am already an Yítóng!"
Thereupon, slaves and servants eagerly rushed out,
and all achieved their ambitions.
After Jǐng's forces had consumed all the grain from Shítóu's granary (常平倉),
he began to plunder the residents.
Thereafter, a liter of rice cost seventy to eighty thousand coins,
and people cannibalized each other;
some even ate their own children.
He also built earthen mountains,
regardless of status,
ceaselessly day and night,
indiscriminately whipping and beating.
The exhausted and weak were killed and used to fill the mountains,
their cries of anguish moving heaven and earth.
The common people dared not hide
and all came out to follow him.
Within ten days, their numbers reached tens of thousands.
Jǐng Yí, together with Fàn Táobàng, secretly coveted generous rewards,
and requested to surrender with two thousand armored soldiers.
They offered to present Hóu Jǐng's head as a bounty.
They sent Wéndé's chief commander Chén Xīn, the leader of the mobile cavalry of the White Horse, to enter by scaling the city wall at night,
and secretly present a memorial explaining the situation.
Jiǎnwén presented the memorial to the Emperor.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and ordered Táobàng to be informed
that if the matter was settled, he would be enfeoffed as the King of Hénán.
An engraved silver tally was given to him.
Jiǎnwén feared it was a ruse,
and hesitated, unable to decide.
The Emperor angrily said:
"Accepting a surrender is a normal principle.
Why are you suddenly so doubtful?"
Zhū Cuōi and Fù Qí both pleaded to accept it.
Jiǎnwén said:
"I am now holding the fortified city,
hoping for external aid.
If external aid arrives,
how can the rebels not be pacified?
If we now open the gates to receive Táobàng,
Táobàng's intentions are still hard to discern.
Should a disaster occur,
it will be too late for regret."
Táobàng further said:
"Now, I will only bring over five hundred of my followers.
When we reach the city gate,
they will all remove their armor.
I beg the imperial court to grant us entry.
When the task is accomplished,
I guarantee to capture Hóu Jǐng."
Jiǎnwén, hearing his words, grew even more suspicious.
Zhū Cuōi thumped his chest with his hand and said:
"This year, the state is lost!"
Soon after, Táobàng's soldier Lǔ Bóhé reported him to Hóu Jǐng,
and both were cooked.
At this time,

Shàolíng Wáng Lún, leading Xīfēng Gōng Dàchūn, Xīngàn Gōng Dàchéng, Yǒng'ān Hóu Què, Nán'ān Xiāng Hóu Jùn, former Cáo Zhōu Cìshǐ Zhào Bózhāo, Wǔ Zhōu Cìshǐ Xiāo Nòngzhāng, and Bùbīng Xiàowèi Yǐn Sīhé, along with thirty thousand cavalry and infantry,
departed from Jīngkǒu,
and directly occupied Zhōngshān.
Hóu Jǐng's faction was greatly alarmed,
and all wanted to flee and disperse.
They sent more than ten thousand men to resist.
Lún greatly defeated them below Àijìng Sì.
When Hóu Jǐng first heard of Lún's arrival,
fear was evident on his face.
When the defeated army returned,
they exaggerated the enemy's might,
making him even more afraid.
He ordered boats to be prepared at Shítóu to cross north.
Rèn Yuē said:
"Having come ten thousand *lǐ* from home,
where do you wish to run?
If the battle is not victorious,
lord and minister will die together.
To beg for survival in the bushes is something Yuē will not do."
Hóu Jǐng then left Sòng Zǐxiān to guard the stronghold,
and personally led elite troops to resist Lún.
He arrayed his forces north of Fùzhōushān,
and stalemated with Lún.
At dusk,
Hóu Jǐng retreated.
Nán'ān Hóu Jùn led several tens of cavalry to provoke him.
Hóu Jǐng turned his army around,
and Jùn retreated.
At that time,
Zhào Bózhāo was arrayed north of Xuánwǔ Hú.
Seeing Jùn retreat,
he then led his army to flee forward.
The allied forces, in the ensuing chaos,
[一０]were thoroughly defeated.
Lún fled to Jīngkǒu.
The rebels captured Xīfēng Gōng Dàchūn, Lún's Sīmǎ Zhuāngqiū Huìdá, Nángé Jiāngjūn Hú Zǐyuē, and Guǎnglíng Lìng Huò Jùn, among others, and brought them to the city wall,
forcing them to say:
"Shàolíng Wáng has already been captured."
Huò Jùn alone said:
"The King suffered a minor setback,
but his entire army has returned to Jīngkǒu.
The city should just hold firm,
and reinforcements will arrive soon."
Before he finished speaking,
the rebels wounded his mouth with a knife.
Hóu Jǐng admired his integrity and released him.
Zhèngdé then seized and killed him.
On this day,
Póyáng Shìzǐ Sì and Péi Zhīgāo arrived at Hòuzhǔ,
and established a camp at Càizhōu.
Hóu Jǐng divided his army to garrison the south bank.
In the twelfth month,
Hóu Jǐng constructed various siege engines, including flying towers, ramming vehicles (*tóngchē*), scaling vehicles, hooking battlements vehicles, ramp vehicles, and fire vehicles.
All were several *zhàng* high,
with some vehicles having up to twenty wheels.
They were arrayed before the palace gate,
attacking the city from a hundred directions.
They used fire vehicles to burn the large tower at the southeastern corner of the city,
[一一]then attacked the city using the fire's momentum.
Those on the city wall set fires,
burning all of their siege engines.
The rebels then retreated.
At this time,
Hóu Jǐng's earth mound was completed,
and the earth mound within the city was also completed.
Tàifù Qīng Wéi Àn was ordered to defend the western earth mound,
and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Liǔ Jīn to defend the eastern earth mound.
From the mound rose a lotus-layered tower,
four *zhàng* high,
decorated with brocade and felt,
and protected by black bamboo screens.
The peaks of the mounds were close to each other.
Dare-to-die warriors were recruited,
heavily clad in robes and armor,
named
"Sēngténg Kè."
They were assigned to the two mounds,
fighting with crossing spears.
The drumbeats and shouts were deafening,
unceasing from dusk till dawn.
The fighting on the earth mounds was bitter,
and the men could not endure it.
Liǔ Jīn ordered a tunnel to be dug
to destroy the outer mound.
They threw fire-tailed torches to burn its battlements and crenellations.
The outer mound collapsed,
crushing almost all the rebels.
The rebels then built "toad vehicles" (*hāmáchē*),
transporting earth and stones to fill the moat.
Warriors ascended these tower vehicles,
which approached from all four sides.
Inside the city, flying stones crushed their vehicles,
and the rebels' dead piled up beneath the city wall.
The rebels also dug under the southeastern corner of the city.
Inside the city, a curved wall shaped like a crescent moon was built to defend against it.
The rebels then retreated.
Cáiguān Jiāngjūn Sòng Ní surrendered to the rebels,
and then devised a plan
to divert the water of Xuánwǔ Hú to flood Táichéng.
The imperial street in front of the palace gate became a vast expanse of water.
They also burned the camps and temples of residents on the south bank,
leaving nothing untouched.
Sī Zhōu Cìshǐ Liǔ Zhònglǐ, Héng Zhōu Cìshǐ Wéi Càn, Nánlíng Tàishǒu Chén Wénchè, and Xuānměng Jiāngjūn Lǐ Xiàoqīn, among others, all came to aid.
Póyáng Shìzǐ Sì and Péi Zhīgāo also crossed the river.
Liǔ Zhònglǐ camped south of Zhūquè Háng,
Péi Zhīgāo camped at Nányuàn,
Wéi Càn camped at Qīngtáng,
Chén Wénchè and Lǐ Xiàoqīn garrisoned Dānyáng Jùn.
[一二]Póyáng Shìzǐ Sì camped south of Xiǎoháng,
all building palisades along the Huái River.
At dawn,
Hóu Jǐng just realized this,
and ascended the gate tower of Chánlíng Sì to observe.
Seeing that Wéi Càn's camp was not yet completely formed,
he dispatched troops to attack it.
Càn was defeated,
and Hóu Jǐng decapitated Càn and paraded his head beneath the city.
Liǔ Zhònglǐ, hearing of Càn's defeat,
had no time to don his armor,
and rushed to the scene with several tens of men.
Encountering the rebels,
he beheaded several hundred,
and more than a thousand rebels drowned themselves in the water.
Zhònglǐ penetrated deeply,
his horse got stuck in the mud,
and he also suffered severe wounds.
From then on, the rebels dared not cross the bank.
Shàolíng Wáng Lún, together with Línchéng Gōng Dàlián and others, assembled on the south bank from the east road.
Jīng Zhōu Cìshǐ Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì sent his Shìzǐ Fāngděng, concurrently Sīmǎ Wú Yè, and Tiānmén Tàishǒu Fán Wénjiǎo as reinforcements.
They camped in front of Xiāngzǐ Àn.
[一三]Gāozhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Qiānshì and former Sī Zhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Yārén also led troops to follow.
Soon after, Póyáng Shìzǐ Sì, Yǒng'ān Hóu Què, Yáng Yārén, Lǐ Qiānshì, and Fán Wénjiǎo led their forces across the Huái River.
They attacked and broke through the rebels' palisade in front of Dōngfǔ Chéng,
and then camped east of Qīngxī Shuǐ.
Hóu Jǐng sent his Yítóng Sòng Zǐxiān to establish a palisade west of the river to oppose them.
Hóu Jǐng's food gradually ran out,
and fifteen or sixteen out of every ten people resorted to cannibalism.
Originally,
when the reinforcements reached the north bank,
their numbers were said to be a million.
The common people, supporting the old and leading the young, waited for the royal army.
But as soon as they crossed the Huái River,
they immediately began to plunder,
and demanded gold and silver.
They set up camps,
mutually distrustful.
Shàolíng Wáng Lún and Liǔ Zhònglǐ were worse than sworn enemies.
Línchéng Gōng Dàlián and Yǒng'ān Hóu Què were more antagonistic than fire and water.
They had no will to fight.
Those among the rebels who wanted to escape, upon hearing this, all stopped.
During the Tiānjiān era,
the śramaṇa Shì Bǎozhì said:
"The bobtail dog goes mad of its own accord,
When it should die but does not, it bites and wounds people,
In a moment's time it will perish on its own,
It arose from Rǔyīn and died in Sānxiāng."
He also said:
"The mountain child truly raises his arm,
And glares like a tiger before the Tàijí Hall."
The 'dog' was
Hóu Jǐng's nickname,
the 'mountain child'
had the appearance of a monkey.
Hóu Jǐng then engulfed the capital
and brutally harmed the imperial family.
He arose from Xuánhù,
which was formerly Rǔnán.
There is a place in Bālíng called Sānxiāng,
where Hóu Jǐng was defeated.
All his words came true.
Hóu Jǐng often told people:
"The character 'Hóu' has 'rén' (人) on the side as the master (主),
and 'rén' (人) below,
this clearly means he is the master of men."
After Tái Chéng fell,
Wǔdì once told people:
"Hóu Jǐng will certainly become emperor,
but not for long.
Breaking down the characters 'Hóu Jǐng' (侯景) forms 'xiǎorén bǎi rì tiānzǐ' (小人百日天子, 'a commoner, one hundred-day emperor'),
he will be emperor for about a hundred days."
According to records, Hóu Jǐng usurped the throne on the nineteenth day of the eleventh month in the Xīnwèi year,
and was defeated on the nineteenth day of the third month in the Rénshēn year,
totaling one hundred and twenty days.
However, Hóu Jǐng went to Gūshú on the first day of the third month,
and he was in the palace for exactly one hundred days.
His words indeed proved true.
Also, during the Dàtóng era,
the Grand Physician Zhū Dān once stayed overnight in the forbidden palace.
He suddenly dreamt of a dog and a sheep each on the imperial throne.
Waking up, he told people:
"Dogs and sheep are not auspicious creatures.
Now that they occupy the imperial throne,
will there be a rebellion?"
Soon after, the Son of Heaven was in distress,
and Hóu Jǐng ascended the main hall.
When Hóu Jǐng was about to be defeated,
there was a monk, Dàorén,
whose disposition was like a madman,
drinking wine and eating meat,
no different from ordinary people.
He had been wandering the world for several decades,
his name and hometown
unknown to anyone.
Initially, his words were hidden,
but after a long time, they proved true.
People all called him Shé Lí.
Hóu Jǐng greatly trusted and respected him.
Hóu Jǐng once shot arrows with his followers in the rear hall,
and Dàorén was present.
He snatched Hóu Jǐng's bow and shot at Jǐngyáng Shān,
shouting loudly,
"I've got the slave!"
Later, Hóu Jǐng again hosted a banquet for his party,
and also invited Dàorén.
Dàorén took some meat, dipped it in salt, and offered it to Hóu Jǐng,
asking:
"Is it good?"
Hóu Jǐng replied:
"My only regret is that it's too salty."
Dàorén said:
"If it weren't salty, it would rot."
When Hóu Jǐng died,
Wáng Sēngbiàn cut off his two arms and sent them to Qí Wénxuān,
and his head was sent to Jiānglíng.
Indeed, five dòu of salt were placed in his belly
and sent to Jiànkāng,
where it was exposed in the marketplace.
The common people vied to butcher and eat it,
even the lord of Lìyáng participated in eating it.
Hóu Jǐng's bones were burned and ashes scattered;
those who had suffered his calamity
mixed the ashes with wine and drank them.
When the head arrived in Jiānglíng,
Yuándì ordered it to be impaled in the marketplace for three days,
then boiled and lacquered,
and placed in the imperial armory.
Before this, there was a folk rhyme in Jiānglíng:
"In Kǔzhú Tīng,
south of the market, there is a good well.
The Jīngzhōu army
will kill Hóu Jǐng."
When Hóu Jǐng's head arrived,
Yuándì handed it to the residence of Cányì Cānjūn Lǐ Jìcháng,
and east of the residence was Kǔzhú Tīng.
When it was put in the cauldron,
they used water from the well south of the market.
[二四]Hóu Jǐng's Yítóng Xiè Dárén and Xíngtái Zhào Bóchāo surrendered to Hóu Tián.
The bandit Xíngtái Tián Qiān, Yítóng Fáng Shìguì, Cài Shòulè, and Lǐngjūn Wáng Bóchǒu were captured alive.
The entire evil faction was pacified;
Fáng Shìguì was beheaded in Jiànkāng market,
and the rest of the party were sent to Jiānglíng.
Initially,
Guō Yuánjiàn, because of his courtesy to the Crown Princess,
was about to surrender,
but Hóu Zǐjiàn said:
"This is a small favor,
not enough to save himself."
So he fled to Qí.
Wáng Wěi's
ancestors were from Luèyáng.
His father, Luè,
served Wèi as the Prefect of Xǔchāng,
and thus resided in Yǐngchuān.
Wáng Wěi was learned in the Zhōu Yì,
and excelled in rhetoric and literary style.
He served Wèi as Xíngtái Láng.
After Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
Gāo Chéng invited him with a letter.
Wáng Wěi wrote a reply to Gāo Chéng on behalf of Hóu Jǐng,
and its prose was very beautiful.
Gāo Chéng read the letter and said:
"Who wrote this?"
Those around him praised Wáng Wěi's writing.
Gāo Chéng said:
"With such talent,
why wasn't I informed earlier?"
Wáng Wěi participated in Hóu Jǐng's plans and strategies;
his proclamations and manifestos were all created by Wáng Wěi,
and when they proceeded with usurpation,
all were Wáng Wěi's initial ideas.
When Hóu Jǐng was defeated,
he and Hóu Zǐjiàn fled together but got separated.
He hid in the grass,
and the commander of Zhídú garrison, Huáng Gōngxǐ, captured and sent him in.
Upon seeing Wáng Sēngbiàn,
he gave a long bow but did not prostrate.
His captors urged him,
but Wáng Wěi said:
"We are both ministers,
why should we respect each other?"
Wáng Sēngbiàn said to him:
"You were a bandit prime minister,
unable to die for your principles,
but seeking survival in the grass,
fallen but not supported,
what use is such a prime minister?"
Wáng Wěi said:
"Rise and fall are matters of time;
skill and ineptitude are up to the individual.
If Hóu had listened to my words earlier,
how could your Excellency have the power you do today?"
Wáng Sēngbiàn laughed heartily,
feeling quite impressed,
and ordered him to be taken out for public display.
Wáng Wěi said:
"Yesterday and this morning I walked eighty lǐ,
I wish to borrow a donkey to ride."
Wáng Sēngbiàn said:
"Your head will travel ten thousand lǐ,
what is eighty lǐ?"
Wáng Wěi laughed and said:
"Today's events
are exactly what I wished for."
The former Assistant Minister of the Left, Yú Zhì, who had once been insulted by Wáng Wěi,
encountered him and spat on his face,
saying:
"Dead slave,
how can you still do evil!"
Wáng Wěi said:
"You do not read,
you are not worth talking to."
Yú Zhì felt ashamed and withdrew.
When Lǚ Jìlüè, Zhōu Shízhēn, and Yán Dǎn were all sent to Jiānglíng,
Wáng Wěi still hoped to be spared.
In prison, he wrote a poem to the important officials under Yuándì, saying:
"Zhào Yī was able to compose a fù,
Zōu Yáng knew how to present a memorial,
Why begrudge the water of the Western River,
and not save the fish in the rut?"
He also presented a five-hundred-character poem to the emperor.
The emperor, fond of his talent, was about to spare him,
but many court officials were jealous,
and pleaded:
"The proclamation Wáng Wěi wrote recently
contained unusual phrases."
Yuándì requested and examined it.
The proclamation read:
"Xiàng Yǔ had double pupils,
yet still suffered defeat at Wūjiāng;
How could the one-eyed man of Xiāngdōng
be the one to whom Chìxiàn would return?"
[二五]The emperor was furious,
and ordered that his tongue be nailed to a pillar,
and his intestines be gouged out.
[二六]His expression remained unchanged.
His enemies carved his flesh,
and he looked down at it,
only until his bones were reached was he executed.
Zhōu Shízhēn and Yán Dǎn were both exterminated to the third degree of kinship.
Zhāo Dás still crossed the mountain range to resist Chén Bǎo-yìng.
Dí then gathered his forces and emerged at Dōngxīng.
Emperor Wén dispatched Commandant Chéng Líng-xǐ to defeat him.
Dí then fled with more than ten men and hid in mountain caves.
Later, he sent someone to secretly go out to Línchuān Commandery to buy fish.
Línchuān Administrator Luò Wén-yá captured him
and ordered him to retrieve Dí himself to prove his loyalty.
He lured Dí out hunting,
ambushed him, and cut off his head.
His head was sent to Jiànyè
and displayed on Zhūquè Bridge for three days.
Liú Yì,
a native of Chángshān, Dōngyáng,
came from a prominent family in the commandery for generations.
Yì was skilled at self-management;
his speech was refined and reserved.
He was a powerful and influential figure in his hometown.
He gathered many unruly youths,
who bullied the poor and humble,
causing distress to all commandery and county officials.
He served the Liáng dynasty
as the magistrate of Jìn'ān and Āngù counties.
During Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion,
he returned to his hometown
and recruited soldiers.
Administrator Shěn Xún, who was assisting the capital,
yielded the commandery to Yì.
Yì sent his nephew Chāo to oversee the commandery affairs
and led his troops to follow Xún to the capital.
When the city fell,
Yì followed Liáng’s Prince Línchéng, Dàlián.
Dàlián entrusted him with military affairs.
Yì was cruel and tyrannical
and lacked long-term strategy.
He privately wielded power and influence,
and everyone resented him.
When Hóu Jǐng’s general Sòng Zǐ-xiān crossed the Zhèjiāng River,
Yì fled back to his hometown,
and soon surrendered to Zǐ-xiān with his forces.
Zǐ-xiān made him a local guide
and ordered him to seize Dàlián.
Upon hearing this, Prince Shàolíng, Lún, said:
