"His surname is spelled with the character for 'depart' (去) and 'stay' (留), and his given name with 'same' (同) and 'different' (異).
It is fitting that he should align with the rebellious traitors."
Hóu Jǐng appointed Yì as Dōngyáng Administrator
and took his wife and children as hostages.
Grand Marshal Liú Shén-mào raised an army to resist Hóu Jǐng.
Yì outwardly allied with Shén-mào
but secretly conspired with Hóu Jǐng.
When Shén-mào was defeated
and executed by Hóu Jǐng,
Yì alone escaped.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Wáng Sēng-biàn sent Yì to console the people of Dōngyáng.
He then fortified himself in strategic mountain strongholds,
and the commanderies and prefectures were wary of him.
When the Wèi dynasty captured Jīngzhōu,
Wáng Sēng-biàn appointed Yì as Dōngyáng Administrator.
When Emperor Wén of Chén pacified Kuàijī,
although Yì provided provisions,
he unilaterally controlled the commandery,
wielding power and influence himself.
In Shàotài 2nd year (559),
for his merit in rendering assistance,
he was appointed Inspector of Jìnzhōu
and concurrently Dōngyáng Administrator,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒngjiā County.
[二九] Furthermore, Emperor Wén’s eldest daughter, Princess Fēng'ān, was married to Yì’s third son, Zhēn-chén.
In Chén Yǒngdìng 3rd year (559),
Yì was summoned to serve as Inspector of Nánxúzhōu,
but he procrastinated and did not take up the post.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he was reappointed as Inspector of Jìnzhōu
and concurrently Dōngyáng Administrator.
Yì frequently sent his Chief Clerk, Wáng Sī, as an envoy to the court.
Sī repeatedly spoke of the court’s weakness,
and Yì believed him.
He became ambivalent
and secretly corresponded with Wáng Lín.
When Lín was defeated,
Emperor Wén dispatched Left Guard General Shěn Kè to replace Yì in the commandery,
effectively sending troops to attack him.
Yì fought Kè,
was defeated,
and then submitted a memorial expressing his apologies.
At that time, the court was preoccupied with Xiāngzhōu and Yǐngzhōu,
so they simply restrained him.
Yì knew he would eventually be attacked,
so he garrisoned troops at Xiàhuái and Jiàndé
to guard the river routes.
After Xiāngzhōu was pacified,
Emperor Wén issued an edict denouncing his crimes
and ordered Minister of Works Hóu Ān-dū to suppress him.
Yì and his second son, Zhōng-chén, fled to Chén Bǎo-yìng.
When Bǎo-yìng was pacified,
Yì was also captured and sent to the capital,
where he was executed in the Jiànkāng marketplace.
His sons and nephews were all put to death,
except for his third son, Zhēn-chén, who was spared because he was married to the princess.
Chén Bǎo-yìng
was a native of Hòuguān, Jìn'ān.
His family had been one of the four prominent families in Mǐnzhōng for generations.
His father, Yǔ,
was capable
and a powerful figure in the commandery.
Bǎo-yìng was treacherous
and full of schemes.
During the Liáng dynasty, Jìn'ān rebelled several times
and repeatedly killed commandery generals.
Yǔ initially incited and facilitated these events,
but later served as a local guide for the government army to defeat them,
thereby gaining control over all military power in the commandery.
During Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion,
Jìn'ān Administrator, Marquis Bīnhuà Xiāo Yún, yielded the commandery to Yǔ.
Yǔ was old,
so he only oversaw commandery affairs,
ordering Bǎo-yìng to command the troops.
At that time, the eastern region experienced famine,
especially severe in Kuàijī,
where seven or eight out of ten people died,
but Jìn'ān alone was prosperous
and its soldiers were strong.
After Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Emperor Yuán then appointed Yǔ as Jìn'ān Administrator.
When Emperor Wǔ of Chén became regent,
Yǔ requested to retire
and asked to pass on the commandery to Bǎo-yìng.
Emperor Wǔ granted his request.
In Shàotài 2nd year (559),
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Hòuguān County.
[三０] When Emperor Wǔ accepted the abdication,
he was appointed Inspector of Mǐnzhōu
and concurrently Administrator of Kuàijī.
When Emperor Wén ascended the throne,
he bestowed the title of Grand Master of Guanglu upon his father,
and furthermore ordered the Director of the Imperial Clan to record his lineage
and include him in the imperial clan.
Bǎo-yìng married Liú Yì’s daughter as his wife.
When Hóu Ān-dū attacked Yì,
Bǎo-yìng dispatched troops to assist him,
and also supplied Zhōu Dí with provisions and grain
to raid Línchuān.
When Commandant Zhāng Zhāo-dá defeated Dí,
Emperor Wén then ordered the suppression of Bǎo-yìng,
and issued an edict for the Director of the Imperial Clan to sever his family registration.
Bǎo-yìng entrenched himself by Lake Jiàn'ān to resist Zhāo-dá.
Zhāo-dá dug deep trenches and built high ramparts, refusing to engage in battle.
Instead, he ordered rafts to be made.
Soon, the water level rose,
and he released them with the current,
breaking through Bǎo-yìng’s water barricades.
Bǎo-yìng’s forces collapsed.
He was captured and sent to the capital,
and executed in the Jiànkāng marketplace.
The commentary states: Hóu Jǐng arose from the border regions,
having endured many hardships and dangers.
From north to south,
he often employed cunning calculations.
At that time, the lands south of the Yangtze River
had seen no warfare.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, in his old age,
indulged in Buddhist teachings,
outwardly loosening the fortifications of his defenses,
and inwardly abandoning the spirit of vigilance.
He made no preparations for the unexpected,
making it difficult to govern the state.
Moreover, traitors were at his side,
secretly engaging in bribery,
allowing Jǐng to seize opportunities and unleash his deceptions,
wantonly carrying out his treacherous acts.
Wáng Wěi served as his chief strategist,
embellishing his words with eloquence.
Emperor Wǔ was swayed by those who understood his tastes
and was misled by these邪 (evil) theories.
This led to his forces crossing directly on rafts,
the Yangtze River losing its natural defenses,
and banners pointing towards the palace gates,
Jīnyǒng losing its strategic advantage.
The people were plunged into misery,
and the imperial altars and temples became ruins.
Consequently, the powerful figures of villages, strongholds,
and the leaders of commanderies, prefectures, and mountain caves
indulged in bullying and violence,
thriving on plunder and becoming dominant.
Emperor Wǔ of Chén responded to the times and took charge of affairs,
pacifying and settling the land.
Xióng Tán-lǎng, Zhōu Dí, Liú Yì, Chén Bǎo-yìng, and others,
though they encountered a flourishing era,
did not change their deluded ways.
Their ambition was to disrupt order,
thus bringing about their own destruction.
This was indeed appropriate.
